articles.title: Will Taiwan vote to revive nuclear power – and why does that matter for AI?
articles.excerpt:
Voters in Taiwan are set to decide whether to bring back nuclear power – 18 months after its last operational reactor was shut down.

A referendum on the issue is being held alongside local elections ...
articles.body_text:
Voters in Taiwan are set to decide whether to bring back nuclear power – 18 months after its last operational reactor was shut down.

A referendum on the issue is being held alongside local elections on Saturday. It is the island’s fourth vote on nuclear power in just eight years.

It comes as demand for electricity to fuel the country’s burgeoning computer chip industry soars and concern grows about how Taiwan would keep its lights on if China, which claims the island as its own territory, cut it off amid escalating tensions.

Voters are being asked whether the government should return to using nuclear power to boost the economy. That would mean abolishing the country’s longstanding “nuclear-free homeland” policy.

The opposition Kuomintang (KMT) proposed the referendum and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) is also backing it. The legislature approved the referendum in August and the Central Election Commission signed it off on August 28.

To pass, ‘yes’ votes must outnumber ‘no’ votes and exceed a quarter of all eligible voters.

The ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), which has long had a policy of no nuclear power in its mandate, is urging ‘no’. DPP legislator Chen Pei-yu called the referendum unnecessary, saying lawmakers could change the policy by amending existing laws instead.

Taiwan once relied heavily on nuclear power. In 1985, its three plants produced 52 percent of the nation’s electricity.

Nuclear power then became one of the most partisan issues in Taiwanese politics. Lev Nachman, an assistant professor at the Graduate Institute of National Development at National Taiwan University, said the divide goes back to the DPP’s founding.

“There was a major group of environmentalists that were part of the party that were very anti-nuclear,” Nachman told Al Jazeera. The nuclear industry, by contrast, was built and run under the KMT.

Polarisation turned that into “a very green-versus-blue issue”, Nachman said, referring to the colours of the DPP and the KMT.

Safety fears run deep. Nachman said Taiwan watched the 2011 Fukushima nuclear plant meltdown in neighbouring Japan very closely.

“There is this sort of fear of any sort of nuclear reaction that would ever happen in Taiwan would just devastate the entire island,” he said. Active geological fault lines run across Taiwan and the question of how to dispose of nuclear waste remains unresolved.

The DPP has governed since 2016, partly on a pledge to phase out nuclear power. In May last year, Taiwan shut down its last reactor at Maanshan in Pingtung County.

Public opinion has been mixed in three previous referendums. In 2018, voters opted to scrap a legal deadline for phasing out nuclear power. But in 2021, they rejected restarting construction on an unfinished fourth nuclear plant. In August last year, a majority vote to restart the Maanshan plant was voided due to low turnout.

Now, nuclear power is back on the agenda because surging electricity demand from Taiwan’s semiconductor and AI industries, along with growing fears about energy security and over-reliance on imported fuel, have renewed the debate over how the island keeps the lights on in an emergency.

According to the Ministry of Economic Affairs, Taiwan imports more than 97 percent of its energy. Natural gas generates about 43 percent of its electricity and coal about 35 percent. Both arrive by ship.

Taiwan only has about 11 days of liquefied natural gas (LNG) in reserve. Japan and South Korea hold between 14 and 20 days.

“There’s two sides to it,” Nachman said. The first is energy security: “If China actually blockades Taiwan and cuts off access to the outside world, then Taiwan only has so much energy it can rely on.”

The second is the chip industry, which requires huge amounts of power and “that’s only going to increase over time”, he said.

The war with Iran this year has added to the pressure by disrupting LNG shipments from the Middle East.

The DPP has already started to shift. In March, President William Lai Ching-te said the government would begin the process of restarting the Maanshan and Kuosheng plants. He cited AI-driven demand and conflicts abroad causing disruption to energy supplies.

On September 24, the Nuclear Safety Commission approved state-owned Taipower’s restart plan for Maanshan. Further safety assessments are still needed before it can operate again.

Nachman said Lai has tried to push his party to rethink its “very dogmatic anti-nuclear stance”. The question is whether DPP voters have come around.

Nuclear power is not Taiwan’s first choice for filling the gap, however. “Investment in LNG – that’s still Taiwan’s kind of number one goal,” Nachman said.

Taiwan is the most important link in the global AI supply chain.

It makes more than 90 percent of the world’s most advanced semiconductors, nearly all of them at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). TSMC has more than 60 percent of the global contract chipmaking market.

Its customers include Nvidia – the world’s most valuable semiconductor company – AMD and Apple. TSMC makes Nvidia’s Blackwell and Rubin AI processors, and Taiwanese firms such as Foxconn and Quanta build most of the world’s AI servers.

That uses huge amounts of electricity and water. In September, Taiwan’s semiconductor industry used more than 4.5 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity for the first time. That was up 11.55 percent from a year earlier, driven by AI demand.

S&P Global estimated that TSMC alone used about 8 percent of Taiwan’s electricity in 2023. That share could rise to almost 24 percent by 2030, it added.

Nachman cautioned against seeing the referendum only through the demand for microchips and semiconductors. “In today’s media, Taiwan has become a single issue, just about semiconductors,” he said. “For a lot of people in Taiwan, the semiconductors aren’t even the priority. It really is the security side.”

Probably not. Beijing does not appear to have commented on the referendum itself.

“The nuclear issue is a completely separate issue from anything related to China,” Nachman said. “It’s much more a matter of domestic politics.”

China has, however, used Taiwan’s energy weakness in its messaging. In March, Chen Binhua, a spokesman for China’s Taiwan Affairs Office, said closer integration with China could help solve Taiwan’s energy problems. He pointed to the island’s reliance on oil and gas from the Middle East.

Taipei rejects unification with Beijing. Analysts writing in The Diplomat called the offer an exercise in optics.

However, it remains a top priority for China. During a speech in Beijing on November 12, President Xi Jinping once again stated that Taiwan and China must be reunified.

The referendum is about civilian power reactors, not weapons. Asked whether Taiwan might seek a nuclear weapon, Nachman said: “No, of course not. This is just about nuclear power.”

Taiwan did secretly pursue nuclear weapons in the 1970s and 1980s. The programme was shut down in 1988 under US pressure, after a senior nuclear scientist, Chang Hsien-yi, defected to the United States.

Since then, Taiwan’s leaders have consistently stated that they will not seek nuclear weapons. Its nuclear facilities are inspected under an arrangement between Taiwan, the US and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

The bigger worry is a blockade by China if it seeks to press reunification in the future. Nachman said large military drills and naval patrols China has held around Taiwan since US House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit in 2022 have all rehearsed one.

Nachman said he is sceptical. “We keep doing it over and over again and it still doesn’t usually pass,” he said. “So my expectations are actually fairly low.”

The outcome will depend on DPP supporters. “It’s really more a matter of whether or not green voters have come around to it,” Nachman said.

If the referendum does pass, he said Lai and the DPP “would probably be largely okay with it”.

The restart process is already under way either way. Supporters say reactors could be running again within 18 months to three years. Opponents say a restart could take five to 10 years and cost several hundred billion New Taiwan dollars.

articles.title: Putin unveils new Russian nuclear-powered submarine with hypersonic weapons
articles.excerpt:
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has unveiled a new nuclear-powered submarine, which Moscow claims is the first equipped with Russian Zircon hypersonic missiles.

The Russians say they will add five ...
articles.body_text:
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has unveiled a new nuclear-powered submarine, which Moscow claims is the first equipped with Russian Zircon hypersonic missiles.

The Russians say they will add five more nuclear submarines to the country’s fleet by 2030.

Putin attended the flag-raising ceremony aboard the Perm at the Sevmash shipyard in the northwestern city of Severodvinsk on Friday, marking the submarine’s formal transfer to the navy, according to video released by the Kremlin.

“Russia is one of the few countries in the world capable of building powerful nuclear submarines of this kind, weapons with global reach and significance,” he said.

Nuclear-powered subs are a key part of Russia’s nuclear deterrent because their ability to operate covertly underwater ensures a retaliatory strike capability in the event of an attack.

Putin said the navy will receive five more submarines by 2030, including three Yasen-M class, the same as the Perm. They can operate in “any part of the world’s oceans” while carrying a range of cruise missiles, he added.

Putin also stated that Russia intends to continue modernising its navy and expressed confidence that all plans to build a powerful naval force will be implemented in full and on time.

articles.title: Hamas chief’s last surviving son escapes Israeli strike in Gaza
articles.excerpt:
Hamas chief's last surviving son escapes Israeli strike in Gaza

Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya’s last surviving son Izzeldeen survived an Israeli assassination attempt on Friday, senior Hamas official ...
articles.body_text:
Hamas chief's last surviving son escapes Israeli strike in Gaza

Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya’s last surviving son Izzeldeen survived an Israeli assassination attempt on Friday, senior Hamas official Basem Naim said. Four of Izzeldeen’s brothers were killed by Israeli forces, including his twin Hamam, who died in a 2025 airstrike in Qatar.

articles.title: Israel kills four in Gaza as Hamas chief al-Hayya’s son survives strike
articles.excerpt:
A son of Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya has survived an Israeli air strike targeting his family in Gaza, said the Palestinian group.

The air raid on Friday came as Israeli attacks elsewhere in the stri...
articles.body_text:
A son of Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya has survived an Israeli air strike targeting his family in Gaza, said the Palestinian group.

The air raid on Friday came as Israeli attacks elsewhere in the strip killed four Palestinians, despite the so-called “ceasefire” agreed over a year ago.

Izzeldeen al-Hayya, 29, and his family survived the Israeli strike at dawn, said Hamas official Basem Naim. Hamas sources told the Reuters news agency that several relatives were wounded, including the daughter-in-law of the Hamas chief.

The family of another of Khalil al-Hayya’s deceased sons, Azzam, also survived.

Naim described Izzeldeen as the Hamas leader’s last surviving son. Four of his brothers were killed by Israeli forces: Hamza in 2008, Osama in 2014, Humam in September last year and Azzam in May this year.

Izzeldeen is the twin brother of Humam, who was killed in an Israeli strike on Hamas leaders in Qatar last year. Khalil al-Hayya narrowly escaped that attack during negotiations. He was named leader of Hamas in July.

Hamas condemned Friday’s attack, describing it as an attempt to “assassinate” al-Hayya’s son and target his family.

The group linked the attack to threats made against its leader by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and accused Israel of seeking to undermine the October 2025 “ceasefire” agreement. Hamas said the “cowardly act” exposes the “complete detachment from human and moral values” of Israeli leaders.

Deadly Israeli attacks continued elsewhere in Gaza on Friday.

A Palestinian was killed and several others wounded in a drone att on a vehicle in northern Gaza, according to the Palestinian Wafa news agency.

Wafa named the victim as Khaled Assaf and quoted witnesses as saying a vehicle was struck in the Bir al-Naaja area, west of the Jabalia refugee camp.

In the southern city of Rafah, Civil Defence teams recovered the bodies of three Palestinians and rescued two wounded people following an attack near Muawiya Mosque on al-Bahr Street, Wafa reported.

Israeli army gunfire injured a Palestinian child in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.

Medical sources and witnesses told Wafa that Israeli forces repeatedly opened fire on tents sheltering displaced people in the area from their positions near the eastern “Yellow Line”.

Friday’s attacks followed a series of Israeli raids on Thursday that killed 10 Palestinians, including a senior education official.

Also on Friday, Hamas described as “ridiculous” the Israeli army’s claim that it used one of the buildings at Al-Ahli Baptist Hospital in Gaza City as an interrogation centre.

The Israeli military and Shin Bet made the allegations on Thursday, claiming Hamas was conducting military activities within the hospital complex.

The Israeli claim “comes as part of the ongoing incitement against hospitals in the Gaza Strip”, Hamas said in a statement.

Hospitals are “public places open to all civil and UN institutions operating in the enclave”, it noted, adding that Israel had never provided evidence to substantiate any of its claims.

The Episcopal Diocese of Jerusalem, which oversees the hospital, said it had no knowledge of any secret interrogation centre on the premises.

According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, Israeli violations of the October 2025 “ceasefire” since it took effect have killed at least 1,705 Palestinians and wounded 6,163. Israel has killed at least 74,772 Palestinians in Gaza since the genocidal war began in October 2023.

articles.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
articles.excerpt:
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves

A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of...
articles.body_text:
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves

A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.

Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.

Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.

Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.

Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.

The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.

Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.

The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.

"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.

The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".

Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.

Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.

The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.

Earlier this week, Mackenzie was also convicted of:

assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child

facilitating the commission of a terrorist act

being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.

Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders

Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.

A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.

His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".

After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.

"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.

Stephen Mwiti, who lost six children to the cult, welcomed the conviction of Mackenzie for murder last month

When the shallow graves were discovered, local men were hired for the horrifying task of exhuming the remains.

"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."

"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."

Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".

Post-mortem records showed many of the victims had died of starvation while the remains of others were mostly skeletal, making the establishment of their cause of death impossible.

Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he had lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.

"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court last month.

"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest. I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."

The deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.

The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

articles.title: ‘Bear trap’: Ukraine hails new operation as Russian casualties mount
articles.excerpt:
Ukraine’s forces liberated more of their land as Russia broke new casualty records and United States negotiators tried to convince Kyiv to give up territory, or NATO membership.

Details emerged on No...
articles.body_text:
Ukraine’s forces liberated more of their land as Russia broke new casualty records and United States negotiators tried to convince Kyiv to give up territory, or NATO membership.

Details emerged on November 20 of a new operation – the fourth this year – in which Ukraine said it cleared Russian troops out of hundreds of square kilometres of land they occupied, this time in the northern Kharkiv region.

That was about a month after Russia said it had encircled 2,000 Ukrainian troops in an enclave adjacent to the Russian border, around the town of Velykyi Burluk.

Ukrainian commanders realised that the troops were in danger of being encircled, and ordered the execution of “Operation Bear Trap”, which relied on deceptive moves and secrecy to attack the enemy from various sides, concealing its main direction.

Ukrainian forces used a Russian T-80 tank and an Abrams M-1 tank to attack the border town of Vilhuvatka, giving the impression that their main blow would land there.

They then attacked Russian reinforcements from the rear as they arrived to shore up defences, and used drones to remotely mine Russian resupply routes.

The Ukrainian command said Operation Bear Trap has so far succeeded in liberating 200sq km (77sq miles) and 14 settlements, and was ongoing.

Russian troops continue to occupy at least four border villages in Kharkiv, including Vovchansk, but their plan to seize almost 500sq km (193sq miles) has been foiled.

It is not the first time Ukrainian forces preempted a Russian pincer movement.

Earlier this year they stopped an attempted encirclement of the “fortress belt” of Sloviansk, Kramatorsk and Druzhivka in the eastern Donetsk region during Operation Vivaldi.

But Kyiv still struggled to defend its skies and nationwide power outages are making life miserable for Ukrainians.

Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces in Donetsk were engaged in active defence, stopping attempted assaults and destroying vehicles.

Retired Ukrainian colonel Konstantyn Mashovets, who analyses the front on his Telegram channel, said Kyiv’s forces had also advanced in southern Zaporizhia, clearing Russian infiltrators out of the northern bank of the Solona river near Novopavlivka.

As Russia continued these assaults, its casualties rose to a record on November 24 of 432,519, Ukraine’s military said. The next day, it set a new monthly record of 55,629 for November, with five days to go in the month.

Despite Ukraine’s battlefield achievements, US mediation offers remained unchanged.

US negotiators had put two proposals before Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported, citing people involved in talks. Both involved an exchange of land for peace.

In one, Ukraine would cede the “fortress belt” of cities in Donetsk and receive full NATO membership, the WSJ said.

But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected the idea of retreating from that well-defended position.

Russian official Dmitry Medvedev reiterated on November 20 that Ukraine’s potential NATO membership was a key reason for the war. He also suggested partitioning Ukraine, proposing that Lviv could be handed to Poland as part of a deal.

“The enemy has not abandoned its goal of destroying Ukrainian statehood,” said Ukraine’s Defence Ministry.

US negotiator Jared Kushner told a Berlin news conference that Russia had accepted a watered-down version of this US proposal – the second option outlined by the WSJ – of creating NATO-style security guarantees for Ukraine in return for freezing the front line.

“We have been able to convince the Russians of this concept that any security guarantees for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” Kushner said. “President Trump is open to it, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest.”

It would be in the US interest, as he explained on social media, if “broader security arrangements made it highly unlikely that the guarantee would ever be invoked. This is why security guarantees for Ukraine cannot be finalised in isolation from post-war European security architecture.”

It appeared, therefore, that Europe would have to assume the burden of a future defence of Ukraine, something Russia has also rejected, because it refuses to accept European forces on Ukrainian soil.

Those NATO-style guarantees would have to be offered from the safety of NATO soil, rendering them less effective.

Zelenskyy told journalists he did not trust a deal between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom Trump referred to as “my friend” on November 19.

He told Bloomberg the US and Russia were effectively in cahoots to bully Ukraine.

“It’s very unfortunate when, during discussions about how to end the war, Starshield either malfunctions or has limitations, and not only are there fewer missiles for Patriot systems, but there are also other issues that prevent deliveries,” he said.

“Politically, it looks as if [the US] is moving in the same direction as what Putin wants: to force Ukraine into unfavourable compromises,” Zelenskyy said.

Europe did not appear to be in a listening mood any more than Ukraine.

“Russia wants more than Ukraine,” German chancellor Friedrich Merz told parliament. “Russia is escalating in the Baltic. Russia is escalating in Poland. Russia is escalating on the Black Sea. Russia is escalating in space, and Russia is escalating massively here in our own country.”

Merz was referring to two Russian missiles and a Russian drone, which crashed in an area of Poland on November 20, where a multinational force of more than 5,000 personnel from Britain, France, Belgium, Estonia, Spain, the Netherlands, Lithuania, Germany, Poland and Sweden was conducting its first military exercise.

Ukraine made its own response to Russia very clear during the past week.

On November 21 it struck the Sparta II, a Russian logistics vessel en route from St. Petersburg to Kaliningrad.

The next day two Ukrainian naval drones struck and sank the Russian corvette Merkury near the Libyan port of Benghazi, in an attack that has caused tensions between Italy and Ukraine.

“The operation involved 7 unmanned boats manufactured in Ukraine, which were transported to the designated location and launched from a ‘mother ship’,” said the Ukraine Security Force (SBU).

On the same day, Ukraine struck another Russian logistics ship, the Angara, also in the Mediterranean.

Ukraine’s strikes inside Russia also continued.

On November 25, Ukrainian forces attacked the Savasleyka airfield, damaging a Mig-31 and two Sukhoi-24 bombers, all used to launch Khinzal missiles. Three days earlier, Russia had fired 84 cruise missiles into Ukraine.

Ukraine struck the Kaleykino pumping station, which sits on the Druzhba oil pipeline and helps export Russian crude, on November 20 and again on November 23. The strikes reportedly destroyed three 50,000 tonne oil tanks.

During the week Ukraine also struck the Novoshakhtinsk, Permnefteorgsintez, Kuibishevsk, and Sizran refineries, all key to supplying the Russian military. The furthest of these was 3,000km (1,800 miles) from unoccupied Ukraine.

Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries have lowered its refining capacity by an estimated one-third, and caused fuel shortages.

Ukraine’s military intelligence estimated that over the three months ending on October 22, Russia imported almost a million tonnes of refined fuels, including 128,000 tonnes of diesel.

articles.title: Low levels of common vitamin could be stealing nearly 30 minutes of your sleep
articles.excerpt:
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel tells 'The Ingraham Angle' the benefits of 'miracle' Vitamin D and why testing is so important and more.

Middle-aged and older adults with low levels o...
articles.body_text:
Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel tells 'The Ingraham Angle' the benefits of 'miracle' Vitamin D and why testing is so important and more.

Middle-aged and older adults with low levels of vitamin D slept about 23 minutes less per night than people with normal levels, according to a new study that tracked sleep with wearable sensors.

The study, led by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and the National Institute on Aging, used data collected from 2012 to 2019 as part of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging.

The researchers looked at blood tests and sleep data from 460 adults ages 40 and older, averaging 71 years of age.

ONE TYPE OF SLEEP LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DEMENTIA, PARKINSON'S AND 81 OTHER DISEASES

After dividing the participants into three groups by vitamin D level, they found that the highest group slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night than the group with the lowest levels.

People with lower levels also stayed awake longer after waking up at night — a pattern that held regardless of age, gender or race.

Middle-aged and older adults with low levels of vitamin D slept about 23 minutes less per night than people with normal levels. (iStock)

The connection between vitamin D and sleep was strongest among Black participants, who made up about 22% of the group.

"Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to White adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels," lead author Diefei Chen, a doctoral candidate in epidemiology at the Bloomberg School, said in a press release.

CAN WEARABLES DETECT HEART PROBLEMS EARLY? DOCTOR BREAKS DOWN REAL DATA

Most earlier studies on vitamin D and sleep relied on people reporting how well they thought they slept. In this study, researchers used blood draws and actigraphs, which are watch-like motion sensors that measure sleep and wake times.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The team also checked vitamin B12, which previous studies linked to sleep. While higher levels correlated with less nighttime wakefulness in women and more in men, the authors noted the results were statistically inconclusive.

Middle-aged and older adults with low blood levels of vitamin D slept an average of about 23 minutes less per night and stayed awake longer after nighttime awakenings than those with normal levels. (iStock)

The findings were published on Oct. 14 in The Journal of Gerontology: Medical Sciences.

Poor sleep and vitamin D deficiency are both widespread among older adults, with previous research linking sleep disturbances to higher risks of dementia, heart disease and diabetes.

The study had several limitations. Because the researchers looked at snapshots of data rather than testing a treatment in a clinical trial, they could only establish a link between vitamin D and sleep.

The findings did not prove that low levels cause poor sleep or that taking supplements will fix it.

Further research is needed to determine whether higher vitamin D levels actually improve sleep health, and whether the findings apply to younger adults or people with cognitive impairment. (iStock)

Because blood tests can't distinguish between vitamin D from sunlight, food or supplements, the study could not determine whether the source matters.

In addition, the researchers did not track whether changing a person's vitamin D levels over several years leads to changes in their sleep.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Because everyone in the study was 40 or older and had no cognitive impairment, the results may not apply to younger people or adults with memory and thinking problems.

"These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health," senior author Adam Spira, a mental health professor at the Bloomberg School, said in the news release.

Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

articles.title: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.excerpt:
China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidents

For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds ...
articles.body_text:
China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidents

For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.

"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."

It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.

But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.

It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .

But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".

Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades

Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.

China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.

Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.

Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.

The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.

Sheznhen, a rich, buzzing city on the soth-eastern coast, has emerged as one of China's star attractions for tech and tourism

China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.

"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."

China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.

This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.

In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.

His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.

That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.

"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.

Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have held three summits so far this year

Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".

The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? "We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."

Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.

"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.

These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.

In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.

Consul-General Wei Xiaodong (in the red scarf) pictured sending people off in January

"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.

Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.

The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.

"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.

Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.

Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.

"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.

"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."

Xinjiang has been sold as an exotic destination, bringing in huge numbers of tourists

When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.

The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".

"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.

"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."

These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.

Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.

"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."

The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.

"They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true."

Karma Rinchen's parents were among thousands who fled Tibet alongside the Dalai Lama in 1959

Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet.

Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed.

Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party.

"Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target."

But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard".

A memorial for Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen who set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York

"For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds.

For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level.

Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture.

The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi.

In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city.

"What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked.

"What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand."

The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says.

He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution."

* Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity

Can China target critics abroad with its new 'ethnic unity' law?

BBC visits heart of Tibetan resistance as showdown looms between Dalai Lama and China

China's hidden camps: What's happened to the vanished Uyghurs of Xinjiang?

Millions of tourists just visited China's stunning Xinjiang region. There's a side they didn't see

articles.title: Eagles kicker didn't get ex-NFLer's memo about not digging into post-game Thanksgiving food
articles.excerpt:
Watch the full postgame press conference from the Philadelphia Eagles after an historic comeback win against the Dallas Cowboys on Thanksgiving.

Thanksgiving is a day for cramming absurd amounts of f...
articles.body_text:
Watch the full postgame press conference from the Philadelphia Eagles after an historic comeback win against the Dallas Cowboys on Thanksgiving.

Thanksgiving is a day for cramming absurd amounts of food into your mouth hole — and giving thanks, I suppose — but one ex-NFLer has a pro tip about when to show a little restraint.

And it would seem that Eagles' Thanksgiving hero Jake Elliott missed the memo.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Back in 2021, Derek Carr also led his team — the Las Vegas Raiders at the time — to a Thanksgiving win over the Dallas Cowboys.

COWBOYS LEGEND RANDY WHITE REVEALS INTENSE ENCOUNTER BETWEEN HIS MOTHER AND EAGLES FANS DURING PLAYING CAREER

Eagles kicker Jake Elliott talks to Fox Sports' Erin Andrews while cradling his Thanksgiving food bounty. (Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images)

As is tradition, he got to help himself to some of the broadcast's Turkey Day grub along with that game's hero, kicker Daniel Carlson.

"I have to share this every year," Carr said on his podcast "Home Grown with David & Derek Carr," per Daily Mail.

Kicker Daniel Carlson (left) and Derek Carr after beating the Dallas Cowboys on Thanksgiving in 2021. (Jerome Miron-USA TODAY Sports)

"So we're up there, we do the interview... and obviously Daniel made his kick. We're like: 'Daniel, you're going to eat the turkey.'"

Of course, few things top a good Thanksgiving meal, but we usually mean one that came straight out of the oven.

"It's definitely cold... [but] he goes to take a bite, and he says: 'Oh, delicious!'" Carr recalled. "And right as we walk away, I said, 'How was it?' He said: 'It was the grossest thing I've ever tasted.'"

It makes sense, especially for a game that goes down to the wire, that the food was prepped well in advance.

Of course, that also means it's not in its optimal eating window.

GIANTS STAR CAM SKATTEBO REVEALS THE ODD PREGAME MEAL THAT CAUSED TO HIM TO PUKE MID-GAME

Philadelphia Eagles kicker Jake Elliott celebrates after defeating the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on Thanksgiving. (Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images)

Well, Elliott must not be subscribed to Carr's podcast because after sealing the Eagles' historic 39-38 comeback win with a 59-yard field goal, he dug right in.

Hey, the taste of sweet, sweet victory goes nicely with food that was probably intended just to be set dressing.

But, lest you think that Elliott had to do his Black Friday shopping while lying on the floor of his bathroom between bouts with food poisoning, think again.

The Eagles' hero was right back at it, getting fans fired up before the Philadelphia Flyers' Black Friday game against the Vancouver Canucks.

Looks like he fared better than most of us did on Thanksgiving, even though our food was much fresher than some stuffing warmed by studio lights.

articles.title: Kenyan cult leader guilty of manslaughter more than 123 starvation deaths
articles.excerpt: A Kenyan court has found cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of manslaughter over the deaths of 123 of his followers, the latest conviction for Mackenzie, the founder and pastor of the Good News Interna...
articles.body_text:
A Kenyan court has found cult leader Paul Mackenzie guilty of manslaughter over the deaths of 123 of his followers, the latest conviction for Mackenzie, the founder and pastor of the Good News International Church.

Mackenzie was convicted on Friday in the coastal city of Mombasa, along with 29 followers, including his wife, Rhoda Mumbua.

Magistrate Alex Ithuku said Mackenzie “gave the directions to fast to death”, Reuters reported. Mackenzie pleaded not guilty, and one of his lawyers said he would appeal after sentencing.

On November 6, Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murder of 191 people, 190 of them children. He had denied forcing the victims to starve, but the court rejected his defence.

He was also convicted this week of child cruelty, assault, radicalisation and “terrorism-related offences”, according to Reuters. He is due to be sentenced on the child cruelty and radicalisation charges in December, The Associated Press reported.

Mackenzie led the Good News International Church in the Shakahola Forest, near Kenya’s Indian Ocean coast.

He told followers to starve themselves and their children to death to meet Jesus before the end of the world.

Police arrested him in 2023 after a tip-off, and authorities began uncovering more than 400 bodies. People familiar with the cult told Reuters that Mackenzie planned the starvation in three phases: children first, then women and young men, and finally, the remaining men.

Mackenzie had been arrested twice before, in connection with the deaths of children, and released.

The killings have shocked Kenya and led to calls for tighter oversight of religious groups.

President William Ruto said in 2023 that he took responsibility as head of state for the government’s failure to prevent the deaths.

Other mass killings linked to cults include one in Uganda in 2000, when a doomsday group killed more than 700 people, and the 1978 massacre in Guyana, where an American cult leader ordered more than 900 followers to drink poison, Reuters said.

articles.title: NBC pulls controversial anti-Israel ad after igniting fury from Jewish groups
articles.excerpt:
NBC pulled a controversial anti-Israel ad after it sparked backlash among Jewish groups and pro-Israel advocates, Fox News Digital confirmed. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

NBC has pulled...
articles.body_text:
NBC pulled a controversial anti-Israel ad after it sparked backlash among Jewish groups and pro-Israel advocates, Fox News Digital confirmed. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

NBC has pulled a controversial anti-Israel ad from its airwaves after sparking backlash over the Thanksgiving holiday, Fox News Digital has confirmed.

During a Thanksgiving-themed "Saturday Night Live" primetime special Wednesday night, NBC aired an ad featuring a girl raising money for a $400 bike, juxtaposing her with a Palestinian girl with a missing leg standing on crutches in front of a pile of rubble.

"Every three seconds, our government sends $400 of taxpayer money to Israel to do this," a narrator tells viewers while showing the injured Gazan child on screen.

MS RACHEL CALLS SILENCE ON GAZA CONFLICT 'F---ED UP,' SAYS IT UPSETS HER SO MUCH SHE NOW SWEARS

The ad, pulled by NBC, featured an injured Palestinian girl standing in front of rubble, telling viewers that U.S. taxpayer money was funding the destruction by Israel. (Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP via Getty Images)

The 30-second ad, funded by the IMEU (Institute for Middle East Understanding) Policy Project, directs viewers to a website named No More For Israel, criticizing what it describes as the U.S. government's weapons "giveaway" to Israel and accusing the Jewish state of "committing a genocide" against Palestinians. The site urges Americans to pressure lawmakers to oppose any weapons deal with Israel.

Jewish groups and pro-Israel advocates criticized the ad as antisemitic, with many pointing out that the ad makes no mention that the ongoing conflict in Gaza began with the Oct. 7 terrorist attack committed by Hamas against Israel.

MANDANI GRILLED ON RHETORIC TOWARD OCT 7, COMBATTING ANTISEMITISM AS JEWISH NEW YORKERS FEAR CURRENT CLIMATE

"NBC took money to tell millions of Americans that our support for Israel is responsible for the horrific injury of a Palestinian child," American Jewish Committee CEO Ted Deutch wrote on X.

"Here’s what the ad leaves out: the vicious Hamas terrorists who launched this war on October 7 by slaughtering, raping, and kidnapping Israelis, dragging hostages into Gaza, and then fighting from among Palestinian civilians, with horrific consequences for Israelis and Gazans alike.

"The suffering of Palestinian civilians is real and heartbreaking. But using that suffering to demonize Israel while writing Hamas out of the story isn’t an honest debate," the former Democratic congressman continued.

"We can debate American policy and assistance to Israel. And yes, this was a paid advertisement. But 'we were paid to run it' cannot be the end of the discussion. Networks decide what they will and will not put on the air every day. NBC chose to take the money and run this ad.

"It should explain why and how an ad this one-sided and manipulative met its standards for what it will put on the air. And if this meets NBC’s standards, Americans deserve to know what those standards are."

The Israeli-American Council (IAC) characterized the ad as a clear example of "antisemitic blood libel aimed at denying the Jewish state its right to defend itself against terrorists and murderers."

"Words and images have consequences," the group shared in a statement to Fox News Digital. "They can normalize antisemitic hatred, embolden people to act on it and endanger innocent lives."

The IAC called on NBC to "come clean about how this advertisement met its own standards and ensure it is not aired again."

Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt also slammed NBC's decision to air the ad.

"Broadcasting an ad that blatantly demonizes the Jewish state and makes false claims about the use of American taxpayer dollars during primetime on the eve of a family holiday isn’t just insensitive. It’s indefensible," he wrote.

"At a moment of escalating antisemitism, there is no rationale to justify fanning the flames with such a twisted narrative."

UK ANTISEMITISM ADVISOR LAUNCHES PROBE INTO BBC, SAYS CULTURE DEMANDS JEWISH STAFFERS 'JUSTIFY' EXISTENCE

"Modern day Nazi propaganda compliments of NBC. Every person who approved this ad buy should be identified and terminated," the advocacy group Stop Antisemitism wrote.

A source familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital that NBC senior leadership was unaware of the controversial anti-Israel ad until it aired. (Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty Images)

A source familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital that senior leadership at NBC was unaware of the ad until after it aired and that the network intends to reevaluate its ad review process going forward. The Wall Street Journal's Joe Flint first reported NBC's decision.

A spokesperson for NBC declined to comment.

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

articles.title: US military says it disabled merchant ship trying to breach Iran blockade
articles.excerpt:
The US military says it has fired on a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman and claims it was trying to breach an American blockade on Iranian ports.

Military aircraft fired “precision munitions” at t...
articles.body_text:
The US military says it has fired on a merchant vessel in the Gulf of Oman and claims it was trying to breach an American blockade on Iranian ports.

Military aircraft fired “precision munitions” at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the “ship’s propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed”, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said in a statement.

US officials say the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel’s destination as Singapore. It is at least the 15th vessel the US military has publicly acknowledged disabling since the blockade began in April, and the sixth since it resumed it in July. The previous vessel was disabled on November 7.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Friday that two tankers attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an “unauthorised” route, claiming that one of them struck a naval mine while the other was forced to turn back.

The claims could not be independently verified.

The commander of the Iranian navy, Shahram Irani, said on Friday on state television that Iran will carry out operations “that will not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region’s waters”.

The US military has maintained a sizeable naval force in the region, including a constant presence of two aircraft carriers and a host of other ships.

American ships have been blockading Iranian ports since April, although the blockade was temporarily lifted during talks with Tehran and resumed in July. Since then, the US military says it has redirected 158 merchant ships and disabled those that refuse to comply.

CENTCOM, which has its headquarters in Florida, has consistently said that American forces issue multiple warnings before firing on the merchant ships.

articles.title: Prosecutors seek 25-year prison term for 'poison seller' Kenneth Law
articles.excerpt:
Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.

Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding t...
articles.body_text:
Canadian prosecutors are seeking a 25-year prison sentence for a man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries.

Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

The 61-year-old will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

She also said Law's motives were financial.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for many of their battles with mental illness.

He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims.

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."

Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.

The sentencing hearing on Friday followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.

Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.

Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

'Poison seller' who sold toxic chemicals online to people across world admits aiding suicides

Man who sold toxic chemicals should rot in hell, says mother of woman who killed herself

Survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair

articles.title: From turkey shortages to helicopter deliveries: The extraordinary history of Thanksgiving during war
articles.excerpt:
House lawmakers on both sides of the aisle spoke to Fox News Digital about what they are most thankful for as they get ready to celebrate Thanksgiving with their families.

In November 1966, 12 Americ...
articles.body_text:
House lawmakers on both sides of the aisle spoke to Fox News Digital about what they are most thankful for as they get ready to celebrate Thanksgiving with their families.

In November 1966, 12 American soldiers stationed at an isolated outpost in a Vietnamese war zone were about as far from a traditional Thanksgiving at home as they could get.

Their only means of resupply was by air. But the U.S. military was determined to get them Thanksgiving dinner anyway.

A mess sergeant at Bien Hoa prepared turkey and all the trimmings, packed the meal into insulated containers and sent it by helicopter into War Zone D, where three officers and nine enlisted men of a 5th Special Forces detachment sat down to Thanksgiving dinner, according to Defense Department records preserved by the National Archives.

The delivery was one piece of a massive logistical effort the U.S. military has undertaken during wars spanning generations to get traditional Thanksgiving meals to troops serving in combat zones.

Soldiers are pictured eating Thanksgiving dinner during World War I, in 1918. (National Archives)

From civilians sending tens of thousands of turkeys to Union troops during the Civil War to helicopters carrying hot meals to soldiers in Korea, the holiday has been observed through some of the nation's most consequential conflicts.

Thanksgiving became a national tradition in the midst of war. President Abraham Lincoln issued his 1863 Thanksgiving proclamation as the Civil War entered its third year, calling on Americans to observe the final Thursday of November as a day of "Thanksgiving and Praise."

By the following year, Americans on the home front were mounting a massive effort to get Thanksgiving dinner to Union troops.

Former War Department official Charles A. Dana later recalled the "great turkey movement" of November 1864. In New York alone, organizers reported having 20,000 turkeys ready to send to the front, according to Dana's account. A Philadelphia committee sought transportation for another 4,000 destined for troops serving under Gen. Philip Sheridan.

U.S. service members stationed at an airbase in Norfolk, England, select turkeys for their Thanksgiving dinners at a local farm on Nov. 6, 1943. (National Archives)

By World War II, the effort to put turkey on troops' Thanksgiving tables had grown so large that it affected whether Americans at home could find one for their own.

In August 1943, the War Food Administration restricted most civilian turkey sales as the government sought millions of pounds for the armed forces. An initial goal of at least 10 million pounds for troops overseas was expanded to include military installations at home, and the government ultimately obtained roughly 30 million pounds before the order was lifted in October, according to wartime government records.

A year later, delivering Thanksgiving dinner near the front could carry its own risks.

102-YEAR-OLD NAVY VETERAN STILL CRAVES HOT WINGS AFTER 102 COMBAT MISSIONS IN KOREA: 'I MIGHT MAKE IT TO 115'

Sailors Leo F. DesJarlait, left, Eulice E. Wheeler, center, and G.J. Lindner eat turkey and trimmings at an advanced U.S. Navy base in the Aleutian Islands on Nov. 24, 1944. Lindner gives a "4.0" sign, meaning "perfect," in response to the Thanksgiving meal. (National Archives)

In Germany's Hürtgen Forest, Lt. Paul Boesch of the 121st Infantry Regiment later recalled being told that hot turkey dinners had arrived for his men amid some of the European campaign's most grueling fighting. Boesch protested that sending soldiers to collect the food would expose them to German artillery, but the order to distribute the meal stood.

His fears proved well-founded. As troops gathered to retrieve the food, German artillery struck the area, killing and wounding several men, according to Boesch's account.

Six years later, American troops were again eating Thanksgiving dinner near the front, this time in the bitter cold of North Korea.

On Thanksgiving Day 1950, Marines around the Chosin Reservoir were served turkey and cranberry sauce, candied sweet potatoes, fruitcake and mince pie. In the subzero temperatures, the food quickly began to freeze.

US NAVY RELEASES PHOTOS OF 'FRESH MEALS,' PUSHES BACK ON REPORTS OF FOOD SHORTAGES ON MIDDLE EAST WARSHIPS

The dinner came as U.S. commanders remained optimistic that the war could soon be over. The following day, Gen. Douglas MacArthur launched an offensive that became known as the "Home-by-Christmas" campaign.

Instead, Chinese forces entered the fighting in massive numbers. Within days of Thanksgiving, Marines around Chosin were surrounded and battling through one of the most brutal engagements of the Korean War.

Pfc. John A. Arnett, left, receives a turkey leg from Cpl. Fred Burks during Thanksgiving dinner in Korea on Nov. 22, 1951. The chow line was set up on the back side of a hill roughly 200 yards from the main line of resistance. (National Archives)

More than half a century later, another generation of American troops was spending Thanksgiving at war in Iraq and Afghanistan.

In 2003, President George W. Bush secretly flew into Baghdad to surprise roughly 600 troops gathered for Thanksgiving dinner at Baghdad International Airport. Air Force One approached with its cabin shades drawn and lights dimmed amid tight security surrounding the trip.

"I was just looking for a warm meal somewhere," Bush joked before addressing the troops and helping serve Thanksgiving dinner.

In Afghanistan, getting that dinner to troops stationed far from major bases could require a different kind of operation.

President George H.W. Bush eats Thanksgiving dinner on the hood of a Humvee while visiting U.S. troops in Saudi Arabia during Operation Desert Shield on Nov. 22, 1990. (National Archives)

On Thanksgiving 2007, helicopters carried turkeys and traditional fixings from Bagram Airfield to soldiers at remote firebases in the Tagab Valley, according to a contemporaneous U.S. military account.

It was the first hot meal some of the soldiers had eaten in months. Because the positions still had to be defended, troops rotated between Thanksgiving dinner and standing watch.

"The white meat was magnificent," Pfc. Matt Lorimer of the 82nd Airborne Division said.

President George W. Bush traveled to Iraq in 2003 to meet with troops without the public's knowledge. (Tim Sloan/AFP/Getty Images)

At another remote Afghan outpost two years later, troops spent a month fattening five scrawny turkeys purchased locally for Thanksgiving. But five birds were not enough to feed roughly 150 soldiers.

Additional turkey was flown from the United States to Bagram Airfield and then transported to the outpost. Even that was not the end of the journey.

A handful of soldiers were manning an observation post on a mountain spur roughly 6,900 feet above sea level. Their Thanksgiving dinner was packed up and flown by helicopter up the mountain to them.
