articles.title: Supplements in the spotlight as longevity doctor shares his personal daily routine
articles.excerpt:
Dr. Kien Vuu discusses how targeted supplements work alongside healthy lifestyle choices to support muscle growth, cellular energy and overall performance.

Nearly eight in 10 Americans take at least ...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Kien Vuu discusses how targeted supplements work alongside healthy lifestyle choices to support muscle growth, cellular energy and overall performance.

Nearly eight in 10 Americans take at least one dietary supplement for their health, according to a September 2026 Pew Research Center survey — yet clinicians warn that routine supplementation isn't always necessary or safe.

Dr. Kien Vuu, a Los Angeles-based physician specializing in longevity and author of the book "Thrive State," spoke to Fox News Digital about the role supplements play in overall health.

"Supplements are a signal," he told Fox News Digital during an event at Soft Bar + Cafe in Brooklyn, New York. "How we live life are signals. How we eat, how we sleep, how we move, how we connect with people, they're all signals to the body — and supplements can play a very important role."

DOCTOR'S 10 RULES FOR LIVING LONGER, CELEBRATING MORE BIRTHDAYS AND MAKING EXTRA YEARS COUNT

Certain supplements can support muscle growth, metabolism and cellular energy, but they work best when they're paired with "lifestyle choices and targeted support," the expert said.

Vuu, a partner with longevity and supplement brand Solaray, shared the supplements he takes on a daily basis.

Certain supplements can support muscle growth, metabolism, cellular energy and overall molecular support, but they work best when they're paired with "lifestyle choices," the longevity expert says. (iStock)

Creatine, an amino acid-based compound, has become popular among fitness enthusiasts, as it has been shown to aid in boosting energy during exercise. The supplement is "really important" for muscle health and recovery, Vuu said.

COMMON GYM SUPPLEMENT COULD HELP FIGHT DEPRESSION, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS

The supplement has also demonstrated cognitive benefits, assisting with memory and processing speed, according to the National Institutes of Health.

Combining creatine with an MBP (milk basic protein) — a whey protein fraction studied for supporting bone formation and reducing bone breakdown — can support both muscle energy and bone health, according to Vuu.

Combining creatine with an MBP (milk basic protein) — a whey protein fraction studied for supporting bone formation and reducing bone breakdown — can support both muscle energy and bone health. (iStock)

NMN, short for nicotinamide mononucleotide, is a compound the body uses to make NAD+ — a vital coenzyme that helps cells convert food into energy and repair damaged DNA.

ANTI-AGING SUPPLEMENTS TAKEN BY MILLIONS MAY UNDERMINE CANCER TREATMENT, STUDY WARNS

As a basic step in his longevity routine, Vuu said he typically takes NMN to support cellular energy as natural NAD+ levels decline with age — though independent researchers note that clinical evidence in humans is still emerging.

Glutathione, a tripeptide antioxidant produced naturally in cells, helps the liver detoxify harmful compounds and protects cells from oxidative damage caused by pollution, stress and aging, according to UCLA Health.

In the body, the compound also plays a vital role in supporting immune and liver function, protecting red blood cells from oxidative damage and facilitating amino acid transport across cell membranes.

Glutathione can help reduce stress by detoxing the body. (iStock)

"When I travel or get super stressed, I like to use glutathione," Vuu said. "I find myself and my nervous system behaving a lot better."

Vuu also takes several staples aimed at filling common nutritional gaps, including vitamin D, magnesium, a multivitamin and fish oil for omega-3 fatty acids.

DR OZ REVEALS 3 FREE WAYS TO BOOST YOUR HEALTH — NO MEDICATION REQUIRED

"What I see very deficient in people these days is vitamin D," he said. "Even if they're out in the sun, our bodies are using so much vitamin D, fighting against some of the stresses we have in life, that it's really low."

The doctor recommends seeing a physician to determine the need for certain supplements. (istock)

Data from the National Institutes of Health shows that roughly one-third of U.S. adults are clinically deficient in vitamin D, and factors like sunscreen, winter sunlight angles, varying skin tones and higher body fat can limit how much the body produces.

"Supplementing with [vitamin D] improves their hormones, it improves their energy, it improves their sex life, improves their immune system," Vuu said — though clinicians note those benefits typically apply to people correcting a true deficiency rather than those whose levels are already normal.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The doctor said he also takes mitochondrial supplements such as ubiquinol — the active antioxidant form of CoQ10 — which supports cellular energy production and helps protect cells from oxidative damage.

While many people fall short on certain nutrients — or could benefit from targeted supplementation — it is possible to overdo it. Vuu said it's important to know your baseline health and to target your specific needs.

"If you're a person looking to supplement, go work with a physician first," he advised. "See where your labs are, see what symptoms you might be having, and then recognize what your goals are."

"The sweet spot is knowing what you need, knowing what the baseline is, and then taking the targeted [approach] to support you … You're not supposed to take everything, and it's going to be different for everyone."

Vuu added that supplements clearly play an important role in how the body functions, noting that "our cells are energetically listening to everything."

The physician recommends connecting with the community as a means of supporting supplement effectiveness. (iStock)

Supplements work best when paired with healthy lifestyle practices, including adequate sleep, regular exercise and social connections, he noted.

Connecting with people and maintaining a sense of community has been shown to be beneficial to health, Vuu said. Pairing a proven supplement like creatine with real-world connection and enjoyment, he said, creates the ultimate "health stack."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Beyond pills and powders, the expert suggested one final daily "supplement" for everyone: vitamin G — which stands for gratitude.

Recognizing life as a gift and feeling fortunate to be alive helps keep fear and anxiety at bay, he said.

"If you can feel gratitude, you're putting your nervous system in a state of calm, which actually improves symptoms and improves your health in the long term."

Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Putin's grip on Crimea tested amid major blackout as Zelenskyy warns of looming Russian strike
articles.excerpt: Fox News senior correspondent Benjamin Hall reports on Ukraine's major strike on the Kerch Bridge in Crimea. Hall details Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's warning to Russia and reports on upc...
articles.body_text:
Fox News senior correspondent Benjamin Hall reports on Ukraine's major strike on the Kerch Bridge in Crimea. Hall details Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's warning to Russia and reports on upcoming peace negotiations led by top Trump aides Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

Russian President Vladimir Putin's control over Crimea faced renewed pressure Thursday as a massive blackout crippled the Russian-occupied peninsula, disrupting public transport and leaving people without heat, according to reports.

The blackout came after Ukrainian strikes had damaged the Kerch Strait Bridge last week, disrupting a key Russian military supply route, and as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Moscow was preparing another large-scale attack on Ukraine.

Russian-controlled utilities blamed the Crimea blackout on an accident at energy facilities outside the region, after reports of explosions and air raid sirens sounded across the Black Sea peninsula, according to the Kyiv Post.

PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

Residential buildings at night during a power outage across Crimea. (Alexey Pavlishak/Reuters)

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence suggested that Russia was preparing to target the country's energy infrastructure, logistics networks and essential services.

"Unfortunately, the Russians are already completing preparations for a new massive strike," Zelenskyy wrote on X Thursday following a coordination meeting. "According to intelligence, energy facilities and logistics infrastructure, as well as essential services facilities in cities and communities, will once again be the targets."

The Ukrainian leader also urged residents to remain vigilant, warning of renewed missile attacks.

"In the coming days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats," Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address Thursday, according to Reuters. "And in Russia, they should know that we will rebuild what is ours and retaliate against every Russian strike."

In Crimea, Russian-controlled electricity provider Sevastopolenergo said that Sevastopol had lost power, while electricity restrictions affected Simferopol, Kerch, Alushta and Yevpatoria, according to Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda.

ZELENSKYY SAYS RUSSIA STRIKES HOMETOWN, CRITICIZES PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING

Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are shown in a side-by-side photo illustration as discussions continue over the future of Ukraine and a potential settlement to the war. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP; Christian Bruna/Getty Images)

Streetcar services were also suspended in Yevpatoria and buses replaced trolleybuses on some routes in Simferopol. Parts of Kerch were also reportedly left without heating.

Russian-installed authorities had issued air raid alerts Thursday morning amid reports of explosions.

The blackout is the latest in a series of disruptions that have hit Crimea since late October, with Russian authorities blaming damage to power infrastructure.

The disruptions come amid mounting pressure on Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014 and has since used as a military and logistics hub for its operations against Ukraine.

The Kerch Strait Bridge, which connects the peninsula to mainland Russia, serves as a critical transportation link for Russian forces and has been targeted by Ukraine since Putin launched his invasion in 2022.

KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION

A view shows the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea, which was targeted in an explosion by Ukraine on Tuesday, June 3. (Alexey Pavlishak/Reuters)

The bridge was built after the Russian annexation and opened in 2018, serving as a symbol of Moscow's control over the peninsula.

Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko also said seven people were wounded in an overnight Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital that damaged a shopping center and two other buildings, Reuters reported.

Zelenskyy also called for additional air defense assistance Thursday, emphasizing the need for interceptors for Patriot air defense systems and National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile Systems (NASAMS).

"I expect a report from Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry on the results of its communication with our partners regarding the supply of air defenses — interceptors for Patriots and NASAMS are the key priority," Zelenskyy wrote.

It was the second time this week Zelenskyy had warned of preparations for another major Russian attack, according to Reuters.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Iran accuses Zelenskyy of 'false flag' Kuwait drone strike op to get Trump's attention
articles.excerpt:
Ret. Navy Vice Adm. Kevin Donegan, former Navy 5th Fleet commander, says the Middle East’s actors have changed ‘dramatically’ since he held command on ‘The Story.’

A former adviser to Iran's nuclear ...
articles.body_text:
Ret. Navy Vice Adm. Kevin Donegan, former Navy 5th Fleet commander, says the Middle East’s actors have changed ‘dramatically’ since he held command on ‘The Story.’

A former adviser to Iran's nuclear negotiating team accused Ukraine on Thursday of orchestrating a deadly drone attack in Kuwait to prove its worth to President Donald Trump, as Tehran continued to deny responsibility.

And while Kuwaiti and Italian officials blamed Iran for the strike, which killed two Italian defense technicians and wounded two others, Iran’s embassy in Rome warned against "false flag" operations it said were aimed at widening the Persian Gulf conflict and now drawing Europe into the crisis.

Mohammad Marandi, who served as an adviser during talks with the U.S. in Pakistan and has been dubbed Iran's "English-language mouthpiece," claimed Ukrainian forces were operating across the Middle East, including in northern Iraq and Syria, also in remarks reported by the Fars News Agency, which is affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

IRAN TARGETS US AIR BASE IN KUWAIT AFTER US DEFENSIVE STRIKES AMID CRITICISM FROM GULF STATES

Smoke rises after a reported Iranian strike near the U.S. Embassy in Kuwait City on Mar. 2, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

"It is widely believed in Iran that the attack on Kuwait was a false flag operation, likely carried out by the Ukrainian regime, because its operatives are now present across the region, including in northern Iraq and Syria. Ukraine aims to demonstrate its potential to Trump," Marandi said on X.

Fars also cited a security source who claimed Ukrainian operatives had deployed thousands of drones and other unmanned aircraft in several Middle Eastern countries, including Iraq's Kurdistan region, according to Iran International.

Kuwait's Defense Ministry said falling debris from the interception of Iranian drones struck a military facility Thursday, initially wounding four people. Two Italian nationals later died of their injuries.

A Kuwaiti national and a Pakistani national were also wounded and taken to a hospital for treatment. The ministry did not disclose the facility's precise location.

Italy's Foreign Ministry confirmed that the two Italian nationals were employees of Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian subsidiary of German defense manufacturer Rheinmetall.

"An explosion caused by a drone attack ... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working," the ministry said in a statement.

The victims were identified as Antonio Saccoccio, 65, of Formia, Italy, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, of Rome, Italian news agency ANSA reported.

EUROPE ASSASSINATION SCHEME EMERGES AS IRAN DENIES DC 'DIRTY BOMB' PLOT AMID TRUMP WARNING

Kuwait’s civil aviation authority released surveillance footage it says shows an Iranian drone crashing into the country’s international airport. (CIVIL AVIATION KUWAIT)

The men had been performing maintenance on detection antennas for the Skyguard air defense system.

Iran's embassy in Rome rejected allegations that Tehran was responsible for the attack, warning of alleged efforts to draw European countries into the Middle East conflict.

"The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran also draws the international community's attention to 'false flag' activities and operations aimed at expanding the scope of the conflict, linking disputes in other regions to the Persian Gulf crisis, drawing Europe into the crisis, and exacerbating the current critical situation, and calls on everyone to remain vigilant in this regard."

Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he had spoken with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and offered to cooperate in an investigation into the deadly incident.

"In calls with my Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts, expressed condolences over deaths of Italian citizens in Kuwait," Araghchi wrote. "The incident is suspicious and looks like a precooked recipe for war.

"We stand ready to cooperate with Kuwait and Italy to determine the cause of the incident," he added.

TOP GULF OFFICIAL OFFERS GLIMMER OF HOPE ON TRUMP-IRAN NUCLEAR TALKS AS THREAT OF WAR HANGS OVER REGION

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi speaks during a joint press conference with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan (not pictured) in Tehran, Iran, Nov. 30, 2025. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via Reuters)

Kuwait, a key U.S. ally in the Persian Gulf, has repeatedly come under Iranian attack since the U.S. and Israel launched military operations against Iran on Feb. 28.

Ukraine has deployed drone specialists and interceptor drones to the Middle East to help defend against Iranian attacks, expanding its regional defense cooperation by sharing technology and military expertise developed during its war with Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in March that Kyiv had sent interceptor drones and specialists to help protect U.S. military installations in Jordan at Washington's request.

Ukraine also announced that teams of military specialists had been deployed to Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia to help defend against Iranian drone attacks.

"Ukraine has the greatest experience in the world in countering attack drones," Zelenskyy said in March, adding that "without our experience, it will be very difficult for the Gulf region, the entire Middle East, and partners in Europe and America to build strong protection."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Thanksgiving storms leave nearly a million without power across the US
articles.excerpt:
Strong winds and heavy storms have knocked out power for nearly a million US homes and businesses and resulted in the rare postponement of Macy’s annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City.

As A...
articles.body_text:
Strong winds and heavy storms have knocked out power for nearly a million US homes and businesses and resulted in the rare postponement of Macy’s annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City.

As Americans marked the annual holiday on Thursday, heavy storms disrupted travel across the country, with more than 2,000 flights to or from US destinations delayed and more than 400 cancelled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.

More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday evening, with the majority in East Coast states, according to the outage tracking website poweroutage.us. New Jersey and parts of New York were placed under a state of emergency.

The US National Weather Service issued wind advisories for northern Georgia, the majority of the mid-Atlantic and southern New England.

Two people were rescued from their cars in New York City due to flooding, according to Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

“There is no destination worth your safety,” Mamdani said. Similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.

In Maryland, nearly two million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were asked to conserve water because of intermittent power disruptions related to heavy rain. The storms also prompted several brief tornado warnings, including for a rare twister southeast of Seattle, Washington.

The Midwestern region witnessed heavy snowfall on Thursday, with some areas of Missouri recording up to 35cm of snow.

Meanwhile, waves driven by high tides caused flooding along the Pacific coast. The conditions were expected to continue into Friday, according to the National Weather Service.

Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations in areas from Humboldt County in the far north to southern Ventura County near Los Angeles.

articles.title: At least 13 Niger soldiers killed in Sanam armed attack
articles.excerpt:
At least 13 members of Niger’s National Guard have been killed and 20 wounded in an attack on their compound in Sanam, in the west of the country, the Defence Ministry has said.

In a statement read o...
articles.body_text:
At least 13 members of Niger’s National Guard have been killed and 20 wounded in an attack on their compound in Sanam, in the west of the country, the Defence Ministry has said.

In a statement read on state television, the ministry said the attack on Thursday was carried out by “numerous heavily armed assailants”, referring to the incident as a “terrorist attack”.

The ministry gave a provisional toll and said soldiers killed several attackers and destroyed their logistical infrastructure. Operations to track down the attackers are ongoing, it added.

The assault took place at about 5am local time (04:00 GMT), local and security sources told the Nigerien outlet ActuNiger.

Sanam is in the Tillaberi region, near the Mali border, where armed groups regularly attack security forces.

It was not clear who was behind the attack.

The attack comes two days after the ministry said 11 soldiers were killed in an attack attributed to Boko Haram in the Diffa region, in the southeast.

In neighbouring Nigeria, suspected members of an armed group killed at least 30 people in villages in the central state of Niger on Tuesday.

They described it as retaliation for the killing of many Fulani herders days earlier.

In Nigeria’s northeast, President Bola Tinubu promised on Wednesday to restore peace to a region hit by a rebellion led by Boko Haram and the ISIL (ISIS) affiliate in West Africa Province, as he campaigns for re-election.

articles.title: Mike Tomlin calls Steelers situation following Aaron Rodgers vs. Mike McCarthy feud 'a dumpster fire'
articles.excerpt: Barstool College Football Show co-host Kayce Smith breaks down the escalating feud between quarterback Aaron Rodgers and Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy after Rodgers criticized the coach following ...
articles.body_text:
Barstool College Football Show co-host Kayce Smith breaks down the escalating feud between quarterback Aaron Rodgers and Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy after Rodgers criticized the coach following his benching and release. Smith also reacts to Crunch Fitness testing dedicated influencer filming zones in Arizona and Florida.

Mike Tomlin coached the Pittsburgh Steelers for 19 years, and although there was a Super Bowl high and that low earlier this year when he decided to quit, he never presided over something like the Aaron Rodgers vs. Mike McCarthy feud going public the past couple of days.

And Tomlin didn't like it. He said the prevailing feeling about the situation now is "just general sadness."

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

NBC broadcast analyst Mike Tomlin before the game between the Los Angeles Rams and Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, Colo., on Sept. 27, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

SUPER BOWL-WINNING COACH MIKE TOMLIN LANDS NBC ROLE ON 'FOOTBALL NIGHT IN AMERICA' BROADCAST

"I'm upset about it," Tomlin said during a halftime interview with play-by-play voice Mike Tirico on NBC's Sunday Night Football broadcast. "Um, you know, it's a dumpster fire. And I don't say that in a judgmental way.

"I've presided over a few dumpster fires in my 19 years. But it certainly is upsetting, and I'm sure, Steelers nation is upset."

AARON RODGERS AND MIKE MCCARTHY DISAGREEMENTS AT HEART OF QUARTERBACK'S BENCHING BY THE STEELERS

On Tuesday the Steelers announced they were benching Rodgers and making him inactive for Friday's game against the Denver Broncos.

On Wednesday, Rodgers responded by going on the "Pat McAfee Show" and claiming McCarthy falls asleep in meetings, snores in those meetings, isn't prepared with the game play as late as Tuesday, misstated what team he coaches while breaking down the team at halftime of a game against the Philadelphia Eagles, and is generally "unwell."

Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin and quarterback Aaron Rodgers (8) leave the field after an NFL football game against the Baltimore Ravens in Baltimore, Maryland, on Dec. 7, 2025. (AP Photo/Stephanie Scarbrough)

Within hours, the Steelers released Rodgers. McCarthy denied falling asleep and missing meetings, and accused Rodgers of presenting him with "an ultimatum" about taking the play-calling away from the coach or he'd ask to be released – something Rodgers confirmed.

AARON RODGERS NFL CAREER SEEMS OVER BUT THREE TEAMS COULD CONSIDER QUARTERBACK AS A LATE-SEASON OPTION

"I had a range of emotions watching those course of events play out yesterday," said Tomlin, who coached the Steelers from 2007 through last season. "I think the prevailing [feeling] is just general sadness. Sad that we might be looking at the end of a legendary career of the quarterback, Aaron Rodgers.

"And just on the macro level, whether it's organizationally or for the game of football at large, to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum. Those are things that kind of run counter-culture to professional football."

Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers, left, shakes hands with his head coach Mike Tomlin following an NFL football game against the New York Jets Sunday, Sept. 7, 2025, in East Rutherford, N.J. (AP Photo/Matt Slocum)

Tomlin coached Rodgers last season and it is no secret he respected and admired Rodgers for year before that. That's one reason the Steelers were interested in signing Rodgers last season.

But Tomlin said it nonetheless shocked him when Rodgers pulled back the curtain on his feelings for McCarthy on national TV.

"It certainly did," Tomlin said. "But, you know, particularly because I know both men involved. Certainly had a lot of intimate work and and development of relationship with Aaron over the last couple of years and have known and competed against Mike, you know, respected and appreciated him as a coach for a long time."

There has been no Steelers player that either publicly or privately has said what Rodgers said untrue. Tomlin was asked how the quarterback is viewed in the Steelers locker room.

"He was beloved, and I'm not, you know, over-exaggerating that," Tomlin said. "He worked at it, and people appreciated his openness to getting to know and understand the Steeler culture, to be engaged with teammates."

Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy looks on during the first quarter against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field in Cleveland, Ohio, on Oct. 1, 2026. (Gregory Shamus/Getty Images)

"Particularly from my perspective, I worked with a lot of veteran players over the years, and at times, they lose a little patience for the process," Tomlin said. "Or they lose patience for relationships with younger guys.

"Man, he seemed to embrace all of that and really embrace it in a real natural way."

STEELERS TEAM PRESIDENT CHOOSES SIDE IN AARON RODGERS, MIKE MCCARTHY SPLIT

So does Tomlin believe McCarthy can effectively lead the Steelers the rest of the way this season after what Rodgers uncovered?

Aaron Rodgers and head coach Mike McCarthy of the Pittsburgh Steelers chat before an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Pa., on Nov. 22, 2026. (Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

And here's a hint to his answer: It's not a definitive yes.

"You know, it certainly created some challenges and challenges is probably an understatement if all of those things are true," Tomlin said. "...But his ability to overcome that, or inability to overcome that, in my opinion, is based on relationships."

That is an unvarnished view of the situation from someone who lived within that Steelers organization and culture for nearly two decades.

It doesn't suggest the Steelers are going to be fine.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

articles.title: Trump downplays Russia, China support for Iran during talks with US troops
articles.excerpt: United States President Donald Trump has claimed Iran possesses missiles capable of reaching Europe and downplayed Russia and China’s support for Tehran while speaking to US military personnel by phon...
articles.body_text:
United States President Donald Trump has claimed Iran possesses missiles capable of reaching Europe and downplayed Russia and China’s support for Tehran while speaking to US military personnel by phone for the Thanksgiving holiday.

Taking questions from reporters at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thursday, Trump said without “peace in the Middle East”, Iran could launch nuclear attacks against Israel and other countries in the region.

“We don’t need Middle East oil. But what we do need is we need peace in the Middle East,” Trump said, as OPEC ministers are scheduled to meet on Sunday to weigh 2027 oil production targets.

The US president and First Lady Melania Trump called US service members deployed across the region to praise their role in the war on Iran, including personnel at the al-Dhafra airbase in the United Arab Emirates and the Prince Sultan airbase in Saudi Arabia.

“Each of you is playing an essential role to protect not only our country today but future generations of Americans by ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” he said.

When asked if the US would renew strikes on Iran, the president said: “If we do something, we will definitely hit Pickaxe Mountain.” Trump also told reporters he spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in recent days.

The US is still offering Iran an opening to negotiate, according to Trump, who said: “We’re trying to be nice. We’re giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives, but I’m not sure if they are gonna take advantage of that.”

He downplayed the importance of intelligence-sharing by Russia and China with Iran, amid reports that the two countries helped Tehran target US bases.

“My meeting with President Xi was an incredible meeting. I think that they’re very little involved with Iran. They could get involved, but involvement to me would mean shooting, not giving them little information,” Trump said during the short news conference.

“We do the same thing, by the way. And you know, when they say that they may be spying on us, well, we spy on them too,” he added.

Trump’s statements come as Iran steps up attacks on US military targets across the region. On Saturday, Bahrain reported an Iranian attack on a civilian industrial facility while Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed it targeted US air defence radars in the country.

Kuwait said on Thursday that an Iranian drone attack on a “vital site” killed two Italian workers and injured four others. Tehran has denied involvement in the attack.

Trump told deployed service members, “You’re going to continue that deployment, and we have victory at hand,” referring to the war on Iran.

“It’s [victory] going to be whenever I want it to be, to be honest,” he added.

articles.title: Asian stock markets rise after earlier tech rout
articles.excerpt:
Asian stocks have opened higher as technology firms enjoy a period of calm following ructions at the start of the week.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 on Friday added 0.7 percent to 57,919.30 in mornin...
articles.body_text:
Asian stocks have opened higher as technology firms enjoy a period of calm following ructions at the start of the week.

Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 on Friday added 0.7 percent to 57,919.30 in morning trading. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.4 percent to 8,800.50. South Korea’s Kospi surged 2.2 percent to 4,812.65.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng edged up 0.4 percent to 22,310.11.

Stocks in Indonesia, Singapore and the Philippines also rose, while New Zealand’s bourse edged down as Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s right-wing coalition lost its parliamentary majority, plunging the country into political uncertainty with a centrist party set to play a decisive role in forming the next government.

Buying of stocks tied to artificial intelligence (AI) has been pushing benchmarks higher, despite some profit-taking that has kept those gains in check.

In Japan, Tokyo Electron and Advantest Corp stocks dropped in morning trading but quickly recovered their losses, underlining the continuing appeal of stocks in the semiconductor and AI sectors.

With Wall Street closed for the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday, traders had no new business-driving catalysts heading into the weekend, though they remain on edge over concerns about the AI boom.

They were also keeping an eye on possible retaliation against US President Donald Trump’s proposed tariffs of up to 20 percent on some of the United States’ biggest trading partners, including China, the European Union, India, Japan and South Korea.

Also in view is the Federal Reserve’s next interest rate decision next month, with speculation swirling that it could opt for a hefty 50-basis-point increase instead of the usual 25 points.

Oil prices extended Thursday’s gains of more than 1 percent amid fresh concerns over an escalation of hostilities in the Middle East after Iran-aligned Houthis struck a Saudi refinery, temporarily halting some operations. That came after an attack on another hub in the Gulf earlier in the week.

In company news, Japan Tobacco rallied more than 4 percent following a report that it was considering joining up with US giant Altria for a takeover of Britain’s Imperial Brands. Imperial jumped 13 percent in London on Thursday.

Japan Tobacco is dealing with an $8.9bn hit after the Russian government seized all seven of its local subsidiaries, as relations with Tokyo worsen following the arrest of a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

articles.title: New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat
articles.excerpt:
If the ruling bloc cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls

New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shap...
articles.body_text:
If the ruling bloc cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls

New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.

It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.

The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.

A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.

Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.

"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.

New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.

Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.

Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.

"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.

Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.

But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.

Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.

Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.

In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.

"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.

A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.

More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.

Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden, moving to Australia.

'Flat', 'tired', 'cynical': Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver New Zealand's tightest election in years

articles.title: Strobe Talbott, former deputy secretary of state and Brookings Institution president, dies at 80
articles.excerpt:
Strobe Talbott, a former deputy secretary of state who once worked at Time magazine, died at age 80.

Strobe Talbott, a former deputy secretary of state whose deep expertise on the Soviet Union shaped...
articles.body_text:
Strobe Talbott, a former deputy secretary of state who once worked at Time magazine, died at age 80.

Strobe Talbott, a former deputy secretary of state whose deep expertise on the Soviet Union shaped U.S. foreign policy before he went on to lead the Brookings Institution, died Thursday at the age of 80.

Talbott’s son, Devin Talbott, said his father died peacefully after a long illness at his home in East Hampton, New York, The Associated Press reported.

An Ohio native, Talbott began his journalism career as an intern at Time magazine while studying at Yale and Oxford, where he was roommates with future President Bill Clinton. Clinton later joked that his job in their shared apartment was to make Talbott breakfast every morning.

NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL

Strobe Talbott, president of the Brookings Institution, right, and Wolfgang Ischinger, chairman of the Munich Security Conference on Security Policy, left, participate in a news conference in Berlin on July 16, 2008. (AP Photo/Franka Bruns)

While at Time, Talbott was tapped to translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former Soviet leader ousted in 1964, which earned him a full-time role at the magazine.

Over a 21-year career there, he focused on U.S.-Soviet relations, led the Washington bureau, and wrote as a foreign affairs columnist.

In 1994, Talbott joined the Clinton administration as deputy secretary of state, helping guide U.S. relations with Russia and other post-Soviet states.

In a statement, Bill Clinton said no one was better suited to advise him on Russian affairs than Talbott, noting that former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton also relied on his counsel.

TRUMP PUSHED NATO TO SPEND BIG — NOW COMES THE HARDER QUESTION: CAN EUROPE ACTUALLY FIGHT?

Strobe Talbott, president of the Brookings Institution, speaks during a news conference in Berlin on July 16, 2008. (AP Photo/Franka Bruns)

"He was analytical, completely devoted to diplomacy, and on the level," Bill Clinton said. "With his expertise, we made real progress building trust between two former adversaries — moving beyond decades of confrontation to reduce the nuclear dangers future generations would inherit and build a Europe where more people could live in freedom and peace, including through the expansion of NATO and resolving ethnic conflicts in the Balkans. Together we laid the groundwork for greater cooperation while putting Russia on a path to democracy."

"Sadly, its current leader has taken the country in a different direction," Clinton added, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

FILE - President-elect Bill Clinton and Strobe Talbott of Time magazine talk privately as they walk along the beach on Hilton Head Island, S.C., Jan. 2, 1993. (AP Photo/James Finley)

He described Talbott as a "good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," and said, "Hillary and I will miss him very much."

After leaving government, Talbott served as president of the Brookings Institution from 2002 to 2017 and chaired the State Department’s Foreign Affairs Policy Board.

President Bill Clinton during his last State of the Union Address before Congress. (Douglas Graham/Congressional Quarterly/Getty Images)

He is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren. His first wife, Brooke Shearer, died in 2009; he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: Zelenskyy warns of major Russian attack as Trump urges Putin to ‘pull back’
articles.excerpt:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine has information that Russia is preparing a new mass strike on the country in the coming days.

“Unfortunately, we have information about a new mass...
articles.body_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine has information that Russia is preparing a new mass strike on the country in the coming days.

“Unfortunately, we have information about a new mass strike being prepared by the Russians,” he said in his nightly video address on Thursday. “In the coming days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats.”

It was the second such warning from Zelenskyy this week. He also had a message for Moscow: “We will rebuild what is ours and retaliate against every Russian strike.”

US President Donald Trump said he had pressed Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease Russia’s military actions in Europe.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he spent “a lot of time” in talks with Putin in China on the issue of Putin pulling back “all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe”.

“Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH,” Trump wrote. He said he hoped that would allow a deal between Russia and Ukraine to be “made quickly”, which he called “a strong possibility”.

Trump said he updated NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on the talks during a meeting at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Wednesday night.

Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, wounding seven people and hitting a shopping centre and two other buildings, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

Moscow said it hit drone-related sites in the city. Russian forces have attacked Kyiv and other cities almost continuously since September.

Ukraine said its drones hit an oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, oil reservoirs at a Transneft facility in Bashkortostan and the Marinovka military airfield in the Volgograd region.

Ukraine has also widened its attacks at sea. On Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine used seven naval drones to hit the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo ship Angara off Libya. Libyan officials told the Associated Press news agency that the Merkury was heavily damaged but not sunk.

At about the same time, a suspected Ukrainian drone struck the Russia-bound cargo ship Sparta II in the Baltic Sea, near Finland. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the attacks a “very dangerous trend“.

At least four Russian vessels have been targeted this month.

European Union leaders are struggling at a summit in Brussels to agree on a new 45 billion euro ($49bn) loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year. It would come on top of a 90 billion euro ($99bn) loan, agreed nearly a year ago, that covers most of Ukraine’s government needs for 2026 and 2027.

Early on Friday in Brussels, European Council President Antonio Costa said that 24 member states supported the new loan, as talks on the bloc’s next seven-year budget stretched on.

The loan is tangled up with the EU’s budget for 2028 to 2034, which includes about $110bn for Ukraine over seven years. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has threatened to hold up the budget unless all member states make a “collective commitment” to Ukraine.

Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (GUR) said on Thursday that North Korea has temporarily halted some military cooperation with Russia after diplomatic tensions between the allies.

It said this includes deliveries of KN-23 ballistic missiles and artillery shells, and Russian military flights over North Korean territory.

GUR said North Korea’s Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui announced the pause last month in response to a Russian deputy foreign minister’s assertion that Moscow would help ease tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang.

GUR also said Pyongyang is holding off on a Russian request to raise North Korea’s military presence in Russia from about 8,500 to 50,000 troops.

It added that North Korean units remain in Russia’s Kursk region and that a North Korean missile unit has been in the Voronezh region since mid-summer, from where Russia strikes Ukraine.

South Korean and Western intelligence agencies have said Pyongyang sent more than 10,000 soldiers to Russia’s Kursk region in 2024, along with artillery shells, missiles and long-range rocket systems.

On November 20, Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine, killing eight people, Zelenskyy said.

It was one of the largest attacks of the war and followed Putin’s vow to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea.

articles.title: Eagles erase 21-point deficit to stun Cowboys with biggest Thanksgiving comeback in NFL history
articles.excerpt:
Terrell Owens plays NFL word association with Julian Edelman, going through a variety of NFL teams.

Look, if you saw the 3-7 Philadelphia Eagles visiting the 5-6 Dallas Cowboys and figured it was tim...
articles.body_text:
Terrell Owens plays NFL word association with Julian Edelman, going through a variety of NFL teams.

Look, if you saw the 3-7 Philadelphia Eagles visiting the 5-6 Dallas Cowboys and figured it was time for your Thanksgiving nap, I get it. The NFL stuck them between Bears-Lions and Chiefs-Bills. When Dallas went up 31-10 late in the third quarter, it looked like you’d timed it perfectly.

Hopefully, someone in your family had the decency to wake you up for the fourth quarter. The Eagles took their first lead Thursday with two seconds left, when Jake Elliott drilled the game-winner from the Cowboys’ star at midfield. Philly’s 39-38 win was the biggest comeback in NFL Thanksgiving history.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Philadelphia Eagles players celebrate after scoring a touchdown against the Dallas Cowboys on Thanksgiving. (AP Photo/Julio Cortez)

If you did sneak in a nap, the first half was the time to do it. By the time the Eagles and Cowboys kicked off, you’d already watched Caleb Williams hit Rome Odunze with three seconds left to give Chicago a 39-35 win. The Bears and Lions came in tied atop the NFC North, and Chicago left Detroit with a one-game lead.

CALEB WILLIAMS, WHO SEEMED TO DISRESPECT NATIONAL ANTHEM MONTHS AGO, SHOWS PATRIOTISM ON THANKSGIVING

Besides, you had to save some energy for Josh Allen vs. Patrick Mahomes on Thanksgiving night. The 9-1 Buffalo Bills were hosting the 8-2 Kansas City Chiefs in arguably the biggest game of the regular season so far.

Philly had already seen what this Cowboys offense could do. Dallas’ 38-21 win in Philadelphia last month kicked off a five-game stretch in which the Cowboys averaged 37.2 points per game. Two Dallas possessions into the rematch, they were already up 14-0.

Javonte Williams capped the 11-play, 77-yard opening drive with a 1-yard touchdown run. Then, on the ensuing Eagles possession, Quinnen Williams stuffed Saquon Barkley on fourth-and-1. Five plays later, KaVontae Turpin caught a short pass from Dak Prescott and sprinted up the sideline for a 31-yard score.

The Eagles finally got on the board with a 48-yard Jake Elliott field goal on their third drive, but Dallas answered right back. Prescott hit CeeDee Lamb for gains of 10 and 19 yards before Javonte Williams ran it in from the 12 for his second touchdown.

Javonte Williams scored three touchdowns in the first half for the Dallas Cowboys against the Philadelphia Eagles on Thanksgiving. (Getty Images)

Eagles quarterback Joe Milton found DeVonta Smith on a 50-yard bomb to cut the deficit to 21-10 with 4:06 left in the first half. Dallas answered again, and the officials got plenty of screen time.

Three Eagles penalties gave the Cowboys 44 yards, including back-to-back pass interference calls that moved Dallas from the Philly 40 to the 1. After two Eagles stops, an offensive pass interference call on CeeDee Lamb wiped out a touchdown pass to Brevyn Spann-Ford and made it third-and-goal from the 12. Javonte Williams caught Prescott’s pass at the 8, dragged an Eagles defender to the goal line and fell across it for his third touchdown of the half.

By halftime, it looked a lot like Sunday against Tennessee. For the second time in five days, the Cowboys scored four first-half touchdowns and took an 18-point lead into the locker room. They led the Titans 27-9 and the Eagles 28-10.

Dak Prescott of the Dallas Cowboys celebrates during the second half of an NFL game against the Philadelphia Eagles at AT&T Stadium. (Getty Images)

For most of the third quarter, it looked like the second half would go the same way, too. Tennessee never got closer than 11 after halftime, and Brandon Aubrey drilled a 59-yard field goal to put Dallas up 31-10 with 3:35 left in the third. Then came two plays worth waking up for.

Milton found Smith for another bomb, this one a 45-yard touchdown with 15 seconds left in the quarter. Just 89 seconds of game time later, Ty Robinson blocked Bryan Anger’s punt, and Kenny Moore II scooped it up at the Dallas 3 and ran it in. Suddenly, it was 31-24 with nearly the entire fourth quarter left.

WHERE DOES AARON RODGERS’ INTERVIEW WITH PAT MCAFEE RANK AMONG THE WILDEST IN SPORTS HISTORY?

Prescott answered by hitting Lamb for 39 yards on second-and-16 and another 12 on third-and-8 before scrambling for a 14-yard touchdown himself. That put Dallas up 38-24 with 10:11 left. The two-touchdown cushion lasted all of 62 seconds.

Britain Covey returned the kickoff 55 yards, Milton found Smith twice, and then the Eagles quarterback ran one in himself from the 15. The Eagles went for two after cutting the deficit to eight, but Milton’s pass to Zach Ertz fell incomplete.

Philly forced a three-and-out, and Covey returned the punt 23 yards. With 7:37 left, the Eagles had the ball at the Dallas 49 with a chance to tie.

DeVonta Smith caught 11 passes for 200 yards, including touchdowns of 50 and 45 yards, in Philadelphia’s Thanksgiving win over Dallas. (AP Photo/Julio Cortez)

But DeMarvion Overshown sacked Milton on second down, and on third-and-15, Cobie Durant picked off a pass intended for Makai Lemon and returned it to the Eagles’ 48.

Dallas drove to the Philly 22, where Aubrey had a chance to make it a two-score game. Naturally, the guy who drilled one from 59 in the third quarter pulled this one wide left from 40. With 3:27 left, the Eagles still trailed 38-30 and had another shot to tie.

Milton took the Eagles 70 yards in four throws, the last a 24-yard touchdown to Makai Lemon with 2:10 left. He went right back to Lemon for the tie. This time the pass fell incomplete, and Dallas still led 38-36.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Because Philadelphia had all three timeouts and the two-minute warning, the Dallas offense needed two first downs to seal the victory. They got the first on a 15-yard strike from Prescott to Brevyn Spann-Ford on a second-and-8 play.

But they couldn't get the second. Javonte Williams had three straight carries to gain nine yards, leaving the Cowboys with a fourth-and-1 on the Eagles' 41-yard line and 55 seconds remaining. Instead of attempting a long field goal or punting, the Cowboys elected to go for a first down and the win.

Ty Robinson, who’d already blocked a punt, sacked Prescott on fourth-and-1. The Eagles got the ball back near midfield with 50 seconds left.

With seven seconds left and the ball at the Dallas 41, Philly sent Elliott out to win it.

articles.title: FLASHBACK: Two presidents pulled off secret Thanksgiving surprises for US troops — see the moments
articles.excerpt: Melania Trump delivers a powerful message of gratitude to military families during a visit to Fort Rucker ahead of Thanksgiving. She honors the profound sacrifices made by military spouses and childre...
articles.body_text:
Melania Trump delivers a powerful message of gratitude to military families during a visit to Fort Rucker ahead of Thanksgiving. She honors the profound sacrifices made by military spouses and children while their loved ones are deployed across the globe. She expresses deep appreciation for their strength and resilience in keeping their homes full of love.

Under a cloak of secrecy, two American presidents made surprise Thanksgiving visits to war zones, bringing a taste of home to U.S. troops serving thousands of miles from their families.

Sixteen years apart, President George W. Bush celebrated with American troops in Iraq in 2003, while President Donald Trump served Thanksgiving dinner to service members in Afghanistan in 2019. Both visits were carried out under tight secrecy, catching troops by surprise as they spent the holiday far from home.

Trump secretly traveled to Bagram Airfield in Afghanistan on Nov. 28, 2019, where he served turkey, posed for photos and thanked American troops for their sacrifices amid the ongoing war.

INSIDE TRUMP’S INTIMATE MEETING WITH NATION’S BRAVEST SOLDIERS DURING WHIRLWIND TEXAS TRIP

President Donald Trump serves Thanksgiving dinner to US troops at Bagram Air Field during a surprise visit on November 28, 2019 in Afghanistan. (OLIVIER DOULIERY/AFP via Getty Images)

"There's nowhere I'd rather celebrate this Thanksgiving than right here with the toughest, strongest, best, and bravest warriors on the face of the Earth," Trump told the troops at the time, later adding, "And you don't even know how much the people of our country love and respect you."

The visit came as roughly 12,000 American troops remained in Afghanistan more than 18 years after the U.S. invasion.

ARMY VET LAWMAKER MARKS ABBEY GATE ANNIVERSARY WITH BLISTERING MESSAGE FOR BIDEN-HARRIS: 'ABJECT FAILURE'

President Donald Trump serves Thanksgiving dinner to US troops at Bagram Air Field during a surprise visit on November 28, 2019 in Afghanistan. (OLIVIER DOULIERY/AFP via Getty Images)

During the visit, Trump met with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani to discuss efforts to end the war and told American troops that the Taliban wanted to reach a deal with the United States. He said his administration was reducing America's military presence in Afghanistan while pursuing a political solution to the more than 18-year conflict.

Less than two years later, President Joe Biden oversaw the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021.

WOUNDED MARINES RELIVE THE HARROWING KABUL AIRPORT ATTACK IN EXPLOSIVE NEW FOX NATION DOCUMENTARY

Trump serves Thanksgiving dinner to US troops at Bagram Air Field during a surprise visit on November 28, 2019 in Afghanistan (OLIVIER DOULIERY/AFP via Getty Images)

The withdrawal unfolded as the Taliban rapidly seized control of Afghanistan, culminating in the fall of Kabul and a frantic evacuation at the city's airport.

Sixteen years earlier, Bush pulled off a similar Thanksgiving surprise in Iraq , secretly flying into Baghdad International Airport on Nov. 27, 2003, to celebrate with American troops just eight months after launching the U.S.-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein's regime.

GEORGE BUSH WELCOMES TOP OFFICIALS TO HIS HOME STATE FOR 9/11 REMEMBRANCE ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF ATTACKS

President George W. Bush helps serve Thanksgiving dinner at the Bob Hope Dining Facility, Baghdad International Airport, Iraq, during a surprise visit with troops, November 27, 2003. (U.S. National Archives and Presidential Libraries)

Bush stunned hundreds of service members when he appeared at their Thanksgiving dinner, emerging to cheers and applause before helping serve a traditional holiday meal and posing for photos with troops stationed far from home.

"I can't think of a finer group of folks to have Thanksgiving dinner with than you all," Bush told the troops at the time.

"We're proud of you," he added. "Today, Americans are gathering with their loved ones to give thanks for the many blessings in our lives."

News of his trip was not even released until Air Force One had already left Iraq.

US FACES ANOTHER MAJOR MIDDLE EAST TROOP WITHDRAWAL, BUT THREAT REMAINS

President George W. Bush carries a platter of turkey and fixings as he visits US troops for Thanksgiving in Baghdad, 27 November, 2003. Bush made the Thanksgiving visit to troops in Baghdad under the greatest secrecy and security. (ANJA NIEDRINGHAUS/AP POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Bush's visit came as American forces battled a growing insurgency following the fall of Saddam Hussein's government earlier that year. Despite Bush's declaration in May that major combat operations had ended, U.S. troops continued to face deadly attacks as the military worked to stabilize the country.

Just weeks later, U.S. forces captured Saddam Hussein in December 2003.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: TPUSA mourns Florida high school chapter president killed with family in devastating plane crash
articles.excerpt: Six family members from Fort Myers, Florida, were killed Tuesday when their small plane crashed off the Mississippi coast while returning from a fishing trip in Louisiana. Those killed were Brent Stok...
articles.body_text:
Six family members from Fort Myers, Florida, were killed Tuesday when their small plane crashed off the Mississippi coast while returning from a fishing trip in Louisiana. Those killed were Brent Stokes, Hunter Stokes, Michael Knox, Arlyn Knox, Charles Holden Knox and Truett Knox. Brent Stokes was piloting the Cessna 210. Divers found all six victims inside the aircraft, two miles off Horn Island, Mississippi. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash.

Turning Point USA's student program mourned the death of a Florida high school chapter president this week after the teen and five members of his family died Tuesday in a plane crash off the Mississippi coast.

The organization said it was "heartbroken" over the loss of Hunter Stokes, 16, who led the Fort Myers High School Club America chapter.

"Hunter was a young patriot who loved his country and led by example," TPUSA Students said in a Wednesday post on X.

SIX FLORIDA FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN PLANE CRASH ON WAY HOME FROM FISHING TRIP IDENTIFIED

Turning Point USA remembered Hunter Stokes, 16, a Florida teenager who was president of the TPUSA Fort Myers High School Club America chapter. Stokes was killed, along with his father and other relatives in a plane crash this week off the Mississippi coast on the way back from a fishing trip. (Facebook; TPUSA Students)

"From attending our Chapter Leadership Summit this summer to helping lead his chapter’s 9/11 Flag Run in honor of the victims of the September 11 attacks, Hunter was dedicated to making a difference in his community," the statement continued. "We are grateful to have had Hunter as part of our TPUSA family. Please join us in lifting his family, friends, and fellow chapter members up in prayer."

Hunter was killed in the crash alongside his father, Brent Stokes, 50; his aunt and uncle, Arlyn and Michael Knox, both 43; and his cousins, Charles Holden Knox, 12, and Truett Knox, 10, according to Jackson County Coroner Bruce Lynd Jr.

DOZENS MISSING AFTER PASSENGER FERRY SINKS AS RESCUERS SCOUR SOUTH PACIFIC COASTLINE

The crash killed Brent Stokes, 50, and his son Hunter Stokes, 16; Brent Stokes’ sister Arlyn Knox, 43, her husband Michael Knox, 43, and their sons Charles Holden Knox, 12, and Truett Knox, 10. (Facebook)

The group was returning to Florida after a family fishing trip.

"They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family," both families said in a joint statement to The News-Press.

The six were aboard a Cessna 210 piloted by Brent Stokes when the aircraft went down two miles off Horn Island, Mississippi, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Officials said the plane entered a descent of 10,000 feet per minute prior to the crash.

White sand beaches are seen at Horn Island in the Gulf of Mexico, Mississippi, on June 26, 2010. (James Edward Bates/Biloxi Sun Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

Air traffic controllers advised Stokes of precipitation and adverse weather shortly before losing contact with the aircraft at about 3:45 p.m. local time, the New York Post and the FAA reported.

Brent Stokes was the president and CEO of Stokes Marine Inc., while Arlyn and Michael Knox led Knox Technologies, an IT company based in Fort Myers.

St. Cecilia Catholic Community on Wednesday said Brent and Hunter Stokes were former parishioners.

"Please keep the Stokes and Knox families in your prayers during this time of loss," the community wrote in a Facebook post. "May the Lord grant eternal rest and the promise of the Resurrection. Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them. May they rest in peace. Amen."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: Olympic trailblazer Anita DeFrantz, longtime advocate for women in sports, dies at 74
articles.excerpt:
Fox News chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt reports on Spain winning the 2026 FIFA World Cup final against Argentina in a match at New York New Jersey Stadium on ‘The Big Weekend Show.’

The sports wor...
articles.body_text:
Fox News chief correspondent Jonathan Hunt reports on Spain winning the 2026 FIFA World Cup final against Argentina in a match at New York New Jersey Stadium on ‘The Big Weekend Show.’

The sports world is mourning the loss of an Olympic trailblazer.

Anita DeFrantz has died, the International Olympic Committee and U.S. Olympic Committe said. She was 74. No cause of death was not immediately disclosed, although DeFrantz was believed to have been in declining health in recent years.

DeFrantz won a bronze medal in rowing at the 1976 Olympics, later becoming a powerful advocate for women in the male-dominated world of Olympic policymaking. She broke barriers throughout her career, becoming the first American woman and first Black American appointed to the IOC in 1986 before becoming the first woman to serve as an IOC vice president in 1997.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Anita DeFrantz speaks onstage during the 2019 Team USA Awards at Universal Studios Hollywood in Universal City, California on Nov. 19, 2019. (Amy Sussman/Getty Images)

DeFrantzalso was vice president of the organizing committee for the LA Olympics in 1984 and served as chair of the IOC’s Women in Sport Commission for two decades.

IOC President Kirsty Coventry, an Olympic swimmer who has credited DeFrantz with helping her rise to the highest position in the Olympic movement, described DeFrantz as "a mentor, a friend and a true inspiration to me, and to so many others around the world."

FIFA AWARDS 2031 WOMEN'S WORLD CUP TO THE UNITED STATES WITH MAJOR REVENUE EXPECTATIONS LEADING THE WAY

"From my earliest days in the Olympic Movement, she showed me what courageous leadership looked like, and what was possible for women in sport," Coventry said.

Edwin Moses, the record-setting hurdler and a contemporary of DeFrantz, said, "every woman who has a high-level position in sports today, they can thank Anita DeFrantz."

DeFrantz won bronze in the 1976 Olympics as captain of the women’s eight team in Montreal. She trained for an Olympic return and, in 1980, gained a sense of the disconnect between athletes and the boardrooms that made decisions on their behalf.

IOC member Anita DeFrantz of the United States attends the start of the 142nd IOC session at the 2024 Summer Olympics on July 23, 2024, in Paris. (AP Photo/David Goldman)

DeFrantz was part of the U.S. team that never made the trip to the boycotted 1980 Moscow Olympics. As spokeswoman for the U.S. athletes’ advisory council, she later led a lawsuit against the U.S. Olympic Committee, which had authorized the boycott under pressure from the Carter administration.

That experience marked the beginning of her effort to earn a seat at the table where those decisions were made.

Before her induction into the Team USA Hall of Fame, DeFrantz recalled realizing how much work remained when she attended her first IOC meeting in 1986.

JAPANESE BOWLING PIONEER RITSUKO NAKAYAMA, FIRST WOMAN TO BOWL PROFESSIONAL PERFECT GAME, DIES AT 84

"I walked in and I thought, ‘This is odd,’" she told The Associated Press in 2025. "It was this cavernous room" and of the 90 or so committee members, she was one of only five women.

"We had to help people open their minds a little," she said.

Anita DeFrantz, spokeswoman for the U.S. Olympic Committee's Athletes Advisory Council, answers questions from reporters outside the White House in Washington on April 4, 1980. (AP Photo/File)

Women made up half of the 10,500 athletes at the 2024 Paris Games. Today, 46 of the IOC’s 106 members are women.

U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee CEO Sarah Hirshland and chairman Gene Sykes remember DeFrantz as "one of the most consequential Olympians our nation has ever known."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Unforgiving rim denies Arkansas a miracle comeback against Michigan State on Thanksgiving
articles.excerpt:
College Basketball is always hectic, but Bruce Pearl believes the field is as wide open as ever

With 1:18 left in a game played on Thanksgiving, Arkansas trailed No. 11 Michigan State by 10 and the S...
articles.body_text:
College Basketball is always hectic, but Bruce Pearl believes the field is as wide open as ever

With 1:18 left in a game played on Thanksgiving, Arkansas trailed No. 11 Michigan State by 10 and the Spartans were at the free-throw line. If you’d offered John Calipari one shot to send the game to overtime, I’m guessing he’d have taken it before you finished the question.

Well, he got his shot. Jordan Smith Jr. pulled up from 29 feet, and the ball found just about every part of the rim at Little Caesars Arena before it finally bounced out. Michigan State escaped Detroit with a 70-67 win to move to 6-1, and Arkansas fell to 4-3.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Arkansas took a 31-27 lead into halftime, pushed it to eight early in the second half and still led 47-40 with 13:31 left. If you’re a Michigan State fan who watched the Spartans lose at Tennessee nine days earlier, I can’t blame you for thinking, "Uh-oh." They’d made all of three baskets in the second half in Knoxville and shot 18% for the game.

MICHIGAN STATE'S PUTRID SHOOTING PERFORMANCE IN LOSS TO TENNESSEE PRODUCES LAUGHABLE FINAL BOX SCORE

Down seven in Detroit, Jeremy Fears Jr. hit a three. Then he found Jesse McCulloch for a hook shot and Coen Carr for the dunk that tied it.

Michigan State’s Jeremy Fears Jr. celebrates during the second half of the Spartans’ 70-67 Thanksgiving win over Arkansas in Detroit. (Getty Images)

Michigan State scored 15 straight, and by the time Kur Teng buried his third three in less than two minutes, the Spartans led 64-51 with 4:55 left. That’s a 24-4 run. The same team that went 3-for-26 after halftime at Tennessee went 17-for-21 (81%) in the second half against Arkansas.

Michigan State still led 68-58 when Fears stepped to the line with 1:18 left. He missed the front end of a one-and-one, but Arkansas still needed 10 points just to pull even.

COLLEGE BASKETBALL GETS A NEW NO. 1 AS THREE TEAMS FALL OUT OF THE AP TOP FIVE IN A SINGLE WEEK

So how did the Razorbacks make it interesting in the final seconds? For starters, Michigan State just couldn’t grab a defensive rebound. The Razorbacks missed two threes on the same possession before Billy Richmond III tipped the ball in with 1:03 to go.

Then Smith picked off a Fears pass. On the ensuing possession, Arkansas rebounded a missed free throw AND a missed three before Smith found Richmond for the three that cut it to 68-64.

Jeremy Fears Jr. made both free throws with 16 seconds left to put Michigan State back up six. Then came the call I’d still be asking about if I were Tom Izzo.

Smith drove to the basket and spun past Fears for a layup. The officials called Fears for a foul, counted the basket and gave Smith a chance to cut it to three with 10 seconds left.

Arkansas Razorbacks guard Jordan Smith Jr. drives to the basket against the Michigan State Spartans during the first half of the CBS Thanksgiving Classic at Little Caesars Arena. (Getty Images)

Did Fears foul Smith? Absolutely. Smith still had his back to the basket and was about 13 feet from the hoop when the contact came. Smith finished his spin, took another full step and then laid the ball in. How much continuation are we giving this guy? Even the CBS crew thought the foul should have been ruled on the floor.

Smith made the free throw with 10 seconds left, Fears missed the front end of a one-and-one with eight seconds left, and guess who came down with the rebound? Smith had six seconds and the length of the floor to find a three. From 29 feet, he came about as close as you can get.

If you laid 5.5 with Michigan State, how good did you feel with 1:18 left? Your team was up 10, and you had a career 81% free-throw shooter at the line. You could give up a couple of garbage-time buckets and still cash.

Fears missed the front end, Arkansas grabbed four offensive rebounds in two possessions, and Michigan State threw the ball away in between. And after all that? You were still covering when Fears hit both free throws to make it 70-64 with 16 seconds left.

Michigan State Spartans guard Jeremy Fears Jr. drives to the basket against the Arkansas Razorbacks during the second half of the CBS Thanksgiving Classic at Little Caesars Arena. (Getty Images)

It took that generous continuation call to put Arkansas back inside the number. Then your 81% free-throw shooter went back to the line with eight seconds left and missed the front end of another one-and-one.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

That left Michigan State bettors rooting for the same guy who’d just cost them the cover. If Smith’s three drops, you get five more minutes to win by six. If you had Arkansas +5.5, on the other hand, you had every reason to cheer when that ball finally bounced out.

Which probably raised a fair question from across the Thanksgiving table: "Wait, didn’t you bet on Arkansas?"

articles.title: Global news agency AFP reports cyberattack, shuts down content platform
articles.excerpt:
Agence France-Presse (AFP) has been hit by a cyberattack, requiring the AFP Forum content platform to be taken offline.

The France-based international news agency’s management said on Thursday that i...
articles.body_text:
Agence France-Presse (AFP) has been hit by a cyberattack, requiring the AFP Forum content platform to be taken offline.

The France-based international news agency’s management said on Thursday that it is currently investigating the circumstances of the cyberattack, including who was behind it.

“AFP was hit by a cyber attack overnight, starting at 1:30 am (Paris time) [00:30 GMT]. The target was AFP Forum, one of the platforms our clients use to browse and download our content,” an internal email from AFP management said.

“As soon as the intrusion was detected, our teams moved immediately to contain the intrusion and took AFP Forum offline as a precautionary measure. AFP Forum remains unavailable until further notice.”

AFP is reportedly offering backup solutions to the agency’s subscribers while the portal is offline.

France’s cybersecurity chief, Vincent Strubel, warned on Thursday that the country faces an unprecedented level of cybersecurity threats and called for collective efforts to strengthen defences against attacks.

“We are facing a level of threat that is unprecedented, with an intensity we have never experienced before,” Strubel said in an interview with France Inter radio.

The incident is the latest in a slew of cybersecurity disruptions across European countries. FIFA, which is based in Zurich, Switzerland, confirmed to Al Jazeera on Thursday that it had been the victim of a cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information.

In October, several French supermarkets were hit by an “unprecedented” cyberattack that raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F).

Temperature spikes were also recorded in stores in 10 other European countries in early November, including the United Kingdom, Germany, Belgium and Sweden.

France accused Tehran of being behind the October attack and summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris to “lodge a very strong protest”.

Iran called Paris’s accusations “baseless” and condemned the “hackneyed policy of levelling accusations against the Islamic republic”.

articles.title: Democrats, Republicans find rare common ground when asked what they're thankful for
articles.excerpt:
House lawmakers on both sides of the aisle spoke to Fox News Digital about what they are most thankful for as they get ready to celebrate Thanksgiving with their families.

An ocean of ideological dif...
articles.body_text:
House lawmakers on both sides of the aisle spoke to Fox News Digital about what they are most thankful for as they get ready to celebrate Thanksgiving with their families.

An ocean of ideological differences separates Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill, but they're largely in agreement over one thing this Thanksgiving, and it's usually miles away from Washington, D.C.

"I'm thankful for family," Rep. Eric Burlison, R-Mo., told Fox News Digital. "It's what drives me to keep going, to keep doing this, keep fighting for the country."

Families across America are gathering for Thanksgiving, kicking off a holiday season that's meant for reflection and refocusing on things that matter most. And members of Congress who spoke with Fox News Digital about that special day are no different.

The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 10, 2026. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"You know, elections can be a bumpy road in many ways, and it's easy to take a shot at somebody who's running — we put ourselves out there. But it's the family, really, and I'm grateful that my wife and my three kids who are in their 20s are so supportive," Rep. John Mannion, D-N.Y., said. "So that's what I'm thankful for."

Reps. Randy Fine, R-Fla., and Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., singled out their children.

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

"I'm very grateful to how great my boys are doing despite the challenges of this job, and just my whole family for putting up with all of this and being there for me," Fine said.

Burchett told Fox News Digital he was "more than blessed."

Rep. Eric Burlison, R-Mo., leaves the Capitol Hill Club after a meeting of the House Republican Conference on March 25, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"I've got a beautiful wife and a daughter, and I never thought I was gonna have a family. And I prayed, asked Jesus that I'd have a family, and I got one, dadgum it, and it is wonderful," Burchett said.

Rep. Mike Quigley, D-Ill., said he was grateful for the U.S.'s ability to still come together despite people's many differences.

SOUND OFF: WILL DEMOCRATS AND REPUBLICANS COME TOGETHER FOR THE GOOD OF THE COUNTRY?

"I'm most thankful that this country still reminds itself that there's more that unites us than divides us," Quigley said.

Two more Democrats said they were thankful for their party’s success in the midterm elections.

Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., arrives for the vote on the budget resolution in the U.S. Capitol on April 10, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"I'm thankful for the excitement of next year, to get things done," said Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill.

Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., said he was thankful for "an opportunity to make a difference in people's lives."

"Democrats got a huge majority, and that allows us to help people," Thanedar, who lost his own re-election bid, said.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com
