articles.title: Trump takes on Somali welfare dependency in Thanksgiving message, lays out who should stay in US
articles.excerpt:
President Donald Trump said Rep. Ilhan Omar could be deported or face jail when asked about questions surrounding her age, calling the Minnesota Democrat "a disgrace to our country."

In a lengthy Tha...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump said Rep. Ilhan Omar could be deported or face jail when asked about questions surrounding her age, calling the Minnesota Democrat "a disgrace to our country."

In a lengthy Thanksgiving message on Truth Social Thursday, President Donald Trump praised a small fraction of the Somali community, saying they should be allowed to remain in the United States, while calling for the immediate removal of those receiving government assistance while unemployed.

The holiday post mixed praise for "AMERICAN PATRIOTS" with criticism of the "Radical Far Left" and Minnesota’s Somali community, which Trump has frequently accused of public assistance fraud in the state.

"I want to thank the 2% of our Somalian population that have a job, and are actually willing to work, without receiving Government Assistance," Trump wrote in the post. "These are wonderful American ‘citizens,’ and should be allowed to stay in our Country, and celebrate Thanksgiving with us. The others should be thrown out, immediately, thereby saving the Great State of Minnesota, which has no chance if they are allowed to stay."

SOMALIS IN MINNESOTA UNLEASH FURY ON TRUMP AFTER FEDS RAID ILHAN OMAR'S DC HOME

President Donald Trump praised a small fraction of the Somali community in a Thanksgiving message, while calling for the majority to be "thrown out" of the United States. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images; YASUYOSHI CHIBA/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump’s remarks echo ongoing criticism from some Republicans regarding public benefit usage and fraud cases within the community.

During a House Oversight Committee hearing in January, Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas, highlighted data on government support programs, noting that 54% of Somali-headed households in Minnesota receive food stamps.

SNAP FOOD STAMP FRAUD HAS NEFARIOUS TERRORISM LINKS, TOP AGRICULTURE WATCHDOG WARNS CONGRESS

A demonstrator waves a flag of Somalia as a vehicle passes by a rally in protest against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), amid a reported federal immigration operation targeting the Somali community, in Minneapolis, Minnesota, U.S. December 8, 2025. (Tim Evans/Reuters)

Elsewhere in the post, Trump claimed that "murderers, drug dealers, and criminals" — who he said illegally entered the U.S. from foreign prisons and mental institutions — have largely been deported.

"They are mostly gone now, brought back to their point of origin and, hopefully, living a beautiful and idyllic life, and promising, ideally, never to kill innocent people again," he wrote.

TRUMP SAYS DEPORTATION PUSH HASN’T PUT 'SAME PRESSURE' ON FARMWORKERS, HOTEL STAFF: 'NOT EVEN CLOSE'

"We won’t have to worry about that, because they are GONE — but, Happy Thanksgiving to them anyway, even though from Faraway Lands," he added. "We miss you dearly, but you will never be back, and America will never allow what you have done to us to happen again!"

Secretary of State Marco Rubio also shared a holiday message on social media, with a video focused on opportunities provided by the U.S.

"We know how special this country is. It's the place that gave us freedom. It's a place that gave us opportunity. It's a place that's given our parents, our grandparents, and many of you the chance not just to do well in life, but to leave our children better off than ourselves," Rubio said in the video.

In the attached caption, he added, "Being an American is a gift unlike any ever afforded to any other peoples throughout human history — we have so much to be thankful for. Happy Thanksgiving."

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: Attack on Saudi’s Jazan refinery kills one person, disrupts operations
articles.excerpt:
An aerial projectile has hit an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s city of Jazan, killing one worker and injuring several other people, according to the country’s Ministry of Energy.

Thursday’s attack on...
articles.body_text:
An aerial projectile has hit an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s city of Jazan, killing one worker and injuring several other people, according to the country’s Ministry of Energy.

Thursday’s attack on the facility on the kingdom’s Red Sea coast caused a fire and temporarily halted some operations, the ministry said.

The statement did not identify who carried out the strike, but earlier the Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said that the Iranian-backed group had ⁠⁠attacked the refinery. It came after Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency had issued an alert about potential danger in Jazan province.

The strike was the Houthis‘ latest blow against key Saudi facilities, a day after the group claimed attacks on Ras Tanura, the kingdom’s largest refinery and a major crude export hub, and the Red Sea ports of Jeddah and Jazan, amid escalating hostilities between the two sides.

The Saudi Ministry of Energy said the worker who died was Nepali, while the injured were of various nationalities.

The injured received medical care, while emergency personnel and specialised technical teams arrived at the site to assess the damage and verify the safety of the facilities following the attack, the ministry added.

The refinery in southwestern Saudi Arabia, near the Yemeni border, is designed to process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.

The Saudi-led coalition, which is backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government in its fight with the Houthis, condemned the strike and threatened a counterattack.

“Targeting civilians and ⁠⁠civilian infrastructure would ⁠⁠be ⁠⁠met with a firm military ‌‌response,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki posted on X.

Later on Thursday, the coalition claimed its forces had destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launch platform in Yemen’s Hodeidah governorate used by the armed group to stage the attack on the Jazan refinery, according to al-Maliki. There was no immediate statement from the Houthis regarding the strike.

On the ground in Yemen, meanwhile, Saudi-backed government forces claimed they had carried out 767 strikes on Houthi positions on Thursday.

In a post on X, the forces’ spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said the strikes had “neutralised” 117 Houthi fighters and destroyed 87 vehicles and combat assets.

Al-Nuzaili added that government forces continued to confront Houthi formations on the front lines in northern and western Marib governorate, as well as in the governorates of al-Jawf, Taiz, Lahj, Shabwah and Hajjah.

Earlier on Thursday, a series of air strikes targeted Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, according to media affiliated with the armed group, which is also known as Ansar Allah – Arabic for Supporters of God.

Elsewhere, Houthi forces targeted Habib al-Sarm and al-Hujalla, as well as al-Aqroud in al-Masrakh district.

The Houthis, who control the most populous areas of Yemen, have launched missiles and drones at Saudi airports, oil facilities and office buildings since the country’s civil war reignited in July, in a spillover from the US-Iran war.

The attacks have previously temporarily disrupted some of Aramco’s operations and caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. They also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including football’s AFC Asian Cup and the flagship FII investment conference.

The fighting has also exacerbated dire humanitarian conditions for Yemeni civilians.

The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that as of Monday, 2,361 people had been killed and 10,982 injured since fighting in Yemen escalated in August. More than 360,000 people have also been forced to flee their homes in Yemen since the start of August, according to the UN.

articles.title: Mexico seeks US talks about suspected SpaceX debris
articles.excerpt:
The Mexican government is seeking talks with aviation authorities in the United States about falling rocket debris following SpaceX launches in Texas.

It is the latest sign of growing tensions betwee...
articles.body_text:
The Mexican government is seeking talks with aviation authorities in the United States about falling rocket debris following SpaceX launches in Texas.

It is the latest sign of growing tensions between Mexico City and Elon Musk’s trillion-dollar company.

“What we are seeking, through the embassy, is a meeting between US and Mexican airspace authorities so that permission for the use of Mexican airspace can be established, how often it would be used, and, if necessary, the relocation of the launch site,” Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Thursday at a news conference in the capital.

“And then there’s the ⁠⁠⁠⁠issue of the debris,” she added.

Earlier this month, Mexican authorities said they had to recover debris after a launch of a SpaceX Starship from its Starbase,Texas, facility near the Gulf of Mexico and nature reserves on both sides of the shared border.

Debris that officials said came from the launch washed ashore along Playa Bagdad in Matamoros in the Mexican state of Tamaulipas, according to PROFEPA, Mexico’s Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection.

It said it had collected material several days after part of the Starship was destroyed and fell into the sea. The debris was taken by the Mexican navy to be stored and PROFEPA said it would ask SpaceX to take possession of it.

SpaceX said it was working with Mexican authorities and disputed the claim that what was found was from its failed Starship launch.

“We continue to stay in contact with the Mexican government and are on standby to send support if authorities in Mexico tell us it is actually needed,” the company posted on X. “Partners on the ground relayed that they have found very little debris in their sweeps of the beach and the small amount they have found is not clearly from SpaceX operations.”

Musk’s SpaceX is seeking permission from the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to dramatically increase activity at the Starbase facility. Previously, the company was allowed 25 launches and 50 landings a year, but now it is seeking permission for 456 launches and 912 landings annually.

Earlier this week, the US Federal Communications Commission granted SpaceX permission to send up to one million satellites into space as part of Musk’s plans to develop data centres in orbit.

articles.title: Kevin Durant dishes on Steelers coach Mike McCarthy’s alleged ice cream snack habits after making NBA history
articles.excerpt: The Pittsburgh Steelers announced they are releasing quarterback Aaron Rodgers after criticism of head coach Mike McCarthy. Renowned sports journalist Peter King, whose book 'The Game' was released in...
articles.body_text:
The Pittsburgh Steelers announced they are releasing quarterback Aaron Rodgers after criticism of head coach Mike McCarthy. Renowned sports journalist Peter King, whose book 'The Game' was released in October, analyzes the impact of the situation.

Aaron Rodgers’ time with the Pittsburgh Steelers ended abruptly just one day before Thanksgiving. The team cut ties with the veteran quarterback shortly after benching him and following his disparaging comments about coach Mike McCarthy during an appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show" on Wednesday.

Rodgers, who was in his second season with the Steelers, made a series of allegations questioning McCarthy’s focus and work ethic. He claimed the coach had been caught "snoring" during team meetings and recently inadvertently ended a speech with "one, two, three, Packers."

Another allegation came from former Steelers defensive lineman Breiden Fehoko, who claimed that a Steelers player sent him a message reading: "McCarthy has a personal assistant who brings him ice cream sandwiches on demand."

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Aaron Rodgers and Head Coach Mike McCarthy of the Pittsburgh Steelers chat before an NFL game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia on Nov. 22, 2026. (Getty Images)

Several sports figures have weighed in on Rodgers’ abrupt departure, with NBA star Kevin Durant among the latest to comment.

"Happy Thanksgiving, hiring a ice cream sandwich assistant for the day, great idea Mike," the Houston Rockets forward wrote on X on Thanksgiving morning.

NEW JERSEY DEVILS MOCK STEELERS COACH MIKE MCCARTHY WITH BRUTAL 'ICE CREAM SANDWICH' JAB

Durant's post surfaced hours after a 3-pointer in the first half of the Rockets game against the Phoenix Suns on Wednesday, made him the fifth NBA player to score 33,000 career points. Houston went to defeat Durant's former team 116-104, with Durant ending the game with 20 points.

Houston Rockets Kevin Durant (7) brings the ball up court against the Phoenix Suns during the Emirates NBA Cup at Toyota Center in Houston, Texas, on Nov. 25, 2026. (Alex Slitz/Getty Images)

McCarthy addressed the allegations raised by Rodgers, telling reporters the team's front office was ""very in tune with everything that goes on in football operations as far as my job responsibility."

Rodgers acknowledged that his time with the Steelers was over, saying, "That ship has sailed."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Mason Rudolph is expected to start when the Black Friday game against the Denver Broncos kicks off. Rodgers suggested he was unaware he wouldn't be the starter going forward until a teammate alerted him.

Steelers owner and president Art Rooney II responded with a show of support for McCarthy, telling the Post-Gazette that he "expects" McCarthy to "be our coach this season, next season and beyond."

The NFL's trade deadline for this season had already passed by the time Rodgers was released, meaning the four-time league MVP will have to go through waivers before another potentially interested team claims him. If Rodgers makes it through waivers unclaimed, he would then be an unrestricted free agent.

The Rockets-Suns game also managed to produce some holiday fireworks, as Durant and Dillon Brooks got wrapped up in a heated verbal back-and-forth. While players jawing back and forth isn't a new phenomenon, the exchange between Durant and Brooks raised eyebrows because it happened during a live play.

Durant untucked his Rockets jersey and pushed his forehead up against Brooks' forehead. Referees whistled for double technical fouls, with Brooks leaving the game due to a technical foul he received a few minutes prior to the confrontation with Durant.

Kevin Durant of the Houston Rockets and Dillon Brooks of the Phoenix Suns exchange words during the Emirates NBA Cup at Toyota Center in Houston, Texas, on Nov. 25, 2026. (Alex Slitz/Getty Images)

Durant address the confrontation after the game, telling reporters, "I mean, I just love basketball. That simple."

"I love to play ball. I love everything about the game, all the details that add up to winning. I care about that and I don't mind if somebody got a grievance with me. I don't mind addressing it right there in the moment. I'm sure he has some. I said some things that he probably didn't like, and he addressed it right there. And I can respect that as a man. And it didn't get farther than that. But if it does get farther than that, I'll be ready for that, too."

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Musk pledges two SpaceX shares for every US child
articles.excerpt: Elon Musk plans to gift every child in the United States two SpaceX shares, as he attempts to build public support for his satellite and artifical intelligence businesses during a period of intense pu...
articles.body_text:
Elon Musk plans to gift every child in the United States two SpaceX shares, as he attempts to build public support for his satellite and artifical intelligence businesses during a period of intense public and political scrutiny of the technology sector.

The world’s richest person announced the share giveaway, which is worth a total of about $18bn, on Wednesday evening just hours after SpaceX won US approval to deploy 1 million satellites for data centres in space.

Musk is seeking to expand SpaceX’s role in the AI industry, even as the rapid growth of computing infrastructure raises concern about its environmental impact and the economic and political influence of technology billionaires.

Opponents of data centre development were among the biggest winners for the Democrats in this month’s US midterm elections.

“The initiative clearly helps broaden public participation in the SpaceX story,” Chez Anbu, head of wealth advisory at OCBC in Singapore, said on Thursday.

“Giving children a direct economic stake in the company creates a powerful narrative around broader participation in the benefits of the AI and space economy,” Anbu added.

The Federal Communications Commission said it approved SpaceX’s satellite constellation proposal to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing.

Astronomers have long been concerned about such developments in space, and the American Astronomical Society said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision.

It warned the proposed constellation would “significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities” and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky.

Children would receive one share from SpaceX and one from him personally, Musk said in a brief post on X.

In a separate post, Musk said the SpaceX company shares would be transferred next month.

“The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year,” Musk added.

SpaceX said earlier on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account, adding that Musk would personally match the number of shares donated by the company.

A Trump Account is a programme designed to give Americans under the age of 18 a stake in the stock market and help build wealth from an early age. The White House said in October it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at $127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly $18bn.

SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment on whether Musk’s SpaceX share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts.

“What it does is build a massive, long-term retail shareholder base,” said Christopher Brankin, global markets adviser at brokerage Mitrade Group.

“It builds immediate market engagement and creates a massive, financially literate client pipeline for trading platforms as that generation comes of age,” he added.

Musk, whose net worth is approximately $824bn, said last month he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in the US. He held about 6.42 billion shares in the company as of June.

“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many,” Musk said in a post on X at the time.

“Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way,” said Musk, most of whose philanthropic efforts have been through the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds more than $14bn in assets.

SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband in October pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under the Trump initiative.

articles.body_text:
OutKick's Craig Carton gives his take on the Aaron Rodgers situation after the quarterback's interview on "The Pat McAfee Show."

Amon-Ra St. Brown came to play on Turkey Day.

The Detroit Lions wide receiver wasted no time in showing off his catching abilities against the Chicago Bears in their Thanksgiving showdown. He was also sure to send a message to the Bears' head coach, Ben Johnson, after the fact.

Barely two minutes into the contest, Detroit quarterback Jared Goff threw a pass to a streaking St. Brown running toward the sideline. Most wideouts wouldn't have been able to haul in the pass, but St. Brown is not like most wideouts, and snagged the football out of the air with just one hand.

Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown stands on the field before the game against the Chicago Bears at Ford Field in Detroit, Mich., on Nov. 26, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

TOM BRADY CALLS OUT NFL'S INCREASINGLY ELABORATE TOUCHDOWN CELEBRATIONS: 'LEARN YOUR ASSIGNMENTS'

After making the one-handed snag for a pickup of 27 yards, St. Brown got up off of the turf and did the stanky leg dance, which was undoubtedly a shot at Johnson, who has pulled out the same dance move inside the Bears' locker room following wins this season.

St. Brown ultimately picked up 46 receiving yards on Detroit's opening drive of the game, although the Lions weren't able to find the end zone after his miraculous catch and settled for a 24-yard field goal.

The Bears-Lions matchup in Detroit is serving as the kickoff to one of the best Thanksgiving Day slates in NFL history.

After the 8-2 NFC foes handle their business, the Philadelphia Eagles and Dallas Cowboys match up in an important clash in the lowly NFC East, with both teams holding losing records still somehow alive in the divisional race.

The Thanksgiving nightcap will feature Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills playing host to Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs in one of the most-anticipated matchups of the NFL season thus far.

Weather, as it typically does in late November, could play a factor, with rain and high winds in the forecast in Upstate New York.

articles.title: Sylvester Stallone endured broke, lonely days cleaning lion cages before Henry Winkler changed his life
articles.excerpt: Sylvester Stallone joins Fox & Friends to discuss his new memoir, The Steps, opening up about his difficult upbringing, the lessons it taught him as a father and the personal experiences that inspired...
articles.body_text:
Sylvester Stallone joins Fox & Friends to discuss his new memoir, The Steps, opening up about his difficult upbringing, the lessons it taught him as a father and the personal experiences that inspired Rocky.

Before Sylvester Stallone became a Hollywood heavyweight, he was a broke, lonely actor living in a cramped New York City walk-up apartment with few friends to lean on — until Henry Winkler came along.

In his memoir, "The Steps," the "Rocky" icon recalls crossing paths with the future "Happy Days" star on the set of 1974's "The Lords of Flatbush." Though Stallone joked they were polar opposites — Winkler, a Yale graduate, and Stallone from "the college of what's the matter [with] you" — the two forged an instant bond.

For Winkler, it didn't take long to see Stallone's fierce determination to make it in Hollywood. It was a drive he witnessed firsthand when he visited his co-star's home on Lexington Avenue for the first time.

SYLVESTER STALLONE'S ADVICE TO THOSE WHO ARE STRUGGLING 50 YEARS AFTER 'ROCKY' CHANGED HIS LIFE

Paul Mace, Sylvester Stallone, Henry Winkler and Perry King are seen on the set of "The Lords of Flatbush," directed by Martin Davidson and Stephen Verona. Stallone and Winkler became fast friends on set. (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)

"He was living there with his first wife and their bull mastiff, who had more slobber than the Atlantic Ocean," Winkler recalled to Fox News Digital.

"He painted his windows black so that he would never be bothered by what time of day it was. He wouldn't be influenced by time. Instead, he just wrote and wrote. And from the minute we met on the set of a movie in which we made no money whatsoever, you could see him. You could see his drive. You could see there was something so special, so funny, so articulate coming out of this, 'I'm going to eat you for breakfast.' And it only continued."

Sylvester Stallone has written a new memoir, "The Steps: A Memoir." (2026 NBCUniversal Media, LLC)

"If you listen to Sly Stallone, you quickly realize he's a philosopher," Winkler shared. "You would never put the two together, but it's true. And he's so open. His upbringing would put any man or woman down. It would put them in a corner shaking for the rest of their life. But his motto is 'keep on punching' and it's true. He kept on punching. And it's been an honor to be his friend."

WATCH: SYLVESTER STALLONE REFLECTS ON CHILDHOOD TRAUMA, ‘ROCKY’ AND WHY ‘TRYING’ MATTERS MOST

In his book, Stallone described how Winkler had to "step over a homeless guy while walking up five flights of stairs" just to see his "shabby place and get a glimpse into my world." Instead of being horrified, Winkler was impressed by the library of tattered books and a shelf holding about 15 screenplays. Stallone had been keeping busy writing.

When Winkler picked up one of Stallone's scripts, he was stunned. Winkler urged Stallone to keep writing.

Sylvester Stallone appears in a scene from "The Lords of Flatbush" (1974) after his character's girlfriend tells him she is pregnant, and he takes her to a jeweler to buy a ring. (FilmPublicityArchive/United Archives via Getty Images)

Stallone told Fox News Digital he never forgot Winkler's kindness and encouragement during a time when hearing "no" was the norm.

"You cannot get two people more different in every aspect," Stallone said with a laugh. "We were, as I wrote, an 'odd couple.' And yet, he gave me such confidence. He's an intellectual, and I didn't think of myself that way. I didn't see myself that way at all. When he saw the writing, he said, 'You wrote all this stuff?' I said, 'It's not good.' He then said, 'That's not the point. You did 15, 15 scripts. It's harder to make it as a writer than an actor. This is impressive.'"

Sylvester Stallone said that despite his differences with Henry Winkler, they became good friends. (Getty Images)

Stallone wrote, "We were an odd couple. He was an intellectual Jewish kid from the Upper West Side who graduated from the Yale School of Drama — the real deal. I had to learn everything the hard way. We were anomalies in each other's lives. To see us together was like watching a zebra hang out with a buffalo. Still, we clicked, because Henry is a genuinely wonderful human being."

Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.

"The Steps: A Memoir" by Sylvester Stallone is available now. (William Morrow)

Years later, after scraping by in New York and taking odd jobs like working at a deli, ushering at a movie theater and cleaning lion cages at the Central Park Zoo, Stallone headed west. He and his then-wife, Sasha Czack, made the cross-country trip to California in hopes of finally getting his big acting break. But they knew no one on the West Coast and didn't have a place to live. Stallone wrote, "We had barely $500 left of the $830 we departed New York with."

Sylvester Stallone was so broke when he married his first wife, Sasha Czack, that he wore a movie costume. (Bettmann Archive)

But there was one person Stallone knew he could call: Winkler. By then, the actor had already moved to California and become a star on "Happy Days."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Sylvester Stallone told Fox News Digital Henry Winkler believed in him early on in his career. (Getty Images)

"When I came out to California, he was the only guy I knew," said Stallone. "It was comforting because, again, he was very complimentary and welcoming. He kept saying, 'Working with you on "Lords of Flatbush" helped me with The Fonz, playing a tough guy.' I kept telling him, 'No, man, you did that all on your own.' But he saw something in me, even before ‘Rocky.’ Yes, this was a long time ago, but that's how great of a guy he was. He still is."

"Really, our relationship goes back to 1972," Stallone said with a smile. "It's amazing. Again, we're so different, yet there's a bond there that he actually instigated. I was a loner, no doubt about that. And yet he would insert himself, talk to me, be very outgoing and witty. He wanted to be my friend. And he was from Yale. He didn't have to be my friend. But he genuinely cared. We bonded and it's terrific."

Henry Winkler won his first Emmy Award in 2018 for his role in the HBO Max show, "Barry." (Neilson Barnard/FilmMagic)

Stallone and Czack eventually settled into a rental in Encino for $300 a month. The house was barely 500 square feet and there was no grass or air conditioning. Still, Stallone said he was determined to make it big in Hollywood.

Sylvester Stallone wrote "Rocky" and starred as boxer Rocky Balboa. (Getty Images)

In the book, Stallone described first arriving at Hollywood and Vine. He had no idea that the nearby Walk of Fame would one day bear his name.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Henry Winkler appears as Fonzie in "Happy Days." (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"That I would have a star there less than 10 years later, and only a few blocks away, still boggles my mind," he wrote.

Sylvester Stallone strikes at a punching bag in a boxing ring while his coach, Burgess Meredith (1908-1997), watches during training at a gymnasium in a still from the film "Rocky," directed by John G. Avildsen. (United Artists/Courtesy of Getty Images)

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Winkler said he never doubted that one day, his friend’s dreams would become a reality.

Sylvester Stallone is seen here on Jan. 12, 1979. (Getty Images)

Henry Winkler and Sylvester Stallone attend the hand and footprints ceremony for Bob Daly and Terry Semel, co-CEOs of Warner Bros., at Mann's Chinese Theater in Los Angeles, on Sept. 30, 1999. (Getty Images)

"I called him one day and I said, 'You're like a fine wine. You were great, and now you have blossomed.' He just kept punching. Isn't he amazing? He punched his way to the top."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: 'One Job Away' campaign is helping SAG-AFTRA members meet work thresholds to keep health insurance
articles.excerpt:
The grassroots online effort launched by actor Cheyenne Jackson has helped fellow SAG-AFTRA members land work and keep union’s medical coverage.

A grassroots social media campaign led by actor and si...
articles.body_text:
The grassroots online effort launched by actor Cheyenne Jackson has helped fellow SAG-AFTRA members land work and keep union’s medical coverage.

A grassroots social media campaign led by actor and singer Cheyenne Jackson has helped fellow SAG-AFTRA members struggling during declining film and TV production earn enough to keep their union health insurance.

Jackson, known for his roles in "American Horror Story," "30 Rock" and "Glee," launched the "One Job Away" movement on Instagram last month to spotlight fellow performers struggling to earn enough to maintain medical coverage through the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists.

SAG-AFTRA requires members to earn at least $28,000 annually to qualify for health insurance, with four quarterly deadlines for meeting that threshold, depending on when they joined the union.

The SAG-AFTRA logo is displayed outside the National Headquarters on Wilshire Boulevard during the actors strike in Los Angeles on Oct. 24, 2023. (AFP via Getty Images)

NEWSOM SAYS FILM TAX INCENTIVES ARE BRINGING HOLLYWOOD HOME BUT INDUSTRY EXPERTS WARN IT MAY BE 'TOO LATE'

For actors working job to job, meeting that requirement has become increasingly difficult as U.S. film and TV production contracts and healthcare costs rise.

"So the success of the project so far at last count is that eight actors have been hired directly and at least 12 to 15 have been pinned or called back or gotten really close," Jackson told Fox News Digital. He described an overwhelming response, including hundreds of direct messages from actors hoping to be featured, many of whom are just a few hundred dollars short of qualifying.

Actor Cheyenne Jackson attends as Academy Award-Winner Kathy Bates hosts Reception On Eve Of California Walk To Fight Lymphedema at Huntley Hotel on June 25, 2016, in Santa Monica, California. (Vivien Killilea)

Among them is William Ngo, who was born and raised in Southern California but relocated to Philadelphia after work dried up following the pandemic and the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike. Ngo, whose credits include The CW’s "The Vampire Diaries," HBO Max’s "The Staircase" and Apple’s "Bad Monkey," is just $500 short of qualifying for SAG-AFTRA health insurance.

Actress and stunt performer Marie Gibeault, whose credits include Netflix’s "The Four Seasons" and multiple commercials, is only $800 short of qualifying. Navy veteran, actor and voice-over artist Jonathan Medina needs one guest role to qualify by the end of the year.

ROB RIGGLE SAYS HOLLYWOOD WORK IS DISAPPEARING FROM LA: 'IT'S THE EXCEPTION NOW'

Actor Alejandro Cardenas reached out to thank Jackson after the campaign helped him book a small role that put him over the earnings threshold.

"After Cheyenne posted my picture and info, an executive from Lionsgate and friend of mine immediately called me and set me up into this job so I could make the money needed to reach the minimum to qualify for my health insurance again," Cardenas told Fox News Digital from the set he was working on in New Jersey.

The actors’ profiles share a common thread: dwindling opportunities in Hollywood during fewer scripted television orders, increased cost-cutting and the continued shift of production elsewhere.

The Hollywood Sign sits in the Hollywood Hills in Los Angeles on Sept. 30, 2025. (Photothek via Getty Images)

TRUMP, SCHIFF FORGE UNLIKELY ALLIANCE AS HOLLYWOOD BLEEDS JOBS

Jackson previously described the industry’s struggles as "systemic" during an interview with The Hollywood Reporter.

"People that have been leads of television shows have worked for years and years and years, and you know their faces, and you know their work. This year, they’re like, ‘What am I going to do?’" he said.

Meanwhile, beginning Jan. 1, quarterly premiums and earnings thresholds are expected to rise by 1%, with additional annual increases of 1% to follow, according to terms negotiated in SAG-AFTRA’s latest contract with streamers and studios.

A petition calling for an audit of the union’s health plan has also gained traction among members.

SAG-AFTRA, which represents approximately 170,000 media professionals worldwide, has faced criticism over the nearly $1.1 million annual salary of its national executive director and chief negotiator, Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, as members struggle financially.

Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, SAG-AFTRA National Executive Director and chief negotiator, joins members of the Writers Guild of America and the Screen Actors Guild as they walk the picket line outside Universal Studios in Burbank, Calif., on Aug. 4, 2023. (AFP via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to SAG-AFTRA’s chief communications and marketing officer, Pamela Greenwalt, for comment. In response, a union representative provided a healthcare fact sheet and a membership termination sheet.

Jackson, who also performs onstage, has expressed a desire to discuss how the system works, noting that actors can have a strong earnings year followed by a lean one that leaves them ineligible for health benefits.

He told Fox News Digital that launching "One Job Away" was a way to pass along kindness he had received.

Last year, for the first time in his 20-year career, Jackson found himself $6,000 short of meeting the health insurance eligibility requirements. Actress Kathy Bates, who had worked with him on "American Horror Story," arranged for him to have four speaking lines on her CBS series "Matlock." The work was enough to qualify him and his family for coverage.

"I really did nothing," Jackson said of launching "One Job Away." He added that several peers, including actresses Jamie Lee Curtis and Sarah Paulson, have reached out to ask how they can help.

"Just this helping one person makes this worth it," Jackson added, expressing disbelief at the outpouring of love he has received for trying to help.

articles.title: Secret Pentagon UFO hunt drew blueprints for hidden Nevada bunker to store ‘exotic’ materials
articles.excerpt:
Newly released clips from the Pentagon’s eighth UAP batch capture U.S. military sensors tracking unexplained objects in 2020, 2023 and 2026.

Buried beneath 15 to 20 feet of Nevada earth, behind 3-foo...
articles.body_text:
Newly released clips from the Pentagon’s eighth UAP batch capture U.S. military sensors tracking unexplained objects in 2020, 2023 and 2026.

Buried beneath 15 to 20 feet of Nevada earth, behind 3-foot-thick reinforced concrete walls, a steel vault door and a heavily guarded access tunnel, a Pentagon contractor drew up plans to build a 5,000-square-foot subterranean fortress.

The bunker was designed to store what was described as acquired "exotic material or tissue" – including recovered hardware and biological samples tied to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP), the Pentagon’s broader term for UFOs and other unexplained sightings in the air, space or sea.

The blueprint was not drawn from science fiction. It is detailed inside a 538-page declassified contractor report released by the Department of War as part of the Trump administration's latest batch of UAP records, exposing how close a private firm came to building a secure repository under a $22 million Pentagon program.

EX-PENTAGON OFFICIAL SAYS UAP FILES REVEAL 'TREASURE TROVE' OF INTELLIGENCE DATING BACK TO THE 1940S

The vault plans highlight the ambitions behind the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program – also referred to in Pentagon correspondence as the Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program.

A section of a July 2009 report by Pentagon contractor Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) details architectural plans for a 5,000-square-foot underground vault in North Las Vegas to store recovered hardware and biological samples. (Department of War)

Launched in 2008 through a $10 million congressional earmark steered by then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., and the late Sen. Daniel Inouye, D-Hawaii, the effort was billed as a study of foreign aerospace threats out to 40 years in the future.

Internal Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) briefing notes from May 2009 say Reid was hunting for radical technological "leaps" across 12 areas – ranging from futuristic propulsion and stealth to directed-energy weapons, space-time travel and how advanced craft affect pilots.

Behind closed doors, however, contractor Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies (BAASS) was preparing to acquire and store physical materials.

'NON-HUMAN' BODIES ALLEGEDLY RECOVERED FROM CRASHED UFO, DOCUMENTARY FILMMAKER CLAIMS

When the DIA solicited bids in August 2008, only one company applied: North Las Vegas-based BAASS, founded by longtime Reid supporter Robert Bigelow. The DIA awarded the contract the following month.

Then-Senate Majority Leader Sen. Harry Reid speaks during a news conference on Oct. 21, 2009, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Within weeks, BAASS moved into a nondescript building on South Polaris Avenue in Las Vegas and began turning it into a fortified compound – installing soundproofed offices, electronic deadbolts, tinted windows, security cameras and an 8-foot perimeter fence while stripping all company names and logos from the exterior.

By May 2009, as the firm's payroll swelled to 47 full-time employees – including scientists, engineers and former military and law enforcement investigators – BAASS began shopping for five additional Las Vegas Valley office buildings to house a 5,000-square-foot laboratory, physical evidence storage and a secure conference room.

At the same time, the company's administrator drew up blueprints for the underground bunker at Bigelow Aerospace's North Las Vegas complex, a site protected by razor wire, surveillance cameras and round-the-clock armed guards with military backgrounds.

UAP WHISTLEBLOWER MAKES STUNNING CLAIM ABOUT SECRETS BEHIND GOVERNMENT’S RECOVERED CRAFT

A satellite image shows a UFO spaceship at night amid an FBI investigation and alien evidence near Area 51, capturing a flying saucer and galaxy survey of a mysterious object in the sky. (Getty Images Creatives)

"The need for a highly secure underground vault operated by BAASS became apparent in line with a BAASS priority to pursue and acquire recovered hardware and biological samples from the corporate world and/or from private individuals and groups located elsewhere, including Brazil," the July 2009 10-month report states.

Plans called for multiple security doors along a concrete access tunnel leading into the buried structure, with any protruding surface components "extensively camouflaged," the filing adds.

To shield the program from broader scrutiny, Reid pushed the Pentagon to place the effort behind one of the military's highest secrecy walls.

On June 24, 2009, Reid wrote directly to Deputy Defense Secretary William Lynn III warning that investigators had uncovered "several highly sensitive, unconventional aerospace-related findings" that required "extraordinary protection."

Reid argued that standard classification protocols were not enough, warning that foreign intelligence services would target the program's methods and that public disclosure could scare off private industry partners.

articles.title: Hamas political official and wife among eight Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza
articles.excerpt:
Dozens of Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in near daily air strikes over the past month

A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes...
articles.body_text:
Dozens of Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in near daily air strikes over the past month

A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.

Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.

A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.

In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.

Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.

In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.

Khaled Abu Nada and his wife Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada were killed in the air strike

In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month.

"No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.

The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.

On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.

At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Ukraine drone attack kills five in Russian-occupied Zaporizhia
articles.excerpt: At least five people have been killed and three others were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russian-occupied Zaporizhia, a Russian-installed official said, as Russian forces hit Ukraine’s capit...
articles.body_text:
At least five people have been killed and three others were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russian-occupied Zaporizhia, a Russian-installed official said, as Russian forces hit Ukraine’s capital Kyiv in a ballistic missile assault.

“Following an enemy drone attack on a parking lot, five people were killed and three others wounded in the locality of Vesioloye,” Moscow-installed governor Yevgeny Balitsky wrote on Telegram on Thursday.

Earlier, Ukrainian forces hit a major Russian military base east of Moscow, damaging five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

Russian authorities also reported repelling drone attacks in the Tuymazinsky district in the Bashkortostan region and in the city of Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and fighting has continued despite a renewed US-backed push to end Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.

Russia has claimed the annexation of the southern region of Zaporizhia, which it partially controls, since September 2022.

The Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, was targeted with ballistic missiles late on Wednesday, striking a shopping centre and two other buildings on the east side of the Dnipro River bisecting the city, with warnings for residents to remain in shelters still in place, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Thursday its forces had carried out a massive overnight strike on Ukraine, hitting military-industrial facilities in Kyiv, the Interfax news agency reported.

The Defence Ministry also said Russian forces had struck a dry cargo vessel southeast of Odesa in the Black Sea overnight, according to the news agency. The ministry alleged the ship was carrying military equipment and dual-use goods to Ukraine.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said the residents heard loud ballistic missile impact sounds late on Wednesday, which injured at least seven people.

“People who live in certain areas of the city that come under frequent attack, they go and spend their nights in the shelter, even before air raid sirens raise alarm,” she said. “Coming into this winter, Russia has really heightened its attacks, especially on energy facilities.”

Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said Russia “is putting pressure on Kyiv’s military infrastructure, straining its air defences, and everything that can support military supply chains”.

“Russia has also been hitting power plants ahead of cold weather. The aim is to wear down morale and inflict economic damage, in addition to all these military effects,” she added.

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, MacAlpine said Ukraine’s energy capacity is below 40 percent of pre-war levels, as a number of the combined heating and power plants in Kyiv and the region have repeatedly gone offline due to attacks.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte urged Russia not to “expand the war” in Ukraine, in a joint statement issued on Wednesday after meeting in Florida.

“We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible,” the statement added.

The joint appeal by Trump and Rutte comes after the US leader described Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” during a meeting in China last week.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has taken issue with Trump’s comments on Putin.

“For us, he is a killer,” Zelenskyy told CNN.

articles.title: Jordan Parliament debates ‘antiterror’ law after deadly Karak church attack
articles.excerpt: Jordan’s Parliament is reviewing proposed amendments to its “antiterrorism” law that would double minimum prison sentences for “terrorism”-related offences after an attack at a church in Karak last mo...
articles.body_text:
Jordan’s Parliament is reviewing proposed amendments to its “antiterrorism” law that would double minimum prison sentences for “terrorism”-related offences after an attack at a church in Karak last month that killed nine people.

House of Representatives Speaker Ibrahim Tarawneh said the chamber had pledged to review legislation and consider amendments after the attack at the church in southern Jordan and the killing of a police officer in the capital, Amman.

The House voted to refer draft amendments to the 2006 Anti-Terrorism Law on Wednesday to its Legal Committee for review. The legislation will return to the chamber for debate and a vote before proceeding to the Senate and, if approved, royal ratification.

On October 23, gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud in a rare attack on Jordan’s Christian minority. Authorities said 34 people were wounded.

Last week, Jordan’s State Security Court sentenced three men to death for the attack.

On Wednesday, the court sentenced another man to death for killing the police officer in Amman. The officer was stabbed while on guard duty near the Sri Lankan embassy on November 5.

The government-backed amendments would raise minimum prison terms to 10 years and up to 15 years in certain cases while retaining the death penalty for the most serious offences, the state-run Jordan News Agency reported.

The proposed amendments drew criticism from First Deputy Speaker Ayatollah Freihat, who said legislation should not be based on knee-jerk reactions to events, FactJo, a Jordanian news agency, reported.

He raised concerns that the amendments could also harm freedom of expression in Jordan.

Freihat called on the government to withdraw the draft amendments and form a committee of legal experts to review the state’s criminal policy, criticising the use of “vague” formulations in defining “terrorism”, including “disrupting public order” and “harming the public interest”.

Earlier, King Abdullah II had said the kingdom would not be shaken by the attack on the church. Opening the new session of parliament this month, Abdullah said “the treacherous hand of terrorism” had reached out “to test the resilience of our state and the resolve of our people”.

articles.title: Trump, NATO chief push Russia to avoid any actions that would 'expand the war' with Ukraine
articles.excerpt: Fox News foreign correspondent Jeff Paul joins ‘The Story’ to comment on a study estimating that more than 700,000 Russian troops have been killed since the war in Ukraine began. He also reports on Po...
articles.body_text:
Fox News foreign correspondent Jeff Paul joins ‘The Story’ to comment on a study estimating that more than 700,000 Russian troops have been killed since the war in Ukraine began. He also reports on Poland’s accusation that Russia violated its airspace, prompting international concern.

President Donald Trump and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte are calling on Russia to avoid making any moves "that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war" against Ukraine.

The declaration came after the pair got together at Trump's Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thanksgiving Eve for what was described as an "outstanding meeting."

However, Russia hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, according to the mayor of the Ukrainian capital.

"The meeting was very impactful, with the war between Russia and Ukraine and the conflict in Iran being the primary subjects, as well as all of the record setting achievements that we have made together at the summits in the Hague and at Ankara," Trump and Rutte said in a joint statement.

"We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," the statement added. "Lastly, we talked about the importance of continuing to expand defense spending and investment in our industrial base, both in the United States and across NATO."

PUTIN'S WAR DEATH TOLL REPORTEDLY TOPS 700,000 AS RUSSIA SCRAMBLES FOR RECRUITS

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte meets with President Donald Trump during a visit to Mar-a-Lago in Florida on Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. (Reuters)

Rutte said in a post on X following the meeting, "It’s clearer than ever that American leadership remains essential as we build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO."

The Kremlin on Thursday accused Ukraine of trying to expand the war after Ukraine sank a Russian warship in Libya using drones and attacked a Russian military-linked cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland this past weekend, Reuters reported.

"As regards the escalation of the conflict in Ukraine, this appears to refer to attempts by the Kyiv regime to expand the geographical scope of this conflict. We are witnessing terrorist activity by the Kyiv regime in the Mediterranean and the Baltic," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted as saying.

NATO SECRETARY GENERAL MARK RUTTE WARNS ON UKRAINE WAR RISKS AHEAD OF TRUMP MEETING

A fire burns in the Desnianskyi district following a Russian ballistic missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. Russian forces attacked the district, causing multiple fires and injuring seven people. (Ukrinform/Ukrinform/Sipa USA/Reuters)

"This cannot fail to cause concern amongst coastal states, and most likely within the Alliance as a whole — the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Of course, nobody would want the conflict to spread geographically, and these are potentially very dangerous actions on the part of the Kyiv regime," Peskov added, according to Reuters.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least seven people were wounded in Russian strikes overnight, hitting a shopping center and other buildings, Reuters also reported.

Russia's President Vladimir Putin and President Donald Trump shake hands at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. (Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

Russia's Defense Ministry reportedly claimed that it struck two sites linked to the production of drones.

Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Parents of potential first Gen Z saint share daughter's powerful final message of hope
articles.excerpt:
Susan and Brian Middleton join 'The Story' to reflect on the life and faith of their late daughter, Maria Middleton, as Catholic bishops take an early step toward her potential sainthood.

The parents...
articles.body_text:
Susan and Brian Middleton join 'The Story' to reflect on the life and faith of their late daughter, Maria Middleton, as Catholic bishops take an early step toward her potential sainthood.

The parents of a Doylestown, Pennsylvania, teenager who could become the Catholic Church's first Gen Z saint are sharing their daughter's powerful message of hope, recalling how she remained steadfast in her faith while braving a terminal brain tumor diagnosis.

"I will not despair. I will choose hope," Maria Middleton told her parents just two weeks after her diagnosis.

Her father, Brian Middleton, recounted the conversation Tuesday on "The Story with Martha MacCallum." Brian, along with his wife, Susan, joined the show to reflect on their daughter's legacy and the movement to canonize her as a saint.

GEN Z FLOCKING TO CATHOLIC CHURCHES IN NYC FOR YOUTH GROUPS, SOCIAL EVENTS AMID CONVERSION BOOM

Brian Middleton, left, and Susan Middleton, right, joined "The Story with Martha MacCallum" to recount their daughter Maria's, center, legacy as she moves toward possible canonization by the Catholic Church. (The Story With Martha MacCallum/Screengrab)

"Maria made a decision that she wasn't going to cling to life, that she was going to spend it in self-transcendent service to others," Brian said, recalling his daughter's determination to not let her diagnosis define her remaining time.

"Two weeks after she was diagnosed, we asked her how she was doing. And she said, 'Mom and Dad, regardless of the circumstances of my life, my mission and purpose remain the same, and it's to know, love and serve God... my emotions will rise and fall, but my faith is not an emotion. It's a commitment and I will not despair. I will choose hope,'" he added.

"Her faith was so well integrated into her life that her decisions were always based on what was good, what was true, what was beautiful," Susan chimed in.

"That's how Maria navigated through life, always going back and saying to herself, and we found this in her journal... 'Only what God thinks matters.'"

FULTON SHEEN BECAME A TV SENSATION PREACHING FAITH, MORALITY AND WARNINGS MICHAEL KNOWLES SAYS STILL RESONATE

Pope Leo XIV arrives for the canonization Mass of Carlo Acutis and Pier Giorgio Frassati in St. Peter's Square at the Vatican, Sept. 7, 2025. (AP Photo/Andrew Medichini)

Maria died in 2020 at just 18 years old, approximately 20 months after being diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumor. Her commitment to faith and serving others has since drawn widespread attention, prompting Catholic leaders to take a preliminary step toward her possible canonization.

On Nov. 17, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops voted to advance Middleton's cause for canonization, marking an early step in a process that could eventually see her recognized as the Catholic Church's first Gen Z saint.

The move comes a little over one year after Pope Leo canonized the first millennial saint, St. Carlo Acutis.

For her parents, the growing movement to recognize Maria as a saint reflects the lasting impact of her message, which they say continues to resonate with people around the world.

"In this world of despair, she's become a patroness of hope because of the way that she lived her life. In this world with anxiety, suicide, and depression, Maria made a decision that she was going to live out her life on a daily basis. She chose gratitude over anger," Brian said.

"And because of this international movement, it's come to the attention of the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, and they're seeing that Maria appears to have lived a life of heroic virtue, and we trust that the church will do a good job."

"But the thing that's undeniable is the impact that Maria has had on so many lives around the world... in this age of despair, she's a light of hope."

articles.title: Is UBI the solution to mass unemployment in an AI economy?
articles.excerpt:
As rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) raise fears of mass job losses, calls for the rollout of universal basic income (UBI) are gaining traction.

UBI is a regular cash payment made to eve...
articles.body_text:
As rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) raise fears of mass job losses, calls for the rollout of universal basic income (UBI) are gaining traction.

UBI is a regular cash payment made to every citizen regardless of employment status, income or wealth.

Proponents of UBI in the United States argue that governments should look to UBI to offset AI’s expected impact on the labour market and prevent extreme poverty and wealth inequality.

The idea of universal payments is not new.

In 1797, Thomas Paine, one of the key thinkers of the American Revolution, proposed an early version of UBI in a pamphlet titled Agrarian Justice. He argued that land was originally common property, shared by all of humanity. Those with no land, he said, were owed compensation as a basic human right.

Under Paine’s proposal, each person would have received a lump sum of 15 pounds when they turned 21, followed by an annual payment of 10 pounds from age 50, paid for by a tax on inherited property.

The idea resurfaced in the 1960s from opposing ends of the ideological spectrum.

US economist Milton Friedman proposed a “negative income tax”, under which the government would top up the earnings of anyone falling below a set threshold. Friedman, a champion of free-market policies, argued that his proposal would be cheaper than existing welfare programmes.

US civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr, in his 1967 book Where Do We Go from Here, called for a guaranteed income as a way to end poverty.

King Jr’s vision came close to being enshrined in law in 1969, when President Richard Nixon proposed the Family Assistance Plan, a minimum income for families with children. Nixon’s proposal passed the House of Representatives but stalled in the Senate, and the plan was eventually abandoned.

After falling out of fashion in subsequent decades, proposals for universal payments have re-entered the mainstream in recent years amid the rise of automation and AI.

Some of the loudest proponents of UBI are the people developing AI.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has been pushing the idea for years.

In a 2024 interview with the All-In Podcast, Altman proposed a twist on UBI that would give everyone a stake in the productive gains of AI.

“I wonder if the future looks something like more like universal basic compute than universal basic income and everybody gets like a slice of GPT 7’s compute and they can use it, they can resell it, they can donate it to somebody to use for cancer research,” Altman said, suggesting that citizens could “own part of the productivity” generated by AI instead of receiving cash.

In April, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk said in an X post that a government-distributed “Universal High Income” would be the best way to deal with large-scale unemployment caused by AI.

Musk said AI and robotics would produce an abundance of goods and services far in excess of the increase in the money supply in future, so there would not be inflation.

Some observers have questioned the motivations of such proposals from billionaire tech executives.

Jonathan Portes, a professor of economics and public policy at King’s College, London, said tech leaders promoting UBI are acting out of “perceived self-interest”. In his view, a basic income could make job losses easier to accept as people are more likely to tolerate AI replacing their work if they are being paid.

“Partly it’s just another cool sounding idea,” Portes told Al Jazeera. “We should not take these people seriously on public policy issues at all.”

Most UBI proposals envision a system paid for by taxes, much in the same way as existing welfare programmes, though some pilot schemes have been funded by private donations.

Unlike traditional social welfare, which typically requires applicants to demonstrate financial hardship, UBI is paid to every member of a population without conditions.

Portes said UBI high enough to support acceptable living standards is not likely to be economically or politically viable in the near future.

While “a realistic UBI could help provide a better level of protection, increase individual autonomy and increase labour market flexibility, getting there would be complex”, he added.

“Many of the claims for it and fears are grossly exaggerated,” Portes said.

While everyone would get some financial benefit, some economists and technologists argue that the biggest beneficiary could be the economy.

In a scenario where AI leads to mass layoffs, people will have less money to spend. From this perspective, UBI would function less as a form of charity than as a way to keep consumer spending going.

That is the case made by Martin Ford, a futurist and the author of Rise of the Robots.

Ford argues that jobs are how purchasing power reaches common consumers, viewing UBI as a way to repair the link between production and spending rather than redistributing wealth for its own sake.

“Jobs are that mechanism that gets purchasing power to consumers so they can then drive the economy,” Ford said in a 2017 TED Talk.

“If, in fact, that mechanism begins to erode in the future, then we’re going to need to replace it with something else, or we’re going to face the risk that our whole system simply may not be sustainable.”

The most common objection is that unconditional cash discourages work. The evidence suggests the effect is real but modest.

In the biggest US trial of its kind, about 1,000 low-income participants were given $1,000 a month for three years.

OpenResearch’s Unconditional Cash Study, backed by OpenAI’s Altman, found that participants worked only 1.3-1.4 hours less each week compared with the control group.

More than half of recipients’ increased spending went on basic necessities such as food, housing and transport.

The study found no significant effect on physical health, and gains in wellbeing faded after the first year.

In the US, paying each family of four a universal payment of $30,000 – slightly below the official poverty line – would cost approximately $8.5 trillion each year, according to the Tax Project Institute.

That would dwarf current levels of spending on welfare.

The US government spent $1.7 trillion on some 90 welfare programmes in 2025, according to the conservative Heritage Foundation.

articles.title: A look at how the Trumps spend their Thanksgiving holiday through the years
articles.excerpt: Melania Trump delivers a powerful message of gratitude to military families during a visit to Fort Rucker ahead of Thanksgiving. She honors the profound sacrifices made by military spouses and childre...
articles.body_text:
Melania Trump delivers a powerful message of gratitude to military families during a visit to Fort Rucker ahead of Thanksgiving. She honors the profound sacrifices made by military spouses and children while their loved ones are deployed across the globe. She expresses deep appreciation for their strength and resilience in keeping their homes full of love.

In keeping with tradition, President Donald Trump marked his sixth Thanksgiving in the executive office with the White House’s annual Turkey Pardon ceremony on Tuesday.

His plans for Thanksgiving Day this year remain unannounced — but previous holidays offer a preview of how the president likes to spend the day honoring those who can't be at home for the uniquely American holiday due to service to the country.

Last year Trump spent Thanksgiving at Mar-a-Lago participating in his favorite pass time — golf. But he also used the time in what is known as the "Winter White House" to call Maj. Gen. Dave Gardner, commander of the 101st Airborne Division and Joint Task Force–Southern Border by video conference and talk with troops deployed along the southern border.

TRUMP AND DANA WHITE HONOR MARINE CORPS BAND WITH SIX-FIGURE CHECKS IN FIRST EVENT ON NEW HELIPAD

President Donald Trump delivers remarks to U.S. troops in an unannounced visit to Al Asad Air Base, Iraq, Dec. 26, 2018. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst)

First lady Melania Trump spent the days ahead of the holiday in 2025 visiting Camp Lejeune and Marine Corps Air Station New River with Second Lady Usha Vance on Nov. 19. They met with military families and made Thanksgiving crafts with children.

In 2020, during the final Thanksgiving of his first term, Trump remained at the White House and made calls to six deployed military units representing every branch of the armed forces, including troops in Kuwait and sailors aboard the USSWinston Churchill in the Red Sea.

Trump famously took a secret trip to Bagram Airfield in Afghanistan on Nov. 28, 2019, where he served turkey, posed for photos and thanked American troops for their sacrifices amid the ongoing war in the Middle East, which not even two years later in August 2021 was brought to an end by then-President Joe Biden.

"There's nowhere I'd rather celebrate this Thanksgiving than right here with the toughest, strongest, best, and bravest warriors on the face of the Earth," Trump told the troops at the time.

"And you don't even know how much the people of our country love and respect you."

President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump greet military personnel at the dining facility during an unannounced visit to Al Asad Air Base, Iraq, Dec. 26, 2018. (Reuters/Jonathan Ernst)

TRUMP SAYS US MAY RECOVER ALL THE EQUIPMENT LEFT BEHIND IN AFGHANISTAN BY BIDEN ADMIN

The visit came as roughly 12,000 American troops remained in Afghanistan more than 18 years after the U.S. invasion.

During the visit, Trump met with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani to discuss efforts to end the war and told American troops that the Taliban wanted to reach a deal with the United States. He said his administration was reducing America's military presence in Afghanistan while pursuing a political solution to the more than 18-year conflict.

President Donald Trump visits with personnel at U.S. Coast Guard Station Lake Worth Inlet in Riviera Beach, Florida, on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 22, 2018. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump spent Thanksgiving 2018 in Florida having a traditional dinner with his family, including Melania and his children and grandchildren.

He also held a video call with deployed troops before visiting Coast Guard members at Station Lake Worth Inlet with his wife, where the first couple thanked them for their service and hurricane rescues.

After that holiday in 2018, Melania and then-Second Lady Karen Pence assembled comfort kits for deployed troops at American Red Cross headquarters.

MOSCOW, TALIBAN FORGE MILITARY ALLIANCE IN POWER GRAB AFTER US AFGHANISTAN EXIT: REPORTS

President Donald Trump speaks to members of the military via teleconference from his Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach, Florida, on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 22, 2018. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)

Trump spent his first Thanksgiving as president at his Mar-a-Lago estate for a traditional Thanksgiving dinner with his family. It came after a day of video-calling deployed troops.

Donald and Melania Trump also visited Coast Guard Station Lake Worth Inlet in Riviera Beach, Florida, where they handed out food and greeted service members.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.
