articles.title: CFP selection committee continues to churn out inexplicable, indefensible rankings | Ian Miller
articles.excerpt:
Finebaum insists he isn't celebrating Indiana's 27-24 overtime loss at Washington, he just conveniently had the obituary ready on First Take.

The College Football Playoff selection committee released...
articles.body_text:
Finebaum insists he isn't celebrating Indiana's 27-24 overtime loss at Washington, he just conveniently had the obituary ready on First Take.

The College Football Playoff selection committee released its updated rankings Tuesday evening to, well, less controversy than a typical week.

There was movement near the top of the rankings, thanks to the UCLA Bruins suffering their first loss of the season in triple overtime at Michigan and the Indiana Hoosiers falling in overtime to the Washington Huskies in Seattle. Then there's the Tennessee Volunteers-Alabama Crimson Tide debate, which this week resulted in a long-awaited changing of the order between the two teams.

After weeks of the Crimson Tide sitting above UT, despite a head-to-head loss, the Volunteers jumped them to sit at No. 5. That might have been reasonable, considering the committee's absurd "logic," but there's plenty from this week's poll that isn't. And it's yet again a sign of how the committee just makes things up as they go.

CFP SELECTION COMMITTEE HAS OFFICIALLY DISCREDITED ITSELF WITH LATEST RANKINGS

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Daune Morris #17 of the Tennessee Volunteers runs the ball for a touchdown during the NCAA football game between the University of Tennessee Volunteers and the University of Kentucky Wildcats at Neyland Stadium, Knoxville, TN Tim Gangloff/CSM/Sipa USA (Credit Image: Tim Gangloff/Cal Sport Media/Sipa USA) (Tim Gangloff/Cal Sport Media/Sipa USA)

First? How they've handled the Hoosiers this season, and particularly the last few weeks.

Just three polls ago, Indiana was ranked No. 4 by the selection committee. After not playing for a bye week, they dropped all the way to No. 9. That was bizarre enough, considering again, they didn't play. The committee's excuse for this was that all of the Hoosiers' Big Ten opponents lost in the same week, devaluing their strength of schedule. We'll come back to that.

After the bye week, Indiana beat the then-No. 18 team, the USC Trojans, at home by two scores. It moved up just one spot to No. 8. Ahead of this week's poll, the Hoosiers lost on the road to overtime to a team now ranked in the selection committee's own poll. They dropped six spots. Six. So it didn't play, beat a top-15 team by two scores, lost on the road in overtime to a ranked team, and dropped from No. 4 to No. 14. This would never happen to a team from say, another conference that enjoys enhanced protection from consequences.

When the Georgia Bulldogs lost, at home, to an unranked Auburn team, they dropped four spots in the AP Top 25. Yes, the AP poll uses a different set of voters, but it's indicative of the different standards applied to different conferences.

BIG TEN FACES ONE-BID NIGHTMARE IN CFP RANKINGS AS SEC EYES FOUR BIDS AND BIG 12 COULD THRIVE

What makes the Indiana ranking even more, shall we say, confusing, is how it compares to say, Alabama. The committee had a golden opportunity to keep their standards consistent when all of Alabama's SEC wins lost in the same week between the second and third polls. Had they applied the same logic to the Tide as they did with Indiana, they'd have dropped multiple spots. They didn't move at all.

This week presented another opportunity for consistency. All of Alabama's SEC wins lost again, except for Mississippi State who beat FCS Tennessee Tech 34-16, which may or may not have counted as a Quality SEC Win™. Alabama dropped just three spots. They're now No. 6, while the Hoosiers are eight places behind them at No. 14. With the same record.

Now, there are multiple ways to evaluate records, strength of schedule and overall resume. But the committee seemingly prioritizes how teams perform against their own rankings. This is a terrible idea that inevitably creates circuitous logic, but it's how they've chosen to operate. Ok, fine.

Taking them at their word, here's how Alabama has done against teams currently ranked in the CFB playoff top-25:

That's it. This is the strength of schedule that boosts the Tide's resume, in the committee's mind, to worthy of being eight spots ahead of Indiana with the same record. Surely though, Indiana must have played an easy schedule that justifies such a lower spot in the poll...right?

Well, for comparison, here's how the Hoosiers have done against currently ranked teams:

So they've played two more games against ranked opponents, and what do you know? They actually won two of those games! Their two losses have come by a combined seven points, including one to a top-5 quality Ohio State team with its starting quarterback healthy. That came down to one of the last plays of the game.

Indiana head coach Curt Cignetti speaks during news conference ahead of the College Football Playoff national championship game between Miami and Indiana, Sunday, Jan. 18, 2026, in Miami. The game will be played on Monday. (AP Photo/Chris Carlson)

We can also look at ESPN's SP+ to point out how absurd the disparity is. While the perception is that Indiana's played an easy schedule, because of its non-conference opponents, nobody makes that claim about the No. 1 Georgia Bulldogs. Even though Georgia, by an objective analytics-driven measurement, has played an easier schedule than Indiana. And a similarly week non-conference slate.

Here's how the two schedules compare in SP+ rankings:

Interesting. Also per SP+, Indiana's schedule ranks as the 38th hardest in the country. Georgia is 44th. Alabama is 14th, so harder than the Hoosiers, but again, they have the same record. The difference does not justify an eight spot differential. Heck, Miami's played a tougher schedule than Georgia, yet they somehow sit at No. 7 in the poll behind not one, not two, but three two-loss SEC teams. Despite the same number of losses, and its one loss coming down to a controversial incomplete pass call late in the fourth quarter on the road to a top-5 team. Not Auburn.

In fact, speaking of SEC teams getting the benefit of the doubt, Tennessee's strength of schedule is just 22nd, and they're 1-1 against teams currently ranked in the top-25. Their non-conference schedule, like Georgia's and Indiana's, is embarrassingly bad. They beat up on Furman 56-9, the same awful Georgia Tech team 45-24, and Kennesaw State 42-9. Its loss to South Carolina looks worse than Indiana's two losses now, and they have fewer wins over ranked teams. Why is it nine spots ahead of Indiana with a relatively comparable schedule?

The answer, as always, is perception. And selection committee chair Hunter Yurachek confirmed that in his typically embarrassing post-poll interview. When asked why the switch between Tennessee and Alabama, Yurachek basically said the committee just felt like it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"When we first ranked Alabama at No. 3 two weeks ago, the resume looked different than it did when we started the ranking process this week. So much so that the committee felt that both Texas and Notre Dame deserved to be ranked ahead of Alabama," he told Rece Davis. "And then you couple that with a UCLA loss, and the Indiana loss, and then a Tennessee win against LSU, Tennessee moves up to a point where they’re now directly comparable to Alabama. You got the head-to-head, Tennessee over Alabama. And that’s the switch where you have Texas at 3 now, Notre Dame at 4, Tennessee at 5, and Alabama at 6."

Why does beating an unranked 6-5 LSU team make Tennessee comparable to Alabama? What has Alabama actually accomplished besides losing its two toughest games of the year?

When asked about Indiana, he gave an even more rambling and incoherent answer.

"For the last six weeks, Indiana's had six one-score games. Three out of the last four have been in overtime. And until Saturday, they had found a way to win those games," he said.

This is wrong. Indiana beat USC 27-13 roughly 10 days ago. Does the committee not know the outcomes of the games? Because that is factually incorrect. Unfortunately for America, he wasn't done there.

"But Saturday, they did not," he continued. "They fell behind the team like a Texas Tech with one loss and then they were in direct comparison with their counterparts in the Big 10 in Oregon and Iowa. You got both of those teams. Oregon has won four games in a row. Iowa has also won four games in a row. Oregon has a win at Ohio State. Iowa lost at home to Ohio State."

Why was Indiana only in direct comparison to other Big Ten teams? Do the two-loss SEC teams not exist? Or is the committee so hopelessly inept and biased that they think two-loss Alabama and Tennessee simply can't be compared to the Big Ten because they're in the mighty SEC and play in big stadiums or something? Four of Indiana's last six games have been against teams currently ranked in the top-25, so why would it be surprising they were close? Though again, it did beat USC by two scores, which Yurachek got wrong.

Does he and the committee also think beating OSU without Julian Sayin is the same as beating it with him? Because Oregon's win was after his injury, and Iowa and Indiana's losses were before the injury. Incompetence all the way down.

Or maybe they're just mad because Cignetti continues to call out the committee's obvious bias.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Alabama Crimson Tide head coach Kalen DeBoer looks on during the second quarter against the Georgia Bulldogs at Saban Field at Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa, Ala., on Oct. 10, 2026. (David Leong/Imagn Images)

Tennessee lost one of its last four games, and their three ensuing wins have come over teams that are a combined 0-9 in their last nine. In fact, Tennessee's resume SP+ is No. 10, while Indiana is No. 11 and UCLA is No. 9. Tennessee is ranked nine spots ahead of Indiana and four spots ahead of UCLA. Guess that doesn't matter though! Cause SEC!

What these inconsistencies and illogical arguments boil down to is that the committee believes losses in the SEC shouldn't matter much. They believe that the SEC deserves preferential treatment it hasn't earned, particularly considering that conference's atrocious record in the playoff the past three seasons. There's a very real chance the Big Ten, which undoubtedly has a stronger middle class than the SEC this year, only gets one team in the tournament. While the SEC will get four. And we already know that the SEC conference championship game can't hurt the loser, a ridiculous fact Joey Galloway thankfully brought up on ESPN's show, to great consternation and disappointment from Rece Davis and Heather Dinich.

Ranked wins don't matter, objective resumes don't matter, the only thing that matters is perception. Which is why this poll will continue to be a discrediting embarrassment.

articles.title: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65
articles.excerpt:
Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's music

Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor foll...
articles.body_text:
Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's music

Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.

Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.

Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".

Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.

Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off

He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.

Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."

They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.

Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".

"Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later."

Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023

Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order,  recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".

Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix."

In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".

US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".

Belinda Carlisle said she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You.

Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".

Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982

Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together."

She said he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".

Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songs

The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.

He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.

The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.

Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.

Duran Duran bridged the sounds of pop, funk, disco, punk and new wave with a sound that remains indelibly tied to the 1980s

Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.

Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.

They became so popular in the US that the press labeled them the leaders of a "second British invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.

During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.

The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.

"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.

"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."

He went on to play on Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.

Taylor quit Duran Duran at the height of their fame in 1985, but rejoined the band several times in the 2000s and contributed to their most recent album, Danse Macabre

After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.

In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.

When the group took the stage, Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.

Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.

Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a true Wild Boy

Duran Duran drummer quits band due to tinnitus

Duran Duran voted into Rock & Roll Hall of Fame

articles.title: FIFA says personal and business information stolen in cyberattack
articles.excerpt: FIFA said it had been the victim of a criminal cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information, although no files from the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project were...
articles.body_text:
FIFA said it had been the victim of a criminal cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information, although no files from the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project were accessed, according to media reports.

FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorised access to a limited set of personal and business information,” a FIFA spokesperson told Al Jazeera.

FIFA strongly condemned the “unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” adding that such actions were “a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy”.

It also said that :”FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement.”

FIFA did not say how many people or organisations were affected, when the attack took place or what the business information included. Its reference to publication did not say whether any data had appeared online, or where.

Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the hack when responding to a post that said more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been leaked.

The person with knowledge of the matter told the Reuters news agency that less than 0.1 percent of the total data held by world football’s governing body was affected.

A FIFA source told The Athletic that the person – or group – responsible for carrying out the cyberattack gained access by impersonating staff rather than a systems or technical failure.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino said in July that his organisation had scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors following a widespread backlash.

The plan ‌involved raising up to $4.2bn by selling a 20 percent stake in a new unit that would run FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup.

articles.title: Dak Prescott's 1,000-yard, 11-touchdown surge over three games makes Cowboys heavy Thanksgiving favorites
articles.excerpt: The Dallas Cowboys beat the Philadelphia Eagles 38-21 to improve to 3-4. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask what grade the Cowboys should get for their performance, and where the Eagle...
articles.body_text:
The Dallas Cowboys beat the Philadelphia Eagles 38-21 to improve to 3-4. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask what grade the Cowboys should get for their performance, and where the Eagles should go from here following their 5th straight loss.

Happy Thanksgiving to all you turkeys out there. I hope your plate is full, your turkey is moist, the stuffing is aplenty, and most of all, that we make a ton of money today. By the time this game comes on, you probably will be either about to start your dinner or heading to the in-laws for the next meal.

What could be better today? Well, a win in this game would be a bit of help, and let’s see if we can get that with the Eagles and Cowboys.

The Philadelphia Eagles were impressive on Sunday, and that’s saying something. The team has been a bit of a disaster this season, specifically with Jalen Hurts and his injury situation. They come into today’s game with a 3-7 record and are probably just trying to play spoiler for any opponent at this point in their season. They aren’t mathematically eliminated from the postseason or anything, but they might as well be. And that’s taking into consideration the win they had Sunday.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Philadelphia Eagles running back Saquon Barkley (26) waves during training camp at NovaCare Complex. (Kyle Ross-Imagn Images)

Before we go and say that Joe Milton III is the answer at quarterback, let’s just admit that the Steelers aren’t exactly a great team. They are fine, but a really bad first quarter did Pittsburgh in for the game. The Eagles only scored six points the remainder of the game, and the Steelers outscored them 16-6 from the start of the second quarter on. A win is a win, but I don’t think want anyone thinking the Eagles have figured something out.

The good news for them is that they at least put up some points against a defense that is certainly better than what Dallas has to offer.

EAGLES QB JOE MILTON SHARES THAT HE SAYS HIS DAUGHTER'S NAME TO CALM NERVES BEFORE THROWING A DEEP BALL

Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott (4) calls a play at the line of scrimmage during the first quarter of the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on Sept. 4, 2025. (Bill Streicher/Imagn Images)

The Dallas Cowboys are basically just running back what they did last season. I hate to bash the team because I was pretty high on them before the season started, but their only method of victory is to have Dak Prescott go bonkers and throw for a million yards and 10 touchdowns a game.

Obviously, I’m exaggerating here, but he does have almost exactly 1,000 passing yards and 11 touchdowns over the past three games. If he had any semblance of a defense this season, he might be in the MVP conversation as I predicted before the year.

BUT… he doesn’t. His defense is awful. They are ranked near the bottom in passing and rushing yards allowed, and they are giving up a ton of points. It means Prescott has to be near perfect for them to win. Even when he was close against the 49ers, they still lost by six because the defense couldn’t give him any help. Dallas is a fun team to watch, but it has to be frustrating for true fans of the club.

COWBOYS STAR QUINNEN WILLIAMS REPEATS SIX WORD ANSWER 12 TIMES IN PRESSER AFTER MAJOR COACHING CHANGE

Dallas Cowboys wide receiver George Pickens (3) celebrates his touchdown catch with quarterback Dak Prescott (4) during the first half of an NFL football game Sunday, Nov. 23, 2025, in Arlington, Texas. (AP Photo/Tony Gutierrez)

Prescott and the Cowboys have already beaten the Eagles once this season. They went into Philadelphia and won 38-21. I’m not really sure why they aren’t bigger favorites in this one, outside of maybe because Philly looked a bit better with Milton under center. I like the Cowboys to cover the -8.5 in this game, and I think their team total is a good look as well. Prescott has been playing great lately and has already shown he can rack up points against the Eagles' defense.

A win from Philly last week also makes me think they will stumble this week. Sometimes a bad team just wants to get a win and then rests a bit the next week. Give me the Cowboys -8.5 and give me their team total over.

articles.title: Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen set up for another shootout as Chiefs face Bills on Thanksgiving
articles.excerpt: Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, Kevin Wildes and Coach Eric Mangini react to the Kansas City Chiefs' AFC West win against the Los Angeles Chargers, the New England Patriots improving to 4-2 and if Wilde...
articles.body_text:
Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, Kevin Wildes and Coach Eric Mangini react to the Kansas City Chiefs' AFC West win against the Los Angeles Chargers, the New England Patriots improving to 4-2 and if Wildes walks throughs the Door of Destiny. The squad also breaks down the Buffalo Bills' shootout win over the Las Vegas Raiders and if it is time to take the Houston Texans and whole AFC North seriously.

I don’t know if you know this or not, but we are at the main course of your Thanksgiving Day with this game.

Sure, you could’ve finished and might be in a food coma by the time this game kicks off, but the NFL has done a great job of giving us one game that we absolutely cannot miss late in the day. Any time the Chiefs and the Bills take each other on, it is must-see television, and that’s precisely what we get this week.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Kansas City Chiefs are one of the best teams in football again. They are coming off yet another win – a 34-7 drubbing of the Arizona Cardinals. I do think it is fair to ask if the Chiefs are actually good, or just taking advantage of an easy schedule.

Their eight wins have been over Denver, Indianapolis, Miami, Las Vegas, Los Angeles (Chargers), New York (Jets), Atlanta, and Arizona. Outside of Denver, whom they played at home and in the first week of the season, there isn’t one quality win in that group. In fact, none of those teams have winning records.

Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes (15) and tight end Travis Kelce (87) walk out with the rest of the team before an NFL football game against the Buffalo Bills Sunday, Nov. 2, 2025, in Orchard Park. New York. (AP Photo/Adrian Kraus)

So, are the Chiefs actually good? Maybe. Patrick Mahomes has played much more like Patrick Mahomes in the past two games, throwing for 672 yards over the two games and eight touchdowns. We know he doesn’t really have a deep receiving corps, but he is making it work. I’ve harped about this for years, but Rashee Rice, Josh Downs, and Xavier Worthy are the options, and I don’t think any of them would be a true No. 1 on almost any other team.

Travis Kelce sporadically looks good, but you can’t really count on it. Kenneth Walker III is a difference-maker at running back, but he has been out the past two weeks, and they really need him to give the Bills defense something different to worry about.

The Buffalo Bills are still one of the best teams in football, and they still have their Superman, Josh Allen.

The Swiss Army Knife quarterback is arguably the best running back in football – certainly for short yardage and goal-to-go situations. He is the reason they win games, and hasn’t really been the reason for their lone loss this year. Even in the loss to the Patriots, the lone blemish on the Bills' season, he had one interception, but threw for one touchdown and ran for another. The Bills defense just couldn’t seem to stop Drake Maye – essentially the only team this season to struggle against him.

Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) drops to throw during the fourth quarter of an AFC Divisional Round playoff game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on Jan. 17, 2026. (Ron Chenoy/Imagn Images)

Perhaps it is worth considering if the Bills have beaten anyone this year, if I’m going to knock the Chiefs schedule. They’ve beaten Houston, Detroit, Los Angeles (both), Las Vegas, Baltimore, Minnesota, New York (Jets), and Miami. Detroit is a good team, but they got them at home.

The Rams are a solid team, but they did play them at least without Myles Garrett. The Vikings defense was still solid in their game, but got no offensive help and forced them to trade for Kirk Cousins after the game. Certainly their schedule has been harder than Kansas City’s, though.

THANKSGIVING WEEK BETTING GUIDE 2026: NFL THANKSGIVING, RIVALRY WEEK, NBA CUP, NHL AND COLLEGE HOOPS PICKS

Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills host Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs on Thanksgiving night, with the AFC’s No. 1 seed in play. (Getty Images)

Any time these two squads get together, you expect fireworks. Since 2020, they’ve played 10 times (including playoffs), and the series is tied 5-5, but in the regular season the Bills are 5-1 against the Chiefs. Which means … the Chiefs are 4-0 against them in the playoffs. In the ten games, the scores have been: 49, 61, 51, 51, 37, 44, 78, 58, 62, and 43. I think we'll see two quarterbacks do their thing tonight and treat us to a shootout. Give me the over 50.5.

articles.title: ‘Symbolic’: Why did UK sanction Yemen’s Houthis amid attacks on Saudi?
articles.excerpt: London, United Kingdom – The United Kingdom has slapped sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis and four of their senior leaders after accusing the Iran-backed group of renewed “aggression” inside Yemen and atta...
articles.body_text:
London, United Kingdom – The United Kingdom has slapped sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis and four of their senior leaders after accusing the Iran-backed group of renewed “aggression” inside Yemen and attacks targeting civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis have escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting the financial district in Riyadh this week, as they engage in a civil war with Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

Fighting has escalated since July as a 2022 United Nations-brokered ceasefire collapsed. Since then, the Houthis have captured the Red Sea port of Mocha and the island of Mayyun, extending control over the Red Sea in a setback to the Saudi-backed government.

The war erupted after the Houthis captured the capital, Sanaa, in late 2014, forcing President Abd Rabbu Mansour Hadi to flee. Saudi Arabia intervened in support of the Hadi government as it saw the Iran-backed group’s rise in neighbouring Yemen as a security threat.

The UK government announced its sanctions on Tuesday, accusing the Houthis of undermining peace and security in Yemen and the region. It froze assets and placed travel bans on the group and its leaders, including Interior Minister Abdulkarim Amir al-Din Hussein al-Houthi and Security and Intelligence chief Abdul Hakim Hashem Ali al-Khaiwani.

Chief prosecutor Sarim al-Din Mufadal, who has been accused of perpetrating “sexual violence, including rape and torture”, also faces an asset freeze and travel ban.

“The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable, and they must be held to account,” said UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who linked the sanctions to attacks on shipping in the Bab al-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea, one of the busiest shipping lanes in the world.

“Today’s measures send a clear message to the Houthis – we will always act in support of British values and interests,” he said in a statement.

The British move comes nearly a month after it decided to deploy fighter jets to defend Saudi Arabia, a close ally going back decades that has increasingly come under missile and drone attacks in recent weeks.

Britain also sent Tornado fighters to Saudi Arabia in the wake of the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait in 1990, according to the Royal Air Force Museum.

The Houthis have also targeted oil installations and a major pipeline that helped Saudi Arabia export its oil while Iran essentially blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint. Tehran said it has blocked the vital waterway, through which most of the Gulf oil and natural gas passes, in response to the US-Israel war on Iran.

The UK has naval and logistics bases in the neighbouring Gulf nations of Bahrain and Oman. In May, it agreed a free trade deal with the six Gulf Cooperation Council states.

Thomas Juneau, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, said the sanctions were imposed during a diplomatic push by Riyadh.

“Saudi Arabia has been asking other countries to list the Houthis as a terrorist entity, to turn the screw on the Houthis and to help in its campaign against the group,” he told Al Jazeera.

The sanctions, Ahmed Nagi from the International Crisis Group (ICG) said, are “intended to send a political message about where the UK stands on the current escalation and the Houthi actions”.

In January 2024, the UK and the United States jointly sanctioned four Houthi figures, including the group’s defence minister and naval commander, over attacks on Red Sea shipping, and a month later, a second package targeted the Quds Force, the overseas unit of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The same month, the UK joined the US in carrying out air strikes on Houthi positions over attacks on ships in the Red Sea, which had disrupted maritime trade. The Houthis had imposed a ban on ships linked to Israel from passing through the waterway in response to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

The Houthis are already under a UN arms embargo, and London is now “going further”, Nagi, who is a senior Yemen analyst at the ICG, said.

This month, the UN Security Council renewed its Yemen sanctions regime until November 2027 through a UK-led resolution.

Raiman al-Hamdani, a Yemeni researcher and analyst, said the UK, as the Security Council’s lead on Yemen, had helped shape that regime and “this latest step continues a longstanding policy rather than breaking from it.”

But Nagi called the UK move “largely symbolic”.

“The four Houthi leaders targeted by the sanctions are unlikely to travel to the UK or hold assets there, so the practical impact will probably be limited.”

Al-Hamdani said the group’s income comes “largely from the black market, smuggling, taxation of local businesses and control of ports and customs, none of which a UK asset freeze touches”.

“The missile and drone programme hasn’t slowed despite years of UN, US, EU and UK listings,” he added.

Juneau from Chatham House agreed the sanctions would not change Houthi behaviour soon but said that while sanctions by individual countries other than the US have little effect alone, they can matter collectively, which is why Saudi Arabia is pressing as many countries as possible to act.

He also pointed to the Houthis’ growing influence in the Red Sea, which has concerned Saudi Arabia as well as its Western allies.

The British foreign secretary on Tuesday pointed out how Houthi actions in the Red Sea were “driving up the cost of living for the British people” and “undermining the stability of the Middle East”.

Analysts pointed out that the UK government statement is silent on the other parties to the war – the Yemeni government forces and Saudi Arabia – even as it said the Houthis’ “reckless aggression is responsible for this conflict”.

Nagi said the omission reflected how London sees the war.

“From London’s perspective, the Houthis are the ones attacking Saudi Arabia and escalating the conflict, rather than the other way around,” he said.

Juneau was blunter. “Sanctions are always political. You sanction your opponents. You don’t sanction your partners or friends,” he said.

Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressed concerns that the sanctions would impact aid organisations engaged in humanitarian work in Houthi-held areas.

“As Yemen relies heavily on imports, curbs affecting commercial goods could also push up food prices,” she told Al Jazeera.

“The sanctions really can have quite devastating impacts for the populations living in territories under Houthi control, even if that’s not what the UK intends by the sanctions,” she warned.

This is the case even though the UK’s sanctions already include a humanitarian exception covering aid and other activities that meet basic human needs, she said.

Moreover, the UK has not proscribed the Houthis under “antiterrorism” laws despite its other Western allies – the US, Canada and Australia – designating the Iran-backed group as a “terrorist” organisation.

Juneau called the aid agencies’ fear that proscription could hamper humanitarian deliveries “a valid concern” although some people argued the Houthis’ diversion of aid has already made such work extremely difficult.

The Houthis have repeatedly denied that they have diverted humanitarian aid.

Al-Hamdani said sanctions have not forced the Houthis to change their tactics. They do not “appear to respond to human rights criticism or listings”, he said, adding that the group “tends to treat detainees and abuses as bargaining chips to strengthen its negotiating position and demands”.

Rather, he said, sanctions “risk deepening polarisation and closing off the political settlement the war needs”.

articles.title: Stone Cold Steve Austin hates slow fishing, Trey McKinney hunts geese & Steven Rinella talks turkey
articles.excerpt: Marsupial Gear co-founder Hannah Graham tells OutKick OutDoors about the pressure of a coveted Arizona elk hunt, the challenges she faced in the field and the emotional relief of harvesting her bull w...
articles.body_text:
Marsupial Gear co-founder Hannah Graham tells OutKick OutDoors about the pressure of a coveted Arizona elk hunt, the challenges she faced in the field and the emotional relief of harvesting her bull with help from friends.

'Field Notes' is a weekly OutKick OutDoors column featuring the biggest hunting, fishing and outdoor stories, viral videos, reader submissions and whatever else Mother Nature throws our way. It runs every Thursday on OutKick.com.

Last year, I struck a nerve with Steven Rinella.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Turns out, the MeatEater host has some very strong opinions about what belongs on the Thanksgiving dinner table. And spoiler alert: It's not turkey.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

"This … OK. This is a major issue in my marriage," Rinella told me.

"MeatEater" host and cookbook author Steven Rinella doesn't like to eat turkey for Thanksgiving. (John Hafner)

You see, Rinella considers himself a Thanksgiving purist.

"I've pointed out to [my wife] that historians don't even think the Pilgrims ate turkey on the first Thanksgiving. They think they were probably eating geese or ducks," he explained. "They ate the best of what they had. They definitely ate deer meat, you know?"

So that's his philosophy. Thanksgiving dinner should be whatever you've recently harvested. Venison, elk, duck — whatever's good and fresh. His wife, Katie, on the other hand, thinks it's downright "sinful" to skip the traditional turkey.

But if you are committed to turkey, Rinella thinks you're probably cooking it wrong.

According to Steve, roasting a whole bird is one of the worst ways to prepare it. By the time the legs are cooked through, the breast is usually dried out. Or, as he put it, "incinerated."

Wild turkey or store-bought turkey for Thanksgiving? Or no turkey at all? You make the call. (Getty Images)

His solution? Break the bird down and cook each part the way it deserves. Smoke the breasts, slow-cook the legs and thighs, and stop trying to make every piece of a very lean animal finish cooking at the same time.

And if you're one of those people who thinks turkey is dry, bland and generally inferior to the mashed potatoes?

"Not the turkey's fault," Rinella deadpanned.

To Rinella’s horror, I’m sure, I come from a bird-in-the-oven family myself. But it was always a treat when my uncle or grandpa would bring home a harvest for the holidays. Hard to beat wild turkey on your plate and Wild Turkey in your glass.

Are you taking the Rinella approach and serving up venison, elk or whatever happens to be in the freezer? Did you save a wild turkey from spring hunting season? Or are you perfectly content shoving a regular ol' Butterball in the oven and calling it a day?

No judgment! Just whatever you do, don't do this:

Send me your menus, photos and strongly held opinions at Amber.Harding@outkick.com. Bonus points if you harvested dinner yourself.

And with that, let's get into this week's Field Notes.

Stone Cold Steve Austin is retired from the ring these days. Now, he's focused on winning off-road championships and — in his downtime — hunting and fishing.

Steve Austin picked up a championship during the 2026 VORRA season. (Jeff Waldaias)

But if the fish ain't biting, Steve ain't happy.

Off the track, the late Kyle Busch was an avid hunter and outdoorsman. In fact, before his death in May, Kyle entered Maine's coveted moose permit lottery. His name was drawn in June, and his son Brexton ultimately went on the hunt in his place.

So I knew the Busch family had an appreciation for the great outdoors.

Still, nothing could have prepared me for the room in Samantha Busch's recent Instagram post.

Samantha is asking for book recommendations, but I'm going to need everyone to direct their attention to the furniture for a moment.

The chair. The antlers. The walls. That little window. Did somebody commission Fred Flintstone to design a hunting lodge?

I have — respectfully — 400 questions about this room, and not one of them is about books.

Tomorrow, it's officially time to start decorating for Christmas. If you're like me (and this buck I'm about to show you), you've already started.

Like a squirrel determined to pilfer bird seed, be ungovernable.

Horse pants! That's it. That's all I have to say.

Back in September, just days after Trey McKinney became the youngest Bassmaster Angler of the Year in history, I caught up with the 21-year-old fishing phenom on "Open Season."

And while we talked plenty about bass fishing, Trey made it very clear he had other things on his mind.

"I basically make my money fishing to spend hunting," he told me.

Trey McKinney, 2026 Bassmaster Angler of the Year, prepares to launch on the final day of The Champions tournament on Old Hickory Lake. (World Bass Enterprises)

He explained that once tournament season wraps up, he trades his fishing rods for shotguns and spends much of the fall and winter chasing waterfowl with his buddies. It's how he unwinds after months on the road.

He just shared a video of himself absolutely hammering geese with Front Range Guide Service.

The fish finally get a break, and now the birds have to deal with this guy.

This week on "Open Season," I sat down with Hannah Graham, co-founder of Marsupial Gear, to talk about her unforgettable first elk hunt in Arizona.

I really appreciated Hannah's honesty in sharing the emotional side of hunting — something that often gets overshadowed by photos of trophy bucks, a freezer full of meat and mounts on the wall.

Taking an animal's life comes with a responsibility that no good hunter takes lightly. And Hannah was refreshingly candid about the pressure, self-doubt and emotions that came with that responsibility.

It's a side of hunting we don't talk about enough, and I think it's a conversation worth having.

articles.title: Houthis target Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports as strikes escalate
articles.excerpt:
Yemen’s Houthi group has struck the port of Jizan on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast as fighting intensifies near the Yemeni city of Taiz.

A Saudi-led military coalition said a Houthi attack on Jizan ca...
articles.body_text:
Yemen’s Houthi group has struck the port of Jizan on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast as fighting intensifies near the Yemeni city of Taiz.

A Saudi-led military coalition said a Houthi attack on Jizan caused only minor damage and no civilian casualties on Wednesday, adding that “efforts are underway to determine the type of projectile” used.

The spokesman for the coalition, Turki al-Maliki, later said in a statement on X that its forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone over Jeddah’s port in Saudi Arabia.

No civilian injuries were reported from falling debris following the interception, he added.

After the coalition’s statement, an explosion was heard in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, according to Al Jazeera’s Nabil al-Yousfi.

The Saudi-led coalition then said its air defences intercepted and destroyed ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh.

The attempted strike on the capital follows a Houthi drone attack on a skyscraper in Riyadh’s financial district on Tuesday, injuring at least 11 people.

The latest incidents mark a further escalation between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia, including strikes from both sides targeting airports, energy facilities and other civilian and economic infrastructure.

The strikes on Saudi Arabian ports come after the Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reported new Saudi attacks on the port of Hodeidah in Yemen.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Houthis threatened to attack Saudi ports if Hodeidah came under attack.

“The port of Hodeidah handles 90 percent of imported goods into Yemen. If it is closed, it could bring the humanitarian situation to the brink of collapse”, said Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Yemen’s capital, Sanaa.

“Some of Saudi Arabia’s recent attacks at the Port of Hodeidah have targeted storage tanks and cranes used to load and unload shipments”, Mawry said.

Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces have been battling the Houthis on several fronts, with the army’s spokesman saying 654 strikes have been carried out against the group on Wednesday.

Yemen’s western front has witnessed the heaviest concentration of recent strikes, according to Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Taiz.

Government forces have said air strikes targeted Houthi positions west of Taiz.

“These strikes are part of an intense and sustained wave of air raids that have continued for approximately 72 hours”, Ali said.

“Particular attention is focused on the most significant mountain range overlooking central Taiz: Jabal Saber and its highest peak, Jabal al-Arus. The government says the Houthis want to seize this strategic peak”, she added.

The Houthis said there have been 105 air strikes and missile attacks by the Saudi-led coalition targeting civilian sites in Sanaa and 10 governorates on Wednesday.

articles.title: Federal judge blocks FCC from reviewing ABC station licenses early as part of agency's spat with network
articles.excerpt:
A judge ordered FCC Chairman Brendan Carr to halt its early review of ABC's broadcasting licenses. (ohn Lamparski/Getty Images for Concordia Annual Summit)

A federal judge ordered Wednesday that the ...
articles.body_text:
A judge ordered FCC Chairman Brendan Carr to halt its early review of ABC's broadcasting licenses. (ohn Lamparski/Getty Images for Concordia Annual Summit)

A federal judge ordered Wednesday that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) halt its early review of broadcasting licenses of eight ABC stations as part of the agency's intense feud with the Disney-owned network.

U.S. District Judge Loren L. AliKhan ruled in favor of ABC, who sued the FCC on First Amendment grounds after the agency announced it was moving up the license renewals of eight stations owned by the network years ahead of schedule.

"This is not a close case," AliKhan wrote in the ruling.

"Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration," an ABC News spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

DISNEY SUES FCC OVER ‘RETALIATORY CAMPAIGN AGAINST ABC,’ SEEKS TO BLOCK EARLY RENEWAL PROCEEDINGS

An ABC News spokesperson called the ruling "important victory for the First Amendment." (Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto)

"While we appreciate the district court denying in part Disney’s request for preliminary injunctive relief, the portion of the decision granting Disney’s motion is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law—as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear," an FCC spokesperson said in a statement. "The FCC looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter. We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations."

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr has called for early renewal of eight ABC-owned stations' licenses in April. The licenses were originally scheduled to be renewed between 2028 and 2031.

KFSN-TV in Fresno, KABC-TV in Los Angeles, KGO-TV in San Francisco, WLS-TV in Chicago, WABC-TV in New York, WTVD in North Carolina, WPVI-TV in Philadelphia and KTRK-TV in Houston were the stations named by the FCC.

FCC BOSS BRENDAN CARR MAINTAINS EARLY ABC LICENSE RENEWAL IS ABOUT DEI PROBE, NOT JIMMY KIMMEL CONTROVERSY

While the FCC maintained the license crackdown was focused on the legality of Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) practices, Carr's announcement came as tensions reignited between President Donald Trump and ABC late-night host Jimmy Kimmel.

Kimmel had quipped First Lady Melania Trump had the glow of an "expectant widow" on his show, a joke made days before a gunman targeted members of the Trump administration at the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner but caught national attention after the assassination attempt. Both the First Lady and President Trump called for ABC to take action against Kimmel at the time.

Carr had previously leveled a thinly-veiled threat against Disney last year over controversial remarks Kimmel made about the assassination of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk.

'THE VIEW' EASED UP ON POLITICAL CANDIDATE BOOKINGS AMID FCC INQUIRY, REPORT SAYS

ABC late-night host Jimmy Kimmel and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr have had an intense feud during the second Trump administration. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images; Alberto Rodriguez/Variety via Getty Images)

The FCC separately launched a probe into ABC's daytime talk show "The View" in an effort to upend its status as a bona fide news program, which exempts the network from abiding by longstanding rules requiring equal time for political candidates.

In previous court filings, ABC has claimed that the actions taken by the FCC has had a chilling effect on the network's free speech, pointing to how "The View" has refrained from inviting political candidates onto the show as a result of the crackdown.

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

articles.title: Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather
articles.excerpt:
New York City mayor on postponing 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade

Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York to Saturday because of severe weather.

Preparations t...
articles.body_text:
New York City mayor on postponing 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade

Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York to Saturday because of severe weather.

Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.

The last time the parade was suspended was during World War Two, but it has never been postponed due to weather. In 1971, Macy's decided to ground the balloons, which often feature beloved characters from pop culture, because of weather.

A powerful coastal storm is set to affect the New York area in coming days.

The balloons will be deflated again and then re-inflated for Saturday

On Wednesday night, New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency for Long Island, New York City and Westchester County

The potent nor'easter is expected to make it too windy and dangerous for the iconic balloons to fly.

Macy's had expected to put 100 inflatables into the sky to mark its 100th parade and feature 10 new balloons, including one depicting the animated dog Bluey wearing a crown and another showing a Minion character riding a banana like a horse.

"While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants and spectators is, and always will be, our top priority," said Will Cross, the parade's executive producer, during a news conference on Wednesday with city officials.

Cross also said the giant balloons would be deflated on Wednesday night and stored at a facility in neighbouring New Jersey until they were reinflated for the parade on Saturday.

Macy's confirmed the new parade date and updated a countdown clock on its website to reflect the Saturday schedule. Meanwhile, broadcaster NBC has said it will show the 2025 parade on Thursday.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who will not attend the parade on Saturday because of a scheduled surgery, said at the news conference that "you have to plan for every possibility" and confirmed that "extreme weather has forced" officials to make the change.

"We know that this is an inconvenience for many who come to visit our city. This decision, however, was made with safety being paramount," he said. "We want to ensure that we're delivering a parade that's not only incredible and spectacular, but one also that doesn't come at the expense of anyone's safety."

Mamdani also said that there would be an expanded police presence along the parade route on Saturday and that there were "no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time".

Cross added that Macy's is working through what costs it could cover as a result of the delay and said the company is in contact with bands, performers and others who travelled to the city for the parade.

BBC Weather's Elizabeth Rizzini looks at the weather that will impact travel over US Thanksgiving.

During some past parades, strong winds and inclement weather have led to the tearing and deflation of the balloons as well as collisions with lampposts that caused injuries.

The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade was due to end.

Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern US as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow, BBC Weather reports.

The governor of the neighbouring state of New Jersey on Wednesday declared a state of emergency across the state's 21 counties, beginning at 18:00 local time (23:00 GMT).

Governor Mikie Sherrill's office said the powerful coastal storm is expected to bring damaging winds, heavy rainfall, and severe tidal flooding through Friday, with coastal and bayside communities facing the greatest risk. Sherrill urged residents to stay off the roads as much as possible once the storm arrives.

Originally called the Macy's Christmas Parade, the celebration, which also features live performers, debuted in 1924 as a way to boost holiday sales. It was founded by Macy's employees and their families.

From 1942 to 1944 New York went without the parade as the US directed materials like rubber and helium toward the country's war effort.

The 2.5mi (4km) procession route begins at Macy's Herald Square flagship store and concludes in Manhattan's Upper West Side, with performers and spectators lining the streets to greet Santa Claus and ring in the holiday season.

Country artist Megan Moroney and Grammy nominee Teddy Swims were slated to perform at the flagship store, but it is unclear whether they, along with the dozens of celebrities and float performers on the roster, would be returning on Saturday.

Departures heading to Miami...

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway on Wednesday evening.

Departures heading to Miami were grounded just after 20:15 local time (01:15 GMT) and all but one runway at the airport was closed, according to the FAA advisory. Flights are expected to resume by around 22:00 local time, the FAA told the BBC.

The airliner that ran past the runway arrived from Memphis. No injuries have been reported. The FAA is investigating the incident.

The ground stop comes on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.

Flight delays in Miami reached one hour but appeared to be declining later Wednesday night.

Passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night were encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport.

"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," Miami-Dade Aviation Department spokesman Greg Chin said in a statement to the BBC.

The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travelers in the country over this holiday week, according to the American Automobile Association.

The Miami-Dade area is under a flood watch until late Wednesday night. Periods of heavy rain throughout the day are expected to cause flooding, according to the US National Weather Service.

A nationwide ground stop earlier this month halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

articles.title: Anthropic CEO Amodei denies wanting humanity to ‘surrender’ free will to AI
articles.excerpt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has denied believing that humanity should “surrender” control to artificial intelligence amid predictions that models potentially far exceeding human intelligence are immine...
articles.body_text:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has denied believing that humanity should “surrender” control to artificial intelligence amid predictions that models potentially far exceeding human intelligence are imminent.

In a lengthy post on X on Wednesday, Amodei said he does not support surrendering “human free will” to AI and has long argued that the frontier technology should be subject to “legitimate democratic processes”.

“If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years,” Amodei said, responding to an Axios report about a purported “consensus” inside Anthropic that some decision-making authority should be passed to the technology.

“But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.”

Amodei’s remarks come amid a flurry of commentary by top industry executives suggesting that AI will soon match or surpass human intelligence.

The prospect of AI that equals or outperforms the best human minds – referred to as artificial general intelligence (AGI) and artificial super-intelligence (ASI), respectively – has fuelled intense debate in Silicon Valley and beyond about whether such technology can be harnessed for good without exposing humanity to catastrophic harm.

AI safety advocates have raised fears that models being developed by firms such as Anthropic, which made history last week in the biggest initial public offering of all time, could slip out of human control, particularly once systems start improving without human input, a process known as recursive self-improvement.

In his X post, Amodei criticised commentary he said conflated the idea of AI taking over specific tasks with surrendering control in a “grand sense of global governance”.

“This is not AI ‘running the world’, but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end,” Amodei said.

“Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc.”

“It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives,” he added. “But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.”

Citing unnamed sources, Axios reported on Wednesday that Amodei and other Anthropic executives believe it would be irrational “or even unethical” not to hand over authority to AI for tasks it can do better than humans, such as curing diseases.

David Krueger, the founder of Evitable, a nonprofit that campaigns against the development of ASI, said Anthropic should pause its work if Amodei is genuinely concerned about humanity losing control of frontier models.

“We don’t have to consciously surrender control to AI to lose it. As AI becomes increasingly capable, there will be mounting pressure to push humans out of decision-making roles across society,” Krueger told Al Jazeera.

“Meanwhile, researchers at Dario’s own company are warning that AI capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to control them. We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”

While there is no universally agreed-upon definition of AGI or ASI, key tech industry figures have over the past week suggested that the milestones are near.

Google DeepMind’s chief AGI scientist and cofounder, Shane Legg, said on Wednesday he believes there is a more than 50 percent chance that “minimal” AGI arrives before 2028.

“We’re getting close now,” Legg said on X.

On Sunday, Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, said ASI is “arriving”, pointing to the announcement that an Anthropic employee had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.

“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in,” Wang said on X.

articles.title: FedEx cargo jet overshoots runway at Miami International Airport and stops just short of busy road
articles.excerpt:
Video shows the scene at Miami International Airport after a disabled aircraft prompted an FAA ground stop on the eve of Thanksgiving (Credit: WSVN).

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued ...
articles.body_text:
Video shows the scene at Miami International Airport after a disabled aircraft prompted an FAA ground stop on the eve of Thanksgiving (Credit: WSVN).

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a ground stop at Miami International Airport Wednesday evening due to a disabled FedEx aircraft after it overshot the runway, disrupting flights amid the busy Thanksgiving holiday travel rush.

Video from the scene shows a large FedEx cargo jet sitting near a fence that runs next to a busy road. The airport confirmed the aircraft overran Runway 26R, prompting all runways to close except for Runway 9R. Miami-Dade Fire Rescue responded to the airport and reported no injuries.

The incident comes nearly three months after a Prime Air cargo jet overran Runway 30 at Miami International Airport, killing five people.

FAA ISSUES GROUND DELAY AT CHICAGO O'HARE DUE TO 'EQUIPMENT OUTAGE'

The Federal Aviation Administration cited a disabled aircraft as the reason for issuing a ground stop affecting Miami-bound flights Wednesday evening. (WSVN)

In a statement provided to Fox News Digital shortly before 10 p.m., the FAA said flights would be "resuming shortly" at the airport.

The FAA said FedEx Flight 910, a McDonnell Douglas MD-11 arriving from Frederick W. Smith International Airport in Memphis, Tennessee, ran off the runway after landing in Miami.

No injuries have been reported, according to the agency.

FedEx confirmed the incident in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying the plane's crew was safe.

articles.body_text:
OutKick's Dan Dakich weighs in on the Aaron Rodgers fallout.

USC pulled its marching band from Saturday's rivalry game at the Rose Bowl following a late-night campus prank at UCLA.

Ahead of the Big Ten matchup between No. 15 USC and No. 9 UCLA, officials barred the Trojan Marching Band from its pregame and halftime shows after members allegedly vandalized signage at the Wasserman Football Center.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The USC Trojan marching band performs at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum in Los Angeles, Calif., on Sept. 12, 2026. (ISI Photos via Getty Images)

The incident capped off a spirited Tuesday night in Los Angeles.

An hour after the latest College Football Playoff rankings dropped, USC held its annual Conquest pep rally featuring a mock fight between the USC and UCLA mascots. The marching band performed and several USC players attended. Head coach Lincoln Riley did not make an appearance.

ARMY CADETS SNEAK INTO NAVY'S STADIUM TO LEAVE A SPECIAL MESSAGE IN THE UPPER DECK

Later that night, according to UCLA's Daily Bruin, band members allegedly crossed town and removed letters from the Wasserman Football Center's exterior sign to spell "ass Football Center."

The USC Trojans band performs the national anthem with a flyover before an NCAA football game between the USC Trojans and the San José State Spartans at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum in Los Angeles on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (MediaNews Group via Getty Images)

The vandalism left the facility temporarily branded as the "ASS Football Center." USC President Beong-Soo Kim responded Wednesday with a formal apology to UCLA.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL CORPORATE OVERLORDS RUIN ANOTHER CLASSIC RIVALRY GAME WITH STUPID NEW NAME

"This morning, we learned that a portion of UCLA's campus had been vandalized by individual students belonging to the Trojan Marching Band. This conduct runs contrary to USC's values and is unacceptable," Kim wrote in a statement to the Trojan community.

"We are cooperating fully with law enforcement and an investigation is underway. Appropriate interim actions will be or have already been taken, and any student ultimately found responsible will be subject to discipline under university policy."

The USC Trojan Marching Band performs during the world premiere of "The Cat in the Hat" on Oct. 25, 2026, in Burbank, Calif. (Getty Images for Warner Bros. Pictures)

The move will sideline hundreds of student musicians for the actions of a few. Kim added that the decision was made jointly with band leadership.

"We want to express our deepest apologies to the entire UCLA community. Our rivalry is one of the great traditions in college athletics, and it has always rested on mutual respect. What happened on UCLA's campus last night has no place in this tradition," Kim wrote.

"Out of respect for UCLA, and to provide time to reflect on the collective responsibility we share to uphold our university's values, the university and Trojan Marching Band's leadership have decided that the band will not take the field for their traditional pre-game and halftime performances at the Rose Bowl this Saturday."

The USC Trojans band performs during the second half against the Nebraska Cornhuskers at Memorial Stadium in Lincoln, Neb., on Nov. 1, 2025. (Getty Images)

The USC Trojan Marching Band performs during the world premiere of "The Cat in the Hat" on Oct. 25, 2026, in Burbank, Calif. (Getty Images for Warner Bros. Pictures)

A USC spokesperson declined to share details on the damages or disciplinary process, telling Fox News Digital.

"The university does not have further comment as the investigation into the matter is ongoing."

UCLA offered Fox News Digital a much looser response: "Go Bruins. Beat SC!"

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Crosstown Showdown has a long history of rivalry week pranks and campus raids. Every November, USC students wrap the Tommy Trojan statue in duct tape to protect it from blue and gold paint, while UCLA students pull overnight shifts guarding the Bruin Bear statue and hiding it under a wooden box.

USC and UCLA kick off Saturday afternoon in Pasadena. No "Tusk" blaring from the sidelines.
