articles.title: Netanyahu declares corruption trial has 'fallen apart' after judges question key charges
articles.excerpt: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu criticized Zohran Mamdani over the NYC mayor’s call for his arrest as large anti-Israel protests descended upon the city during his address to the UN General ...
articles.body_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu criticized Zohran Mamdani over the NYC mayor’s call for his arrest as large anti-Israel protests descended upon the city during his address to the UN General Assembly.

The decade-long legal battle against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suffered a major blow Wednesday after judges cast doubt on key corruption charges, prompting the Israeli leader to declare that his trial had "fallen apart" and demand an immediate end to the proceedings.

A three-judge panel at the Jerusalem District Court suggested that Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara consider dropping the most serious case against Netanyahu, questioned whether a criminal offense occurred in a second case and recommended resolving a third through a plea deal.

"Today, the trial fell apart," Netanyahu said in an evening address following the proceedings, according to The Times of Israel.

FROM INTELLIGENCE SHARING TO MISSILE DEFENSE, HOW ISRAEL'S PARTNERSHIP PROTECTS AMERICAN SECURITY

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attends his trial on corruption charges at the district court in Tel Aviv March 12, 2025. (Yair Sagi/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

"Ten years ago, I said, ‘There will be nothing because there was nothing.’ But it took 10 years for this truth to be revealed to everyone," he said.

"Citizens of Israel, this trial must end immediately. And what also needs to end immediately is what came out of it — the hatred, the incitement, the division."

The court's intervention dealt a major setback to prosecutors more than six years after Netanyahu's trial began and roughly a decade after authorities launched the initial probe into him.

Judges had summoned Baharav-Miara to court Wednesday amid concerns over the strength of the prosecution's evidence and whether continuing the cases served the public interest.

"We’re now at a crossroad and need to rechart a new path," Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman told the attorney general, according to The New York Sun.

"Public interest dictates a need to rethink."

NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO'

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, center, waves from the stage next to his wife Sara during a Jewish New Year greetings event attended by Likud party members in Tel Aviv Sept. 17, 2026. (Jack Guez/AFPvia Getty Images)

She and her colleagues, Judges Moshe Bar-Am and Oded Shaham, stressed that their comments were preliminary, did not constitute a verdict and applied only to Netanyahu because they still had to hear the other defendants’ testimony, The Jerusalem Post reported.

Baharav-Miara signaled that prosecutors would review the judges' recommendations and weigh their options.

Netanyahu faces charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust stemming from three corruption investigations.

Prosecutors announced the charges in November 2019 and formally filed the indictment in January 2020, and Netanyahu consistently denied wrongdoing.

The most serious charge, Case 4000, centers on allegations that Netanyahu granted regulatory favors to Israeli telecommunications giant Bezeq in exchange for favorable coverage on the Walla news website, which was then controlled by businessman Shaul Elovitch.

Judges questioned whether prosecutors presented sufficient evidence to secure a conviction. In Case 2000, prosecutors also allege Netanyahu negotiated for favorable coverage from Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper publisher Arnon Mozes in exchange for legislation to weaken rival newspaper Israel Hayom.

TRUMP WANTS LARGEST-EVER ISRAELI HEAVY BOMB TRANSFER — BUT PROPOSAL HAS CONGRESS PREPARING FOR $2.8B FIGHT

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivers remarks during a toast by heads of Israel's political factions on the day of the inauguration of Israel's 26th parliament at the Knesset in Jerusalem Nov. 10, 2026. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)

The proposed deal never materialized, and judges questioned whether a criminal offense had happened.

Case 1000 centers on allegations that Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, received almost $300,000 in gifts from Hollywood producer Arnon Milchan and Australian billionaire James Packer.

Judges suggested resolving that case through an agreement. Zion Amir, an attorney who previously represented Netanyahu in the proceedings, rejected the prospect of a settlement.

In his address Wednesday, Netanyahu also accused investigators of pressuring his political associates to testify against him and described the toll the investigations had taken on his family.

"Ten years of terrible suffering for me, my wife and my sons," he said.

"Of delusional interrogations. Of character assassination. Of grave incitement that wounds the soul. Who will give us back those 10 years?"

Netanyahu, who requested a presidential pardon in November 2025 without admitting guilt, also called on his political opponents to set aside their differences and form a unity government.

"The boycotts must end, and now," Netanyahu said.

"I know what enormous and immediate dangers the State of Israel faces. There is only one way to deal with them. To unite in order to deal with them. We must unite to secure the future of Israel — no less than that, and immediately."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over?
articles.excerpt:
Some analysts fear Somali security forces may not be able to handle the nation's security without external support

Somalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing,...
articles.body_text:
Some analysts fear Somali security forces may not be able to handle the nation's security without external support

Somalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing, funding for its security forces comes under pressure and a bitter political dispute threatens to derail plans for the country's first direct democratic elections in decades.

The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions.

Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu.

The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) troops supporting the government.

The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control.

Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year.

Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission, is also reportedly planning to withdraw about 3,000 troops. The country has 2,500 troops authorised under the AU mission and roughly 5,000 under a bilateral agreement with Somalia. It is not clear whether the reported withdrawals would be from the AU contingent, the bilateral force, or both.

The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of $500m UNSOS's annual budget, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations.

With military support uncertain and the government facing mounting political challenges, analysts question whether Somalia's security forces are ready to stand on their own.

The concerns were heightened recently when al-Shabab claimed to have killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an attack. The government acknowledged the attack but did not disclose the number of casualties.

Abdisalam Guleid, a former deputy director of Somalia's National Security Agency, told the BBC the security situation was increasingly precarious.

He warned that the withdrawal of foreign troops could leave Mogadishu vulnerable to a takeover similar to that of Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2021, following the withdrawal of US and Nato forces.

"I don't think Mogadishu will be able to defend itself. The Taliban style [takeover]… that's the most likely scenario I can envision now," he said.

The Taliban took over control of Afghanistan between 6-15 August 2021 in a rapid offensive, following the withdrawal of US and NATO forces.

Such a scenario has played out in Somalia in the past, Guleid explains.

Why is Uganda fighting in 'hellish' Somalia?

Somalia has experienced the collapse of central authority before.

In the early 1990s, clan-based rebel groups advanced on Mogadishu from several fronts, forcing then-President Mohamed Siad Barre from power.

His overthrow triggered a devastating civil war and a prolonged humanitarian crisis. The collapse of state institutions subsequently created conditions in which Islamist militant groups, including al-Shabab, were able to expand their influence.

Guleid says Ugandan troops have been central to preventing a similar collapse since their first deployment to Somalia in 2007.

They played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns, while protecting strategic installations, including the airport, seaport, government institutions and diplomatic missions.

Troops from Burundi, Djibouti, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Ethiopia later joined the AU mission, while countries including Turkey and the US maintained separate military deployments and provided training and equipment to Somali forces.

But Guleid argues that years of international assistance have not translated into sufficient military independence for the Somali government.

He says the authorities have become so reliant on foreign protection that they have neglected to adequately prepare their own forces to take over.

Somalia's Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud rejected suggestions that the country would be unable to cope with the withdrawals.

He told the BBC that Somali troops had already taken over some positions vacated by Ugandan forces and were prepared to assume greater responsibility for the country's security.

He said Somalia could not depend indefinitely on foreign troops for its protection.

"I believe there is no reason for concern over this issue. There will be no change in the country's security situation or in the areas they have vacated," he said.

President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has also been seeking continued international backing.

During a visit to Uganda on 23 November, he and President Yoweri Museveni called on the international community to continue supporting Somalia to consolidate security gains.

Uganda troops were first deployed to Somalia in 2007

Not everyone believes the withdrawal will necessarily result in a security collapse.

Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa argues that years of international military support have helped Somalia establish the institutions needed to take greater responsibility for its security.

He says the withdrawal will provide an opportunity to assess how much progress has been made.

It will also force Somalia's political leaders to put aside their differences and take greater responsibility for the country's future, he adds.

But other analysts warn that the timing could hardly be worse.

Omar Mahmood, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, says Somali forces are  under considerable pressure as they fight al-Shabab while attempting to take over positions previously held by foreign troops.

This is a major undertaking for an army that is still developing, he says.

The military is also facing pressure in the Bay region of the South-West state, where forces loyal to ousted regional President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed have been fighting the federal government.

The withdrawal of Ugandan troops from the Lower Shabelle region could create further security challenges, Mahmood adds.

Mahmood further points to the long-delayed elections, which need to be secured, as another issue compounding the security situation.

Somalia has been attempting to move away from an indirect electoral system in which clan elders select lawmakers, who then elect the president, towards a system of direct voting.

Beyond the military situation, Mahmood says, the government must also resolve a growing political dispute over the timing and format of the country's elections.

But the proposed changes have divided the government and opposition, with disagreements over how the elections should be conducted.

The dispute escalated this year after Mohamud pushed through constitutional amendments extending the presidential term from four to five years, effectively delaying the next elections until 2027.

Al-Shabab militants still pose a big threat against the government

This month, the Supreme Court ruled against the extension, ordering political leaders to agree on an electoral roadmap within 30 days and to hold elections within three months.

A day before the ruling, Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed. He and other judges in the case have filed a suit against Somalia over the dismissals at the East African regional court in Tanzania.

The Somali government has since rejected the Supreme Court's decision, with its implementation now uncertain.

Mahmood says the political and security crises are closely connected, with the absence of consensus over the elections making it harder for the government to focus on the fight against al-Shabab.

Guleid also warns that the threat to Somalia's stability comes not only from the militant group but from clan-based militias increasingly challenging the federal government.

"Today, we have clan loyalists fighting alongside al-Shabab against the federal government," he said.

He added the country's leadership appears unable to anticipate the scale of the challenges ahead.

Who will fill the gap left by foreign partners?

Somalia's security challenges are compounded by its heavy dependence on international financial support.

Latest data from its finance ministry shows that donor grants amounting to $878.8m accounts for two-thirds of its planned $1.36bn budget in 2026.

Despite that, the ministry said it had only received about $314m of grants in the first nine months of the year, equivalent to 35% the expected annual aid.

Mahmood believes that although some international military support is declining, other partners could help bridge the gap through bilateral agreements and continued assistance.

But Guleid is sceptical that countries such as Turkey, Qatar and Egypt could quickly replace the military and financial contributions of Uganda and the US.

He argues that Somalia's dependence on external support makes it particularly vulnerable when international partners change their priorities.

That dependence has also contributed to increasingly strained relations with some foreign governments.

Somalia's challenges are compounded by its heavy reliance on foreign support

Somalia has accused the United Arab Emirates of funding armed groups and undermining its sovereignty, in the latest dispute involving an external power with significant security and economic interests in the country.

The UAE has rejected the criticism and hit back at the Somali leader, describing him as an "outgoing president" in reference to the dispute over his presidential mandate.

The two countries formally severed ties earlier this year, although the UAE has long been an important security and economic partner in Somalia.

The dispute illustrates the difficult relationship Somalia has with foreign partners on whom it relies for security, funding and political support.

For Egesa, the withdrawal of foreign troops could ultimately provide an opportunity for Somalia to demonstrate how much progress it has made in rebuilding its security institutions.

He believes the staggered departure of troops will allow Somali forces to assume responsibility gradually, while also forcing rival political factions to work together.

He argues that unless Somalia addresses its military weaknesses, political divisions and growing influence of armed groups, it risks losing the security gains made.

For now, it faces the difficult task of fighting an entrenched insurgency, managing rival political interests and preparing for a contentious electoral process, all while some of military partners are preparing to leave.

Whether Somalia can withstand these pressures without renewed instability remains an open question.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un says North Korea should widen deployment of tactical nukes
articles.excerpt:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has urged his country to focus on deploying tactical nuclear weapons “across multiple domains for different missions”.

Kim said North Korea’s nuclear material producti...
articles.body_text:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has urged his country to focus on deploying tactical nuclear weapons “across multiple domains for different missions”.

Kim said North Korea’s nuclear material production capacity was being systematically expanded on Thursday, according to state media KCNA.

Maintaining North Korea’s status as a nuclear-weapons state was “absolutely inviolable”, Kim said during an inspection of nuclear material production and weapons research facilities. KCNA did not identify the facilities or their locations.

The country’s status would not change because of what he called “denuclearisation rhetoric from forces that ignore objective reality and failed to recognise the changed situation”.

“Our nuclear capability is now a reality,” he said, calling recent achievements in nuclear weapons production a major success in carrying ⁠⁠out the country’s nuclear policy.

Any attempt to deny North Korea’s nuclear status, which it enshrined in its constitution in 2023, would be regarded as “an open declaration of war”, he said.

Kim said diversified use of tactical nuclear weapons was an “important and urgent task raised from tactical nukes’ military value in modern warfare and from the inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state”.

Kim’s statements come during a growing border dispute with South Korea over a landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), a heavily fortified territory between the two countries, on September 21.

Seoul demanded an apology from Pyongyang in October after a joint South Korea-United Nations investigation found that North Korea had planted the landmines more than a year ago.

Pyongyang sent a letter to the UN Security Council in response, accusing Seoul of fabricating the explosion, and fired about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast into the Sea of Japan less than a week later.

South Korea estimates that North Korea possesses between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads.

articles.title: Aaron Rodgers' ex-Packers teammate makes bold prediction about QB’s NFL future after shocking Steelers exit
articles.excerpt: Nick Wright, Danny Parkins, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes reacted to Aaron Rodgers’ shocking release from the Pittsburgh Steelers. Plus, Danny Parkins served up his picks for the NFL’s Week 12 mat...
articles.body_text:
Nick Wright, Danny Parkins, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes reacted to Aaron Rodgers’ shocking release from the Pittsburgh Steelers. Plus, Danny Parkins served up his picks for the NFL’s Week 12 matchups.

Aaron Rodgers’ time with the Pittsburgh Steelers ended abruptly just one day before Thanksgiving. The team cut ties with the veteran quarterback shortly after benching him and following his disparaging comments about coach Mike McCarthy during an appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show" on Wednesday.

Rodgers, who was in his second season with the Steelers, alleged that McCarthy had been sleeping through team meetings.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"That ship has sailed," Rodgers said about his stint in Pittsburgh. While his future in the NFL remains unclear, but former longtime Green Bay Packers teammate Clay Matthews offered a bold prediction.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers (8) walks off the field following an NFL football game against the Cincinnati Bengals in Cincinnati Thursday, Oct. 16, 2025. (AP Photo/Carolyn Kaster)

"I think this is the last time we see him in the league. I don't think another team wants him as their quarterback." Matthews said on Netflix ahead of the Los Angeles Rams and Green Bay Packers kicked off for the NFL's first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game.

The Packers drafted Matthews in the first round in 2009. Matthews went on to spend a decade with Rodgers, helping Green Bay win Super Bowl XLV during his second season.

WHAT’S YOUR TAKE: WILL AARON RODGERS PLAY ANOTHER SNAP THIS SEASON?

"It's sad, (Rodgers is) one of the greatest quarterbacks we've ever had in this National Football League. For him to end his career like this, walking off the football field like this, that's very sad," Pro Football Hall of Famer Michael Irvin added.

Green Bay Packers quarterback Aaron Rodgers and linebacker Clay Matthews celebrate after the Packers defeated the Pittsburgh Steelers 31-25 in Super Bowl XLV in Arlington, Texas on Feb. 6, 2011. (TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images)

The NFL's trade deadline for this season had already passed by the time Rodgers was released, meaning the four-time league MVP will have to go through waivers before another potentially interested team claims him. If Rodgers makes it through waivers unclaimed, he would then be an unrestricted free agent.

Mason Rudolph is expected to start when the Black Friday game against the Denver Broncos kicks off. Rodgers suggested he was unaware he wouldn't be the starter going forward until a teammate alerted him.

AARON RODGERS AND MIKE MCCARTHY DISAGREEMENTS AT HEART OF QUARTERBACK'S BENCHING BY THE STEELERS

Rodgers said Steelers tight end Pat Freiermuth said during a phone call, "I can't believe they're doing this."

Although his ending wasn't ideal, Rodgers expressed appreciation for his time with the Steelers.

Aaron Rodgers and Head Coach Mike McCarthy of the Pittsburgh Steelers chat before an NFL game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia on Nov. 22, 2026. (Getty Images)

"I thanked Mike T [Tomlin] last year for giving me that joy and passion back. I mean, in the two years I've been here, I've made some super tight friendships, and we got such a good group of guys, such a great veteran leadership, guys that give a s---, guys that play hard, great personalities all over the board," he said.

articles.title: Photos: Storms and an El Nino-charged king tide batter California’s coast
articles.excerpt:
California and other parts of the United States West Coast have experienced record-high water levels, causing flooding, destruction and dangerous waves.

On Wednesday, the National Oceanic and Atmosph...
articles.body_text:
California and other parts of the United States West Coast have experienced record-high water levels, causing flooding, destruction and dangerous waves.

On Wednesday, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) announced that the fishing community of Charleston, Oregon, notched its highest-ever coastal water level, roughly 1.12 metres above the mean high water level.

It was as high as 3.4 metres above the mean low water mark.

Other NOAA stations recorded some of their highest water levels on record, including San Diego, Los Angeles and Santa Barbara, all on the southern California coast.

Further north, the L-shaped municipal pier in Pacifica, a city south of San Francisco, crumbled into the surf after a wave as tall as its platform crashed into it.

In a video on social media, bystanders could be heard voicing astonishment at the sight. “Oh my god, it’s gone. Oh my god,” one person said.

The pier had faced multiple closures in recent years, as seawater weakened its concrete structure, but experts say this week’s conditions were more dangerous than normal.

The high coastal water levels were spurred by a combination of factors, including a phenomenon popularly known as king tides.

The term is applied to the highest tides of the year, created when both the sun and the moon are aligned to create a larger-than-normal tidal bulge, pulling the water with their combined gravitational force.

The king tides have been exacerbated by the El Nino weather pattern as well as human-fuelled climate change.

While El Nino is a regular occurrence, this year’s edition is projected to be stronger than normal, according to forecasters, leading to record-warm waters off the Pacific coast. That warming, in turn, helps churn up powerful storms that contribute to waves battering the shoreline.

San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie announced on Wednesday that his city had made it through the worst of this week’s surge with flooding and waves up to 9 metres, but he warned of more king tides to come.

“The last two weeks have been an important reminder to get prepared for the rest of El Nino season. We’re expecting more king tides in December and January,” he wrote on social media. “We need to take these events seriously, prepare ahead of future storms, and stay alert.”

articles.title: Ukraine attacks Russian military base, says five planes struck

Ukrainian forces have hit a major Russian military base east of Moscow, damaging five aircraft used to launch missiles and bombs, according to the Ukrainian General Staff.

Ukraine struck the Savasleyka airbase in the Nizhny Novgorod region, the General Staff said on Wednesday, adding that three MiG-31 jets were used to fire hypersonic missiles and two Su-34 fighter-bombers were damaged.

Russia did not immediately comment on the report by the General Staff, which said the Savasleyka airbase had been hit in the latest long-range attacks aimed at crippling Moscow’s war effort.

The operation followed a series of high-profile strikes by Ukrainian forces in recent days in which two Russian ships were hit in Libyan waters and a Russian vessel was struck in the Gulf of Finland.

Last week, Ukraine destroyed the road portion of Russia’s prized bridge to the Crimea peninsula after consecutive attacks.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and fighting has continued despite a renewed US-backed push to end what has become Europe’s worst conflict since World War II.

Kyiv is trying to dent Moscow’s military might as it struggles under a renewed campaign of attacks on its energy system and mounting Russian strikes on front-line cities.

Ukrainian forces are hunting Russian ballistic-missile launchers used to carry out many of those attacks, striking 16 over the past several months, Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said this week.

Renewed Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian oil refineries’ processing volumes by 45 percent since late October, industry sources said this month. Kyiv has said it will stop striking Russian energy targets only when Moscow does the same.

Total Nonstop Action Wrestling (TNA) successfully put on a thrilling Destination X pay-per-view earlier this month despite a ground stop that hampered travel for millions in North America.

Several TNA wrestlers were affected by the flight issues. Many made it work, while others were forced to skip the show. Still, the show went on. KC Navarro ended up winning the men’s Ultimate X match and earning a shot at the X Division Championship.

But Navarro wasn’t exempt from the chaos.

"Me and Tasha Steelz were actually on the same flight," he explained to OutKick Dropkick. "Funny enough, the two winners of the Ultimate X were on the same flight, almost didn't have winners. articles.title: California warns of flooding as King Tides peak over Thanksgiving
articles.excerpt:
High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communities

Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Wa...
articles.body_text:
High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communities

Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.

The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.

Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.

Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.

Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.

Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.

In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.

In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.

Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.

King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.

While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record.

Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.

On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.

Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.

"Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.

The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.

The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.

The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.

The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.

Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.

Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.

King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

articles.title: Carla Babb Named Head of Content for Military Times and Defense News
articles.excerpt: Carla Babb is joining Military Times and Defense News as our new Head of Content. In nearly two decades covering national security and international affairs, Babb has earned a reputation for fearless,...
articles.body_text:
Carla Babb is joining Military Times and Defense News as our new Head of Content. In nearly two decades covering national security and international affairs, Babb has earned a reputation for fearless, fact-driven journalism and deep relationships across the U.S. defense establishment.

Recognized as one of the nation’s most candid and well-sourced defense journalists, Babb has broken major stories, pressed senior military leaders for answers and reported from conflict zones around the world. In her new role, she will spearhead editorial initiatives, lead enterprise projects and expand the publications’ presence at major events while developing new ways to engage military, defense industry and national security audiences.

Babb will work alongside Editor-in-Chief J.D. Simkins, who continues to lead coverage by the Military Times and Defense News newsroom. Under Simkins, the newsroom has published its 10 most-read stories of all time within the last year. Simkins was also a recent recipient of the Timothy White Award for Editorial Integrity at SIIA’s Jesse H. Neal Awards. Together, they will lead the next chapter for the brands.

“Carla is one of the most respected and versatile journalists covering national security, and she is the right person to help lead what comes next for Military Times and Defense News,” said Kelly Facer, Senior Vice President at Sightline Media Group, which publishes Military Times and Defense News. “For decades, the military and defense community has trusted these brands to tell them what is really happening. With Carla and J.D. leading our editorial work together, we will build on that trust as we expand into new coverage areas, programs and events for our audience.”

Babb most recently served as national security correspondent for Newsmax and spent more than a decade as Voice of America’s Pentagon correspondent, reaching a global audience of hundreds of millions. She has also reported for Military Times and Defense News.

Babb’s scoops include the 2020 Iranian missile attack on U.S. troops at Iraq’s Al-Asad Air Base, U.S. military interdictions of illicit oil tankers in 2025, and troop deployments and military operations during the 2026 war with Iran. Her interviews with senior military leaders have generated headlines across major national outlets, including The Washington Post, Newsweek, Fox News and NBC News.

“Military Times and Defense News are where service members and their families turn for unvarnished insight and accountability on the issues that shape their lives, and I’m excited about where we can take them next,” said Babb. “I’m eager to get to work with Jon and this newsroom to chase the stories our readers need, widen our coverage and shape national security conversations.”

A prominent advocate for independent defense journalism, Babb serves as vice president of the board of Military Reporters and Editors.

Later this week, Babb will receive the prestigious Prize of Excellence from the Association of Foreign Correspondents in the United States for her outstanding contributions to journalism and distinguished national security reporting. Her work has also earned recognition from the Gerald R. Ford Presidential Foundation, the Press Club of Atlantic City, and regional Associated Press and Society of Professional Journalists chapters.

articles.title: Could renewed strikes on Hodeidah port worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis?
articles.excerpt:
The Saudi-led coalition has launched renewed attacks on Houthi targets at Yemen’s port of Hodeidah as the armed group fights Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

The strikes come amid signi...
articles.body_text:
The Saudi-led coalition has launched renewed attacks on Houthi targets at Yemen’s port of Hodeidah as the armed group fights Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

The strikes come amid significant Houthi territorial gains in recent weeks and escalating attacks by the group on Saudi Arabia.

Hodeidah, which has repeatedly been attacked over the past decade, is critical to both Yemen’s economy and the supply of essential goods to millions of people in Houthi-controlled areas.

The port of Hodeidah, situated on Yemen’s western Red Sea coast, is the country’s principal commercial seaport and has been under Houthi control since 2014.

It serves as a major entry point for food, fuel and other commercial goods as well as humanitarian assistance, supplying the densely populated northern and western regions of Yemen, including the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa.

The port had eight berths and the capacity to accommodate 6,500 standard shipping containers in 2023. However, attrition due to Yemen’s more than a decade of conflict has reduced the number of operational berths and damaged cranes and storage facilities.

Despite this, in September 2025, the United Nations Mission to Support the Hodeidah Agreement estimated that the port handled about 70 percent of commercial imports and 80 percent of humanitarian aid coming into Yemen, calling it a “lifeline”.

“The closure or disruption [of the port] under the current circumstances would delay the arrival of food, medicine and fuel; increase transport costs and prices; and exacerbate the suffering of families already facing an acute humanitarian crisis,” said Abdusattor Esoev, Yemen Chief of Mission for the International Organization for Migration.

“At a time when millions of people in Yemen depend on humanitarian assistance and face severe food insecurity, Hodeidah remains a critical lifeline. The port is essential for bringing in food, fuel, medicines and other basic goods needed by civilians across northern Yemen,” said Francesca Quinto, the programme manager for Yemen for Doctors Without Borders.

However, the Houthis have long been accused of using Hodeidah’s port for both civilian and military purposes. Investigations have found that the group exploits commercial port facilities to smuggle in weapons from Iran, its chief ally.

“The ports of Hodeidah are key to commercial flows. However, the Houthis’ increasing militarisation of vital civilian infrastructure by smuggling and storing arms, fuel and narcotics is undermining the humanitarian functions they serve in wartime,” Ibrahim Jalal, a senior researcher and policy adviser, told Al Jazeera.

Tawfiq al-Hamidi, a Yemeni lawyer and human rights activist, told Al Jazeera that the port has been misused by the group for smuggling despite its importance for Yemen’s population.

“Nevertheless, efforts must be made to protect the port as a civilian facility, and the Houthi movement must provide genuine guarantees,” he said.

Yes. Since the start of Yemen’s civil war in September 2014, the port and its surrounding area have repeatedly come under attack from the Saudi-led coalition, the United States, the United Kingdom and Israel. Pro-Yemeni government forces also tried to capture it in a 2018 offensive.

About 70 percent of Yemenis live in Houthi-controlled areas in the country’s west, where most goods arrive from the rest of the world through Red Sea ports. Humanitarian aid continues to enter through other ports, including Mocha and a major government-held port in Aden, but renewed fighting has made the overland flow of this aid to the country’s interior difficult. Humanitarian operations in Houthi-controlled areas have also been severely curtailed because of the detention of UN staff by the group.

In March 2015, shortly after launching its military intervention in support of the Yemeni government, the Saudi-led coalition began a partial maritime blockade on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.

A UN-brokered nationwide truce in April 2022 led to an easing of restrictions on fuel imports through Hodeidah. Further restrictions on commercial imports were lifted in early 2023, which also helped to revitalise the port.

But that recovery was then jeopardised by a campaign of US, British and Israeli strikes on Houthi-controlled areas beginning in 2024 and lasting into the next year, in retaliation for Houthi drone and missile attacks on Israel and Red Sea shipping, carried out ostensibly in the name of supporting Gaza during Israel’s genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave.

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen announced on Wednesday that it had launched new strikes against the Houthis at the port, days after it warned civilians to evacuate the area. The Houthis have promised not to let strikes against the port go unanswered.

Since the return of full-scale war to Yemen in September, the Houthis have made sweeping territorial gains across Yemen, pushing back the forces of the internationally recognised government.

A government counteroffensive launched in early October has failed to stem Houthi advances despite heavy air support. Government forces are now scrambling to defend Aden, the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

“Broadly speaking, the strikes [on Hodeidah’s port] were a response to the shift on the battlefield in favour of the Houthis,” Ali al-Dhahab, a Yemeni military and strategic analyst, told Al Jazeera.”

“They were aimed at undermining and crippling their economic and logistical capabilities, including infrastructure, such as ports and airports, as well as their military capabilities,” he said.

Escalating Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia targeting airports, oil infrastructure and commercial buildings also played a role in the decision, al-Dhahab said, mentioning Thursday’s attack on the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund in Riyadh.

The following day, the Saudi-led coalition urged civilians near Hodeidah’s port to evacuate without providing specifics.

Before Wednesday’s strikes, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree reiterated a threat of retaliation on Saudi seaports on the Red Sea, naming Jeddah’s port in particular.

Nabil Al-Bukairi, a Yemeni researcher and policy expert, told Al Jazeera that Saudi Arabia’s strikes on the port should not be taken as a warning. “I believe the strikes have gone beyond being merely symbolic,” he said.

“Continued bombardment would inevitably lead to its closure and render it inoperable once its infrastructure and logistical capabilities have been targeted,” he warned.

Even without a closure, strikes that disrupt the operations of the facility risk delays of critical aid as Yemen’s war shows no sign of an imminent end.

articles.title: UK military ‘moving aircraft to hangars in case of drone attacks’
articles.excerpt: Britain’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) says it takes “the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously,” after media outlets reported the Royal Air Force (RAF) had taken new precautions ...
articles.body_text:
Britain’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) says it takes “the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously,” after media outlets reported the Royal Air Force (RAF) had taken new precautions against possible drone attacks.

The Times and Sky News reported on Wednesday that planes would be moved to hangars and hardened shelters overnight, and anti-drone nets would be installed to protect any warplanes that remained exposed.

The MoD did not confirm the reports, but in a statement said it was “always adapting to counter any potential threats”.

Justin Bronk, a senior researcher at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) think tank in London, told Al Jazeera that the RAF’s reported tactics would be “a sensible, logical response if there is intelligence suggesting a likely drone threat”.

“The main bases used for RAF fighters, Coningsby, Marham and Lossiemouth all still have hardened aircraft shelters from the Cold War era that have been maintained in usable condition for both aircraft storage, protection and limited maintenance work,” Bronk said.

However, Bronk cautioned that there were not enough hardened shelters to protect all of the jets at each airbase, after squadrons were consolidated into ‘super bases’ following the end of the Cold War, and a “mistaken assumption” that such protection was no longer important.

The MoD said it was investing an additional 470 million pounds ($615m) “to strengthen security at military sites, including better physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities”, and that 15 million pounds ($19.6m) had already been invested “in drone and counter-drone technology and introduced restricted airspace over 44 critical Defence sites”.

British authorities have regularly issued warnings about threats posed by Russia and Iran, and the government has urged the country to be prepared for different contingencies. In a report in October, members of Parliament warned that Britain’s military needed to make “dramatic progress” to be ready for a potential attack by Russia on a NATO country.

On Tuesday, Britain’s domestic MI5 intelligence service and the MoD issued a joint alert warning UK military suppliers to Ukraine about increasing sabotage attempts by Russia.

“Aircraft inside a standard hangar or a hardened aircraft shelter are protected from attacks by infiltrated adversary cells or terrorists with small drones,” explained RUSI’s Justin Bronk. “But only those in hardened shelters are protected from larger one-way attack drones like the Geran 2/3/4 series during a hypothetical wartime attack,” he added, referring to the Geran drones manufactured and operated by Russia, based on an original Iranian design.

Bronk said that even though hardened aircraft shelters seem old-fashioned, they are a “relatively low-risk, inexpensive and effective way to improve fighter fleet resilience in wartime.”

“They provide almost total protection from drones due to thick concrete and blast doors, and also mean that any unintercepted cruise missile can only destroy a single jet at most with a direct hit.”

Earlier this month US forces responded to possible unauthorised drone activity over a military base in the United Kingdom, hosting American warplanes.

“No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected” at the eastern RAF Lakenheath base, a US Air Force spokesperson said in a statement at the time.

There was also an Iran-linked security scare on September 27 at the southwestern RAF Fairford base, which was used by the US planes. A group of men allegedly drove three vans up to a village near the site and abandoned them with filled petrol barrels inside, sparking a bomb scare and evacuation.

Washington had used the airbase in its war on Iran, and days after the September incident withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the base. Two men have since been charged in a UK court over the incident, and three in the United States.

The US military also withdrew its planes from RAF Mildenhall, near Lakenheath, on November 9 , following a threat from Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal and The Financial Times.

articles.title: Japan to use Indian ranges for long-range missile training under new pact
articles.excerpt: NEW DELHI — India will allow Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at its firing ranges for the first time as Tokyo looks overseas for facilities to test its long-range missile capabil...
articles.body_text:
NEW DELHI — India will allow Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at its firing ranges for the first time as Tokyo looks overseas for facilities to test its long-range missile capabilities including surface-to-ship missiles.

The signing of a Letter of Intent (LOI) regarding the use of the Indian ranges was announced on Nov. 19, following a meeting between the two countries’ foreign and defense ministers in Tokyo.

The move marks a significant step in deepening defense cooperation between the two Asian countries.

Japanese officials visited India in October to assess whether its missile ranges could accommodate training with anti-ship missiles and smaller attack drones.

Chief of Staff of the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force Masayoshi Arai told reporters in Tokyo last month that the visit’s aim was to determine how to conduct training that makes full use of the roughly 1,000-kilometer range of Japan’s Type-25 surface-to-ship missile, which he described as “a major challenge.”

Limited space in the island country for long-range live-fire exercises has prompted officials to look for training options overseas. Access to Indian ranges could help overcome that limitation.

To bolster its military strength amid growing concerns over China’s military activity in the region, Japan began deploying long-range missiles on the southern island of Kyushu this year. The deployment is part of Japan’s effort to strengthen its deterrence and stand-off defense capabilities as it makes a significant shift in its post-World War II security posture.

A joint statement by the two countries after last week’s meeting welcomed the signing of the Letter of Intent, “whereby Japan Self-Defense Forces would, for the first time, conduct live-fire training etc., including those involving surface-to-ship missiles, at firing ranges in India.”

Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the arrangement was significant not only for expanding the scope of training for Japanese forces but also as a demonstration of a new phase in Japan-India cooperation.

The meeting between the Indian and Japanese defense ministers – their third in the last four months — also focused on enhancing military and arms industry cooperation between the two countries.

They agreed to accelerate negotiations toward finalizing their first-ever defense technology cooperation initiative under which India and Japan are jointly developing and manufacturing advanced integrated communication antenna systems for Indian Navy warships.

Developed for the Japanese navy, the Unified Complex Radio Antenna (UNICORN) system helps reduce the radar signature of naval vessels. Under the proposed agreement, a state run Indian company will collaborate with Japanese defense firms to co-produce the advanced mast for future Indian navy warships.

New Delhi has been seeking greater Japanese involvement in its defense industry and access to advanced technology as part of its efforts to strengthen domestic manufacturing.

After the talks in Tokyo, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said potential areas for collaboration between the two countries include naval shipbuilding, unmanned and autonomous systems and advanced defense technologies.

Amid their deepening defense cooperation, Japan deployed its fighter jets in India for the first time in September during a bilateral air exercise held in the Indian city of Jodhpur. Tokyo sent F-2A fighter aircraft for the exercise, known as Veer Guardian 2026.

At the recent meeting, both sides agreed to incorporate unmanned systems and increase the complexity of future exercises.

articles.title: Five Russian military jets hit in airfield strike, says Ukraine
articles.excerpt:
A Russian MiG-31 military jet (file photo)

Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.

Three MiG-31 and...
articles.body_text:
A Russian MiG-31 military jet (file photo)

Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.

Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.

The airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.

The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.

Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line – the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.

"Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said.

Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.

Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.

"Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry said, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes.

Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.

On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities.

But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv.

Ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills senior Hamas security official and family in Gaza City
articles.excerpt:
The strike caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment

An Israeli air strike in the Gaza Strip has killed a senior Hamas security official and three members of his family, according ...
articles.body_text:
The strike caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment

An Israeli air strike in the Gaza Strip has killed a senior Hamas security official and three members of his family, according to local doctors and the Hamas-run interior ministry.

Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters died when their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City was bombed at dawn, the ministry said.

The Israeli military said Abu al-Ouf was a "terrorist" and that he was eliminated "to remove the threat he posed".

On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.

Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza

Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says

Wednesday's strike in Shati caused extensive damage to the Abu al-Ouf family's apartment.

Photos showed the exterior wall and several interior walls were destroyed, with rubble and broken furniture left scattered across the floor.

An interior ministry statement said that Abu al-Ouf was killed along with his wife Noura, 41, and their daughters Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13.

It condemned the attack as a "heinous crime" and accused Israel of targeting security personnel in Gaza "in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society".

Hamas's internal security service is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting the group's infrastructure and rooting out informants.

Israel's military said in a statement that Abu al-Ouf was a "significant figure" who had served as "a key source of expertise" in efforts to restrict Israeli counter-terrorism operations in Gaza.

"His elimination is a blow to the apparatus's leadership capabilities and follows yesterday's elimination of his commander," it added.

On Tuesday, an Israeli drone strike in western Gaza City killed Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service.

He had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid in Gaza City by Israeli special forces.

Near daily Israeli strikes continue in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreed in October last year.

At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.body_text:
Fans in the comments section thanked Taylor for his contributions to music. (Fin Costello/Redferns)

Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor has died at age 65 of prostate cancer, Fox News Digital confirmed.

Taylor died peacefully at home surrounded by family on Monday, according to a joint statement from his family and former bandmates.

"To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather," his wife, Tracey, said on behalf of the family.

In a tribute on the band's website, lead singer Simon Le Bon wrote, "There’s a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart."

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

articles.title: Pat Freiermuth sidesteps Aaron Rodgers' claims about Mike McCarthy and Steelers coaching staff
articles.excerpt:
OutKick's Dan Dakich weighs in on the Aaron Rodgers fallout.

If the Pittsburgh Steelers thought they'd get a relaxing Wednesday before Thanksgiving, they were mistaken.

Because now-former signal cal...
articles.body_text:
OutKick's Dan Dakich weighs in on the Aaron Rodgers fallout.

If the Pittsburgh Steelers thought they'd get a relaxing Wednesday before Thanksgiving, they were mistaken.

Because now-former signal caller Aaron Rodgers went scorched earth on Steelers coach Mike McCarthy during an appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show," even claiming that the coach has been known to doze off in meetings.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Now, players like tight end Pat Freiermuth found themselves in front of microphones just minutes after Rodgers' bombshell interview and in a brutal spot.

AARON RODGERS NOT RETURNING TO STEELERS, SAYS MIKE MCCARTHY FALLS ASLEEP IN MEETINGS AND IS 'UNWELL'

"Yeah, listen: anything I say about the situation is going to be tough, and obviously (the situation) is tough," Freiermuth said. "Y'know, I'm here, and we're just focused on trying to get a win against Denver."

The former Penn State Nittany Lion was then asked if he had confidence in the Steelers coaching staff and the team's current direction.

Steelers tight end Pat Freiermuth did his best to toe the line when it came to questions about the Steelers' split from quarterback Aaron Rodgers. (Bill Streicher-Imagn Images)

WHAT’S YOUR TAKE: WILL AARON RODGERS PLAY ANOTHER SNAP THIS SEASON?

Freiermuth was especially in a bind, as Rodgers claimed that the tight end was the one who broke the news that he was being benched in the first place. He was asked about the conversation he had with Rodgers over the phone.

"I was just checking in on a close friend, from what I heard," Freiermuth said. "That's all I have to say about that."

Freiermuth also steered clear of a question about whether the situation between Rodgers and the organization could've ended differently.

Aaron Rodgers and head coach Mike McCarthy of the Pittsburgh Steelers chat before an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Pa., on Nov. 22, 2026. (Getty Images)

"Again, I'm sorry, but I'm just going to focus on Denver," he said.

It's a wise choice to put as much focus on the Broncos as possible. With the Steelers already facing a Black Friday meeting with the top team in the conference, the last thing they need is some noise creating distractions.

And, boy, is there a lot of drama here, and likely more to come.

articles.title: North Korea expels Swiss diplomat in sanctions row
articles.excerpt:
Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang

North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for t...
articles.body_text:
Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang

North Korea has ordered Switzerland's diplomatic representative to leave the country within 48 hours and called for the office to close, in a row over sanctions.

It followed Switzerland's decision to place sanctions on the Songdowon international children's camp in the eastern city of Wonsan, which is attended by Russian and Chinese children among other nationalities.

The camp has been accused of involvement in transferring children from Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.

North Korea's state-run news agency KCNA called the sanctions "a blatant hostile act".

Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang.

Confirming the expulsion, KCNA said: "The Foreign Ministry of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) declared the head of the Swiss Diplomatic Office in the DPRK persona non grata and urged him to leave the country within 48 hours."

The diplomatic rebuke comes weeks after Swiss foreign minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially reopened the office and discussed normalising relations.

Swiss authorities said relations between the two countries would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing.

Diplomatic links with North Korea were first established in 1974 and Switzerland opened a co-operation office in Pyongyang in 1997. It was closed during the pandemic and remained shut for six years.

Switzerland's Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis (C) and his wife Paola Cassis (R) were greeted by a North Korean official at Pyongyang Airport on 29 October

Switzerland's department of foreign affairs said the country "distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries".

It added: "The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."

Thousands of North Korean soldiers have been deployed to help support Russia's war with Ukraine.

In August, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles.

Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says

North Korean weapons are killing Ukrainians. The implications are far bigger

Why a fresh wave of North Korean soldiers may fight in Russia's war in Ukraine

articles.title: Trump's birthright citizenship restrictions struck down again by DC federal judge he called 'hater'
articles.excerpt: Fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn analyzes President Trump's new executive orders targeting birth tourism and birthright citizenship, plus the legal battle with the ACLU and a Texas hospital settleme...
articles.body_text:
Fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn analyzes President Trump's new executive orders targeting birth tourism and birthright citizenship, plus the legal battle with the ACLU and a Texas hospital settlement. Urbahn discusses the constitutional battles ahead.

A DC federal judge, previously dubbed by President Donald Trump as an "anti- Trump Hater," blocked Trump's second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship in a Wednesday ruling.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who was recently in Trump's crosshairs after ruling against efforts to shut down the Kennedy Center for renovations and add Trump's name to the cultural institution, issued a 67-page ruling striking down an August executive order that barred U.S. -born children whose parents are suspected terrorists or gang members, or children born through surrogacy to foreign parents, from citizenship eligibility.

Cooper's ruling comes months after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's initial executive order, signed on his first day back in office. The order attempted to deny birthright citizenship to U.S.-born children whose mothers were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor green card holders.

WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER

Demonstrators hold up an anti-Trump sign outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, after the justices curbed nationwide injunctions in a case stemming from President Donald Trump's initial bid to end birthright citizenship. (ALEX WROBLEWSKI/AFP via Getty Images)

"As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws," Cooper ruled.

Trump's second executive order was already partially blocked on Sept. 2 by U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland, whose injunction protected U.S.-born children of mothers who were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents.

Cooper's ruling expanded protections beyond that class to include additional children born to certain foreign government and international organization employees, parents deemed "alien enemies" by the administration and foreign parents who used commercial surrogacy services in the U.S.

"The merits in this case are clear-cut. The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law," Cooper wrote.

In addition to the Supreme Court's June ruling in Trump v. Barbara, Cooper referred to the high court's ruling in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which determined that a man born to Chinese immigrants was a protected U.S. citizen under the 14th Amendment.

SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS

President Donald Trump speaks during a news conference in the James S. Brady Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on nationwide injunctions in litigation over his first birthright citizenship executive order. (Mehmet Eser/Middle East Images via AFP)

Cooper noted that Wong Kim Ark established narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship, including for children of foreign diplomats, children born aboard foreign public ships and children of enemy forces occupying American territory.

"While the Fourteenth Amendment may theoretically permit new exceptions beyond those listed in Wong Kim Ark, Congress has not authorized any such exceptions," Cooper wrote.

Cooper argued that membership in a terrorist organization alone does not satisfy the historical exception to birthright citizenship for children of enemy forces occupying U.S. territory. He criticized the Trump administration's contention that foreign invaders could occupy American territory without actually holding it as an "outside-the-box understanding" of what constitutes an occupation.

"To recap, a parent’s purported status as an alien enemy, standing alone, cannot strip a U.S.-born child of his right to birthright citizenship," Cooper wrote. "The alien-enemy exception, properly understood, applies only to children born to hostile enemy forces in temporarily occupied U.S. territory."

Cooper also rejected Trump's attempt to deny birthright citizenship to children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements involving foreign parents, finding that the circumstances of their birth do not exempt them from U.S. jurisdiction.

"Indeed, foreign parents choose surrogacy arrangements in the United States precisely to have the child be governed by U.S. law and have the surrogacy process ‘supervised by a court.," Cooper wrote.

TRUMP TO ASK SUPREME COURT TO REHEAR BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CASE AFTER 'INSANE DECISION'

Demonstrators gather outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on May 15, 2025, in support of birthright citizenship during litigation over President Donald Trump's first executive order narrowing citizenship eligibility for children born on U.S. soil. (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty)

He noted that, prior to Trump's second executive order, the State Department recognized the citizenship of children born on American soil regardless of whether they were born through surrogacy.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the decision and request that the executive order be temporarily enforced while the litigation works its way through the courts, a process that could take months.

"This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Obama attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court."

The Justice Department could seek temporary relief from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit or seek intervention from the Supreme Court. Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE WITH TIES TO ANTI-TRUMP CONSPIRACY THEORY HIT WITH MISCONDUCT COMPLAINT

In addition to ruling against Trump's Kennedy Center renovation efforts, Cooper ruled that Trump's Department of Government Efficiency must turn over records requested in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.

Trump has called Cooper one of the "Radical Left Democrats."

Cooper is also married to Amy Jeffress, who was Biden’s personal lawyer in 2025 and previously did some work for the Jan. 6 committee.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

articles.title: UConn head coach Geno Auriemma goes scorched earth on his team after loss to South Carolina
articles.excerpt: Dakich: "She's absolutely right. Now you want all this attention, so you're not getting people that go, ‘Oh my God, this is so great. Women are playing.' No, no no no. You're getting sports fans, real...
articles.body_text:
Dakich: "She's absolutely right. Now you want all this attention, so you're not getting people that go, ‘Oh my God, this is so great. Women are playing.' No, no no no. You're getting sports fans, real sports fans, sports fans from other sports coming in watching, and they're going to treat you like you want to be treated allegedly like a real serious league, but you can't handle it."

UConn women's basketball coach Geno Auriemma has never been shy about speaking his mind.

The fiery legend recently took his entire sport to task over the rampant NIL paydays being awarded to incoming freshmen, showing that he still won't hesitate to empty the tank and tell it like it is.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Auriemma's sights were turned inward today, though, as he went scorched earth on his own team following their defeat at the hands of the South Carolina Gamecocks.

GENO AURIEMMA, DAWN STALEY SHAKE HANDS AFTER HOSTILE SCRAP LAST SEASON, AS NCAA MAKES HANDSHAKE RULE CHANGE

UConn head coach Geno Auriemma watches a play late in the second half of a Sweet 16 game of the NCAA college basketball tournament against North Carolina in Fort Worth, Texas, on March 27, 2026. (LM Otero/AP Photo)

The loss dropped the Huskies to 4-3 on the season, and in his postgame news conference, an exasperated Auriemma clearly wasn't happy with the results so far.

"I'm having a really hard time coaching this team. You might be able to tell that," Auriemma said at the podium. "I've got to figure it out. But it would be nice if I could get a little help."

DUKE COACH JON SCHEYER SAYS BLUE DEVILS' UPSET LOSS TO MICHIGAN STATE FELT LIKE AN 'OUT-OF-BODY EXPERIENCE'

While all of their losses have come against top-ranked teams, UConn has never lost three games in the month of November, and Auriemma is clearly not handling this skid (or his team's demeanor) very well.

"It's just so out of character for anybody that's watched UConn play for 30-some years," he said. "I don't even recognize it."

IS IT WEIRD FOR A COACH TO NOT TALK TO HIS TEAM AFTER A GAME, OR IS IT EXTREMELY WEIRD?

Dawn Staley of the South Carolina Gamecocks argues with Geno Auriemma of the UConn Huskies during the second half of an NCAA Women's Final Four semifinal game at Mortgage Matchup Center in Phoenix, Ariz. on April 3, 2026. (C. Morgan Engel/NCAA Photos via Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Auriemma bemoaned his team's inability to handle any sort of adversity, something his eight championship-winning teams were clearly adept at.

The 18 turnovers certainly didn't help, nor did shooting 27% from the field.

Now, Auriemma is faced with a turnaround that he isn't used to, and although there's plenty of season left, this is uncharted territory for a program that has become accustomed to winning and winning big.

UConn head coach Geno Auriemma reacts to a play during the first half of a Sweet 16 game of the NCAA college basketball tournament against North Carolina in Fort Worth, Texas, on March 27, 2026. (Julio Cortez/AP Photo)

I don't doubt a coach like Auriemma's ability to right the ship, but he's clearly fed up with the current iteration of his team, and it's hard for anyone to blame him.

articles.title: 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed: What to know
articles.excerpt: Kurt 'CyberGuy' Knutsson joins 'The Faulkner Focus' to discuss recent airport disruptions due to severe weather and technological glitches. He also guides viewers on how to handle any delays or frustr...
articles.body_text:
Kurt 'CyberGuy' Knutsson joins 'The Faulkner Focus' to discuss recent airport disruptions due to severe weather and technological glitches. He also guides viewers on how to handle any delays or frustrations during the holiday travel weekend.

The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed ahead of a nor'easter in New York City, marking the first time the parade has been moved because of weather.

The parade has been moved from Thursday to Saturday, amid a forecast of strong winds and heavy rain, according to The Associated Press.

"With severe weather expected on Thanksgiving Day, and out of an abundance of caution, in partnership with the City the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will be postponed," Macy's said in a statement.

WORST AIRPORTS FOR THANKSGIVING TRAVEL CHAOS RANKED AS MAJOR US HUBS TOP LIST

A Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade float is seen on the Upper West Side of Manhattan in New York City, on November 25, 2026. (Photo by Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images)

"Our team is now working through the complex operational logistics required to bring the Parade to life on Saturday, and we will share additional details as they are finalized," the statement continued. "We are incredibly grateful to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who make this extraordinary tradition possible. We can’t wait to celebrate 100 years of Parade magic together on Saturday."

A Thanksgiving storm is expected to hit New York City, as well as the tri-state area, with heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding in some places expected.

The Charlie Brown balloon is seen during the 90th annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on Nov. 24, 2016, in New York City. (WireImage)

The iconic parade draws thousands of spectators along the 2.5-mile route, which begins in Manhattan's Upper West Side to Herald Square on 34th Street, the site of the Macy's department store.

Police officers detain a protester during the 98th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City, U.S., November 28, 2024. (Brendan McDermid/Reuters)

An area of low pressure developing off the Southeast coast will push northward into the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast beginning Wednesday night. The storm is expected to intensify through Thanksgiving Day before clearing out on Friday, according to the FOX Forecast Center and the National Weather Service.

This story is breaking. Please check back for updates.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.
