articles.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
articles.excerpt:
Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.

The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jense...
articles.body_text:
Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.

The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower.

The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks.

Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft closed the day lower, though Meta and SpaceX were in positive territory by the end of the trading day.

Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower.

The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after revelations of his extramarital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.

Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.

The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.

The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs.

But share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.

Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away

Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.

Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off.

"It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending, but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.

Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.

Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by just over 3%.

The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.

articles.title: Shane Gillis wishes ex-girlfriend 'the best' after tell-all essay accusing him of cheating and 'red flags'
articles.excerpt:
Comedian Shane Gillis, left, and Grace Brassel attend the 2025 ESPY Awards at the Dolby Theatre on July 16, 2025, in Hollywood, Calif. The couple has since split up. (Maya Dehlin Spach/WireImage)

Com...
articles.body_text:
Comedian Shane Gillis, left, and Grace Brassel attend the 2025 ESPY Awards at the Dolby Theatre on July 16, 2025, in Hollywood, Calif. The couple has since split up. (Maya Dehlin Spach/WireImage)

Comedian Shane Gillis’ ex-girlfriend wrote a lengthy piece this week about their yearlong relationship, saying his controversial "Saturday Night Live" joke about women at the gym reflects how he treats women behind closed doors.

In an essay published by The Cut, content creator Grace Brassel wrote that the comedian pressured her into quitting her job, isolated her from friends and family and cheated on her before their split in August 2025.

Speaking to Fox News Digital, Gillis responded to Brassel’s claims, saying, "Grace and I had some good times together. Breakups are tough, and I wish her the best."

'SNL' CAST MEMBER MICHAEL CHE SHRUGS OFF SHANE GILLIS' MONOLOGUE JOKE SAYING, 'THAT'S COMEDY'

Comedian Shane Gillis delivered the opening monologue while hosting NBC’s "Saturday Night Live" on Oct. 10, 2026. (Will Heath/NBC via Getty Images)

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Brassel said she wrote the essay to help other women.

"I wrote this essay to help other women, and for them to know there is a life past it, these kinds of relationships. The beautiful DMs I am receiving mean so much to me. No matter what age you are, this can happen to you, and I always wished someone could have told me sooner. I hope it can help more girls speak out and stand up for themselves," Brassel said.

Brassel referenced Gillis’ recent controversial comments regarding women’s gym attire on "SNL" being that of "whores," writing that she wasn’t the "least bit surprised."

"Until last August, I was in a yearlong relationship with Shane, and his comments didn’t faze me. After our time together, how do I think he feels about women? He doesn’t like them much," Brassel wrote.

The pair began talking in May 2024 after Brassel sent him direct messages on Instagram, and she initially described their whirlwind romance as a "dream." However, she explained that when they eventually moved in together, it was a "nonstop party," which made it difficult for her to keep up her day job as a social media manager.

Social media content creator Grace Brassel arrives on the red carpet at the 2025 ESPY Awards at the Dolby Theatre on July 16, 2025, in Hollywood, Calif. (Maya Dehlin Spach/WireImage)

She claimed Gillis encouraged her to quit, and when they moved to Pennsylvania to shoot his Netflix series "Tires," she felt as though his expectations of her changed.

"I felt like I was turning into a 25-year-old housewife, someone who cooked, cleaned, did the laundry, and waited for her man to come home from a long day at work. I never said I was capable of all that, but it felt like an expectation," Brassel wrote. "When things weren’t exactly to his liking, he would tell me that I wasn’t ‘being good.’ You know, the way you would talk to a dog."

'SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE' STAR WOULD SIT SHANE GILLIS DOWN 'LIKE A LITTLE KID' OVER PROVOCATIVE MONOLOGUE

She added that she ignored many "red flags," claiming he would say something "remarkably cruel" and play it off as a joke, and noted she felt she needed to start dressing more "conservatively."

"I cried every day. I would call my mom in tears, telling her that I didn’t know if I was meant for this life. My six-month free trial of Sweet Shane Gillis had run out, and it was time for me to start paying," she wrote.

Brassel alleged that things came to a head on the Fourth of July, when she said she discovered Gillis’ infidelity after going through his phone and finding explicit messages with another woman that had been going on for months.

"I scrolled and realized they had been sexting for months and had probably had in-person encounters as well. The floor seemed to give way beneath my feet," she recalled.

Comedian Shane Gillis appears before a college football game between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Texas Longhorns at Neyland Stadium on Sept. 26, 2026, in Knoxville, Tenn. (Roger Wimmer/ISI Photos via Getty Images)

Brassel admitted she "snapped" when confronting him. She described punching a hole in the bathroom wall and throwing her phone and a chair before the two eventually went through an on-and-off breakup. She claimed they had considered reconciling, but that Gillis said they could never mend things after she began telling others how he treated her.

BROADCAST BIAS: FEMINIST FREAKOUT OVER SHANE GILLIS COMMENT IS THE REAL JOKE

Brassel added that the outrage over Gillis’ recent monologue on "SNL" gave her "some kind of closure."

"He had flown too close to the sun, and people were finally seeing the man I knew. I had spent so long protecting this part of my life, afraid to speak publicly about it, and then he just did it himself. Finally, some initiative," Brassel wrote at the end of the essay.

She also addressed the attention the essay has gotten in a video posted to her 124,000 followers on Instagram, saying she’s been working on the essay for a month and was fully aware of the "discourse" it would cause.

Musical guest Rosalía, left, host Shane Gillis, center, and cast member Kenan Thompson film promotional segments for "Saturday Night Live" at Studio 8H on Oct. 8, 2026, in New York City. (Rosalind O'Connor/NBC via Getty Images)

"I'm well aware of the discourse that was going to happen," Brassel said. "And I weighed out my options, and I think that it is a net positive, no matter what. I can handle the heat. I'm in the kitchen, girl. I can handle the heat."

SWIFTIES CLAIM TRAVIS KELCE DID THE UNSPEAKABLE BY LIKING SHANE GILLIS' 'SNL' MONOLOGUE & THEY'RE NOT HAPPY

Gillis addressed the controversy he spurred on "SNL," telling host Joe Rogan earlier this month that he had promised the show’s producers "no controversy."

"Not to defend ‘SNL,’ they don't approve it. I mean, they could shut it down," Gillis said on "The Joe Rogan Experience."

"But you don't write your set and give it to them," he added. "Unless you’re not a comedian. I’m sure non-comics, they write the set for them. They have writers that write the monologue for them."

"The funniest part was... they were like, ‘What’s going on with the monologue?’ And I was like, ‘It’s not great, but I don’t say anything bad.’ The whole time, I was like, ‘Fellas, I’m giving you a solid C-minus of a monologue, but I promise there’s no controversy. I’m calling myself fat for f---ing 10 minutes. That’s it.'"

Gillis drew criticism from entertainment figures, including actor Dan Levy and former "SNL" cast member Ego Nwodim, after joking during his opening monologue last month that women at gyms "just dress like whores now."

The appearance marked his third time hosting the NBC sketch seies, which briefly hired and then fired him in 2019 as a cast member over a podcast appearance where he made jokes deemed offensive.

Fox News Digital’s Taylor Penley contributed to this report.

Madison Colombo is a writer for Fox News Digital’s Flash, Media, and Culture team, covering daily breaking news and trending topics with an award-winning background in broadcast and digital journalism.

articles.title: At least 30 killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
articles.excerpt:
Huge fire erupts near Cairo killing at least 30 people

At least 30 people have been killed and 19 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health...
articles.body_text:
Huge fire erupts near Cairo killing at least 30 people

At least 30 people have been killed and 19 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.

Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.

Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.

Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.

The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.

The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.

It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.

Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.

Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.

Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished

The tanker crossed the highway's central reservation before overturning and bursting into flames, local media report

The health ministry said 39 ambulances had been dispatched to respond to the fire, while it posted images of Egypt's health minister overseeing the treatment of the injured at one of Cairo's hospitals.

Road collisions are also common in Egypt, often attributed to lax maintenance and the widespread flouting of traffic laws.

Nearly 6,000 people died on Egypt's roads last year, official figures show, a rise of several hundred on the previous year's total.

Emergency responders have since cleared the highway and allowed it to reopen, state broadcaster NMA reports.

A bulldozer could earlier be seen at the scene clearing the burnt-out wrecks of cars.

articles.title: Thanksgiving flights booked after key hour face double the risk of major delay
articles.excerpt:
Fox News' Max Gorden joins 'Jesse Watters Primetime' to discuss how extreme weather and flight delays may impact Thanksgiving travel.

As U.S. airports brace for a brutal Thanksgiving rush, travel ana...
articles.body_text:
Fox News' Max Gorden joins 'Jesse Watters Primetime' to discuss how extreme weather and flight delays may impact Thanksgiving travel.

As U.S. airports brace for a brutal Thanksgiving rush, travel analysts are warning passengers about a common scheduling mistake that raises the odds of a disrupted trip: booking a flight after 9 a.m.

"Flights departing after 9 a.m. are generally twice as likely to be delayed as those departing between 5 a.m. and 8 a.m.," according to Hopper data.

The alert lands at an uneasy moment for American flyers, with 69% now ranking delays and cancellations as their top booking concern, according to a Hopper consumer survey.

TSA DETECTS SUSPICIOUS MOVEMENT IN TRAVELER'S SUITCASE DURING SECURITY SCREENING

A storm system bringing heavy rain, wind and thunderstorms has already swept across the Gulf Coast and Southeast and is bearing down on major Mid-Atlantic and Northeast hubs through Thanksgiving Day, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Confidence has also been tested by recent technical scares.

As U.S. airports prepare for the Thanksgiving rush, travel analysts warn passengers about a common scheduling mistake. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Travelers were shaken by the Nov. 13 FAA ground stop sparked by telecommunications instability.

The ground stop halted departures nationwide, resulting in more than 12,400 cancellations, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation and the FAA.

TRAVELERS BUSTED AT AIRPORT WITH OVER 3,000 TARANTULAS HIDDEN AWAY IN THEIR SOCKS

An isolated outage also prompted a brief ground stop at Chicago O'Hare International Airport on Nov. 24, as Fox News Digital previously reported.

Across U.S. domestic flights from 2023 through 2025, just 11% of departures scheduled before 8 a.m. arrived 15 or more minutes late, according to Bureau of Transportation Statistics data analyzed by DelayGuard.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Because commercial jets typically fly multiple legs a day, a storm or runway bottleneck in one hub can affect later routes. Late-arriving aircraft are responsible for 41% of all U.S. delay minutes, an AirDelay analysis noted.

Sunrise departures sidestep that chain reaction.

"The aircraft has spent the night at the airport, so there is no late inbound flight to wait for," DelayGuard reported. Morning crews are also just beginning their shifts, so earlier snags on the schedule will not hold up boarding, according to DelayGuard.

Airplanes are shown lined up at O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, Illinois, on May 11, 2024. Since commercial jets fly multiple legs a day, a storm or runway bottleneck in one hub can cause delays in another hub. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)

Passengers whose morning flights are disrupted have far more later departures available to rebook.

Evening snags leave fewer options, according to AirDelay and CLEAR.

In addition, travelers willing to brave a 4 a.m. alarm often score lower fares on a 6 a.m. flight than on a 10 a.m. departure, The Points Guy reported.

"Taking a morning flight gives you a greater chance of having a plane and crew ready to go," Gary Leff, a Texas-based travel industry expert and author of the blog "View From The Wing," told Fox News Digital.

Travelers willing to brave a 4 a.m. alarm often score lower fares on a 6 a.m. flight than on a 10 a.m. departure, experts point out. (Mehmet Eser/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"There's an opportunity to address maintenance issues overnight. So [there's] a likelihood of starting the day with an aircraft that's ready," Leff continued.

"Crew have limits in their duty day. They could run out of allowable time with late flights that get delayed," he added. "Early flights mean starting fresh, and you aren't risking your pilots or flight attendants 'timing out.'"

Picking the right day of the week can sway the odds as well.

Tuesday consistently ranks as the most punctual day at major U.S. airports, with fewer than 19% of departures arriving late — followed closely by Wednesday, according to Bureau of Transportation Statistics records reviewed by DelayGuard.

Sunday sits at the bottom, with a quarter of flights running behind schedule, DelayGuard reported.

Delays can stack during the day, making evening flights especially risky, a travel expert said. (Getty Images)

"Delays stack throughout the day. If you're on the third or fourth flight operated by your crew or aircraft that day, there were several opportunities for them to get delayed during the day," Leff said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

During peak holiday windows, timing can protect a traveler's wallet, too.

Flying home on Sunday can be the costliest option, with round-trip domestic fares averaging $604 compared with roughly $350 for passengers who wait until Monday or Tuesday, according to Hopper's 2026 Holiday Travel Index.

"Early flights mean more recovery options."

Aviation officials urge passengers to build extra buffer time into their commute, to stay subscribed to airline alerts and to check real-time airport conditions through the FAA's National Airspace System status portal.

"Early flights mean more recovery options," said Leff. "Not only are there more same-day options left on the schedule, but available seats are less likely to have been taken by other passengers that were delayed."

Jessica Mekles is an editor on the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

The details have come out on Puka Nacua's season-ending injury, and the details are grotesque.

The Los Angeles Rams star suffered the injury on the final offensive play of the team's 20-13 win over the Washington Commanders in Week 9. The 25-year-old sustained a grade 3 MCL tear, which means the ligament completely tore off the tibia, which is the shinbone, according to ESPN's Adam Schefter.

In addition to the MCL tear, Schefter said that Nacua "had a tear off the posterior oblique portion of the MCL as well."

LA Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua heads to the locker room after the Washington Commanders game against the Los Angeles Rams at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Md., on Nov. 8, 2026. (Justin Cooper/Cal Sport Media/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)

"So that wouldn’t have healed with the stability that they needed, and, essentially, it would be performance-limiting with a higher chance of earlier degenerative changes," Schefter said on "The Adam Schefter Podcast." "So they had to go in and repair the knee."

Losing Nacua is a massive blow for a 6-4 Rams team that is fighting for a playoff spot. Although Nacua missed two games earlier this season due to injury, he has been incredibly productive when healthy. In seven games, the two-time Pro Bowler has 70 catches for 715 yards and four touchdowns.

Rams coach Sean McVay said earlier in November they were targeting a return for the team's matchup against the Green Bay Packers on Wednesday, but he remains on injured reserve and is out.

articles.title: Winter rains threaten 1,000 Gaza shelter sites, councils warn
articles.excerpt: Gaza’s municipalities have warned that winter rains could flood about 1,000 camps and other sites hosting displaced Palestinians in the war-torn enclave, adding that damage to drains and sewers, and a...
articles.body_text:
Gaza’s municipalities have warned that winter rains could flood about 1,000 camps and other sites hosting displaced Palestinians in the war-torn enclave, adding that damage to drains and sewers, and a shortage of pumps, have left their crews with little means to clear the water.

After a meeting in Gaza City on Wednesday, the Union of Gaza Strip Municipalities singled out al-Mughraqa and al-Zahra in central Gaza, where water levels in Wadi Gaza could rise suddenly. Across the territory, about 200,000 tents need replacing, and more than 2,000 damaged buildings are at risk of collapse, the union said. Gaza’s Government Media Office had warned on Tuesday that it expected another storm within days.

This is Gaza’s fourth winter since Israel launched its war in October 2023. The union said storms in early November flooded about 70,000 tents and affected more than 350,000 displaced people. During a winter storm this November, families piled sand at tent entrances to keep out the rain. Others carried their children out and salvaged what belongings they could.

One displaced mother said she had cut up the burial shroud she had bought for her son and used it to patch her tent. She wanted to keep the family’s bedding and clothes dry. “I couldn’t get a tarpaulin,” she said.

When the first rains hit, Gaza’s civil defence crews reached only a minority of those who called for help. Most of the other callers received advice by phone, Al Jazeera reported.

In Brussels on Wednesday, the European Commission called on Israel to reopen all Gaza crossings to humanitarian aid. Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova said tents were waiting on trucks outside Gaza because Israel had not allowed them or the equipment needed to put them up to enter.

The UN said earlier this month that more than 150,000 tents were awaiting entry into Gaza.

Al Jazeera’s open-source unit (Ar.) measured a queue of trucks stretching about 1.1km (0.7 miles) along the Egyptian road to the Rafah crossing in a November 17 satellite image, up from about 460 metres (1,510 feet) on October 6. The images do not establish what the trucks carried. Freight from Egypt is routed through the Karem Abu Salem crossing, known as Kerem Shalom in Israel, for inspection rather than entering Gaza through Rafah.

COGAT, the Israeli military body that coordinates aid, said that nearly 100,000 tents had entered Gaza since the start of a winter aid programme. It said Israel would allow reconstruction equipment into Gaza only after Hamas had fully disarmed.

Inside Gaza, aid workers have cleared drains, installed flood barriers and reinforced shelters. The UN’s humanitarian affairs office reported on November 20 that teams had recorded such work at 162 of the 356 flood-prone locations they had identified. Gaza’s municipalities are asking for pumps, backup generators and fuel before the next storm, as well as 10,000 tonnes of cement for emergency repairs and mobile homes that can withstand wind and rain.

articles.title: Charlie Sheen swung bat, threatened to ‘break’ Emilio Estevez’s head open before cops swarmed teen brawl
articles.excerpt:
Charlie Sheen and Emilio Estevez reflected on their tumultuous relationship growing up. (Getty Images)

Charlie Sheen and Emilio Estevez may have eventually shared the screen in films like "Young Guns...
articles.body_text:
Charlie Sheen and Emilio Estevez reflected on their tumultuous relationship growing up. (Getty Images)

Charlie Sheen and Emilio Estevez may have eventually shared the screen in films like "Young Guns" and "Men at Work," but growing up, their off-camera dynamic was rocky at times.

During a recent appearance on Sheen’s "Mostly Sheenius" podcast, the brothers reminisced about their "toxic" and "dangerous" teenage rivalry.

"We didn't always get along. And we fought a lot as siblings do," Estevez said, admitting that even filming Super 8 movies together in their youth turned into an "insane" battle over creative control.

DENISE RICHARDS SAYS SAMI 'STANDS UP' TO DAD CHARLIE SHEEN AND THAT HE NEEDS IT

Sheen has previously opened up about the complicated dynamic between the two, including feeling excluded during Estevez’s rise in the 1980s "Brat Pack" era.

Long before they were competing for Hollywood roles, however, they were clashing at home — including one explosive high school fight that ended with Sheen swinging a baseball bat and sheriff’s deputies arriving at their front door.

Sheen recalled gearing up for his first high school date at 16 and didn't want to show up in his "piece of s--- Ford Escort," so he turned to his brother, who turned him down.

"I said, ‘OK, but like, you don’t mean "no" no, because this really matters to me, this is important, man. This girl's really pretty, I think she likes me, and if I had your car I think everything would work out,'" Sheen recalled pleading, while Estevez admitted he was "just being a douche" by refusing.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Emilio Estevez and Charlie Sheen once got into an argument so bad the police were called. (Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

Sheen snapped in what he described as a "blackout" rage and hurled a sandwich toward Estevez. Realizing he was "in trouble," Sheen bolted down the hallway and locked himself in his bedroom.

"I was like, 'All right, he's going to die tonight,'" Estevez said, remembering how he stalked down the hall yelling, "'You clean it up right now!'"

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

When Estevez kicked the bedroom door open, Sheen was frantically swinging a baseball bat to keep some distance between them. Estevez remembered him yelling, "Don't come near me. I'll break your head open."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Sheen said he and his brother learned the art of acting the night the police were called on them.  (Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)

"I was saying, ‘I’ll kill you! I'll kill you!'" Estevez remembered, adding that the windows were open. Sheen said that he egged him on, with Estevez saying, "Then you said, ‘Do me a f---ing favor, kill me, kill me!’"

Around 10 minutes later, the brothers shared, there was a knock at the door, and when they opened it, four sheriff's deputies were there, ready to intervene.

Facing law enforcement, the future Hollywood stars immediately pivoted to damage control.

"We both became brilliant actors in that moment," Estevez said, recalling how he draped an arm around Sheen with a forced laugh and told the deputies, "'Why would I want to kill my brother? We were just kidding ... rehearsal.'"

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

articles.title: US Education Department probes Virginia schools after sexual abuse scandal
articles.excerpt: The United States Department of Education says it is launching an investigation and withholding funding from a district in the state of Virginia after local officials shut down all of its schools in t...
articles.body_text:
The United States Department of Education says it is launching an investigation and withholding funding from a district in the state of Virginia after local officials shut down all of its schools in the wake of a child sexual abuse scandal involving its employees.

“Parents should never have to question whether their child’s school is aiding and abetting child predators,” US Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said in a statement on Tuesday. “The Trump Administration is taking decisive enforcement action to hold those responsible accountable and ensure Virginia schools are safe places for children to learn.”

Officials in Albemarle County, Virginia, announced they were closing all 29 schools in the district last week, after learning that more than 500 staff had not been subjected to a routine background screening for a history of child sexual abuse. The school system has about 2,800 employees, and only a fraction of its $284m budget comes from the federal government.

Local officials emphasised that none of the 524 employees is suspected of abuse.

Approximately 14,000 students attend the schools, and parents have scrambled to find childcare, while many who depend on free school meals for their children have had to look for other sources of food.

Bob Beard, a member of the Albemarle school board, told Al Jazeera that families were struggling to deal with the shutdown, but schools would reopen on Monday.

The child abuse allegations have shaken the county and caught the attention of the Trump administration.

A former elementary school teacher was arrested for possession of child sexual abuse material earlier this year, while a counsellor at another school was put on leave and later indicted on 20 counts of sexual crimes involving seven different children, according to the Albemarle County Police Department.

Two county school officials and a school principal were later charged with failure to report child abuse, and the county’s superintendent of schools resigned.

Jason Grant, a spokesman for Albemarle County Public Schools, told Al Jazeera that none of the individuals implicated in those cases was among the 524 employees who were hired without the proper screening required to check for a history of child sexual abuse.

“This was not about having the policies in place, this was about processes that were not followed,” Grant said. He said officials were working with the state to “make sure the processes are in place to make sure this doesn’t happen again.”

Grant said all employees in the district undergo several stages of vetting, including a criminal background check and an attestation that they have no history of child abuse or neglect. Then the school system submits their information to the Virginia Department of Social Services to verify that they are not part of the agency’s abuse and neglect database.

For three years, it appears that vetting procedures were not consistently applied. Putting employees hired over that period on leave to carry out background checks meant schools would not be able to run, so officials decided to close them until next week.

“Those were for every range of employee, from teachers to bus drivers to substitutes and across the division, so we couldn’t get coverage for that amount of people,” Grant said.

All but three of the 524 employees have now been properly vetted, and none had background issues, Grant said, adding that the county will reopen schools on Monday.

The Trump administration has long called for the dismantling of the Department of Education. The US president  signed an executive order last year that tried to set that in motion.

The department, which distributes federal funding to states for use in schools, also traditionally investigates whether local officials are complying with civil rights laws banning discrimination against minorities and marginalised groups.

Since returning to office in 2025, the Trump administration has cut more than half of the department’s staff and subjected it to wider changes it says are aimed at rooting out “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) policies.

articles.title: Maddow says Democrats can abolish Electoral College if they 'swing for the fences'
articles.excerpt:
MS NOW host said getting rid of the Electoral College was "doable" for the Democrats if they swing for the fences during an interview on Saturday.

MS NOW host Rachel Maddow said during an interview o...
articles.body_text:
MS NOW host said getting rid of the Electoral College was "doable" for the Democrats if they swing for the fences during an interview on Saturday.

MS NOW host Rachel Maddow said during an interview on Saturday that getting rid of the Electoral College was "doable" for Democrats if they "swing for the fences."

MS NOW's Jacob Soboroff asked Maddow about her thoughts on Democrats getting rid of the system, which has received criticism after the last two Republican presidents won their first elections despite losing the national popular vote.

"My whole life, it has been this kind of theoretical, you know, this hypothetical math problem. You know, if ever enough states to speak for 270 electoral votes all got into this agreement, then it would go into effect, and it always just seems so pie in the sky," she said.

GOP WIPEOUT GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE AS DEMS QUIETLY SCORE ANOTHER MAJOR WIN WITH BIG RAMIFICATIONS

Maddow said she felt it was doable for the Democrats after speaking with Ben Wikler, a Democratic advocate for eliminating the Electoral College.

Rachel Maddow appears in an interview with host Seth Meyers on Sept. 29, 2026. (Lloyd Bishop/NBC via Getty Images)

Soboroff and Maddow said that Democrats could use the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement that makes it so a state will award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential candidate wins the overall national popular vote — regardless of who actually won the vote inside that individual state.

GAVIN NEWSOM EXPRESSES 'OPENNESS' TO PACKING SCOTUS, CALLS ELECTORAL COLLEGE SYSTEM 'PERVERTED'

Eighteen states have signed the compact, in addition to Washington, D.C., which means the compact has 222 electoral votes pledged to it — 48 short of the 270 needed to take effect. However, Democrats now control the governor’s office and both chambers of the state legislatures in the swing states of Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada.

Those legislatures' combined 50 electoral votes would push the compact to 272 and activate it should they vote to sign the compact.

PROGRESSIVES UNVEIL $25 MINIMUM WAGE PUSH TO SOLVE AFFORDABILITY CRISIS DESPITE ECONOMIST INFLATION WARNING

MS NOW host Rachel Maddow is seen in conversation with David Remnick during the 2024 New Yorker Festival at Webster Hall on Oct. 27, 2024, in New York City. (Craig Barritt/Getty Images for The New Yorker)

"There are enough Democratic states right now who have a Democratic trifecta — governor and the full legislature — that puts you way over 270 if they all decided to do it, and you don't need very many states to act right now for that to be operative," Maddow said. "It's doable. I mean, raising the minimum wage is doable. Getting rid of the Electoral College is doable, age limits for Supreme Court justices might be doable. I mean, the Democrats have big majorities and if they decide to swing for the fences, they could do a lot right now."

KAMALA HARRIS CALLS TO EXPAND SUPREME COURT, ADD STATES IF DEMS TAKE CONGRESS

Former Vice President and 2024 Democratic nominee Kamala Harris called for major institutional changes in October during an interview, which included "changing" the Electoral College.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"I believe that we need to expand the Supreme Court. We need more justices on the Supreme Court so that we can have a court that actually reinforces the spirit and principles behind the Constitution of the United States," Harris told podcast host Keke Palmer.

"I believe that we should be pushing for what is possible around changing the Electoral College. Right?" she added.

Harris also lost the popular vote in 2024, making her the first Democratic White House candidate to do so in 20 years.

The system allocates 538 electors to the 50 states and Washington, D.C. A majority of 270 is needed to win the presidency.

Proponents argue, among other benefits, that the Electoral College ensures that all parts of the country play a part in choosing the president, rather than just major population centers.

Hanna Panreck is an associate editor at Fox News.
