articles.title: Israeli air strike kills senior Hamas security official in Gaza
articles.excerpt:
An Israeli strike on Gaza has killed a senior Hamas security official and wounded several others, according to local authorities.

In a statement, Gaza’s Ministry of Interior and National Security ide...
articles.body_text:
An Israeli strike on Gaza has killed a senior Hamas security official and wounded several others, according to local authorities.

In a statement, Gaza’s Ministry of Interior and National Security identified the official killed in Tuesday’s attack as Brigadier General Naim Abu Nahl, director of the Internal Security Service.

Abu Nahl was 50 years old and head of Hamas’s internal security across the Gaza Strip. A statement from Gaza’s Interior Ministry said the official was walking in the street when a drone strike killed him.

Four others, including a Palestinian woman, were wounded and taken to al-Shifa Medical Complex. The area where the missile struck is crowded with displaced people and shelters.

Hamas has condemned the assassination as a war crime, saying the killing is part of Israel’s efforts to create a “state of chaos” in the Gaza Strip.

“We affirm that these cowardly assassinations will not succeed in breaking the will of our people, nor will they deter our security and police forces from carrying out their national duty in protecting the internal front and preserving security and stability,” the group’s statement read.

Gaza’s Interior Ministry said the assassination came after the Internal Security Service had made significant gains against what it described as “gangs collaborating with the occupation and operating in areas under Israeli military control”.

Israel’s army and its Shin Bet domestic security service said in a joint statement that they had struck a senior Hamas figure, without identifying him, adding that further details would be provided later. Israel’s public broadcaster Kan later said the target was Abu Nahl. Citing Israeli sources, Kan said Abu Nahl had succeeded Moein al-Arbeid, who was detained by the Israeli army and Shin Bet during a special operation in September and remains in Israeli custody.

Several Palestinians were already reported killed earlier on Tuesday, including a child and police officers, while dozens were injured in Israeli air strikes on various parts of the Gaza Strip, according to local health officials.

There have been daily violations of the so-called “ceasefire” in Gaza, with Israeli air strikes continuing regularly in its genocidal war, with at least 1,680 people killed and 6,100 injured since the ceasefire was signed on October 11 last year.

Hamas also called on the guarantor states of the “ceasefire” agreement to intervene immediately “to rein in the occupation, impose a halt to its crimes, and obligate it to adhere to the agreement’s path”.

articles.title: Former chief of staff to Pentagon chief Hegseth says 'it’s time for Pete to call it quits': report
articles.excerpt: Impeachment efforts against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth fail in the House after 11 Democrats miss the vote. Host Paul Gigot joins Kim Strassel and Kate Odell to discuss the roll call that referred t...
articles.body_text:
Impeachment efforts against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth fail in the House after 11 Democrats miss the vote. Host Paul Gigot joins Kim Strassel and Kate Odell to discuss the roll call that referred the matter to the House Judiciary Committee. The panel also explores political setbacks for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and President Donald Trump's negotiation strategy.

Joe Kasper, who served as chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth during the early days of the Trump administration last year, has now said that Hegseth should resign.

"Pete's ability to be effective has been constrained and very soon he’ll have lost any ability to be effective," Kasper said, according to Politico. "For that reason and others, it’s time for Pete to call it quits."

"Pete's been belligerent in his stewardship of an office that will outlive him or any memory of his service," Kasper asserted, the report states.

The outlet reported that Kasper suggested that Hegseth would not be able to work with the nation's legislature or obtain appropriate funds for department priorities.

"He’s not just burned bridges up on the Hill," Kasper reportedly said. "He’s napalmed them. … He’s going to be suffocated, and it’s not like it’s going to be a slow suffocation. It’s going to be a quick asphyxiation."

PENTAGON SUED BY THE INTERCEPT, FREEDOM OF THE PRESS FOUNDATION OVER ALLEGED 'BLACKLIST' OF NEWS OUTLETS

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth attends a Halloween event hosted by first lady Melania Trump at the White House on Oct. 29, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

According to Politico, Kasper noted that he understood within a week of joining the Pentagon that Hegseth's focus was "all about Pete rather than the institution and the men and women who support it."

"There’s quite an emphasis on the showmanship," Kasper reportedly said. "The virtues of humility and basically service before self and those things have disappeared. I didn’t see those at the start, and see them ever less so now."

The Pentagon chief "overindulged in ego, in attitude, and in entitlement," Kasper said, according to the report.

He noted that he would rate Hegseth near the bottom 10% of defense secretaries in U.S. history, Politico reported. "I think history will be much crueler to him than I could be," he said.

MASSIE'S PUSH TO IMPEACH HEGSETH SPLITS CONSTITUENTS IN HIS OWN BACKYARD: 'PURE SPITE'

War Secretary Pete Hegseth and President Donald Trump during a roundtable in the East Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Due to an executive order that was issued last year, the administration now refers to the Defense Department as the Department of War and to Hegseth as the secretary of war.

The department did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's comment request on Tuesday.

A senior Pentagon official declared on behalf of the War Department in a statement to Politico that it was not surprising a "disgruntled former staffer—someone who could barely survive ninety days in the building—is now peddling made up gossip to the media."

"Secretary Hegseth is laser focused on restoring lethality to the force and supporting our warfighters, while Mr. Kasper is more focused on rewriting history to cover for his own failed tenure," the person stated, according to the outlet.

PETE HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT EFFORT DIES IN THE HOUSE AS ABSENT DEMOCRATS COULDN'T BEAT THE TRAFFIC

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon on Nov. 10, 2026 in Arlington, Va. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

A bid to impeach Hegseth failed to clear the House of Representatives earlier this month.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: McDonald's taps into Grand Theft Auto hype with Discord ordering feature as experts share concerns
articles.excerpt: Psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert addresses concerns surrounding major video game releases, noting that while violent games do not cause real-world crime, excessive screen time can strain health and rel...
articles.body_text:
Psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert addresses concerns surrounding major video game releases, noting that while violent games do not cause real-world crime, excessive screen time can strain health and relationships.

Right on the bumper of the Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) video game release, McDonald's has launched a food ordering feature within Discord, an app widely used among gamers to talk with each other while playing.

Now, those who are still in the midst of a GTA 6 marathon can stay fueled up without too much disruption by utilizing an "Order McDonald's" option in Discord that allows players to get McDelivery through Uber Eats, entertainment outlet IGN reported.

The integration, which also includes a game called Fast-Lane Feast, is available in the Apps section of all Discord servers, channels and direct messages.

'GRAND THEFT AUTO VI' MANIA COMES WITH SERIOUS HEALTH RISKS, DOCTORS WARN

While players won't need to get up from their couch, they will probably have to pause their game, as the food ordering is done through an external Uber Eats link, IGN noted.

McDonald's is making it easier for gamers to order from the fast-food giant without ever leaving their homes. (Charles-McClintock Wilson/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to McDonald's for comment.

The add-on has a few red flags in the eyes of some healthcare experts.

FORMER MCDONALD'S EXEC SPILLS THE BEANS ON WHY HEALTHIER MENU FAVORITE GOT THE AXE

"Making food ordering part of a gaming platform adds convenience, but it also raises questions about how food marketing and distracted eating intersect," Geremy Kerr, an Ohio-based registered dietitian, told Fox News Digital.

"Eating while absorbed in a game can make it easier to lose track of how much you've eaten."

Gamers can now order McDelivery through the Discord app thanks to a new add-on from McDonald's and Uber Eats. (iStock)

A McDonald's Big Mac meal with a medium fry and medium Coca-Cola contains 1,170 calories, according to the company's website.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"For gamers, a practical approach is to take a break for meals, decide what and how much to order before returning to the game and keep water within reach," Kerr said.

"I play video games myself and enjoy comfort food at times, but I still make a point of carving out time in my schedule for exercise and my health, because enjoyment and wellness don't have to be at odds."

The new feature arrives at a time when a growing number of young Americans are getting diabetes diagnoses.

By 2060, an estimated 220,000 kids and teens are predicted to be diagnosed with type 2 diabetes, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recently reported.

Healthcare professionals caution against the combination of unhealthy food and long periods of sitting. (iStock)

It's possible to delay or prevent type 2 diabetes by making healthy lifestyle choices, according to the CDC.

"Gaming often means hours of sitting, and when comfort food is only a click away without ever pausing the game, the line between leisure and an unhealthy habit gets even thinner," Dr. Swapnil Patel, a physician at Hackensack Meridian Health Center in Farmingdale, New Jersey, told Fox News Digital.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"In excess, that combination can contribute to obesity, high cholesterol and type 2 diabetes."

However, that doesn't mean that someone needs to stop gaming altogether, Patel added.

The recent release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) has captivated the video game community. (Richard B. Levine/Getty Images)

"I play video games myself and enjoy comfort food at times, but I still make a point of carving out time in my schedule for exercise and my health, because enjoyment and wellness don't have to be at odds," Patel said.

Currently, the Discord add-on is only available in the U.S. in areas where McDelivery is available, cybersecurity and information outlet Cybernews reported.

Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Colombia at a Crossroads: Searching for peace amid conflict

A decade after Colombia’s peace accords, former FARC fighter and artist honours killed signatories with a mural.

Yuheni Izquierdo, a former FARC fighter turned artist, paints a mural commemorating fe...
articles.body_text:
A decade after Colombia’s peace accords, former FARC fighter and artist honours killed signatories with a mural.

Yuheni Izquierdo, a former FARC fighter turned artist, paints a mural commemorating fellow peace signatories killed since Colombia’s 2016 Havana peace accords. More than 50 years of armed conflict formally ended with the agreement, but hundreds of signatories have since been killed as armed groups carry out reprisals and fight for territorial control.

Yuheni fears that the escalating violence threatens to return the country to a past that claimed more than 450,000 lives and hopes her mural will inspire Colombians to believe that a lasting peace is possible.

Colombia at a Crossroads is a documentary film by Rodrigo Vazquez Salessi.

articles.title: Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies of measles in state's ninth fatal case this year
articles.excerpt: Dr. Marc Siegel warns that dropping measles vaccination rates could cost the U.S. its elimination status. The Fox News senior medical analyst joins hosts Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino to discuss the ris...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Marc Siegel warns that dropping measles vaccination rates could cost the U.S. its elimination status. The Fox News senior medical analyst joins hosts Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino to discuss the rise to over 5,000 cases in 2026. Siegel outlines what is driving the decline and explains how communities can protect public health.

Pennsylvania health officials announced Monday that a resident unvaccinated against measles died from the virus after testing positive, making it the ninth measles-related death in the state this year.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed the death less than a week after the United States lost its measles elimination status, ending a public health achievement that had been maintained since 2000.

Officials said the victim was a resident of Centre County, located in the middle of the state and most known for being home to Penn State University.

The state has 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties this year, including 49 new infections that were reported Monday.

A measles screening sign is posted at the entrance of Geisinger's Hospital for Advanced Medicine in Danville, Pennsylvania, on Nov. 21, 2026. (Paul Weaver/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK

Hospitalizations rose from 315 to 330, according to the state’s measles dashboard. Just five of the confirmed infections involved vaccinated residents.

Last week, officials confirmed the state’s eighth measles death, an unvaccinated Clinton County resident.

Pennsylvania and federal health authorities continue to urge residents to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, saying it the best defense against the disease.

Pennsylvania has been battling a measles outbreak since April and now leads the nation in cases, accounting for more than a quarter of all U.S. infections.

One-year-old River Jacobs is held by his mother, Caitlin Fuller, while he receives an MMR vaccine from Raynard Covarrubio, at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025, in Lubbock, Texas. (Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images)

TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM

The sharp rise in cases — largely in rural and Amish communities with historically low vaccination rates — has prompted state health officials to ramp up immunization efforts.

The state health department has administered more than 7,400 doses of the MMR vaccine at nearly 300 pop-up clinics. Officials plan to set up dozens more of these temporary immunization sites over the coming weeks and months.

For months, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have sparred over the response to the ongoing measles outbreak in the state.

Shapiro has accused Kennedy of spreading misinformation about the MMR vaccine and vaccines in general, something the nation's top health official has denied.

Josh Shapiro, governor of Pennsylvania, speaks during the Bradford County Democrats Breakfast at the Sayre VFW in Sayre, Pennsylvania, on Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026. (Photographer: Heather Ainsworth/Bloomberg)

AMISH FACE NEW YORK VACCINE MANDATE IN SUPREME COURT FIGHT, MIGHT HAVE TO ‘PACK THEIR WAGONS’

Overall, Kennedy has given a mix of answers about his stance on the MMR vaccine. When testifying before the House in May 2025, he said he would "probably" vaccinate his children against measles.

When he was asked the same question in August 2024, prior to becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy said he would not give his kids the MMR vaccine.

Kennedy, meanwhile, has accused Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak and suggested that some of Pennsylvania’s reported measles deaths may have been "fabricated."

Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. speaks during an event at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services building on Oct. 5, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

The Pan American Health Organization’s decision last Wednesday to revoke the U.S.’ measles elimination status means the virus is once again considered endemic in the country. This means it is circulating regularly at a relatively predictable level, much like the seasonal flu and chickenpox.

The difference is, measles is around 12 times more contagious than the flu and twice as contagious as chickenpox, according to Unicef.

People infected with measles — especially babies and young children — also face the risk of severe complications, including a weakened immune system or encephalitis, a type of brain swelling that can cause seizures and intellectual disabilities.

James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

articles.title: A $17 million bill for an AD who never actually started? Michigan's Trev Alberts mess gets uglier
articles.excerpt:
Former Michigan tight end held nothing back against the College Football Playoff committee and their strange rankings they've released so far.

The Michigan athletic department has another problem on ...
articles.body_text:
Former Michigan tight end held nothing back against the College Football Playoff committee and their strange rankings they've released so far.

The Michigan athletic department has another problem on its hands, and it could be a very expensive one, thanks to the vetting process of what was supposed to be its new leader in Trev Alberts.

Last week, the former Texas A&M athletic director announced he was leaving the school to accept the same position at Michigan starting in December.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The move was a somewhat stunning one, as incoming Michigan Pres. C. Cybele Raver was tasked with leading this search with the help of the Board of Regents in Ann Arbor.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

So, when Alberts agreed to be the next athletic director after signing an MOU with the school over the past week, folks at Michigan were under the impression this was all but finalized.

This is where things took a turn for all parties involved, thanks to a story published last week.

Athletic Director Trev Alberts stands on the field before the game against the Iowa Hawkeyes at Memorial Stadium in Lincoln, Neb., on Nov. 26, 2021. (Getty Images)

The Wolverines might end up learning the hard way about what transpires when you do not complete a full background check on an incoming employee that will be tasked with also restoring an athletic department that has been marred in scandal over the past six years.

When Trev Alberts decided to accept the Michigan job, he informed Texas A&M that he was moving on to his third school in nearly six years.

Turns out, the school he had already interviewed with and accepted a job at had themselves a very big problem coming their way that pertained to Alberts' time as athletic director at Nebraska.

A lawsuit filed by a Nebraska women's basketball player in 2024 alleged that Alberts violated her civil rights by encouraging her to leave the team after not ordering an investigation into a romantic relationship the athlete had with an assistant coach.

When deposed under oath related to the lawsuit, Trev Alberts was asked if he had understood the Nebraska policy on consensual relationships under the school's personnel handbook.

According to a story by FOIABall.com, Alberts was grilled over whether he understood that coaches should not be involved in romantic relationships with student athletes.

FORMER MICHIGAN COACH SHERRONE MOORE RECEIVES PUNISHMENT FROM STALKING CASE STEMMING FROM FIRING

Did the Nebraska athletic director concede that it was ok for this situation to occur?

As outlined in his answer to the question, according to FOIABALL.com, Alberts provided this answer to plaintiff counsel.

"I mean, you know, it just depends," he added, claiming that COVID eligibility rules led to older players, who may be closer in age to coaches, which makes the situation more "nuanced."

Trev Alberts also reportedly admitted that he did not know the answer to that same question as the current leader of Texas A&M athletics.

Was this taken out of context and did Michigan react without fully understanding the way in which this was answered? That's up to them to discuss over the next few days.

But, Trev Alberts made it clear in a statement that he felt like he had been fully vetted by Michigan, after already starting to work on behalf of the Wolverines.

"The egregious characterization of words taken out of context from a deposition regarding an incident that occurred years ago is wrong and unfair," Trev Alberts said in statement. "I was informed that Michigan's General Counsel had spoken with the General Counsel of both Texas A&M and the University of Nebraska, as well as Nebraska's outside counsel, to inquire about the deposition.

"I was further told that all three of those lawyers told Michigan's GC that I had done nothing wrong or inappropriate and had followed all applicable university polices and procedures. I am proud of my long tract record of standing up for student-athletes and for following the rules and my core values."

When this story was released late last week, multiple sources tell OutKick that Board of Regents members at Michigan were shocked to learn of the answers that Alberts provided in the deposition.

On Tuesday, the University of Michigan released the following statement.

"The University of Michigan's search for its next athletic director is ongoing. As we navigate a rapidly changing landscape in intercollegiate athletics, the values that define Michigan will guide our decisions and reinforce our commitment to excellence and integrity, both in the classroom and in competition."

Trev Alberts, athletic director for the Nebraska Cornhuskers, talks with head coach Matt Rhule before the game at Camp Randall Stadium on Nov. 18, 2023, in Madison, Wis. (Getty Images)

Given that the Wolverines were still dealing with the aftermath of the Sherrone Moore situation, which led to him being fired for having an affair with a female staffer in the football building, it was a pretty bad look for the incoming AD not to understand school policy over student-coach relationships.

The Michigan Board of Regents held an emergency call to discuss the hiring of Trev Alberts, knowing the ramifications that would be coming if made official.

This then led to incoming president C. Cybele Raver informing the board that she did not feel comfortable with the school moving forward with the hiring of Trev Alberts and needed to move in a different direction, quick.

If there is anything we've learned over the past six years regarding the University of Michigan, it's that anything is possible when it comes to a disaster of epic proportions.

Trev Alberts had already resigned from Texas A&M, which also led to him signing an MOU with the school. His contract, when fully executed, would pay him $17 million with a buyout if not fired for cause.

Was there language in the MOU that said his full hiring was contingent upon a background search? Attorneys for Alberts believe there was not that type of language, while Michigan officials are holding firm that there is an "out" for the school to avoid paying him $17 million that would come if he had been actually fired upon taking the job.

According to the contract obtained by OutKick, there is language in the MOU that says it is a "binding contract."

"Pending the completion of the Agreement this MOU shall form a binding contract between you and the University," the MOU states in the second paragraph.

Another snag for Alberts — and there are seemingly plenty — is the roughly $4 million buyout he owes Texas A&M, which Michigan agreed to cover in the MOU.

So, you have a guy that owes the Aggies millions, while at the same time fighting Michigan over what his attorneys feels as though he is owed for an MOU that might be binding.

Michigan Wolverines head coach Sherrone Moore leaves the field following the NCAA football game against the Ohio State Buckeyes at Michigan Stadium in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on Nov. 29, 2025. Ohio State won 27-9. (IMAGN)

There are plenty of things we could say about the University of Michigan and its knack for creating public relations' nightmares inside their own house, but this latest fumble by the school shows us why it's hard to give them the benefit of the doubt on anything related to athletics.

The school puts out one dumpster fire, only to start another one a few yards away.

There will obviously be a fight over buyout money related to the MOU signed by both Michigan and Trev Alberts.

All the while, Texas A&M has appointed an interim athletic director and has already started a national search for its new leader.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

articles.title: Cameroon separatist leader pleads not guilty at war crimes trial in Norway
articles.excerpt:
Cameroonian separatist leader Lucas Cho Ayaba has pleaded not guilty in a Norwegian court to being an accessory to war crimes and “terrorism”, charges that carry a sentence of up to 30 years.

The 54-...
articles.body_text:
Cameroonian separatist leader Lucas Cho Ayaba has pleaded not guilty in a Norwegian court to being an accessory to war crimes and “terrorism”, charges that carry a sentence of up to 30 years.

The 54-year-old, who appeared in a court in Oslo on Tuesday, is accused of involvement in planning two attacks in Cameroon from Norway, helping to select targets and pay for explosives.

Prosecutors say Ayaba, also known as Cho Lucas Yabah, remotely led the separatist Amazonia Governing Council and commanded its armed wing, the Amazonia Defence Forces, from 2017 until 2024, when he was arrested in Norway, where he has lived since 2008.

Francophone-majority Cameroon has been gripped for nearly 10 years by conflict between state security forces and separatists demanding the independence of two Anglophone regions in the country’s west to form what supporters call “Ambazonia”.

In February 2023, three improvised devices exploded during a mountain run race near Buea in southwestern Cameroon, killing a 38-year-old woman and injuring 19 civilians.

In February of the following year, another improvised device killed a 15-year-old girl during a Youth Day celebration in Nkambe, northwestern Cameroon. More than 90 civilians were wounded, with some undergoing amputations.

Ayaba is also alleged to have encouraged or ordered the murder or attempted murder of captives and to have orchestrated the torture or humiliation of four women accused of having intimate relations with Cameroonian soldiers.

“Messages on WhatsApp are key evidence in this case,” prosecutor Carl Fredrik Fari told the AFP news agency.

“Wrap a rope around his neck and send him to hell,” Ayaba allegedly said in an audio message sent on WhatsApp in October 2023, after receiving videos showing a mistreated prisoner believed to be a Cameroonian soldier.

Ayaba’s lawyer, Morten Engesbak, told AFP that Ayaba “sees himself as the leader of a struggle to liberate a population that has been oppressed for very many years by the Cameroonian authorities”.

The unrest began in late 2016 after Anglophone lawyers and teachers protested against the appointment of Francophone magistrates unfamiliar with British common law to courts in English-speaking regions, and French-speaking teachers unable to communicate fluently in English.

The protests were met with a violent government crackdown and eventually gave rise to a separatist movement seeking independence for the two regions.

The UN says at least 6,000 civilians have been killed since 2016. More than 330,000 people were displaced within Cameroon in 2026 and another 100,000 took refuge in neighbouring Nigeria.

The trial in the Oslo district court is expected to last until March 12.

articles.title: Billy Bob Thornton urges viewers to learn the real history behind Thanksgiving on Fox Nation's 'The Mayflower'
articles.excerpt:
"Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower" is streaming now on Fox Nation. (Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)

The stars were out on Monday night in New York City to celebrate Fox Nation’s "Billy Bob Thor...
articles.body_text:
"Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower" is streaming now on Fox Nation. (Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)

The stars were out on Monday night in New York City to celebrate Fox Nation’s "Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower" as the iconic actor seeks to educate viewers, just in time for Thanksgiving.

"The Mayflower," which is now streaming on Fox Nation, is a three-part historical docudrama that aims to strip away the myth of Plymouth Rock and inform viewers on everything from the deadly voyage across the Atlantic to Thanksgiving and one of America’s bloodiest wars. Fox News Media executives, Fox News Channel anchors, the show’s creators and other special guests gathered at The Whitby Hotel for an exclusive screening of the debut episode.

"Thank God for Fox Nation, because they’re willing to tell stories of our history, which is awesome," Thornton told the crowd.

BILLY BOB THORNTON SAYS HE’S A HOLIDAY ‘PURIST’ AS HE BRINGS BACK ‘TRADITIONAL’ THANKSGIVING AT HOME

Billy Bob Thornton attends the New York screening of "Billy Bob Thornton Presents: The Mayflower" hosted by Fox Nation at Whitby Hotel on November 23, 2026, in New York City.  (Dominik Bindl/Getty Images)

"The Mayflower" traces the Pilgrims’ death-defying Atlantic crossing, the fragile alliance forged between the English settlers and the Wampanoag people, and the devastating conflict that ultimately transformed Britain’s colonies into the earliest foundations of an American identity.

"One of the things that I think we're quickly losing around here is our history. History is very important, and if you don't know where you came from, it's hard to live now," Thornton said.

"I love history, I’ve always studied it. My dad was a history teacher, and I always want to learn more about stuff and I didn’t know this," he continued. "I knew the story they told us in elementary school."

BILLY BOB THORNTON PUSHES BACK ON CELEBRITY ACTIVISM: ‘I DON'T KNOW ANYTHING ABOUT POLITICS’

"The Mayflower," which is now streaming on Fox Nation, is a three-part historical docudrama that aims to strip away the myth of Plymouth Rock. (FOX News Media)

The Academy Award-winning writer, actor and director said most people simply think, "’Oh, that’s great, the native tribe came over, and they had turkey'" — but the truth is far more complex.

"The people who came over here on [the Mayflower]… a lot of people got sick, a lot of people died," Thornton said.

He called for viewers to keep the trials and tribulations of the Pilgrims in mind when celebrating Thanksgiving with loved ones this week.

"When you say your blessings to the people, maybe remember the people that suffered to get us where we are," he said.

Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott, Fox News Media President and Executive Editor Jay Wallace, Fox News Media Chief Digital and Marketing Officer Jason Klarman, Fox News' Bill Hemmer, Dan Perino, Lawrence Jones, Martha MacCallum, Emily Compagno, Eric Shawn, Lisa Boothe, Paul Mauro and "House of Cards" actor Michael Kelly were among the guests for Monday’s screening and cocktail reception.

FOX NATION TEAMS UP WITH JACK CARR TO TAKE VIEWERS INSIDE THE GLOBAL MANHUNT FOR CARLOS THE JACKAL

Billy Bob Thornton praised Fox Nation for telling stories of American history.

While developing "The Mayflower," the team consulted a range of historical resources and experts, including historians at Plimoth Patuxet Museums, where portions of the series were filmed, as well as acclaimed historian Nathaniel Philbrick.

The series is produced by AIRtime Projects and Terminal B TV with Thornton as an executive producer, alongside Geyer Kosinski, Tom Forman, David Metzler, Jordan Rosenblum and showrunner and executive producer John Ealer.

"My only wish and prayer from you all is that you watch this as people who want to learn something and watch something wonderful that these wonderful producers and director put together with Fox Nation," Thornton said.

Thornton currently stars in the hit Paramount+ series, "Landman," for which he received Critics' Choice Award and Golden Globe Award nominations for Best Actor in a Television Drama. His recent projects have also included the Amazon series "Goliath" and the critically acclaimed FX series "Fargo."

Thornton has also starred in such movies as "Bad Santa," "The Alamo," "Bandits," "The Man Who Wasn’t There," "Friday Night Lights," "Sling Blade," "A Simple Plan," "Armageddon" and "Monster’s Ball," among other critical and commercial hits.CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fox Nation programs are viewable on demand and from your mobile device app but only for FOX Nation subscribers. Go to Fox Nation to start a free trial and watch the extensive library of your favorite FOX Nation personalities.

Fox News Digital’s Laura Carrione contributed to this report.

Brian Flood is a media editor/reporter for FOX News Digital. Story tips can be sent to brian.flood@fox.com and on Twitter: @briansflood.

articles.title: Biden's first-year fundraising fails to crack 1% of Obama's library haul as questions swirl over legacy
articles.excerpt:
Ohio State accounting professor Brian Mittendorf examines the Obama Foundation's financial health, assets and endowment as construction costs hit $1 billion.

Former President Joe Biden has raised a s...
articles.body_text:
Ohio State accounting professor Brian Mittendorf examines the Obama Foundation's financial health, assets and endowment as construction costs hit $1 billion.

Former President Joe Biden has raised a shockingly small amount of funds for his presidential library compared to former President Barack Obama.

The figures are fueling skepticism about how history will remember Biden's single term in the White House.

In 2017, Obama’s first year out of office, the two-term president managed to bring in $232.6 million in donations and contributions to fund the foundation behind his presidential library. By comparison, Biden secured just $1.5 million in 2025 for his presidential library foundation, per tax filings.

This is less than 1% of what his former boss raised in the same amount of time after leaving office.

Even before leaving office, President Donald Trump’s library foundation has already dwarfed that of his predecessor by raising tens of millions of dollars from a variety of sources, including companies that settled lawsuits with him.

OBAMA CENTER ISN'T A TRADITIONAL PRESIDENTIAL LIBRARY. CRITICS SAY IT'S AN ACTIVISM CENTER.

Former US presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden shake hands during the opening of the Barack Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, Illinois, on June 18, 2026. (Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images)

Though the Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation has yet to decide on a construction site, it’s already running a deficit, spending $600,000 more than it raised in 2025. A Biden library official claimed that it wasn’t actively fundraising in 2025 in a statement shared with CBS News.

The lack of enthusiasm for Biden’s legacy has led some to claim that Americans may simply forget about his presidency as the years go on.

"Presidencies usually fade," Axios’ Zachary Basu wrote of his legacy. "But in just one year, Biden’s has been reduced to a footnote by a successor committed to dismantling every pillar of Washington’s old liberal order."

Heritage Action press manager Doug Blair told Fox News Digital, "Joe Biden spent half a century in Washington and did nothing to benefit the American people."

"The anemic fundraising for his presidential library is a fitting bookend for a failed presidency Americans are eager to forget," he added. "Joe Biden left Americans worse off by every conceivable measure and his legacy will be a southern border blown wide open, the disgraceful image of him checking his watch as fallen American troops returned home from Afghanistan, and endless scandals and investigations surrounding him and his corrupt family.'

BIDEN'S BATTLE WITH ADVANCING CANCER RENEWS FOCUS ON PROSTATE DISEASE

Allies of the former president point to the fact that Biden presided over the end of the COVID-19 pandemic, influential pieces of domestic legislation and America’s withdrawal from Afghanistan, parts of his legacy that could contribute to historical staying power.

A January 2025 Gallup poll found that 54% of U.S. adults believed history would remember Biden as a "below-average" or "poor" president.

Former U.S. President Joe Biden attends the dedication ceremony for the opening of the Barack Obama Presidential Center in John Lewis Plaza (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)

A source close to Biden’s foundation told CBS News that it ramped up its fundraising in 2026, pulling in multiple multi-million-dollar contributions, including two $5 million donations.

Another source told the outlet that some of Biden's close allies are frustrated that Democratic donors aren’t stepping up to support the former president’s library.

Further complicating Biden’s fundraising efforts, and his ability to nurture his public image, is his advanced age and Stage 4 prostate cancer, which has metastasized to his bones.

OBAMA CENTER OPENS AFTER YEARS-LONG SAGA AS LOCALS WARN ‘MONSTROSITY’ COULD PRICE THEM OUT

Former President Barack Obama and the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, where construction costs are now projected to reach approximately $1 billion, nearly triple the upper end of the original estimate. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images; Talía Sprague/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

While the increase in funds is no doubt encouraging for Biden’s allies, it still puts them far behind Obama, who raised $164.8 million for his foundation in 2018.

Obama ultimately spent nearly $1 billion on his presidential library in Chicago, a sum Biden likely will not be able to reach given his current fundraising levels.

The Joe and Jill Biden Presidential Library Foundation and the Obama Foundation did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Tuesday.

articles.title: US sanctions on Lebanon’s Hezbollah-affiliates may have limited impact
articles.excerpt: Beirut, Lebanon – New United States sanctions on an organisation linked to the Iranian-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah will have a limited impact beyond the political messaging the punishment provides...
articles.body_text:
Beirut, Lebanon – New United States sanctions on an organisation linked to the Iranian-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah will have a limited impact beyond the political messaging the punishment provides, analysts have told Al Jazeera.

The organisation – a charity called Wa Ta’awanu Association – was among the entities and individuals targeted by the US Treasury in new sanctions announced on November 18, accusing it of being a “front organisation” for Hezbollah. The Treasury said the sanctions were an effort to disrupt Hezbollah’s financing networks.

The sanctions are part of a US campaign against Hezbollah, a Shia political and military group. Washington has put pressure on the Lebanese government to make progress on disarming Hezbollah, which has been engaged in an on-off war with Israel for the past 40 years.

But experts told Al Jazeera, the sanctions will do little to change Lebanon’s domestic situation, in which Hezbollah has been one of the major powers – if not the major power – over the past two decades.

“[The US] is threatening to impose sanctions on political, judicial and security figures but that won’t change the reality,” Qassem Kassir, a Lebanese journalist close to Hezbollah, told Al Jazeera. “Sanctions or the threat of sanctions will not change the reality inside Lebanon.”

Lebanese media reports have suggested that the US, frustrated by the Lebanese government’s lack of progress in disarming the Iran-backed group, could apply sanctions beyond direct Hezbollah affiliates and start to target bankers and businessmen.

“There are other packages, a second, third, maybe a fourth [round of sanctions],” Ali Hamade, a Lebanese journalist with Annahar, claimed in a video posted to social media. “It will focus on Hezbollah funding and money smuggling efforts and may involve several bankers, figures in the world of Lebanese finance and business, in the real estate sector and contractors.

He added that politicians, security personnel, judges, and figures in Lebanese public administration were unlikely to face sanctions yet.

Hezbollah, a Shia-dominated movement which emerged during the Lebanese civil war, is part of a wider network of Iran-linked groups in the region. The group is believed to receive direct financing from Tehran, as well as its own financing networks.

In its sanctions announcement, the US Treasury claimed that the Wa Ta’awanu Association “provides cover for Hizballah’s activities under the guise of delivering humanitarian services”.

But Kassir said the group provided assistance to needy Lebanese people.

“Unfortunately, the Americans and some Lebanese parties want to prevent any assistance or service from reaching people,” he said. “However, sanctions will not stop the work of the Wa Ta’awanu Association, just as it has not been able to stop the Al Qard Al Hassan, educational institutions, construction companies and Jihad Al-Binaa.”

Al Qard Al Hassan, a financial institution, and Jihad Al-Binaa, a construction company, are part of a wide array of Hezbollah-affiliated organisations that have been sanctioned by the US, though both companies also employ or serve people not affiliated with Hezbollah.

Israel has continued to attack what it says are Hezbollah targets in Lebanon intermittently, despite a “ceasefire” agreement earlier this year.

It also continues to hold territory it invaded up to 10km (6.2 miles) into Lebanese territory.

Israel – backed by the US – has tied its withdrawal from Lebanon to the full disarmament of Hezbollah. Talks between the Israeli and Lebanese governments were held earlier this year and led to a Framework Agreement in June, which designated so-called “pilot zones” where Israeli troops would withdraw, and the Lebanese army would deploy to disarm Hezbollah.

But the pilot zone programme has had little success, as Israel still refuses to withdraw from new territories and accuses the Lebanese army of failing to disarm Hezbollah in the existing pilot zones.

In the meantime, the US has looked for other means to pressure Hezbollah, as it continues attacks against the group’s patron, Iran.

“The US treats sanctions as one of several forms of pressure that it can exert on Hezbollah’s financial networks,” David Wood, the senior Lebanon analyst with International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera. “Washington has also targeted Hezbollah’s efforts to raise money outside of traditional financial systems – such as receiving physical cash – by insisting that the Lebanese state exert more control over the country’s airport, seaports and border with neighbouring Syria.”

But Wood argued that sanctions against the group and individuals connected to it are only likely to have a limited effect.

“The threat of US sanctions might change the behaviour of some Lebanese elites, but that source of leverage largely disappears after imposing sanctions, because it is not straightforward to lift them,” Wood said. “Imposing US sanctions seeks to raise the cost of doing business with Hezbollah, especially for alleged associates of the party who enjoy lucrative sources of private income. This tactic is probably less effective in relation to direct affiliates of Hezbollah, which are more likely to operate outside traditional financial networks already.”

Analysts also argue that the US’s use of sanctions is politically driven, showing that it is not a neutral or balanced actor when it comes to brokering deals between Beirut and Tel Aviv.

“The US is not a fair or equal decision-maker because it is a strategic partner of Israel and that’s the motivation behind sanctions,” Karim Safieddine, a Beirut-based nonresident fellow at the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, told Al Jazeera. “Sanctions by, say, the UN or independent bodies or courts that actually assess Hezbollah’s criminal culpability are one thing. But partisan sanctions that are part of warfare obviously only induce further [divisions] in Lebanon and have had lots of repercussions on people who are not Hezbollah.”

The US pressure campaign is still having an adverse effect on Lebanese people who do not support, or in some cases, actively oppose Hezbollah, due to the affiliation of the Shia community with the group – a connection the group itself also stresses at times.

“There are real repercussions on normal Lebanese people, especially Shia, because of supposed affiliations within a party that is very embedded in a community,” Safieddine said. “And it’s very hard to disembed it, as opposed to the genocidal tactics used by Israel. But the issue with sanctions is that they’re not actually based on criteria of human rights respectability.”

articles.title: 'Worst nightmare' as Delta flight comes to sudden halt due to cabin disruption
articles.excerpt:
Aviation safety expert and former airline captain Steve Arroyo explains how crews that are lined up for departure must communicate with tower controllers when an animal roams free inside a cabin.

Pas...
articles.body_text:
Aviation safety expert and former airline captain Steve Arroyo explains how crews that are lined up for departure must communicate with tower controllers when an animal roams free inside a cabin.

Passengers aboard a morning flight out of Boston faced an unusual pause on the tarmac recently after a four-legged traveler broke free in the cabin.

A Delta Air Lines flight was taxiing toward the runway at Logan International Airport on Nov. 20 when a passenger's pet slipped out of its carrier, Delta Air Lines confirmed to Fox News Digital.

The plane was preparing to depart for Tampa, Florida, when the pilot asked air traffic control for a quick stop, according to audio on ATC.com.

TRAVELERS CLASH OVER WHETHER CRUISE LINES SHOULD ALLOW DOGS AND CATS ON BOARD OR NOT

"We got a situation in the cabin. We need to hold somewhere for a minute," the captain told controllers.

"Thanks for accommodating," the captain said, according to ATC.com. "We had a cat loose in the cabin."

A passenger's cat slipped out of its carrier aboard a taxiing Delta Air Lines flight (not pictured) at Boston's Logan International Airport on Nov. 20. (iStock)

"That's a new one," the controller replied. "And have a good day. Meow."

The jet soon resumed taxiing, took off without further trouble and landed in Tampa on schedule, the airline said.

Steven Arroyo, a Florida-based aviation expert and a retired United Airlines captain, told Fox News Digital that pilots are required to halt takeoff procedures whenever passengers are out of their seat or if an animal gets loose in the cabin.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"It is incumbent upon the pilots to communicate what's going on in the cabin, whether it's for an animal [or] a passenger," Arroyo said. "We can't have people up and about."

He recalled a similar scare of his own in the early 1990s, when one of his dogs chewed through a nylon carrier while his family was flying from South Florida to New York.

The aircraft in question (not pictured) had to stop on the taxiway while the loose cat was safely placed back inside its cabin crate.  (iStock)

Under the Delta Air Lines pet travel rules, small cats and dogs flying in the cabin must stay inside a closed, ventilated kennel tucked under the seat in front of their owners throughout the trip.

The airline's website warns that travelers who fail to follow pet policies or keep their animals secured inside a carrier risk losing the ability to bring pets on future flights.

The escape led to plenty of jokes and travel stories on Reddit, where users weighed in on how easily cats can slip out of carriers.

"That's the best part of the story," one commenter wrote about the air traffic controller's "meow" sound over the radio.

Several pet owners shared their own stories of animals breaking free during trips.

"My cat was always fine in her carrier. It's a backpack that has some mesh windows. Then one day she decided to unzip it and let herself out," one commenter wrote.

Travelers who fail to keep their pets secured inside a carrier during flights could lose the ability to bring their animals on future flights. (Smith Collection/Gado)

"I work for a wildlife agency and was called to a plane to pick up a turtle that had been found wandering the aisle by a [flight attendant] during a flight," another user shared.

Not everyone found the idea of a loose cabin pet amusing — with some travelers pointing out problems with allergies and phobias.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"This would be [my] worst nightmare as someone [who is ] terrified of cats," one commenter wrote.

"I would have an allergic reaction that [would last] days," another user added.

Kelly McGreal is a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. She and the team cover travel, food and drink, health, relationships and more. She also produces the weekly American Culture Quiz and handles other special projects.

I don’t know about you, but as exciting as all the football we get over the next few days is, I’m equally jazzed up about the college basketball tournaments. To me, this is one of the best times of the year for college basketball. We usually see some fun tournaments, with good teams facing each other. Then, once these are over, the conference games start fairly soon after. It really marks the start of the main portion of the season for college basketball. Tonight, we get what should be a great game between Baylor and Alabama.

The Baylor Bears come into the game with a solid 4-1 record for the year. They’ve had a fairly easy schedule to start the year. In their four wins, they’ve taken down Northwestern State, Arkansas-Pine Bluff, Yale, and Jackson State. None of those games were particularly close, either. They won each of them by at least 20 points. The lone loss they had did come at a neutral site, but it is an easily justifiable loss as they fell to Texas. It was a close game, with the Longhorns winning that one by three points.

Baylor Bears center Caden Powell goes up for a layup against Jackson State Tigers guard Dorian McMillian during the second half at Paul and Alejandra Foster Pavilion in Waco, Texas, on Nov. 18, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Baylor has some solid pieces on its team. Unfortunately for them, they are mostly made up of guards. They have five guys averaging 10 or more points per game in the early season, and four of them are guards. The lone addition is a forward, and he is the lowest-scoring. That could prove difficult when they need to get some action close to the rim. To their credit, after the four guards, their next five players are all forwards and centers, but they are only averaging anywhere from 3.2 points per game to 10 points per game.

The Alabama Crimson Tide are perfect to start the year, but the reality is that they really haven’t had a test yet. Sure, Sam Houston might be okay, and Seton Hall should be pretty good, but this is the first non-home game they’ve played this season, and it is the first time they have a team that might give them a real challenge. They’ve also beaten Arkansas State, Oakland, and Kennesaw State. The only game that was reasonably close was the one against Seton Hall, and they still won that game by six points.

Guard Aden Holloway of the Alabama Crimson Tide talks to a referee during the college basketball game between the Alabama Crimson Tide and the Georgia Bulldogs on March 3, 2026, at Stegeman Coliseum in Athens, GA. (Jeffrey Vest/Icon Sportswire)

This team is built around a bit more balance, but it does skew toward guard play as opposed to forwards. They have Aden Holloway and Amari Allen both averaging 16 points per game, and then the next five guys on the roster averaging eight or more points per game. Four of those five players are forwards, so I do think they have a bit more balance. Holloway and Allen have had some very hot shooting to start the year, with both of them hitting 50% or better from beyond the arc. I don’t know that it will last, considering this is the first time they have to look at a different shooting eye and play on a different court.

articles.title: Nvidia shares slide as Trump's role in Jensen Huang's comeback questioned by US politicians
articles.excerpt:
How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

Shares in Nvidia dipped on Tuesday as US politicans questioned President Donald Trump's role in the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive.

...
articles.body_text:
How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

Shares in Nvidia dipped on Tuesday as US politicans questioned President Donald Trump's role in the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Huang was handed back his job at the AI microchip maker on Monday less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.

Trump has said he played a big role in the 63-year-old's reinstatment, which has led to questions and backlash from US lawmakers.

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the annoucement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price was down almost 8% on Tuesday, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's shock return was revealed.

However, Nvidia was not the only semiconductor chip company to experience share price declines on Tuesday, with rival AMD down more than 10%.

Broadcom and Marvell Technology shares were also lower, suggesting that investors were continuing to weigh up concerns over potential regulation by newly-elected Democrats, as well as the central question as to whether the huge amounts being invested in AI will pay off.

Nvidia's share price for example, is down almost 30% over the past six months and had been on the decline before the scandal involving its co-founder emerged earlier this month.

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn on its original position. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

Trump said he had spoken to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump told CNBC. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

There has been bipartisan political anger over Huang's reinstatement.

Republican representative Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang", while Republican senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions", and Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.

The US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.

articles.title: Zimbabwean convicted in South Africa of trying to fight in Ukraine
articles.excerpt:
A group of South Africans returned from the war in Ukraine earlier this year

A Zimbabwean national has been convicted by a court in South Africa of planning to go to fight in Ukraine.

The country ha...
articles.body_text:
A group of South Africans returned from the war in Ukraine earlier this year

A Zimbabwean national has been convicted by a court in South Africa of planning to go to fight in Ukraine.

The country has strict laws which restrict unauthorised involvement in overseas wars.

Twenty-four-year-old Wesley Sothole, who pleaded guilty, was handed a five-year suspended prison sentence and was ordered to be deported from South Africa.

He is one of five Zimbabweans who were arrested at OR Tambo Airport in Johannesburg on 8 November. South African prosecutors have not confirmed which side the Zimbabweans allegedly intended to fight for.

Sothole's four co-accused have yet to enter pleas and are due to return to the Kempton Park Magistrates' Court on 1 December for further plea and sentencing proceedings.

Another four Zimbabweans were arrested at a hotel in Johannesburg at the same time in a joint operation and are facing a different court process.

The investigation has involved South African police, Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies.

South Africa's Foreign Military Assistance Act was passed in 1998 at a time when the government was concerned about members of the former apartheid security services going to fight elsewhere in Africa.

There has been growing concern across Africa over the recruitment of its citizens to fight in the war in Ukraine, with some reportedly being lured to Russia by promises of lucrative civilian employment.

A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.

Some have been captured and are being held as prisoners of war.

In March, Kenya estimated that 252 of its citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia.

Kenyan Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue. He said an agreement had been reached for Russia to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.

In the same month, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.

The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 of its nationals who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.

In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.

South Africa's government said it condemned "the exploitation of young vulnerable people by individuals working with foreign military entities".

Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.

Additional reporting by Khanyisile Ngcobo in Johannesburg.

articles.title: Florida Gators head coach Jon Sumrall takes swipe at predecessor Billy Napier in Monday press conference
articles.excerpt: "Alabama brought their paddle, you know, and Lane Kiffin brought his celebrities like he brought Kevin frickin Costner to get off the bus with him. He's got Shaq, Angel Reese, Paul Skenes, Livvy Dunne...
articles.body_text:
"Alabama brought their paddle, you know, and Lane Kiffin brought his celebrities like he brought Kevin frickin Costner to get off the bus with him. He's got Shaq, Angel Reese, Paul Skenes, Livvy Dunne, the side show circus is starting to piss people off in Baton Rouge."

You might not be able to tell by sifting through the thoughts of the lunatic fringe of social media, but things are going quite well for the Florida Gators football team this season.

While the Orange and Blue are still a far cry from their dominant teams of the 90s and 2000s, this year's edition of the Gators are showing signs of life for the first time in a while.

Florida is 7-4 with three wins over top-15 teams, and boast a winning conference record as well as a top-20 ranking in November, both firsts for the program since 2020.

Not exactly national championship caliber stuff, but hey, it's progress.

Head coach of the Florida Gators Jon Sumrall in the tunnel with team before the game between the Florida Gators and Florida Atlantic Owls at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium on September 05, 2026 in Gainesville, Florida. (Photo by Dustin Markland/Getty Images) (Dustin Markland/Getty Images)

This fact is not lost on first-year head coach Jon Sumrall, who, while being a maniacal psycho who demands perfection, is still able to see the forest for the trees and recognize that there's tangible growth from his squad compared to the last several years in Gainesville.

URBAN MEYER JOINS DAN DAKICH, GUSHES ABOUT NEW FLORIDA HEAD COACH JON SUMRALL: 'I LOVE THAT GUY'

That's not lip service, either, as the always candid and blunt coach said as much in his Monday morning news conference.

Sumrall was answering a question about resourcing and booster buy-in when he dropped a quote that may have gone unnoticed to the uninitiated, but if you've been paying attention - particularly to the previous staff - you know exactly what was being insinuated.

EX-FLORIDA GATORS COACH BILLY NAPIER RIPPED TO SHREDS BY FORMER PLAYER DURING PODCAST APPEARANCE

"I think there's probably, in fairness, people who wanted to see some proof of concept to make sure I wasn't an idiot, and I knew, at least how to get 11 guys on the field, or run a formation, or us win a close game," Sumrall said.

Jon Sumrall speaks during a press conference introducing him as the new Florida Gators football head coach at the University of Florida in Gainesville, Fla., on Dec. 1, 2025. (Getty Images)

For those of you who aren't keenly aware of what Sumrall is referencing here, allow me to explain.

Sumrall's immediate predecessor at Florida was a man named Billy Napier.

JAMES MADISON COACH BILLY NAPIER CONTINUES SELF PITY TOUR, REFUSES TO TAKE ACCOUNTABILITY FOR PAST FAILURES

I've written extensively about Napier's disastrous tenure in Gainesville, but the CliffsNotes version that you need to know is that Sun Belt Billy had a losing record while coaching the Gators, a feat no full-time coach had "accomplished" since World War II.

Oh, and he was notorious for sending the wrong number of players out on the field for special teams plays, so frequently, in fact, that his staff hilariously bought a mat with 11 circles on it to signify how many men needed to be in to kick a field goal.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The head coach for the University of Florida, a program that has won three national championships and eight SEC titles, couldn't do something most toddlers learn while watching The Count on "Sesame Street."

A fan wears a Fire Billy Napier bag over their head between the Florida Gators and Mississippi State Bulldogs during the second half at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium on Oct. 18, 2025. (Matt Pendleton/Imagn Images)

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Was Sumrall referencing Napier with these comments? We may never know definitively, but the veil is so thin it's almost laughable.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

And I loved it, as I'm sure most of Gator Nation did.

Napier took a once-proud college football program that was already on the decline and drove it into the dirt in record time.

So, while a top-20 ranking and a winning record in SEC play may not seem like a reason to throw a parade, just remember how low the bar was before Sumrall arrived.

articles.title: French ex-President Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to face trial
articles.excerpt: Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money...
articles.body_text:
Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.

The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.

Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.

Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.

In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.

In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.

The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president.

Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.

At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file – the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.

So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face the charge of "criminal conspiracy to commit fraud as part of an organised group and receiving stolen goods related to witness tampering". They deny any wrongdoing.

French ex-president Sarkozy begins jail sentence for campaign finance conspiracy

Nicolas Sarkozy illegal campaign financing conviction upheld

Sarkozy releases prison diaries about his 20 days behind bars

articles.title: Ukraine’s drone strike on Russian warship in Libya risks ‘serious escalation,’ former official warns
articles.excerpt: Drones strike and sink a Russian warship as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirms the successful military operation on Telegram. Foreign correspondent Jeff Paul reports on the escalating co...
articles.body_text:
Drones strike and sink a Russian warship as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirms the successful military operation on Telegram. Foreign correspondent Jeff Paul reports on the escalating conflict as continuous Russian bombardment sparks emergency rescue efforts in Kyiv.

The Ukrainian sea drone strike that capsized and sank a Russian warship in Libya on Sunday risks a "serious escalation" of the nearly five-year war, a former U.S. national security adviser warned Monday, calling the operation a "giant tantrum" by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Morgan Murphy, a former press secretary to the secretary of defense, also told Fox News Digital that the nighttime attack on the Russian corvette Mercury in the Libyan port city of Benghazi could further strain relations between Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump, while echoing frustrations that he said also plagued former President Joe Biden's administration.

"The strike on the Russian corvette Mercury in North Africa — in Libya specifically — is a serious escalation of the war in Ukraine," Murphy claimed.

"Calling the Benghazi strike a giant tantrum could be one interpretation of it, and it's not unusual behavior for him," Murphy said of Zelenskyy.

RUSSIAN WARSHIP SINKS OFF LIBYA AS SUSPECTED UKRAINIAN STRIKES TAKE WAR BEYOND BLACK SEA

The port of Benghazi after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base. (Vantor/Handout via REUTERS)

Murphy also argued that Zelenskyy's willingness to pursue military objectives that complicate Washington's diplomatic priorities has frustrated previous administrations.

"This is why I think the Biden administration was frustrated with Zelenskyy, and why the Trump administration has been frustrated with Zelenskyy: he's acting like an independent player and not an ally," Murphy said.

Biden had reportedly lost his temper during a June 2022 phone call after Zelenskyy requested additional military assistance shortly after the White House announced a $1 billion aid package for Ukraine.

In his recently released memoir, Biden also revealed private frustrations with Zelenskyy, describing the Ukrainian leader as moody, stubborn and less grateful than expected.

UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC

U.S. President Biden and Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine's president, left, meet in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 1, 2021. Photographer: Doug Mills/The New York Times/Bloomberg via Getty Images (Doug Mills/The New York Times/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Murphy went on to suggest the Benghazi drone strike could also complicate Trump's efforts to broker an end to the war, particularly after the president met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a historic summit without Zelenskyy.

"The President just had a successful meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, and he met them without Zelenskyy present, as is the right of the President of the United States to meet with whom he likes when he pleases," Murphy said.

"Zelenskyy was clearly upset about that, and this attack is him showing the President of the United States that he's still very relevant."

The operation, coordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and armed forces, targeted the Russian vessel in port, raising questions about where the drones originated and whether the conflict could spread further beyond Ukraine's borders.

Zelenskyy praised the strike Monday in a post on X, calling it "An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war."

Murphy argued that the Ukrainian leader is increasingly under pressure to demonstrate Kyiv can still deliver significant military victories as Trump pursues a diplomatic resolution.

"What he's looking for here is, I believe, a victory, because Ukraine has found more aid and sympathy on the world stage when it's winning," Murphy said.

Ukraine initially drew widespread international support after resisting Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, defying expectations that Moscow would quickly overwhelm Kyiv.

"Ukraine performed much better against an enemy five times its size, and human nature loves an underdog."

"There was a deep outpouring of sympathy — and more importantly, support — for Ukraine after that initial flop of a Russian invasion," Murphy said.

UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

President Donald Trump met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the White House Aug. 18, 2025, where Trump said a ceasefire agreement is not necessary.  (Getty Images)

But as the conflict has dragged on, Murphy argued, Ukraine has struggled to sustain the enthusiasm that followed Russia's initial setbacks, with the fighting descending into what he described as a "stalemate and a war of attrition."

"Zelenskyy is having a harder time building support," he said of the current state of play.

"As he saw the President meet with Russia and meet with Xi Jinping in China, he needed a victory, and he needed a dramatic attack — so an asymmetric attack was on the board."

The Benghazi strike also underscores Ukraine's expanding ability to target Russian military assets thousands of miles from its territory, although questions remain about how the operation was carried out.

"Ukraine has taken credit for it, but they've been coy about where it was launched from," Murphy said.

"There's some speculation that it was launched from within Libya. Others say that it came from a mothership, which is totally plausible — that they took an innocuous-looking cargo ship and launched these drones out of it."

Murphy said the operation reflects a broader transformation in modern warfare, with military planners still grappling with the implications of increasingly sophisticated drone attacks.

"What we are watching unfold in real time is a total shift in the nature of warfare. It's really unheralded," he said.

UKRAINE’S DRONE REVOLUTION SHOWS RUSSIA IS DANGEROUSLY UNPREPARED. BUT, SO IS AMERICA

A Russian corvette before and after the explosion in Benghazi and with Libya's eastern-based government saying the explosion was caused by a suspected drone attack. (VANTOR/ Reuters)

"It will take time — planners' time and nations' time — to understand how to react to this kind of aggression."

Beyond the military implications, Murphy warned that the strike could undermine diplomatic efforts in Washington to negotiate an end to the conflict.

"There is a very concerted group of diplomats and thought leaders in D.C. who want to see a diplomatic end to this conflict sooner rather than later," Murphy said.

"They see that as being in the best interest of the United States and the world, but most importantly, they see it in the best interest of the Ukrainian people."

Murphy said those pushing for a negotiated settlement would likely view the reported strike in Libya as a setback to Trump's peace efforts.

"A lot of thinkers in Washington want this to end, and they'll see this escalation in Libya as counterproductive to what the President is trying to do."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.
