articles.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
articles.excerpt:
Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space

Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any...
articles.body_text:
Nato chief Mark Rutte and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz respond to reports of Russian plans to launch nuclear weapons into space

Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.

Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".

The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".

Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.

"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.

Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.

Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".

"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.

A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".

Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.

Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.

In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation.

"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.

In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

US confirms for first time it has deployed space weapons

articles.title: SEC threatens the nuclear option as LSU’s rebellion puts conference future at risk, RJ Luis plans to sue
articles.excerpt: LSU faces a federal judge's order to amend its court filing in an SEC court battle over football recruitment. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill strongly defends her team, stating she will not apo...
articles.body_text:
LSU faces a federal judge's order to amend its court filing in an SEC court battle over football recruitment. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill strongly defends her team, stating she will not apologize for her lawyers doing their job. The legal dispute intensifies after allegations of citation errors, highlighting the high stakes in collegiate sports litigation.

UPDATE: On Monday night, RJ Luis' attorney reportedly said that the basketball player would be suing the SEC and commissioner Greg Sankey for damages related to the conference violating a judge's order that led to LSU no longer rostering his client.

In addition, Clayton made it very clear that he is looking to get SEC Presidents on the record through depositions on whether they were acting in collusion with Greg Sankey to undermine RJ's attempt at playing basketball this season. This, along with others, is a reason why the SEC has such a problem with how LSU has conducted themselves, even if they were not directly tied to the situation.

The SEC’s ongoing feud with LSU now comes with a threat that would have once seemed unthinkable: kicking the Tigers out of the conference in a meeting Dec. 3.

In a federal court filing Monday, the Southeastern Conference said it will hold a special meeting next month to consider whether to "terminate" LSU’s membership amid the ongoing fight involving RJ Luis and two football players.

Whether conference leaders would actually take that step is another question. But after months of legal threats, courtroom showdowns and last-minute roster decisions, the SEC is putting LSU’s future on the table.

LANE KIFFIN’S ROSTER FIGHT SET THE STAGE, WILL WADE JUST THREW A GRENADE IN LSU-SEC WAR WITH RJ LUIS

The latest escalation follows Will Wade’s decision to play Luis against Louisiana-Monroe last week, six days after a Baton Rouge judge granted the former professional basketball player an injunction allowing him to compete.

That appearance reignited a fight that began months earlier, when Lane Kiffin’s football program considered rostering two players with NFL experience in the preseason.

On the eve of LSU’s season opener against Clemson, school officials ultimately decided against adding Dae’Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris to the roster, despite a judge’s order permitting them to play.

By then, the dispute had already spilled into federal court.

The day before that roster decision, SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey testified in the football players’ eligibility lawsuit against the conference and NCAA. That same day, the SEC filed a federal lawsuit against LSU President Wade Rousse and other university officials, including Kiffin.

DEION SANDERS TO THE NFL? CRAIG CARTON EXPLAINS WHY HE CAN SAVE A FLOUNDERING NFL FRANCHISE?

LSU president Wade Rousse, left, and athletic director Verge Ausberry, right, pose with new head football coach Lane Kiffin after after an introductory news conference, Monday, Dec. 1, 2025, in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. (Michael Johnson/The Advocate via AP)

The conference argued that using a court order to circumvent its eligibility rules interfered with its First Amendment right to govern its membership.

LSU has since asked a federal judge to dismiss the lawsuit. While both sides await a ruling, the SEC’s latest filing adds another layer to a fight that keeps finding ways to get uglier.

The possibility that LSU would roster Luis was always going to create another confrontation.

This is the same school that kept the SEC guessing about Wright and Harris until the final hours before football rosters were due. When Luis added the conference to his eligibility lawsuit last month, another showdown seemed inevitable.

LSU LEAVES FORMER PRO-ATHLETES OFF FINAL ROSTER, ONE NIGHT BEFORE SEC TAKES LANE KIFFIN AND TIGERS TO COURT

Even though a judge granted Luis an injunction to play, there was an expectation within the SEC president's circle that the Tigers would not actually put him on the court.

To make matters worse, one of the attorneys representing RJ Luis, Tony Clayton, filed a motion to hold Greg Sankey in contempt of court on the same day.

SEC ACCUSES LSU OF DEFYING ITS RULES AS WILL WADE’S BASKETBALL ROSTER ADDS FUEL TO A BURNING FIRE

RJ Luis Jr. #12 of the LSU Tigers poses for a photo during media day at Pete Maravich Assembly Center in Baton Rouge, La., on Oct. 1, 2026. (University Images via Getty Images)

According to Greg Sankey, that expectation came from assurances by Wade and LSU athletic director Verge Ausberry.

"Before Defendants rostered Mr. Luis on Nov. 17, 2026, as discussed below, LSU officials indicated to me on multiple occasions—including a text message from Defendant Ausberry to me on September 5, 2026 and a phone call between Defendant Wade and me on October 14, 2026 — that Mr. Luis would not play for LSU’s basketball team," Sankey said on Monday in a declaration filed in federal court.

LSU PRESIDENT WADE ROUSSE ENDS LANE KIFFIN’S SEC SHOWDOWN, BUT THERE IS STILL RELATIONSHIPS TO MEND

Then Wade sent RJ Luis into the game last Wednesday, and whatever understanding existed between LSU and the conference went out the window.

It was the following day, according to multiple sources, that LSU President Wade Rousse took a phone call from Sankey to let him know the seriousness of what had just transpired the previous night and that SEC presidents were preparing to discuss how to penalize the Tigers on teleconference taking place later that afternoon.

That evening, Rousse released a statement announcing that he had instructed Wade to stop playing Luis.

While that might have calmed the waters for about 20 minutes, SEC presidents were furious that LSU would once again put them in a position to potentially act.

The prospect still seems unlikely. Expelling LSU would require a two-thirds vote (11), and scheduling a meeting to consider that option does not mean the votes are there, yet.

But dismissing this as another empty threat would ignore how far the dispute has escalated.

After LSU and Will Wade pulled the pin and throwing the grenade last week by playing RJ Luis, the conference is now prepared to discuss the matter further.

INSIDE A LOUISIANA COURTROOM: SEC-LSU LEGAL CIRCUS PLAYED OUT LIKE A JOHN GRISHAM NOVEL IN STUNNING SHOWDOWN

Also, none of the shenanigans involving LSU over the past four months happened without President Wade Rousse, and even Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry, giving the athletic department permission to test the SEC's power.

"That was the final straw for SEC leaders, they were ready to penalize them (LSU) in some form or fashion," one source familiar with the discussions told OutKick last week. "You can only poke the bear so many times before they decide to pounce, and they (SEC Presidents and Chancellors) had seen enough nonsense from LSU.

"Who knows if they would have actually boycotted games, or even tried. But lawyers from schools within the conference were going through their options. This whole thing is just annoying. Like, get your s— together, and I mean everyone involved."

President Wade Rousse, new head coach Will Wade and athletic director Verge Ausberry pose for a photo at Wade's press conference at the Pete Maravich Assembly Center in Baton Rouge, La., on March 30, 2026. (University Images via Getty Images)

LSU’s repeated challenges to the conference have unfolded with the backing of Rousse and Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry. The school has shown a willingness to test how much authority the SEC can exercise when a judge has cleared an athlete to play.

That is the heart of this fight: LSU has leaned on court orders allowing athletes to compete, while the SEC has defended its right to enforce conference eligibility rules.

Playing Luis made clear that LSU was willing to push that conflict further, even with a federal lawsuit hanging over the dispute in an Alabama courtroom.

For now, the immediate question is how far SEC leaders are willing to go. What began as an eligibility dispute now carries consequences that reach well beyond a roster spot.

The SEC has put its most drastic option on the table. Next month, we find out whether conference leaders are prepared to act on it — or whether the threat itself is the point.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

articles.title: Drone attack on police base in Colombia injures three, including infant
articles.excerpt:
A drone attack on a police base in the Colombian city of Cucuta has injured at least three civilians, including an infant, and damaged 60 homes.

Officials did not immediately say who was responsible ...
articles.body_text:
A drone attack on a police base in the Colombian city of Cucuta has injured at least three civilians, including an infant, and damaged 60 homes.

Officials did not immediately say who was responsible for the attack on Monday that struck the base belonging to the Norte de Santander police.

Orlando Roa, who lives near the base, told local media that his 18-month-old grandson was among those injured and was being treated at a nearby hospital.

The attack came as far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella steps up an offensive against rebel groups and drug gangs that has resulted in the military capturing several mid-level commanders.

Armed groups have responded by attacking military bases and police stations with small drones, rockets made with gas canisters and roadside bombs. De la Espriella, who took office in August, has cancelled peace negotiations with rebel groups that were under way under his predecessor, leftist Gustavo Petro.

Cucuta, a city near Colombia’s border with Venezuela, is a major trade hub and a centre for criminal groups profiting from the drug trade and other kinds of smuggling. Rebel groups, including the National Liberation Army and the FARC-EMC, also operate in the nearby Catatumbo region.

In 2016, a peace deal between the Colombian government and the FARC led to the demobilisation of more than 14,000 fighters.

However, some border areas in Colombia have seen a surge of violence as smaller armed groups try to seize territory abandoned by the FARC, where the government has been slow to provide security and basic services.

Another police station in the Cesar region was also attacked with drones on Monday, injuring a police officer. On Saturday, one soldier was killed, and 12 others were injured during an attack with drones and rockets on a military base also in Cesar.

Both incidents remain under investigation, according to local officials.

articles.title: NATO warns Putin could strike before European army responds, points to US as military model
articles.excerpt: Polish airspace violations by suspected Russian missiles trigger a stern warning from NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, as Jon Scott reports. Rutte declares that the alliance will defend every inch o...
articles.body_text:
Polish airspace violations by suspected Russian missiles trigger a stern warning from NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, as Jon Scott reports. Rutte declares that the alliance will defend every inch of Polish territory. This escalation coincides with a devastating Russian missile strike on a residential apartment building in Kyiv, where rescuers search the ruins.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned Monday that creating a separate European army could undermine the alliance’s ability to respond quickly to a Russian attack, as Moscow continues to ramp up its military capabilities during the ongoing war in Ukraine.

Speaking at the 72nd annual session of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, Rutte cautioned that competing military command structures could hold up decisions in a crisis, warning that Russia’s "war machine" is running at full throttle and could also pose a threat to Europe long after the war ends.

"What I would counsel against is having all the nations with their own militaries working together in NATO and then on top of that having a big European structure, because then if Putin attacks, we will first need two or three weeks to agree who will do what, and then he will probably end up in Rotterdam before we have decided. So that has been my argument," Rutte said, according to Ukrainska Pravda.

NATO JETS SHOOT DOWN DRONE IN LITHUANIAN AIRSPACE AS RUSSIA GROWS 'INCREASINGLY RECKLESS,' RUTTE SAYS

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte speaks to the media during a joint news conference with the members of the Bosnian Presidency in Sarajevo, Bosnia, Monday, March 10, 2025. (Armin Durgut)

Rutte pointed to the United States as a model for an integrated military, arguing that European countries would also need to move beyond separate national forces to establish a unified army.

"My point has always been that if you have a European military, you cannot also have national militaries. The United States has one military."

"There is not a specific army or navy for the state of New York or for the state of California. It is an integrated United States military. If Europe is able to pull that off, fine," Rutte said.

Rutte said it was Russia's expanding military production and cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea that pose a long-term threat to NATO, regardless of how the war in Ukraine ends.

"We face great dangers coming from Russia and the fact that Russia works so closely together with Iran, China, and North Korea, we know that Russia's war machine at the moment is running at full speed," Rutte also said at the assembly in Berlin.

FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE

Plumes of smoke rise from fires at an oil refinery following what authorities said was a Ukrainian drone strike during the Russia-Ukraine conflict in Moscow, Russia, on Sept. 20, 2026. (REUTERS/Stringer)

"Its war economy keeps growing, and it won't stand still when the war against Ukraine hopefully will end one day. That whole machine is there and will continue."

Rutte also rejected the idea that only countries bordering Russia or Ukraine face a direct military threat, warning that Moscow's long-range missiles put capitals across Europe within striking distance.

"Let me say once again to everyone here who is not on the eastern flank: I have news for you. You are on the eastern flank too. These latest Russian missiles need only five minutes longer to reach Lisbon, Rome or The Hague, my hometown, than to reach Tallinn, Warsaw or Helsinki," Rutte said.

"So we are all on the eastern flank here. Let's put an end to this discussion about whether or not you are on the eastern flank. We are all on the eastern flank."

The NATO chief's remarks came amid plans to deploy an early-warning aircraft to Poland after Polish prosecutors said three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles landed on Polish territory Friday during strikes against Ukraine.

NATO WARNS RUSSIA: 'WE WILL BREAK' FORCES, DESTROY 'ANYTHING AND EVERYTHING' IF YOU ATTACK

Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski during an inteview with Fox News Digital in Warsaw, Poland. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)

Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said that NATO would deploy an Airborne Warning and Control System, or AWACS, aircraft to strengthen surveillance along the alliance's eastern flank, according to Reuters.

"This is a very good system that gives us even deeper... operational awareness which allows us to respond better to this kind of threat," Zalewski told reporters following a NATO meeting in Brussels.

The aircraft can monitor large areas of airspace and provide allied forces with a shared picture of potential aerial threats, improving NATO's ability to detect and respond to missile and aircraft activity.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also warned Monday night that intelligence indicated Moscow was preparing a new wave of strikes against Ukraine.

Beyond Russia's ongoing military threats, Rutte said that Europe's interconnected infrastructure, including energy networks and communications systems, is vulnerable.

RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT

Smoke rises in the city during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine August 31, 2026. (Gleb Garanich/Reuters)

"We are all targeted, that we are all affected when it comes to our pipelines, our cables, our energy grids, and our economies."

"They are all interconnected, and that means that we are all in this for the long term. And therefore, we must step up to the plate to ensure that we stay ahead of danger."

Rutte said defending NATO countries demands civilian preparedness, pointing to northern European nations that have begun teaching residents about their responsibilities in the event of war.

"This really takes the whole of society," he said.

"And that's in the end, I think, still Norway and Sweden, and Denmark and Finland, and maybe one or two others who are really ahead of the pack here, and having made clear to their citizens what they need to do in case war breaks out, at least not to get in the way of the military, but to be helpful and also how they make sure that the police and the ambulance services and fire, the fire fighting departments work together, supporting the military wherever possible."

Rutte's warnings come amid uncertainty over Ukraine's long-term security arrangements and whether Western allies will offer guarantees resembling NATO's Article 5 collective defense commitment as part of a future peace agreement.

U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner said Sunday that President Donald Trump was willing to consider Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine as part of a broader postwar security arrangement for Europe.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell filed a federal lawsuit Monday seeking to block ICE from making civil immigration arrests inside state courthouses without a judicial warrant.

Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration on Monday to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from carrying out civil arrests in the state's courthouses, arguing that such arrests without judicial warrants are illegal under state law.

The lawsuit filed by Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell challenges a 2025 ICE directive that authorizes agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants, which she says violates the PROTECT Act, a new state law passed ​by the Democratic-led legislature that prohibits civil immigration arrests in state courthouses without judicial warrants. The courthouse protections took effect Nov. 3.

Campbell said the ICE directive interferes with the state's authority to operate its judicial system, disrupts court proceedings, undermines constitutional principles and public safety and spreads fear, chaos and confusion.

"The Massachusetts PROTECT Act makes it illegal for ICE to conduct civil arrests in our courthouses without a judicial warrant. ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable," Campbell said in a statement.

DOJ SUES TO STOP OHIO COURT BLOCKING COURTHOUSE ARRESTS

Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration to block ICE agents from carrying out civil arrests in the state's courthouses. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images)

"ICE is misleading the public by suggesting that these arrests make us safer when, in fact, ICE's actions are preventing criminal cases from moving forward, denying a victim’s ability to obtain accountability, violating a defendant’s due process, and leaving open the possibility that someone facing serious criminal charges could ultimately be released from ICE custody without their criminal case ever being resolved," she continued.

The attorney general said more than 1,110 people have been arrested at her state's courthouses since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, including more than 600 people in 2025 and more than 500 during the first 10 months of 2026.

Campbell said ICE has ignored the new state law and arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants in the two and a half weeks since the courthouse protections went into effect.

"I, along with our district attorneys, share the goal of holding defendants accountable for crimes, yet ICE’s unlawful tactics to arrest someone for a civil immigration violation is not the same as holding them accountable for a crime," Campbell said.

FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS

The attorney general said more than 1,110 people have been arrested at her state's courthouses since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. (Getty Images)

Campbell said that ICE's courthouse arrests have continued in Massachusetts despite a federal ruling handed down in June by U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in California that vacated the Trump administration's courthouse arrest policy ​in a separate class action lawsuit.

In Monday's lawsuit, Campbell argues the ICE policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act since it was adopted without taking into account the impact it would have on states and because the Immigration and Nationality Act does not explicitly authorize courthouse arrests.

The lawsuit also alleges that the ⁠policy violates the U.S. Constitution's Tenth Amendment, which protects states' rights to maintain authority over their own judicial systems.

"The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety. When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe," Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement. "We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law."

The lawsuit challenges a 2025 ICE directive that instructs agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment.

In a statement to Reuters, a DHS spokesperson argued that making immigration arrests at courthouses "conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already ​know where a target will ​be," adding that "the ability of law enforcement ⁠to make arrests of criminal illegal aliens in courthouses is common sense."

A similar lawsuit against ICE arrests at state courthouses was filed in October by California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

articles.body_text:
Who: Arsenal vs Borussia Dortmund
What: UEFA Champions League
Where: Emirates Stadium, London, United Kingdom
When: Tuesday, November 24 at 8pm (20:00 GMT).
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 17:00 GMT before our live text commentary stream.

Premier League holders Arsenal face German giants Borussia Dortmund for the first time in more than a decade, as the Champions League returns for matchday five action.

Arsenal and their fans were left frustrated at the weekend despite opening up a six-point lead at the top of the Premier League with a 2-2 draw at Newcastle United.

But a firm grip on their English top-flight title defence and a 10-game unbeaten streak across all competitions give Mikel Arteta’s side plenty of reasons to be optimistic for Tuesday’s UCL fixture in north London.

Dortmund, too, have been impressive in their own ways. Unbeaten in Germany this season, they sit two points clear of defending champions Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga table. Niko Kovac’s team are also on an eight-match unbeaten run.

Eberechi Eze, who also scored in the last game, has been Arsenal’s leading scorer in this year’s Champions League with two goals so far, while fellow stars Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard have also bagged a goal each.

In the Dortmund camp, veteran striker Serhou Guirassy is the outright leader with four goals – figures that also make him the joint fourth-highest in the competition.

Arsenal are third in the league phase standings, with 10 points from four games. The Gunners have won three games – against Napoli, Lille and Slavia Prague – and drawn once, with Bayern.

Only Paris Saint-Germain and Real Madrid have performed better than Arsenal, with 100 percent records.

Dortmund are 12th in the standings with nine points. They have won three games – against Villarreal, Sabah and Real Betis – and lost once, to Bodo/Glimt.

The last time the two teams met in a competitive match was in the 2014-15 season.

Dortmund won 2-0 in Germany in their first encounter and Arsenal beat them by the same scoreline in England in the reverse leg.

Opta’s supercomputer has picked Arsenal as favourites.

They are predicted to have a 65.2 percent chance of winning, while Dortmund’s odds of victory are 15.8 percent. A draw is a 19 percent probability.

(Last five matches across all competitions; latest game first)

Goalkeeper David Raya is doubtful after he was forced off in the second half against Newcastle with a shoulder injury and missed Monday’s training session.

Winger Saka has been sidelined for another month with a thigh injury and midfielder Martin Zubimendi, who picked up a hamstring injury on international duty, is out for a few weeks.

Kepa Arrizabalaga; Jurrien Timber, Ezri Konsa, Gabriel, Riccardo Calafiori; Bruno Guimaraes, Declan Rice; Noni Madueke, Martin Odegaard, Eberechi Eze; Kai Havertz

Dortmund have a long list of injured players, including Carney Chukwuemeka (muscle) and Emre Can (ACL).

Gregor Kobel; Waldemar Anton, Nico Schlotterbeck, Ramy Bensebaini; Julian Ryerson, Joey Veerman, Felix Nmecha, Daniel Svensson; Jobe Bellingham, Fabio Silva; Serhou Guirassy

articles.title: India's 'cockroach' party leader says he was stopped from flying to UK
articles.excerpt:
Saurav Das said that he was supposed to deliver a series of lectures in the UK

A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to th...
articles.body_text:
Saurav Das said that he was supposed to deliver a series of lectures in the UK

A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.

Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".

It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.

Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests, said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.

He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.

"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," he wrote on X.

A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.

Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.

"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.

Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.

In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .

In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.

The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.

There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.

In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.

In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

articles.title: Trump's Nixon-to-China moment: There's an immigration move only he can make
articles.excerpt:
President Donald Trump joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss the recent FBI hack, bipartisanship and his recent trip to China.

"Maybe we could touch the subject of immigration." That was President T...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss the recent FBI hack, bipartisanship and his recent trip to China.

"Maybe we could touch the subject of immigration." That was President Trump’s suggestion to host Kayleigh McEnany during his Nov. 21 appearance on Fox News’ "Saturday in America."

If the president deploys his power of pardon for a defined class of illegal immigrants, it will be a "golden touch" for them that will enshrine his memory among their communities and add another achievement of enormous significance to his already lengthy column of them.

Such an act of presidential mercy would be unprecedented—without a parallel mass grant of grace in American history—and it would be approved of by supermajorities of Americans and certain to be counted among his greatest achievements as president by citizens of all political persuasions who have long desired an actual breakthrough on this stalemated front.

TRUMP AND IMMIGRATION REFORM: WILL DEMOCRATS MAKE HIM AN OFFER HE CAN'T REFUSE?

The president’s carefully phrased suggestion to McEnany is a good topic for a Thanksgiving dinner conversation: "What should we as a country do about or to the country’s illegal immigrant population?"

"What do we think about a presidential pardon for, say, the 10% of the illegal immigrant population, people whom everyone here could agree ought to be left alone and free of the fear of deportation?"

The best studies estimate the population of illegal immigrants in the country at between 15 and 20 million. Some crossed the border right up to the day President Trump returned to office, but very few have arrived in the country since the spring of 2025. Trump sealed the southern border, and it remains, for all practical purposes, shuttered. "The Wall" has now been built over more than 750 miles. Another 600 miles of wall are planned between now and the end of Trump’s second term. The Border Patrol is funded through the end of Sept. 2029.

President Trump delivered on his promise to close the border.

On Nov. 8, after being asked by Ross Douthat of "60 Minutes" about deportation policy in the past two years, the president said, "I think it was too tough." President Trump then added, "I think it might be too tough, yeah."

TRUMP CAN FINALLY DELIVER THE IMMIGRATION BARGAIN REAGAN WAS PROMISED

Some of the election results on Nov. 3 were "because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally."

"Now, there is a large part of the country that thinks that they should be put out," he added. "And there's a large part of the country that thinks that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."

So, what should be done? What should President Trump do?

FOX NEWS POLL: MAJORITY SAYS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT HAS CROSSED THE LINE

Democratic leaders in Congress have a wide-open door to the Oval Office to negotiate a reasonable set of statutory reforms that are not "amnesty" and don’t involve a "path to citizenship."

But as President Trump has noted on a few occasions, he doesn’t have to wait on them, as he has the "very powerful power of the pardon," which is indeed complete and within his sole control.

He could use the power of pardon on any segment of the illegal immigrant population before COB today or on Thanksgiving if he wanted to.

What might a presidential pardon look like that would (1) reflect the views of a supermajority of Americans and (2) not create an incentive for immigrants to think they should come toward our country or overstay visas?

A number of violations of federal statutes could be the subject of a presidential pardon. Illegal entry into the country is a crime, as is an illegal return after deportation. It is also a civil offense—still within the pardon power—to have entered legally but to have overstayed the permitted time of presence in the country.

TRUMP'S IMMIGRATION OLIVE BRANCH THREATENS TO OPEN PANDORA'S BOX AS EXPERTS WARN OF FAR-REACHING FALLOUT

So ask the people around the table: What would you think of any sort of presidential pardon for those who have broken these laws? Is there a version of one you could endorse and even applaud?

President Jimmy Carter’s pardon of draft dodgers who had broken the Selective Service laws of the Vietnam era is a model and included this language:

"I, Jimmy Carter, President of the United States, do hereby grant a full, complete and unconditional pardon to: (1) all persons who may have committed any offense between August 4, 1964, and March 28, 1973, in violation of the Military Selective Service Act or any rule or regulation promulgated thereunder; and (2) all persons heretofore convicted, irrespective of the date of conviction, of any offense committed between August 4, 1964, and March 28, 1973, in violation of the Military Selective Service Act, or any rule or regulation promulgated thereunder, restoring to them full political, civil and other rights."

On its face, the pardon of 50 years ago was narrowly tailored, and its accompanying language specifically excluded those whose Selective Service violation involved force or violence and those who committed violations in connection with employment as an agent, officer, or employee of the Selective Service System.

It also did not cover military deserters or people who had gone AWOL from the armed forces.

TRUMP SAYS DEPORTATION PUSH HASN’T PUT 'SAME PRESSURE' ON FARMWORKERS, HOTEL STAFF: 'NOT EVEN CLOSE'

President Trump thus has it within his power to immediately and carefully address the excesses of deportation policy that he knows were "too tough."

Thus, President Trump is in a position to do a Nixon-to-China on illegal immigrants. There might be a "Trump-Schumer-Jeffries Regularization Act" a year down the road, a statute that should not include a general "amnesty" and cannot provide a "pathway to citizenship." Such a statute could provide a detailed legislative change to grant a right of continued residence to a defined subset of illegal immigrants upon a showing of certain conditions, such as no felony arrests, past or future, for people in the country for a decade or more.

But President Trump does not have to wait on Democrats, and indeed he shouldn’t, to make clear it was his decision. Pardon seekers would have to present proof of near-continuous employment and such other evidence of character and commitment as President Trump details in the language of the pardon. A pardon could be very focused and also include such conditions and exclusions as the president deems fit.

President Trump could issue such a pardon today. He can act tomorrow. He can act on Thanksgiving or Christmas. The pardon power is unlimited. If President Trump deploys it carefully, the public would first be thunderstruck and then almost wholly united in praising his act of mercy.

There is a very deep and broad sense of justice and fairness in the American public. The deportation of long-time residents who have worked hard and are raising families—especially those with children born in the country—deeply disturbs most Americans of all political persuasions. Continued deportation of individuals whose life circumstances jar ordinary voters especially upsets legal residents, family members, and friends of illegal immigrants.

Hardly a week goes by without a story of a deportation that elicits the pity of most Americans while triggering anger at government officials who are just applying the law. President Trump can unilaterally defuse the worst assaults on the collective American sense of justice. There will be critics, and they will be loud, but they would actually represent only a tiny portion of the country.

TRUMP BORDER CRACKDOWN DRIVES ENCOUNTERS TO RECORD OCTOBER LOW AS ZERO-RELEASE STREAK HITS 18 MONTHS, DHS SAYS

The deportation excesses of the past two years are also going to be a barrier to the return of Republican majorities in either the House or the Senate if they do not end. Reasonable people will disagree on the specifics of a presidential pardon (or of a statutory "regularization" bill down the road), but—assuming the Bell Curve applies to illegal immigrants—there are more than a million illegal immigrants who ought obviously to be deported as soon as possible and at least a million who are just as obviously good people and community members who should not be rousted out of their lives and deported.

The online world separates quickly from the reality of the American center on this issue, but President Trump intuits he has to course-correct on deportation policy. Thus, there is a great opportunity right now for a legacy achievement via his pardon power and down the road via statutory compromise, if Democrats do not overreach and seek political advantage from a "regularization" bill.

Presidents Obama and Biden could not bring themselves to do the necessary thing prior to such a statute, which was to have built the border wall.

President Trump has provided the necessary precondition to a wide-ranging pardon: He has shown that the border is secure. Now he can accomplish an immediate and vast good via the pardon power and begin negotiations on a breakthrough, provided the Democrats do not allow their extremists to poison the political well, even as center-right to conservative Republicans reject the instant denunciation of a pardon and every bill as "amnesty," which regularization efforts would not be.

The question for the adults at the Thanksgiving table on Thursday: If President Trump were to issue a pardon, to whom should it apply and what limits on that pardon should there be?

If I were White House Counsel Will Scharf, I would urge President Trump to begin with a fairly narrow pardon and one with explicit parameters that excluded felons and people who have been arrested for violent crimes. It should—at least in the first round—require those seeking its benefit to be able to show unbroken residence in the country prior to, say, January 21, 2020. It might also require proof of having worked and paid taxes and perhaps be limited to adults with children who are American citizens. There are a lot of fine points and exclusions to be debated here. The White House Counsel and his team could prepare many pardon options, and President Trump could decide among them.

TRUMP TELLS DHS CHIEF TO WORK WITH DEMOCRATS ON IMMIGRATION REFORM, BUT NO AMNESTY

The debate in the comments below or on a related Reddit forum will be angry but unrepresentative of the whole of the public, and President Trump already knows he must course-correct. If a pardon from President Trump does issue, it ought then to be the subject of careful consideration by serious people of goodwill, and their reactions should be guided by reason.

A carefully crafted pardon would be life-changing for more than a million people who would thereafter brook no criticism of Trump. It would lift an enormous burden from intact families of law-abiding people who work hard and have no inclination to break the law and who have had children in this country who are citizens. It should be easy to understand and to apply in practice. Its successful implementation could yield permission to remain in the country contingent on not committing a serious offense.

Such a pardon would immediately refocus the debate around deportation away from the deportation cases that trouble three-quarters or more of Americans. If you pay attention to these stories, you know there are many, many cases that jar ordinary Americans.

"Maybe we could touch the subject of immigration," said President Trump.

He is right to make that touch. If he did so with a pardon that was satisfactory to the vast majority of Americans, that touch would indeed be a golden one.

Hugh Hewitt is a Fox News contributor and host of "The Hugh Hewitt Show" heard weekday afternoons from 3 PM to 6 PM ET on the Salem Radio Network, and simulcast on Salem News Channel. Hugh drives Americans home on the East Coast and to lunch on the West Coast on over 400 affiliates nationwide, and on all the streaming platforms where SNC can be seen. He is a frequent guest on the Fox News Channel’s news roundtable, hosted by Bret Baier weekdays at 6pm ET. A son of Ohio and a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Michigan Law School, Hewitt has been a Professor of Law at Chapman University’s Fowler School of Law since 1996 where he teaches Constitutional Law. Hewitt launched his eponymous radio show from Los Angeles in 1990. Hewitt has frequently appeared on every major national news television network, hosted television shows for PBS and MSNBC, written for every major American paper, has authored a dozen books and moderated a score of Republican candidate debates, most recently the November 2023 Republican presidential debate in Miami and four Republican presidential debates in the 2015-16 cycle. Hewitt focuses his radio show and his column on the Constitution, national security, American politics and the Cleveland Browns and Guardians. Hewitt has interviewed tens of thousands of guests from Democrats Hillary Clinton and John Kerry to Republican Presidents George W. Bush and Donald Trump over his 40 years in broadcasting. This column previews the lead story that will drive his radio/ TV show today.

articles.title: Pennsylvania reports ninth measles death in ongoing state outbreak
articles.excerpt:
Pennsylvania health officials have reported another death linked to the ongoing measles outbreak, bringing the state’s death toll associated with the highly contagious viral disease to nine.

The stat...
articles.body_text:
Pennsylvania health officials have reported another death linked to the ongoing measles outbreak, bringing the state’s death toll associated with the highly contagious viral disease to nine.

The state Department of Health confirmed on Monday the death of an unvaccinated resident of Centre County in central ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Pennsylvania who tested positive for measles.

Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, has recorded 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties so far in 2026, including 330 hospitalisations.

The nine deaths were recorded across five counties, as Lancaster County accounted ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌for three deaths, while Jefferson County reported two.

Virginia recorded its first measles-related death in more than three decades on Friday, just days after the United States lost its hard-fought designation as having eliminated the highly contagious virus.

Meanwhile, Wisconsin has reported two deaths, and New York state has recorded one child death linked to the disease.

However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reported only six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, without specifying the ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠states where the deaths were recorded.

The discrepancy between state and federal tolls emerged earlier this year after the health agency, under US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.

The US Department of Health and Human Services said it ⁠⁠⁠⁠was “saddened to hear of another death in Pennsylvania”, adding that the CDC has provided the state with nearly $4m in one-time emergency funding for ⁠⁠⁠⁠response efforts in 2027.

A total of 5,838 measles cases were confirmed across the country this year as of November 19, according to CDC data. The figure is the highest number reported by the CDC since 1991.

Children below the age of five account for 18 percent of cases, while children between the ages of five and 19 make up 41 percent of cases.

The number of confirmed cases in November 2026 is more than double the 2,289 confirmed measles cases reported for the full year of 2025.

articles.body_text:
Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, Kevin Wildes, and Danny Parkins discuss the coolest stats entering week 11, including Joe Burrow’s path to MVP, the Jacksonville Jaguars being underrated, and the Denver Broncos’ winning ways.

Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow, the MVP frontrunner, was heading into another Primetime slate on "Monday Night Football" with NFL history on the line, as he could’ve been the first player ever to tally four or more touchdown passes in six straight games.

Well, he didn’t accomplish that, but against the 31st-ranked pass defense in the NFL, surely he was able to lead the Bengals past the Commanders, right?

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Well, he seemed to do so with a strong, "Thank you!" to kicker Evan McPherson for drilling a 56-yard field goal with 46 seconds left through the wind.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels looks to pass during the first quarter against the Cincinnati Bengals at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Md., on Nov. 23, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

That is until Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels spoiled an 8-2 start for the Bengals through 10 games with a gutsy game-winning drive of his own to upset Cincinnati, 20-19, at Northwest Stadium on Monday night.

Daniels led the Commanders on five straight scoring drives before the Bengals retook their lead late in the fourth quarter, but they weren’t for six points. Rookie kicker Drew Stevens was called upon for all of them, but he kept the Commanders in the game by doing his job and knocking through three points each time.

On the final drive, Daniels needed to get Stevens into range to make it a perfect five for five, which would win Washington the game. The problem is Daniels had no timeouts left, making things a bit tricky.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

However, Antonio Williams, the third-round pick out of Clemson who had a fantastic night, came through in the most clutch way for Daniels when he hauled in a 22-yard strike to quickly get the ball to midfield. Then, after spiking the rock, Daniels linked up with Williams again, this time for 42 yards, giving Stevens a 26-yard field goal for the win.

He drilled it, and the Commanders and their fan base at home went ballistic as, for the second straight week, they came away with a miraculous victory to keep their NFC East division title hopes alive at 4-5-1. The New York Giants, whom the Commanders shocked on the road in a "Thursday Night Football" thriller last week, sit in first place at 6-3-1, but the Commanders have the tiebreaker over them now due to the win in Week 10.

Burrow and the Bengals couldn’t believe it, but this game certainly wasn’t what their offense has been doing of late.

The first half pouring rain didn’t help matters, but both defenses were suffocating the quarterbacks on the gridiron. Burrow and Daniels couldn’t get anything going, that is until the rain started to lighten up before the first half came to a close.

Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels winds up a pass under pressure during a game against the Bengals at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Md., on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. The Bengals led 10-7 at halftime. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Burrow finally found the end zone when he dropped in another perfect ball this season to Tee Higgins. How in the world Higgins came down with the touchdown grab, as the ball wasn’t fully secured in one of his hands, was a feat.

However, Jacksonville Jaguars fans won’t be happy as it was eerily similar to Parker Washington’s no-touchdown call on Sunday against the New York Giants. This time, referees confirmed Higgins was in bounds and had control for the first touchdown of the game.

Daniels, though, made things very interesting for the second half when he ripped off a 47-yard run to get into the red zone for the first time. A few plays later, Jacory Croskey-Merritt, playing his first game since suffering a groin injury against the Giants in Week 5’s tie at home, scored to make it a 10-7 game.

Burrow was able to find Colbie Young in the third quarter for his first career touchdown, giving the Bengals a 17-10 lead. But back-to-back punts, while the Commanders continued to tack on points, made things tight down the stretch.

Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow throws the ball during the third quarter against the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium in Landover, Md., on Nov. 23, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Cincinnati looked like they escaped with a win, but Washington continues to show the NFL that, until the clock hits zero, it’s simply not over.

articles.title: Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
articles.excerpt:
A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia

Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two wee...
articles.body_text:
A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia

Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over a reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company came under pressure by Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring him back.

But now both Trump and Nvidia are facing bipartisan backlash from lawmakers, just as Huang is due to testify before Congress next week.

The CEO's comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that left the S&P 500 in correction territory, and added nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value.

Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday - adding about $1tn to the company's market value.

But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price.

As Asian stock markets opened, Nvidia racked up more gains and helped lift other share prices across the tech sector.

Asia markets jump as Nvidia boss Jensen Huang reinstated after spy scandal

Watch: Nvidia's stock skyrockets after Jensen Huang reinstated as CEO

Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said in a statement earlier in the day: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

It was only last Tuesday that the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman, Alice Huang, who was alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO.

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

In a brief interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to bring back Huang. Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating the CEO.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.

The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.

The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang

How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?

The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.

Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years".

"I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they go him back in," he says.

Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.

Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to lead the House of Representatives as Speaker when Democrats take control in January called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible" and vowed that Congress will conduct "a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation".

"We will not allow America's national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," he said, echoing many lawmakers on Monday who said that Congress must pass strong export control legislation.

Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December.  Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee once Democrats take control of the chamber in January, said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".

"The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement," she also said.

"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," said Republican Representative Don Bacon, who chairs a House subcommittee on cyber security.

"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."

The chair of the Senate's select committee on intelligence, Republican Tom Cotton said: "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."

Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns

Faisal Islam: Why Jensen Huang proved too big to fire

US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal

Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.

A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he  purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.

The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.

Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.

Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.

The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon and Rachel Clun

articles.title: WHO chief visits Cuba as healthcare system deteriorates
articles.excerpt:
The World Health Organization’s top official is in Cuba, as the island continues to suffer under an ailing healthcare system amid an economic crisis deepened by United States sanctions.

WHO Director-...
articles.body_text:
The World Health Organization’s top official is in Cuba, as the island continues to suffer under an ailing healthcare system amid an economic crisis deepened by United States sanctions.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus visited a paediatric cardiology centre in Havana on Monday alongside the country’s Public Health Minister Dr Jose Angel Portal Miranda.

“Hola, Havana!” Tedros wrote in a post on X during his tour. “Here for a visit to discuss Cuba’s health situation, challenged by sanctions, fuel and electricity shortages.”

The WHO leader arrived Sunday at the invitation of health authorities in the Caribbean nation for a three-day visit, the second time he has visited Cuba as WHO director-general.

Portal Miranda welcomed Tedros, saying it was an opportunity for him to see firsthand the reality of the Cuban healthcare system and the challenges that it faces.

Cuba’s once-vaunted system of free universal healthcare has deteriorated sharply.

Analysts say the crisis has been compounded by fuel shortages that they blame on stricter US sanctions on the island’s energy sector, worsening an economy that already had been limping for years.

A government report released in June said that the survival rate for children with cancer had fallen to 65 percent from 85 percent, before the energy blockade began in January.

Hospitals across Cuba face shortages of supplies including syringes, gauze, vaccines and anaesthetics. They also lack spare parts to repair equipment such as haemodialysis and CT scan machines.

“The situation is shocking,” said Mario Cruz Penate, the Pan American Health Organization and WHO representative on the island.

He noted that Cuba has long enjoyed health indicators comparable to those of developed nations, including low mortality, high life expectancy, broad vaccination coverage and widespread prenatal care.

Play during Monday night's NFL game between the Cincinnati Bengals and Washington Commanders stopped briefly after the field lights went out.

Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels and wide receiver Stefon Diggs were lined up on third down when the stadium suddenly went dark.

While the main overhead lights shut off, the smaller signs and video boards around the stands stayed lit.

articles.title: Mexico to try ‘El Chapo Isidro’ despite US extradition request
articles.excerpt: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro”, will be tried in Mexico despite an extradition request by the US, in a move that could worsen already-strained relations...
articles.body_text:
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro”, will be tried in Mexico despite an extradition request by the US, in a move that could worsen already-strained relations between the two countries.

Attorney General Ernestina Godoy told reporters on Monday that Mexican authorities “are going to put him on trial in this country”.

Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured after an hours-long firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen on Friday at a compound in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa. He was flown to Mexico City the following day.

He faces local charges for weapons offences and methamphetamine possession with intent to sell.

Earlier on Monday, Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said Washington had requested Meza Flores’s extradition after his capture in the northern state of Sinaloa.

President Claudia Sheinbaum said US authorities provided intelligence support but did not participate directly on the ground.

US surveillance drones were authorised to help track Meza Flores before ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠the raid, authorities added, despite sensitivities over US anti-drug operations in the country in recent months.

Four Mexican soldiers and 16 alleged cartel gunmen were killed in the overnight operation, according to the Mexican Secretariat of National Defence.

Meza Flores is accused by US authorities of leading a major trafficking network that moved heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, marijuana and fentanyl across the border.

The US Department of Justice said he faces six charges in the US that include running a continuing criminal enterprise, narcoterrorism, money laundering conspiracy and weapons offences.

His arrest is the latest in a series of high-profile anti-cartel operations by Mexico, including the February killing of Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera, as US President Donald ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Trump presses ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌the Sheinbaum government to crack down on organised crime.

articles.title: Coast Guard boards 2 foreign ships bound for US amid reports of Iranian hacking probe
articles.excerpt: U.S. Central Command said U.S. Marines in the Gulf of Oman "boarded M/T Celestial Sea, an Iranian-flagged commercial oil tanker suspected of attempting to violate the U.S. blockade by transiting towar...
articles.body_text:
U.S. Central Command said U.S. Marines in the Gulf of Oman "boarded M/T Celestial Sea, an Iranian-flagged commercial oil tanker suspected of attempting to violate the U.S. blockade by transiting toward an Iranian port." (Credit: CENTCOM)

The U.S. Coast Guard deployed specialized cyber teams to board two foreign-flagged commercial ships bound for U.S. ports in August after indications that their networks had been compromised by "foreign cyber actors," a Coast Guard spokesperson told Fox News Digital on Monday.

The offshore operations took place Aug. 21 and 24 in the Gulf of America, with teams mitigating the threats before the vessels reached U.S. ports.

The confirmation came as The Wall Street Journal also reported Monday that U.S. authorities are investigating whether Iran was involved in dozens of cyberattacks targeting energy tankers.

FEARS OF CHINA SPYING ON US MILITARY PROMPT GOP HAWKS TO DEMAND RETALIATION AGAINST THE SHIPPING GIANT

The U.S. Coast Guard and Homeland Security Investigations conducted a joint boarding operation aboard the tanker in the Port of Los Angeles. (Department of Homeland Security)

"The U.S. Coast Guard (USCG), in close coordination with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and federal cybersecurity experts, recently conducted joint offshore security boardings of two inbound foreign-flagged commercial vessels in the Gulf of America," a Coast Guard spokesperson said.

"The measures were designed to ensure the integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised by foreign cyber actors."

The Coast Guard said a specialized team of law enforcement personnel, Coast Guard Cyber Protection Team members, a vessel inspector and FBI Cyber Action Team operators boarded the first vessel Aug. 21 to investigate the suspected cybersecurity breach.

"The captain, crew, and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," the spokesperson added.

A similar multiagency boarding and safety verification operation was conducted Aug. 24 aboard the second vessel, also in the Gulf of America, the Coast Guard said.

FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE

The Coast Guard (pictured here in Miami) has complete authority to make sure ships comply with US law and international law. (iStock)

No operational disruptions, vessel instability, threats to crew safety or environmental impacts have been reported.

The Coast Guard said it is coordinating with port operators, vessel owners and local maritime stakeholders to ensure port operations continue safely and without interruption.

According to The Wall Street Journal, attackers exploited vulnerabilities in Fortinet networking equipment, prompting Coast Guard boardings after crews received bomb threats warning that "traitor ships will burn in hell."

STRAIT OF HORMUZ CRISIS TRAPS 6,000 SAILORS AS ATTACKS ON SHIPS MOUNT, UN MARITIME CHIEF SAYS

A Coast Guard MH-65 Dolphin helicopter crew. (U.S. Coast Guard photo by Chief Petty Officer David Mosley)

As many as 50 vessels carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemicals and other potentially explosive cargo are believed to have been targeted, the outlet reported, citing U.S. officials.

A European shipping executive also said officers received threats on their cellphones.

A ransom letter addressed to the captain of the Liberian-flagged supertanker Prosperity, which was carrying about 2.3 million barrels of oil, described the operation as a "planned execution."

Hackers reportedly breached one vessel's propulsion and navigation systems, disrupting communications for about 30 hours and forcing the crew to switch to manual procedures, potentially delaying energy shipments to Asia and Europe.

AMERICA MUST DEFEND OUR DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE, HERE AND OVERSEAS, TO WIN THE NEXT WAR

The U.S. Coast Guard will be ending admissions for college students wanting to commission as officers that take race into consideration as part of the Trump administration’s continued anti-diversity, equity and inclusion initiative, Fox News Digital has learned. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

"The Marine Transportation System is vital to America's economic prosperity and national security, and safeguarding it against potential cyber risks is a standard part of the United States Coast Guard's safety and security mission," the Coast Guard spokesperson said.

"Just as we monitor for mechanical or weather-related hazards, we incorporate cyber risk management into our routine, professional approach to facilitating commerce and ensuring safe vessel transits into and from our ports and waterways.

"While confirmed cyber disruptions in the maritime domain remain uncommon, even isolated technical issues can cause avoidable commercial delays.

"We encourage all maritime stakeholders to leverage Coast Guard Cyber Command’s free, non-regulatory technical resources to maintain strong digital hygiene and report any suspected anomalies to the National Response Center," the spokesperson added.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Newly elected Florida commissioner's son shot dead inside tent during camping trip
articles.excerpt:
Carey Washington Vinson was fatally shot inside his tent along Florida's Blackwater River on Sunday night.

A newly elected Florida politician is mourning the death of his son after the young man was ...
articles.body_text:
Carey Washington Vinson was fatally shot inside his tent along Florida's Blackwater River on Sunday night.

A newly elected Florida politician is mourning the death of his son after the young man was fatally shot inside his tent during a weekend camping trip, his father confirmed Monday.

Joe Vinson, who made history earlier this year as the first non-party-affiliated county commissioner elected in Escambia County, announced the tragedy on Instagram, revealing that his son, Carey Washington Vinson, was killed while camping with friends near the Blackwater River in the Florida Panhandle.

"I don’t know how to say this," Joe Vinson wrote. "Our son Carey Washington Vinson is dead. He was camping with friends on the Blackwater River last night when a gunshot from outside their campsite struck him in his tent."

CALIFORNIA NURSING STUDENT AND MOM ARRESTED MONTHS AFTER MAN’S BODY TURNS UP IN RAVINE: POLICE

Carey Washington Vinson was killed while camping with friends near the Blackwater River in the Florida Panhandle, his father confirmed Monday. (@joepensacola / Instagram)

He added, "It’s an ongoing investigation, and I don’t have any more details at this time. We are shocked and heartbroken about our sweet boy."

According to the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office, officers were dispatched to the Blackwater River area on Sunday following a 911 call about a shooting.

First responders arrived to find a male victim with a gunshot wound to the head and pronounced him dead at the scene.

RUSH HOUR ROAD RAGE SUSPECT’S BAIL REVOKED AS SLAIN UTILITY WORKER’S SUPPORTERS SHOUT AT ACCUSED MURDERER

Joe Vinson was elected this year as the first non-party-affiliated county commissioner in Escambia County history. (Escambia County)

Carey, 19, and his friends had been camping on sandbars along the river since Friday, Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office Chief Deputy Randy Tifft told People Magazine.

Law enforcement has not yet said whether they believe the shooting was intentional or accidental.

Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons offered condolences to the commissioner's family on Facebook.

"There are simply no words that can ease the pain of losing a child," Simmons said. "I ask that you join me in keeping Joe and his entire family in your thoughts and prayers during this incredibly difficult time. May God grant them strength, comfort, and peace in the days ahead."

LOUISIANA MAN ACCUSED OF RANDOM NATURE TRAIL MURDER, KILLING COWORKER WITH CROSSBOW DAYS LATER

Law enforcement has not yet said whether they believe the shooting was intentional or accidental. (iStock)

Detectives are urging anyone who was in the area or witnessed suspicious activity to come forward.

"This incident remains under active investigation," a spokesperson for the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office told Fox News Digital in an email. "We will provide updates as additional information becomes available for release."

Fox News Digital reached out to Joe Vinson for comment.

Sophia Compton is a Writer at Fox News Digital. Sophia was previously a business reporter covering finance, energy and tourism and has experience as a TV news producer. She graduated with a journalism degree in 2021 from the University of Hawaii at Manoa. Story tips can be sent to sophia.compton@fox.com.

First responders arrived to find a male victim with a gunshot wound to the head and pronounced him dead at the scene.

RUSH HOUR ROAD RAGE SUSPECT’S BAIL REVOKED AS SLAIN UTILITY WORKER’S SUPPORTERS SHOUT AT ACCUSED MURDERER

Joe Vinson was elected this year as the first non-party-affiliated county commissioner in Escambia County history. (Escambia County)

Carey, 19, and his friends had been camping on sandbars along the river since Friday, Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office Chief Deputy Randy Tifft told People Magazine.

Law enforcement has not yet said whether they believe the shooting was intentional or accidental.

Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons offered condolences to the commissioner's family on Facebook.

"There are simply no words that can ease the pain of losing a child," Simmons said. "I ask that you join me in keeping Joe and his entire family in your thoughts and prayers during this incredibly difficult time. May God grant them strength, comfort, and peace in the days ahead."

LOUISIANA MAN ACCUSED OF RANDOM NATURE TRAIL MURDER, KILLING COWORKER WITH CROSSBOW DAYS LATER

Law enforcement has not yet said whether they believe the shooting was intentional or accidental. (iStock)

Detectives are urging anyone who was in the area or witnessed suspicious activity to come forward.

"This incident remains under active investigation," a spokesperson for the Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office told Fox News Digital in an email. "We will provide updates as additional information becomes available for release."

Fox News Digital reached out to Joe Vinson for comment.
