articles.title: Nine million jobs are in limbo, and Congress can fix it before Christmas
articles.excerpt: Billy Downs, president of Ford's Garage, tells Fox News Digital the challenges of balancing employee compensation with affordability for diners as select Florida franchise locations experiment with a ...
articles.body_text:
Billy Downs, president of Ford's Garage, tells Fox News Digital the challenges of balancing employee compensation with affordability for diners as select Florida franchise locations experiment with a different approach to covering labor expenses.

Ask most Americans who owns the McDonald's on the corner, the Holiday Inn off the interstate, or the gym down the street, and they'll tell you it's a big corporation. They're wrong. Most of those businesses are owned by local entrepreneurs who put their own savings on the line, sign the lease, make the payroll, and live in the town they serve. There are roughly 832,000 of these franchise small businesses in America, and together they support about nine million jobs.

Yet for more than a decade, Washington hasn't been able to answer a simple question for them: Who is the employer?

The answer has flipped with every change in administration. In 2015, the Obama labor board's Browning-Ferris decision blew up decades of precedent and said a parent brand could be on the hook for a franchisee's workers based on "indirect" or even unused control. A 2020 rule restored common sense. In 2023, the Biden board went further than Browning-Ferris, declaring that merely reserving the right to control was enough, before a federal court struck that rule down. The standard has now changed four times since 2015, and another court case could change it again in the next few months. No small-business owner can plan a five-year expansion around a rule that changes every four.

CHICK-FIL-A IS ONE OF AMERICA'S TOUGHEST FRANCHISES, AND THE STARTUP COST MAY SHOCK YOU

This isn't an abstract legal fight. When the International Franchise Association and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce studied the damage from the expanded standard, they found it cost the economy $33.3 billion a year, led to as many as 376,000 fewer job opportunities, and drove a 93% increase in lawsuits against franchise businesses. Ninety-two percent of the brands and owners surveyed said the rule meant less support from their brand.

That last number is the one that should bother Congress most. Under a sprawling joint-employer test, every bit of help a franchisor gives — a training program, an HR template, a workplace-safety manual — becomes evidence that it is really the boss. So the brands pull back. The national company with the lawyers and the compliance staff protects itself. The owner of three sandwich shops is left on her own. A rule sold as protecting workers ends up kneecapping the small employers who hire them.

The fix is sitting in front of Congress right now. The American Franchise Act (H.R. 5267 / S. 3525) writes one permanent, franchise-specific standard into federal law under both the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act. A franchisor would be a joint employer only if it both possesses and exercises substantial, direct, and immediate control over essential terms of employment like wages, hiring, and scheduling. Setting brand standards, offering training, or requiring safety qualifications would not, by themselves, make a franchisor the employer. That is how franchising worked for most of its history, and it is how it should work.

Most important, it would be the law — not a board decision that the next administration can toss out on a party-line vote.

This is that rarest of things in Washington: a genuinely bipartisan bill. It was introduced by seven Republicans and seven Democrats. It has 158 cosponsors in the House, cleared the House Education and Workforce Committee in July, and has the backing of the White House. Members like Rep. Kevin Hern of Oklahoma, who owned and operated McDonald's restaurants before he came to Congress, understand from the inside what it means to meet a payroll under rules that won't sit still.

REP ROGER WILLIAMS: 250 YEARS OF HARD WORK PAYS OFF FOR MAIN STREET BUSINESSES

At Unleash Prosperity Now, our new paper, "Nine Million Jobs at Stake: Why Franchising Needs Regulatory Certainty," lays out what's on the line. One in eight American businesses with at least one employee is a franchise, and nearly two-thirds of local franchise owners are first-time business owners. This year alone, franchising is projected to create more than 150,000 new jobs. The conclusion is plain: Clarity is the cheapest pro-growth policy Congress can pass. It would also lift a compliance headache off small-business owners and free them to keep prices down at a moment when Americans have made clear that affordability is what they care about most. It doesn't cost the Treasury a dime, and it lets hundreds of thousands of small employers get back to hiring.

The clock matters. If the American Franchise Act doesn't pass before this Congress adjourns, it dies, and the whole process starts over, with a future labor board free to swing the pendulum back again. (iStock)

The clock matters. If the American Franchise Act doesn't pass before this Congress adjourns, it dies, and the whole process starts over, with a future labor board free to swing the pendulum back again. Franchise owners have already spent 10 years in limbo. They shouldn't be made to wait for another election cycle.

The lame-duck session is usually remembered for what Congress fails to do. Here's a chance to do something useful for Main Street before Christmas. Pass the American Franchise Act.

Stephen Moore is an economist and co-founder of the Committee to Unleash Prosperity.

articles.title: At least 15 killed in Ukraine’s Kyiv region as Russia intensifies attacks
articles.excerpt:
Rescuers in Ukraine have raced to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike after attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people.

...
articles.body_text:
Rescuers in Ukraine have raced to find residents trapped under the rubble of a block of flats that partially collapsed in a Russian strike after attacks on the Kyiv region killed at least 15 people.

Moscow has been pummelling Ukraine with nightly drone and missile barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter while the full-scale invasion grinds through its fifth year.

An overnight strike on Dymer, about 45km (30 miles) north of the Ukrainian capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least 11 people, Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko said on Monday.

“Rescuers recovered the body of another person from beneath the rubble,” Tkachenko wrote on Telegram, confirming the death toll had risen to 11.

Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said earlier on Telegram that the dead included a teenager.

It said rescuers were searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”.

Rescuers had managed to pull out survivors from the rubble, including a 79-year-old woman and a child, Tkachenko said.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said people were believed to still be under the rubble.

“Rescuers are still at the site, working to try to pull people out from under the rubble dead or alive,” she said.

A Russian strike on a supermarket killed three other people and wounded 15, including three children, in Vyshneve, a city just south of Kyiv, Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on Facebook.

“People had simply gone to the store to buy groceries. An ordinary shopping trip turned into a tragedy due to a Russian attack,” Tkachenko said.

A strike on a private home in nearby Bila Tserkva killed one more person and set the building ablaze, he added.

Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said on social media.

Moscow has ramped up attacks on Ukraine and its energy network in particular as temperatures drop to around freezing.

Putin promised on Thursday that Russia would respond to Ukrainian attacks on the Kerch Bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule over Ukraine’s Russian-annexed Crimean Peninsula, with “much more painful” attacks.

Ukraine hit the bridge three times in a week, severing the part of it used by vehicles and halting train services.

Meanwhile, drones attacked oil storage facilities in Russia’s Tatarstan region, damaging several, but there were no immediate reports of deaths or injuries, according to the Interfax news agency, which quoted local authorities.

“A fire broke out there,” Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova reported from Moscow, adding that the attack targeted the facility in Tatarstan’s Almetyevsk area.

Shapovalova said drone attacks were also reported in the Novoshakhtinsk area in Rostov, hitting a petroleum products plant and causing a fire in a storage tank.

She added that an attack was also reported in the city of Perm in the Volga region, where a large oil refinery is located.

Our correspondents said the attacks in Tatarstan, which is about 1,000km (620 miles) away from the Ukrainian border, demonstrate Kyiv’s ability to penetrate deep inside Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine’s forces sank the Russian corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest ships, commissioned in 2023, near the coast of Libya using seven Ukrainian-made naval drones.

Zelenskyy said they hit a second target, the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara. The Ukrainian president said it was used by Russia to transport weapons.

“We continue operations in designated waters,” he said on Telegram.

Zelenskyy added that a Russian Ka-27 combat helicopter was destroyed along with the corvette.

articles.excerpt: More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war has turned Gaza into “a toxic wasteland”, with poisoned water and contaminated soil threatening the survival of Palestinians in the enclave of 2.3 milli...
articles.body_text:
More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war has turned Gaza into “a toxic wasteland”, with poisoned water and contaminated soil threatening the survival of Palestinians in the enclave of 2.3 million people.

Israel’s use of explosives and incendiary weapons has caused environmental contamination across more than 99 percent of Gaza, according to a new report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS).

“Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come,” said Amitabh Behar, Oxfam’s international executive director.

“The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival. This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law,” he said in a statement.

“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins in multiple ways through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris.”

The report shows how Israel’s destruction of buildings and the environment has contaminated the air, soil, food and water in the enclave.

It also emphasises the urgent need for a full independent investigation to identify and reduce the risks to Palestinian lives.

Pollutants from bombardment, fires, rubble and untreated sewage can reach Palestinians through the air they breathe, the water they drink and the food they eat.

Oxfam’s report, which uses satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, gives a comprehensive picture to date of the impact of the Israeli assault on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called “ceasefire” was signed in October 2025.

In September 2025, a UN international commission of inquiry said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. And the International Court of Justice is hearing a case of genocide against Israel. In January, the ICJ said it was plausible that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

The report came a day after world leaders failed to reach a consensus on climate change at the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) of the United Nations.

Explosions, fires and the destruction of buildings and infrastructure release pollutants that settle on rubble and soil.

Wind, traffic and debris clearance send them back into the air. Oxfam’s analysis points to the highest concentrations in Gaza City, Jabalia and the North Gaza governorate.

Israel’s continuous bombardment has also generated substantial greenhouse gas emissions, with further emissions expected from clearing debris and rebuilding.

A study cited in the report estimated direct conflict emissions at more than 1.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) by January 2025.

By October 11, 2025, Israeli ground operations directly affected about 283sq km (109sq miles) of Gaza’s 365sq km (141sq miles), or 78 percent of the area, Oxfam estimates.

The UN Environment Programme estimates that the assault since October 7, 2023, generated 61 million tonnes of debris, which is about 29 tonnes of rubble per person living in Gaza now. More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, most of them multiple times.

Oxfam estimates that the mountains of rubble would require 2.1 million dump truckloads to clear them, equivalent to 736 trips around the circumference of the entire planet.

The amount of rubble that needs to be cleared is about eight times the 7.65 million tonnes estimated in Iraq’s Mosul during the 2017 conflict.

The report identifies at least one potential contamination source across more than 99 percent of Gaza. Gaza City, Khan Younis, Rafah, Jabalia and the Salah al-Din Street corridor showed the greatest overlap of potential hazards.

Unexploded munitions can leach contaminants into soil and groundwater as their casings corrode. Damaged vehicles, batteries and fuel stores add to the risks along military routes and former positions.

A study cited by Oxfam estimated emissions across the wider conflict cycle at 33.2 million tonnes of CO2e, including an estimate of 31.4 million tonnes of carbon emissions that will occur from reconstruction.

According to a report by Palestinian Water Authority cited by Oxfam, Gaza’s daily water supply fell from 334,107 cubic metres before October 2023 to 54,747 cubic metres in June 2024, a drop of about 84 percent. By April 2026, emergency repairs had brought it back to 130,315 cubic metres a day, still 61 percent below pre-assault levels.

Nine of 61 reservoirs were operational, with combined storage sufficient to provide 18 litres per person for one day.

Gaza’s Coastal Aquifer historically supplied 81 percent of the territory’s water. Oxfam says 97 percent of the aquifer was already chemically polluted before October 2023.

Decades of overpumping amid Israel’s air, land and sea blockade of Gaza allowed seawater to seep in. Untreated sewage, farm runoff and waste disposal added to the pollution.

In July 2026, Gaza’s Ministry of Health detected faecal coliforms in 15 of 79 groundwater wells (19 percent) tested. Oxfam identified North Gaza, Gaza City and Deir el-Balah as the areas most at risk from contaminated drinking water. An assessment in 2021 reported faecal coliforms in 2 percent of wells.

July tests found that 61 of 79 wells (77.2 percent) had total dissolved solids above 1,000 milligrams per litre, 400mg above the level at which the World Health Organization says water becomes increasingly unpleasant to drink.

By April 2024, Israel’s assault had destroyed all six of Gaza’s wastewater treatment plants. An estimated 40,000 cubic metres of raw sewage enter the Mediterranean daily, enough to fill 16 Olympic-size pools.

By April 2026, 19 percent of pumping stations and about 30 percent of the sewer network still functioned at least partly.

Gaza’s waste collection fleet fell from 261 vehicles to 48.

Both main landfills remained inaccessible. Of at least 56 temporary dumps, only 11 were accessible and operating.

These sites generally lack barriers to protect soil and groundwater. By April 2026, an estimated 1.45 million people lived in areas affected by rodents and other pests.

Before October 2023, Gaza’s farms supplied about 95 percent of the fresh vegetables people ate. By late 2025, more than 87 percent of cropland was damaged.

Oxfam says only 3 percent was accessible and undamaged.

By October 2024, the UN had reported that more than one million olive trees had been uprooted.

Oxfam identified more than 7,200 damaged greenhouses and documented the destruction of facilities that preserved and distributed Palestinian seeds.

Before the assault, Gaza’s fisheries produced about 4,660 tonnes of fish a year, with fish farms adding 750 tonnes.

In July 2026, an estimated 1.2 million people (59 percent) faced crisis levels of acute food shortages or worse, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, cited by the report.

The report also records the loss of roughly 95 percent of cattle and a collapse in fishing.

The average daily catch from October 2023 to April 2024 was 7.3 percent of its 2022 level. Oxfam warns that contaminants could enter crops and seafood as production resumes.

Gaza’s gross domestic product fell by 83 percent in 2024 to $362m, the report says.

Damage to farms, workshops and factories has stripped people of income and the means to resume work. Debris removal, repairs and farming could expose workers to asbestos, silica and other hazards for years.

Among the commerce and industry establishments assessed, 92 percent sustained damage, including 72 percent that were destroyed.

A joint World Bank, European Union and UN assessment, cited by Oxfam, put direct physical damage at $35.2bn and economic losses at $22.7bn by October 2025.

It estimated recovery and reconstruction needs at $71.4bn over a decade, including $26.3bn in the first 18 months.

Disease prevalence in Gaza recorded more than 1.9 million cases of acute respiratory infection and about 81,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in January and February 2026. More than 36,000 of the diarrhoea cases were among children aged below five years. Gaza recorded more than 496,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in 2025.

In 2024, vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 was detected in Gaza’s wastewater. A child was later diagnosed with paralytic polio, Gaza’s first reported case in 25 years. The report also cites the detection of multidrug-resistant pseudomonas in water at primary healthcare centres.

Oxfam says the destruction of Gaza’s water, food and sanitation systems may be relevant to alleged crimes under the Rome Statute and to assessing whether Israel violated the Genocide Convention.

A genocide finding requires proof of intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part. Oxfam calls for full reparations where violations are established.

Its five-stage plan calls for securing access and reducing exposure, testing for contamination, screening sites and making essential repairs, treating contaminated sites and managing hazardous waste, then rebuilding with safeguards and long-term monitoring.

articles.title: Georgia officer shoots 13-year-old after traffic stop linked to earlier shooting, police say
articles.excerpt:
A Milledgeville, Georgia, police officer shot a 13-year-old during a traffic stop involving a vehicle linked to a separate robbery and shooting, authorities said.

A Georgia police officer shot and wo...
articles.body_text:
A Milledgeville, Georgia, police officer shot a 13-year-old during a traffic stop involving a vehicle linked to a separate robbery and shooting, authorities said.

A Georgia police officer shot and wounded a 13-year-old Sunday night while conducting a traffic stop linked to an earlier shooting, according to authorities.

The teenager is suspected of being involved in a Jones County robbery and shooting that left one man with a gunshot wound.

Jones County Sheriff Butch Reece said the teenager had met with four men from Macon for a gun sale on Etheridge Road when the group allegedly tried to rob the teenager. The teenager then opened fire, shooting one of the men.

GEORGIA DEPUTY FIRED AFTER HARASSING MOM WITH FAKE FACEBOOK PAGE

A Georgia police officer shot and wounded a 13-year-old Sunday night while conducting a traffic stop linked to an earlier shooting. (Milledgeville Police Department)

Authorities said the teenager fled the scene before being tracked down to the Milledgeville Mall parking lot, where Milledgeville police attempted to stop a vehicle determined to be linked to the Jones County shooting.

During the traffic stop, an officer shot the teenager, who sustained a single gunshot wound, Milledgeville Police said. A firearm was also recovered at the scene.

The teenager was alert and conscious following the shooting and was transported to a hospital in the Macon area for medical treatment. (Milledgeville Police Department)

The teenager was alert, conscious and speaking following the shooting and was transported to a Macon-area hospital for medical treatment, where the juvenile was listed in stable condition, Milledgeville police said.

THREE TEENS, ADULT CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER WOMAN FINDS HER TEENAGE SON DEAD IN ABANDONED HOME

The circumstances surrounding the shooting were not immediately known, including whether the teenager attempted to shoot the officer. (Google Maps)

The circumstances surrounding the shooting were not immediately clear, including whether the teenager attempted to shoot the officer.

Milledgeville police said the Georgia Bureau of Investigation has been asked to respond and will take over the investigation.

articles.title: Artificial superintelligence ‘arriving’, warns top Meta executive
articles.excerpt:
Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that superintelligence that far exceeds the human intellect is imminent.

Meta Chief AI Officer A...
articles.body_text:
Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that superintelligence that far exceeds the human intellect is imminent.

Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang issued the warning on Sunday after an employee at AI giant Anthropic announced that he had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.

Wang said the breakthrough dwarfed any human achievement for “sheer intellectual might”.

The 29-year-old executive said the milestone showed that emerging AI models will be “clearly superhuman” at improving themselves, as well as “massively accelerating” research in fields such as biology, armaments and economics.

“Superintelligence is arriving,” Wang said on X.

“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in.”

Wang, who co-founded Scale AI before joining Meta as the tech giant’s first chief AI officer last year, said it is unlikely humankind will be able to control AI that achieves unconstrained recursive self-improvement or is “1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”

“Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully,” Wang said.

AI safety advocates have identified recursive self-improvement – where AI models become capable of advancing without human input – as a critical tipping point after which humanity could lose the ability to control the technology.

While the risks of frontier AI have stoked intense debate in Silicon Valley, there is no consensus on how to maximise the benefits of the technology without exposing humanity to catastrophic risks.

Meta has largely positioned itself on the more optimistic side of the debate, with CEO and cofounder Mark Zuckerberg rejecting calls by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman for a coordinated slowdown in development to beef up guardrails.

In an essay published in August, Zuckerberg lamented that discussions about AI were “filled with doom” and said the technology should lead to “more people sharing greater prosperity, health and freedom.”

In his post on Sunday, Wang criticised “lazy thinking” within the AI industry that he said treated superintelligence as inevitable.

“We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI. We should endeavour ourselves to build a technology which delivers a positive future for humanity, where all humans have greater agency and empowerment,” Wang said.

“I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.”

articles.title: Inside the Thanksgiving turkey hotline that's been saving holiday dinners for 45 years
articles.excerpt:
FOX News goes behind the scenes at the Illinois call center where culinary experts have spent 45 seasons helping Americans navigate Thanksgiving cooking emergencies.

NAPERVILLE, IL – Thanksgiving din...
articles.body_text:
FOX News goes behind the scenes at the Illinois call center where culinary experts have spent 45 seasons helping Americans navigate Thanksgiving cooking emergencies.

NAPERVILLE, IL – Thanksgiving dinner can bring plenty of questions, especially when a frozen turkey, a crowded kitchen and hungry guests are involved. But for 45 seasons, Americans have had somewhere to turn when holiday cooking doesn't go according to plan.

Inside Butterball's Turkey Talk-Line in suburban Chicago, dozens of culinary professionals spend the holiday season helping home cooks with everything from thawing their turkeys to figuring out whether dinner is ready to serve.

The operation began in 1981 with just six female home economists answering calls by telephone, using a Rolodex to help guide their conversations.

"When the talk line started, it was just a mere six all-female home economists," said Nicole Johnson, director of the Turkey Talk-Line. "They were manning all of the phone calls, kind of old school Rolodex."

AFFORDABLE FOOD IDEAS AND TURKEY TIPS FOR THANKSGIVING THIS YEAR

An archival photograph shows six women from Butterball's original Turkey Talk-Line team, which began answering Thanksgiving cooking questions in 1981. (Courtesy of Butterball)

Today, the team has grown to more than 50 chefs, dietitians and food scientists who answer thousands of questions each holiday season. While the telephone remains part of the operation, home cooks can now reach experts through text messages, email, online chat and social media.

The questions have evolved, too. Johnson said callers aren't always standing in front of an oven. Some reach out while shopping for Thanksgiving groceries, with the sound of shopping carts in the background as experts help them decide what to buy.

Others need advice about side dishes, ham or which meat thermometer to use. Home cooks can even send photos when they're having trouble explaining a problem.

A roasted turkey and Thanksgiving side dishes are displayed inside Butterball's Turkey Talk-Line facility in Naperville, Illinois.  (Olivianna Calmes)

Preparing to answer such a wide range of questions takes practice. Each October, the team goes through training known as Butterball University, testing cooking techniques and reviewing common holiday challenges. That includes some less conventional methods, such as cooking an entire turkey in the microwave.

The experts also experiment with recipes in a test kitchen, including ways to use Thanksgiving leftovers.

The annual preparation comes as more Americans say they plan to cook their own holiday centerpiece. New research from FMI – The Food Industry Association found 59% of shoppers planning to serve turkey expect to prepare it from scratch this year, up from 43% in 2025.

Regardless of experience, one question comes up repeatedly: How long does it take to thaw a turkey?

Experts recommend allowing about 24 hours in the refrigerator for every four pounds, meaning a 20-pound turkey needs roughly five days to thaw. For cooks running short on time, cold-water thawing takes approximately 30 minutes per pound, with the water changed every half hour. The turkey should be cooked immediately afterward.

But answering questions isn't always as straightforward as providing a cooking time or temperature.

Bill Nolan, a retired chef and culinary educator, has spent 10 seasons helping home cooks through Butterball's Turkey Talk-Line.  (Olivianna Calmes)

"We're turkey counselors, we're turkey detectives," said Bill Nolan, a retired chef and culinary educator who has worked on the Talk-Line for 10 seasons.

Nolan said callers sometimes reach out in a panic, leaving experts to piece together what went wrong before they can offer a solution.

'FOOD BABE' DECLARES WAR ON THE 'HOLIDAY DEATH AISLE' AHEAD OF THANKSGIVING

And after a decade of conversations, some have stayed with him for reasons that have little to do with cooking.

A prepared Thanksgiving turkey is displayed in the test kitchen at Butterball's Turkey Talk-Line facility in Naperville, Illinois.  (Olivianna Calmes)

"A gentleman called up, he had lost his wife, and he wanted to cook dinner for his family and his grandkids, and he'd never done it," Nolan recalled. "And I took the time to walk him through the process."

"It's those types of calls that really hit you right here," he added.

The Talk-Line continues operating through Dec. 24, with experts available at 1-800-BUTTERBALL or by text at 844-877-3456.

Olivianna Calmes joined Fox News in 2024 as a Multimedia Reporter based in St. Louis, Missouri.

articles.title: Widowed amid war and displacement: Sudanese mothers struggle to survive
articles.excerpt:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of sexual assault that some readers may find disturbing.

Port Sudan, Sudan – In Sudan’s displacement camps, the stories of residents often follow similar pat...
articles.body_text:
Warning: This story contains descriptions of sexual assault that some readers may find disturbing.

Port Sudan, Sudan – In Sudan’s displacement camps, the stories of residents often follow similar paths, but each loss and hardship is a deeply personal experience.

Arafa Abdelaziz endured a dangerous 15-day journey from Omdurman to a displacement camp in Port Sudan in late 2023, after losing her husband and one of her two sons, who died early in the war.

Her husband died just days after fighting broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023, leaving her to care for her remaining two children as their home city of Omdurman in Khartoum State came under bombardment.

Five months later, her eight-year-old son was killed by a stray bullet during clashes near Omdurman’s market.

“My son was playing outside the house with his friends when I suddenly heard a loud noise. When I went outside, I found that his head had been shattered by gunfire,” said the 33-year-old.

With the fighting between the SAF and RSF continuing in Omdurman, one of the centres of the power struggle between the two former allies at the start of the war, Arafa eventually decided to flee the city with her six-year-old son, who has a brain condition affecting his development.

She describes the journey to Port Sudan as a prolonged and horrifying ordeal. Near Jebel Aulia, south of Khartoum, RSF fighters intercepted the vehicle they were in and the passengers were robbed and assaulted.

“They asked every woman carrying a child how she wanted her son to be killed. I told them to kill me before they touched my son,” Arafa recalled.

When she confronted the fighters as they attempted to assault her child, one of them hit her with the butt of his rifle, leaving her unconscious for more than an hour.

“When I regained consciousness, I saw RSF fighters raping the young women who were travelling with us on the bus. Some were raped in front of their fathers. I felt it was the end,” she said.

In October 2026, UN Women reported that 12.7 million people, mostly women and girls, needed support for gender-based violence in Sudan – four times the pre-war figure.

The agency warned that sexual violence is being used as a weapon of war, with women and girls at risk while fleeing areas of fighting, in displacement camps and while searching for food, water and shelter.

Arafa said her greatest fear throughout the ordeal was for her younger son’s safety. When the fighters asked what valuables she had, she told them she owned nothing. They took two gold rings from her fingers and after severely beating her, let her continue her journey.

“I arrived in Port Sudan with nothing, having lost my husband. My son’s condition had worsened because of what we went through on the journey and because he could not receive his medication regularly,” she said.

It was Arafa’s first time in Port Sudan, so, having no family or friends there to support her, she headed to a school sheltering displaced families. She was later transferred to another displacement camp, where she now lives with her son. But reaching relative safety was not the end of her struggles. Her son’s condition fluctuates, and she remains worried about his health and future.

“Sometimes he imagines strange things because of his illness,” she said. “Yesterday, he told me he could see a lot of blood on the ground. It makes me think every day about his future with this condition.”

Arafa cannot afford his medication, so she has resorted to giving him medicine only when his condition deteriorates. She depends largely on aid distributed in the camp, as her needs and those of her son continue to grow.

“I’m afraid to leave him alone at home, out of my sight, in case he has a seizure or hurts himself,” she said.

The war in Sudan has killed as many as 150,000 people and forced millions from their homes, often to camps in impoverished neighbouring countries.

Income levels have dropped to 1992 levels and extreme poverty rates are worse than in the 1980s, according to the United Nations. Due to conscription, fatalities and emigration to other regions and countries for work, women have become the sole guardians in many displaced Sudanese households.

The UN’s 2025 Gender Snapshot found that 75 percent of female-headed households in Sudan were food insecure – three times the rate among male-headed households.

The Mashad Observatory has documented 72,202 cases of widowhood since the outbreak of war in Sudan in April 2023. That constitutes a complex humanitarian crisis which can lead to the collapse of household incomes, stability and protection systems. In the long term, it means transmitting deprivation, economic vulnerability and psychological trauma from one generation to the next.

These cumulative impacts can weaken social cohesion, exacerbate inequalities and undermine the capacity of local communities to recover from the consequences of war. This growing burden means fewer opportunities for women to work and increased dependence on humanitarian assistance, with long-term economic implications for Sudan, the group said.

“Their suffering is further compounded when women lose the primary source of household income or are forced to abandon their homes and communities without adequate financial resources or social support networks. Such circumstances may expose them to heightened risks of economic exploitation, gender-based violence, forced or early marriage involving their daughters and the interruption of their children’s education,” a spokesperson for the organisation told Al Jazeera.

“These pressures may also contribute to deteriorating mental health as a result of cumulative trauma, overwhelming responsibilities and the absence of appropriate psychosocial support services.”

With humanitarian agencies saying that Sudan’s 2026 response plan, which aims to reach 20.4 million people and requires $2.9bn, has received only 47% of the funding needed, there will be challenges in providing these families with the necessary support.

“Addressing this challenge therefore requires a transition from temporary emergency relief towards a comprehensive national strategy that places widows and female-headed households at the centre of Sudan’s recovery and reconstruction plans,” said the organisation.

“Such a strategy should include sustainable cash assistance, economic empowerment programmes, vocational training, access to decent employment, improved access to finance and productive enterprises, as well as guaranteed access to education, healthcare, legal protection and psychosocial support.”

Zahra Idris, 39, fled Khartoum with her husband and two children as shelling intensified, arriving in Port Sudan three years ago.

Her husband initially rented a house in the working-class neighbourhood of Al-Kasara. But when they could no longer afford the rent, the landlord evicted them. The family moved to a school shelter before being relocated to a displacement camp at the start of the school year.

Two months ago, Zahra’s husband died of heart disease, leaving her to care for their two children with little support beyond humanitarian assistance, which has become increasingly limited.

“Since my husband died, my fears have grown. I cannot go out to look for work until I complete the mourning period prescribed in Islam, which lasts four months and ten days,” she said.

Her 12-year-old son has an intellectual disability and requires regular medical care, something the family cannot afford given the rising cost of living.

“There is no one to help me. I just want my son’s condition to improve enough for him to attend a school for children with disabilities,” she said.

“Going from one organisation to another, looking for someone to cover my son’s medical treatment and education, cost me around 100,000 Sudanese pounds. That money could have covered our household needs for several days.”

articles.title: Kenya and DR Congo agree to restore ties after tensions over conflict
articles.excerpt:
The meeting between Kenya's President William Ruto (left) and DR Congo's Félix Tshisekedi (centre) was hosted by Denis Sassou Nguesso (right)

Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterp...
articles.body_text:
The meeting between Kenya's President William Ruto (left) and DR Congo's Félix Tshisekedi (centre) was hosted by Denis Sassou Nguesso (right)

Kenya's President William Ruto and his Congolese counterpart Felix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic ties between the two countries following tensions over the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo.

Relations between the two countries have soured since 2023 when DR Congo accused Kenya of hosting leaders launching a rebel alliance, including the M23.

This led DR Congo to recall its envoy to Nairobi. Relations deteriorated further when Kinshasa refusing to accredit Kenya's nominated ambassador.

On Sunday, the two leaders affirmed their commitment to "sovereignty, territorial integrity, non-interference in the internal affairs of states".

The agreement was announced in a joint statement issued after the summit held in the town of Oyo in Congo-Brazzaville, facilitated by the nation's President Denis Sassou Nguesso, with Togolese leader Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé as mediator.

Tshisekedi and Ruto also agreed to "good neighbourliness and peaceful settlement of disputes" as well as "strengthen cooperation within regional mechanisms".

DR Congo and Kenya are both members of the East African Community (EAC).

DR Congo, which joined in 2022, is the latest entrant to the bloc, but its membership has been complicated by its accusation that Rwanda, a fellow member, backs the M23 rebels. Rwanda denies the claims despite overwhelming evidence.

DR Congo has also accused Kenya of hosting Congolese political and rebel leaders whom it says are working to destabilise the country.

When the Congo River Alliance (AFC), a political-military alliance including the M23, was launched in Nairobi in 2023, DR Congo responded by recalling its ambassador to Kenya.

The tensions were stoked further in March last year after Kenya named a consul-general to Goma, the capital of DR Congo's North Kivu region, after it fell to M23 forces, who control many eastern parts of the country.

DR Congo said naming the envoy amounted to disrespect for the country's territorial integrity and seemed to legitimise the group's occupation.

Suited and booted: How Joseph Kabila went from president to rebel leader

Relations deteriorated further after Kenya hosted a meeting of Congolese opposition figures, including former President Joseph Kabila, in October 2025.

Kabila was in 2025 sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself.

He has since been named the leader of the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), the new rebel coalition that took over from the AFC.

Sunday's meeting between Ruto and Tshisekedi also included other issues including deepening trade cooperation, economic development, and regional integration.

The two also sought to collaborate to control the spread of the Ebola virus.

On Sunday, the head of the World Health Organization (WHO), Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said the frequency of attacks across the country's east had increased since the end of October, seriously affecting the Ebola response.

Tedros said heavy fighting in an area close to where the Ebola outbreak first emerged had disrupted work and the wider Ebola response.

More than 5,700 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.

The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, has spread beyond DR Congo borders, with cases reported in Kenya, Uganda and Nigeria.

articles.title: Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears
articles.excerpt:
Jump in price follows slowdown in Qatar supplies and depleted summer stocks due to heatwaves

European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the cont...
articles.body_text:
Jump in price follows slowdown in Qatar supplies and depleted summer stocks due to heatwaves

European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the continent’s over depleted supply this winter and costly household bills.

The Dutch month-ahead contract – the European benchmark for gas prices over the next four weeks – rose by as much as 8.6% to €96.08, before settling up 4% at €92.50.

The jump in gas prices comes as much of north-west Europe braces for a tough winter, when energy demand is at its highest.

Europe’s gas supplies have been hit by a slowdown in exports from Qatar due to the war in the Middle East, as well as an increase in consumption during the summer to power refrigeration and cooling during the prolonged heatwave.

Storage levels on the continent are now well below the seasonal average, at about 69% full against a typical level of 80%.

In the UK, energy system operators have said the country will have enough gas and electricity to meet demand during the coldest months, partly because of paying higher market prices than neighbours to secure imports.

However, it means British households will probably pay some of the highest energy bills in Europe this winter.

This week the energy regulator Ofgem is expected to announce a 26% rise in its quarterly price cap from January, adding an extra £443 to an average annual bill for a dual-fuel household. It could be one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record.

The charity Citizens Advice has said it expects a wave of more people seeking emergency help. Its chief executive, Clare Moriarty, said every day its “advisers see people whose budgets have been completely wiped out by years of compounding crises.”

“Millions of households are entering the coldest months of the year with nothing left,” she said.

Last month, the chancellor, John Healey, used his first budget to announce a giveaway of £100 to 20m households in council tax bands A to D to help with energy bills. But Moriarty said that, while the top-up was welcome, it “simply won’t stretch far enough for those who need the most support”.

“Many households will quickly burn through it, leaving them at risk of deeper debt or being unable to top up their prepayment meter just as winter bites.

“The government must take action before the cold weather takes hold. A targeted top-up to the warm home discount and an emergency support credit for prepayment customers are vital, practical lifelines that will stop households being left in the cold and dark this winter.”

Chris O’Shea, the chief executive of British Gas owner Centrica, has also said he is “hugely concerned” about the forecast jump in energy bills, warning that the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their bills would rise in the new year.

He told the BBC on Sunday that there was a “massive problem” with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some without the means to do so and an “increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills”.

articles.title: Trump says Iran unleashed missile, drone surge after midterms
articles.excerpt:
President Donald Trump claimed that the war with Iran will end "right after" the midterm elections in the U.S.

President Donald Trump said Sunday that Iran has launched more missiles and drones over ...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump claimed that the war with Iran will end "right after" the midterm elections in the U.S.

President Donald Trump said Sunday that Iran has launched more missiles and drones over the past week than at any point in more than a year, adding that U. S. forces shot them down without any damage and as tensions escalate following the U.S. midterm elections.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump also tied the surge in Iranian attacks to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress amid voter frustration over the war with Iran and rising fuel costs.

"As everyone remembers, I predicted two things concerning the November 3rd Midterm Elections," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

TRUMP RESPONDS AFTER VANCE BLAMES IRAN WAR FOR MIDTERM LOSSES, VP SAYS HIS JOB IS TO SUPPORT PRESIDENT

President Donald Trump said Iran has launched more missiles and drones over the past week than at any point in more than a year, claiming U.S. forces intercepted them all without damage. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

"One, that if the Democrats win, the Stock Markets would go down, substantially, which they have, and two, that the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has killed 81,000 protestors as of today, will grow more aggressive in their attacks, which has also occurred. "

Trump also said that Iran launched "more drones and missiles over the past week than at any time for over a year," though he said U.S. defenses neutralized the threat.

"Don't worry, they've all been knocked down, and done no damage," Trump said.

"Iranian leaders consider the Democrats weak, ineffective, and Country destroying, but I won't let that happen!" he added.

The remarks also came days after the Senate rejected a war powers resolution in a 48-51 vote on Nov. 19, leaving Trump's military authority intact.

TRUMP WARNS OF NEW STRIKES AGAINST IRAN AFTER NEW YEAR, CALLS NEGOTIATORS ‘PROFESSIONAL TAP DANCERS’

President Donald Trump monitors U.S. military operations in Iran following an Israeli strike in Tehran on Saturday, Feb. 28, 2026. (@WhiteHouse/X)

Speaking to Fox News earlier Sunday, Trump said he is inclined to resume strikes on Iran after the new year if diplomatic talks fail to produce a deal, warning that Iranian vessels testing the U.S. naval blockade would end up "at the bottom of the sea like the rest of the navy."

In his social media post Sunday, Trump accused both Democrats and Iran of trying to keep fuel prices high ahead of the midterm elections and separately questioned the integrity of the vote without providing evidence.

"Both the Dems and Iran fought like hell to keep the Oil price up as long as possible and, since the Election, the Oil price has dropped by a record level," Trump wrote, adding that it was too bad voters "didn't understand this before they pulled the trigger."

"The whole Election was very 'strange,'" he said. "In the end, America will win! "

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Russian warship sinks off Libya as suspected Ukrainian strikes take war beyond Black Sea
articles.excerpt: Russia faces a record Ukraine drone attack as more than 1,400 drones strike overnight, damaging the prized Crimean Bridge. Host Harris Faulkner covers the escalating war before analyzing the arrival o...
articles.body_text:
Russia faces a record Ukraine drone attack as more than 1,400 drones strike overnight, damaging the prized Crimean Bridge. Host Harris Faulkner covers the escalating war before analyzing the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt in the Middle East. Retired Blackhawk helicopter pilot Lt. Col. Darin Gaub joins 'The Focus' to discuss these rising global conflicts and U.S. military positioning.

A Russian warship capsized and sank Sunday after suspected Ukrainian sea drones struck a naval base in eastern Libya, triggering an explosion and fire, according to Libyan officials.

Hours later, a second drone attack also hit a commercial ship off the coast of Benghazi, Reuters reported.

The first ship, the Russian navy corvette Merkury, was docked at Benghazi Naval Base when two explosive-laden sea drones struck the vessel, according to Libyan military officials who spoke to The Associated Press.

UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC

Fire burns after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at Benghazi port in Libya. (Reuters)

At least four other drones were intercepted and destroyed, the officials said.

Satellite images showed most of the warship capsized and submerged, with only its bow remaining above water. Smoke could be seen rising from the ship's superstructure, and debris was scattered along the pier.

Ten people, including Russian and Libyan nationals, suffered minor injuries in the attack and were receiving treatment in Benghazi, medical sources told Reuters.

The warship had stopped at the port to refuel and resupply while returning to Russia under a maritime cooperation agreement with Libya's eastern-based government, officials said in a statement.

Libyan military officials said an initial investigation indicated that Ukrainian sea drones had been launched from a base in western Libya, according to The AP.

UKRAINE STRIKES DEEP INTO RUSSIA’S ARCTIC GAS HEARTLAND AS TRUMP PUSHES PUTIN TOWARD PEACE

The port of Benghazi after an explosion aboard a Russian ship docked at the Benghazi naval base. (Vantor/Handout via REUTERS)

Hours after the warship was struck, a Maltese-flagged commercial ship was also hit by a sea drone off Benghazi, two Libyan military sources told Reuters.

Libyan naval forces rescued the commercial ship's crew, while health officials reported that some crew members sustained minor injuries and were in stable condition.

Libyan naval and air forces also intercepted more than 20 drone boats off Benghazi on Sunday evening, the military sources told Reuters.

The attacks prompted Libya's eastern-based government to seek an international investigation.

Prime Minister Osama Hamad said his government had submitted a formal request to the United Nations General Assembly and Security Council to investigate the attacks, including suspicions that the drones were launched from western Libya.

RUSSIA DEPLOYS NORTH KOREAN MISSILE UNIT TO UKRAINE; MOSCOW-PYONGYANG AXIS DEEPENS: REPORT

A Russian corvette before and after the explosion in Benghazi, with Libya's eastern-based government saying the explosion was caused by a suspected drone attack. (VANTOR/ Reuters)

Hamad also called for an investigation into the possible presence of Ukrainian military experts in Libya and requested an explanation from Kyiv about their activities.

The eastern government insisted that Libya was not a party to the war between Russia and Ukraine and condemned attempts to use its territory to settle foreign conflicts.

"The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts," the government said.

Benghazi is controlled by forces loyal to Gen. Khalifa Haftar, whose self-styled Libyan National Army dominates eastern and southern Libya and maintains close ties with Russia.

Libya has been divided since the 2011 NATO-backed uprising that toppled longtime dictator Moammar Gadhafi.

UKRAINE UNLEASHES MORE THAN 400 DRONES NEAR MOSCOW IN ONE OF WAR'S BIGGEST ATTACKS

Putin is testing the boundaries of NATO with aircraft incursions, allied states say. (Ramil Sitdikov/Pool/Reuters)

A U. N. recognized government operates from Tripoli, while a rival administration controls much of the east.

The suspected attacks also come as Ukraine has expanded its campaign against Russian naval assets beyond the Black Sea. In December 2025, Ukraine said it struck a Russian-linked oil tanker with aerial drones in the Mediterranean Sea.

In March 2026, Russia accused Ukraine of attacking a Russian liquefied natural gas tanker with naval drones launched from the Libyan coast.

Libyan officials previously told the AP that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating from military facilities in western Libya, including an air base in Misrata and sites in Tripoli and Zawiya.

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Ukrainian forces have used explosive-laden sea drones and missiles to strike Russian warships and naval installations, primarily in the Black Sea.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Poland says Russia tried to assassinate Ukrainian rapper twice
articles.excerpt: Polish authorities have said Russian intelligence services tried to kill a Ukrainian-American rapper visiting the country in August, after Copenhagen said Moscow had allegedly targeted the same man on...
articles.body_text:
Polish authorities have said Russian intelligence services tried to kill a Ukrainian-American rapper visiting the country in August, after Copenhagen said Moscow had allegedly targeted the same man on Danish soil.

The alleged assassination plan targeted Albert Vasiliev, a rapper who performs under the name Kyivstoner and holds Ukrainian and US citizenship, according to Danish media.

Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Maciej Wewior confirmed the alleged plot to kill Vasiliev in Poland to The Associated Press news agency on Sunday.

On Friday, in response to Denmark’s statement about the alleged assassination plan, Poland’s Foreign Ministry had written, “It is the second assassination attempt against the same person. The first one was foiled on the Polish territory in August 2026.”

It also said that a Russian national had been arrested.

Polish authorities detained the suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Moscow, on August 7.

Denmark announced the expulsion of a Russian diplomat on Friday after it accused Moscow intelligence of plotting the assassination during a concert in a Copenhagen suburb in September.

Denmark’s intelligence agency, PET, said on the same day that it suspected Russia of planning the assassination with the help of a banned Danish gang.

Two Danish men appeared ⁠in court near Copenhagen on Friday, charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and attempted murder.

Russia dismissed the allegations through its embassy in Copenhagen, saying they were unsubstantiated.

Previously, on August 13, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed that a plot to kill a Ukrainian-American in Warsaw was thwarted. He did not disclose Vasiliev’s name at the time but said the target “was uncomfortable” for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s government.

Vasiliev has expressed his support for Ukraine amid Russia’s ongoing war on the country and was performing across Europe this year before his concerts were cancelled for security reasons.

Russia’s domestic security service, the FSB, accused Vasiliev of being involved in supplying drones for an alleged Ukrainian attack on a defence enterprise in the Moscow region. It said he was “acting under the patronage” of Ukraine’s internal security service, the SBU.

Danish broadcaster DR reported that Vasiliev denied the FSB accusations.

Danish Minister for Foreign Affairs Lars Lokke Rasmussen told reporters on Friday that Denmark was also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russians.

Poland’s Foreign Ministry said it backed the move.

“Poland supports measures Denmark suggested to limit the access and freedom of travel of Russian nationals on the EU territory,” it said on X.

Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title: Purdue professor, 2 daughters killed in apparent murder-suicide after daughter’s terrifying 911 call
articles.excerpt:
Julie Tkach, a Purdue University professor, and her daughters, ages 16 and 17, were found dead alongside the father in their Indiana home.

This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is ...
articles.body_text:
Julie Tkach, a Purdue University professor, and her daughters, ages 16 and 17, were found dead alongside the father in their Indiana home.

This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

A Purdue University professor and her two teenage daughters were killed in an apparent murder-suicide last week after the father reportedly opened fire on his family before turning the gun on himself, according to Indiana authorities.

Preliminary autopsy results identified the mother as Julie Tkach, 53, of West Lafayette, who died from multiple gunshot wounds, with her death ruled a homicide, the Tippecanoe County Coroner’s Office said Friday. Julie was a clinical assistant professor in Purdue University's Department of Hospitality and Tourism Management, according to her LinkedIn profile.

The father, Thomas Tkach, 51, died by suicide from a gunshot wound to the head, officials said. He was employed by the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office as a courthouse security officer after previously serving as a jail deputy, according to local outlet Star City News., according to local outlet Star City News.

KANSAS CONVICTED FELON, SEX OFFENDER ALLEGEDLY KILLS FELLOW FAMILY MEMBERS BEFORE TAKING HIS OWN LIFE: POLICE

Julie and Thomas Tkach and their daughters, Katharyn and Lauren, pose for an undated photo in Indiana. (Tom Tkach/Facebook)

Their daughter, Katharyn, 17, died from multiple gunshot wounds to the head, while their other daughter, Lauren, 16, died from multiple gunshot wounds, the coroner's office said.

West Lafayette Police said the family members were found inside their West Lafayette-area home Wednesday evening, Nov. 18, after officers responded to a 911 call shortly after 8:30 p.m. The coroner's office was subsequently notified of multiple deaths at roughly 1:50 a.m. Thursday.

According to emergency dispatch audio obtained by Star City News, authorities received a separate concerning call shortly before the bodies were discovered. A dispatcher described receiving a call from one of the daughters.

"She advised that her father had a gun and was threatening to shoot the family. I heard multiple gunshots go off and the line is now silent," the recording said.

TWO TEEN SUSPECTS HELD AFTER 5 FAMILY MEMBERS KILLED IN 'TARGETED MASS SHOOTING'

Julie Tkach and her daughters, Katharyn, 17, and Lauren, 16, were killed in an apparent murder-suicide at their West Lafayette, Indiana, home. (Julie Tkach/Facebook)

While officials have not disclosed a motive behind the killings, the coroner’s office urged anyone struggling with mental health challenges to seek help through available resources. Residents can call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

Indiana State Police is leading the investigation because Thomas Tkach was employed by the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office.

The West Lafayette Police Department described the incident as a "terrible night" that deeply affected its personnel, as well as those at the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office, which also responded to the scene.

"Many people on my team and other teams have had a very difficult time with the incident that took place on Wednesday night," the sheriff’s office said.

"The things seen and heard the other night will be remembered for the rest of their lives," the office added.

DISPATCH AUDIO RELEASED IN MICHIGAN FAMILY MURDER-SUICIDE AS TROUBLED FAMILY'S SECRETS EMERGE

Julie Tkach, a Purdue University professor, and her husband, Thomas Tkach, a courthouse security officer, were found dead in their West Lafayette, Indiana, home last week. (Julie Tkach/Facebook)

According to LinkedIn, Julie had spent more than 20 years teaching and mentoring students in the hospitality industry. Prior to Purdue, she worked at South Dakota State University for eight years as a lecturer and instructor.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Purdue offered its condolences and said it would provide support to those affected.

"We are saddened by this tragedy and the death of Julie and her family. We offer our condolences and support to her colleagues, peers, students and all who are affected," the university said.

"The Tippecanoe County Coroner’s Office extends its deepest condolences to all who have been impacted by this tragedy. These deaths have affected many people across our community, including friends, neighbors, and others who knew the family," the office said.

The emergency response required a multi-agency effort involving the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office, West Lafayette Police Department, Indiana State Police, emergency medical services, fire crews and the coroner's office, according to West Lafayette police.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Tippecanoe County Sheriff's Office and Purdue University for more information.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital
