articles.title: ‘Music was our teacher’: the sound system pioneers reviving the scene in Manchester and beyond
articles.excerpt:
Manchester-based Megatone Sound Foundation and Baron Turbo Charge have rejuvenated the culture to offer a sense of belonging and empowerment

For a generation of young Black Mancunians, some of the hi...
articles.body_text:
Manchester-based Megatone Sound Foundation and Baron Turbo Charge have rejuvenated the culture to offer a sense of belonging and empowerment

For a generation of young Black Mancunians, some of the history lessons that mattered most were not taught in classrooms, but through towering stacks of amps and speakers, turntables and Jamaican records.

“We didn’t know where we fit in. We didn’t know our history. Our parents were busy working two or three jobs,” says Errol “Barzy” Beaumont, a founder member of Baron Turbo Charge, Manchester’s long-running reggae sound system. “It was the records – Burning Spear, Bob Marley, Culture, that were telling us about our culture, which wasn’t on the school curriculum. For us, the sound system was not just entertainment – it was an education.”

More than 50 years since the sons and daughters of Windrush-generation pioneers adapted their parents’ music, DJing culture and technology to forge a Black British youth movement, Manchester’s sound system scene is enjoying a revival.

Keithly Brandy, an archivist of Manchester’s postwar Black history, has been working with museums and universities to preserve the flyers and paperwork that documented the scene in the 1970s and 80s and Winston Jones, the founder of Trafford Bar Studios, has been producing a podcast series about it.

It has come full circle. Manchester once looked to Jamaica for inspiration, but in recent years the Megatone Sound Foundation has set up and supported sound systems across the Black diaspora, from Kingston to the Gambia and Ethiopia, and Baron Turbo Charge are keeping reggae alive in the heart of Moss Side.

And, just as sound systems provided a lifeline for young Black people with few places to express themselves in postwar Britain, half a century later they are once again offering a sense of belonging and community to those same people, now in their 60s.

For Marcus, of Megatone Sound Foundation, the journey began in his parents’ front room in Old Trafford in 1976, when he was nine years old. Without his mother’s knowledge, he dismantled the family’s wooden stereogram, removing the turntable, speakers and valve amplifier before reassembling them in homemade cabinets upstairs.

“I started to build a little system called Conqueror. It was just like a house thing,” he says. “And then from there, it grew.”

Back then the emergent scene was concentrated in the house parties, community functions and youth clubs of Manchester neighbourhoods such as Hulme, Moss Side and Old Trafford.

The records varied depending on the venue and the company. Bob and Marcia’s anthem, Young, Gifted and Black, was a staple record parents approved of. But, away from the more conservative older generation, youth clubs such as Aquarius, Proctor’s, Birley and the Hideaway rocked to the sounds of Dillinger and Johnny Clarke. In what could be a male-dominated scene, 1980s sounds such as Kilowatt drew a female following with lovers rock.

No one could have imagined that ephemera from Manchester’s scene – such as a contract from the broadcaster David Rodigan’s appearance at the PSV club, the reggae venue founded by the city’s Black bus drivers – would one day be displayed in a museum. That contract – which features in the V&A East’s The Music is Black: A British Story exhibition in London – is among items preserved for decades by Brandy.

Back in 1976, Brandy set up his own sound system, Tyban Sounds, with two friends, “Big” Trevor Bell and “Young” Trevor Bell, inspired by the older generation of Manchester soundmen, including Lord Cass, Bugga Levi, Count Leroy, Count Sam, Rocket and Angel Hi-Fi, who had brought the culture with them from the Caribbean. “You would see these people at weddings and christenings – and be in awe of them,” Brandy says.

Brandy still recalls the excitement of bringing London’s Conqueror sound system to Manchester Carnival and the after-party at Abasindi’s women’s co-operative – having persuaded his mother, the carnival pioneer Locita Brandy, to give the young people a chance.

The sound system – a competitive collective of DJs, MCs, sound engineers, crew and their mobile, custom-built, bass-heavy audio set-up – was invented in 1940s Jamaica, with the original sounds playing American R&B and mento music in Kingston.

In the US, the culture would shape hip-hop, after the Kingston-born DJ Kool Herc set up a sound system in the Bronx, while in the UK, sound system culture evolved through time, bringing everything from roots reggae and lovers rock to house, garage and jungle records to the mainstream.

Despite that winding journey – shaping artists including Soul II Soul, Maxi Priest and Massive Attack along the way – reggae is the essence of the culture.

“Back then the music was like a newspaper,” Jones says of 70s reggae. “It was teaching us about history, it was teaching us about Marcus Garvey, about Nelson Mandela. It was teaching us that Africa was our home – the music was our teacher.”

At the heart of Trafford Bar Studios, the creative space Jones founded and funded with compensation from his experiences as part of the Windrush scandal, young people can learn skills such as DJing, photography, videography and podcasting without charge. It echoes the ethos of the sound system movement: collective and individual empowerment through music and creativity.

“It’s about resilience,” Jones says. “A kid leaves school and believes he can’t do anything, but we give you hope when you come in here.”

Jones funded the Pioneers of Manchester’s Soundsystem era podcast to ensure voices from a significant chapter in Manchester’s Black cultural history are preserved for posterity. “All these soundmen, everybody have a story to tell,” he said.

The Baron Turbo Charge founder Errol Beaumont set out into the scene with his friends Junior Wilson and the late Melvyn “Wizzydan” Joseph as teenagers in the mid-70s, when Black people faced an unofficial societal colour bar.

The trio saved £10 each to buy a secondhand valve guitar amplifier to add to the records, speakers and old turntable they already had.

On the day of the dance, realising their speakers had no cabinets, they nailed together boxes using timber from a building site and hauled the gear up the staircase of flats on Bonsall Street, on the edge of Manchester’s long-demolished, brutalist Hulme Crescents estate.

“We hadn’t tested the system or anything. The party was on the fourth floor, we built it on the first, and by the time we got to the second floor, it fell apart,” Beaumont laughs. From that moment on, the boys decided to “get serious”.

Awareness that his generation was facing a different kind of exclusion motivated Beaumont, now 67, to return to playing dances after a decades-long hiatus.

“There’s nothing really for my generation now, as entertainment,” he says. “That was one of the reasons we brought the sound back out – because there’s a lot of people like ourselves who still want to put on their nice clothes and go out, just like we did back in the day.”

This makes the West Indian Sports and Social Centre – the historic Moss Side community hub – a key venue, one of the few places where large sound systems can still recreate the old atmosphere.

Meanwhile, as well as establishing sounds in Africa and the Caribbean, fundraising for charitable causes, and organising events celebrating community elders, the Megatone Sound Foundation is feted by audiences in France, Greece, Hungary and Poland.

“What makes Manchester sounds special is that Manchester people have this warm demeanour, and a multicultural attitude to things,” Jones says. “If you go back to the days of [Moss Side nightclubs] the Nile and the Reno, white people, Black people, everybody was rubbing shoulders. It’s a working-class attitude, it’s a solidarity.”

articles.title: Race to lead Senate Democrats the latest battlefield in party’s tussle over Israel
articles.excerpt:
Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer represent conflicting visions on issue that has become ‘litmus test’ for Democratic voters

The race to lead the Democratic Party’s incoming Senate majority has beco...
articles.body_text:
Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer represent conflicting visions on issue that has become ‘litmus test’ for Democratic voters

The race to lead the Democratic Party’s incoming Senate majority has become the latest battlefield between two conflicting visions for how the US should relate to Israel – a once unquestioned ally whose collapsing standing among the US public has become a defining feature of American politics.

Chuck Schumer, the veteran New York Senator and current Democratic minority leader, is one of Israel’s most reliable supporters in Congress. As he views it, according to an interview he gave last year, his “job” is to “keep the left pro-Israel”.

On the other side is Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland senator and challenger to Schumer for Senate leadership, who in recent years emerged as a steadfast advocate for Palestinian rights in the Senate. He supports sanctions, voted to block sales of weapons to Israel, and advocates for the families of US citizens killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers, as well as against the detention of Palestinian children by the Israeli military.

The two represent two opposing sides of the Democratic party’s approach to Israel at a time when a majority of Democrats hold unfavorable views of it. Van Hollen has repeatedly visited the occupied West Bank. In January 2024 he traveled with Oregon’s senator Jeff Merkley to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and Gaza, where they denounced Israel’s restrictions on humanitarian aid.

While he has in recent years criticized Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and called him a “major obstacle” to peace, Schumer has been an unflinching supporter of Israel throughout his political career, repeatedly referring to himself as “Shomer Yisrael” or “guardian of Israel”. Earlier this year, he said he views it as part of his job to fight for “all the aid that Israel needs”.

He has opposed the Iran nuclear deal, the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement, and a UN resolution affirming that Israeli settlements in occupied territory are illegal, and supported the US Embassy move to Jerusalem. During the war in Gaza, he has repeatedly voted against measures seeking to restrict military aid and weapons sales to Israel. He did, however, vote in favor of a failed resolution that would have required the state department to produce a report on Israeli human rights abuses in the West Bank, and has supported efforts to impose sanctions on individual settlers.

Schumer’s office did not respond to a request for comment. In a statement, Van Hollen’s office said that “the Israeli government has become increasingly hardline in its approach, diminishing the possibility of a two-state solution, including through its indiscriminate attacks on Gaza and its complicity in the escalating violence in the West Bank”.

“The senator has urged the United States to use its leverage to push the government of Israel to comply with US policy and law.”

While the Senate leader has ample discretion to set the party’s legislative priorities and move bills to the floor for votes, he would not necessarily be able to influence the outcome of specific votes – or foreign policy – especially for the remainder of Trump’s term.

Van Hollen has stressed that his challenge to Schumer is about delivering the “change from the status quo” that drove historic numbers of US voters to elect Democrats earlier this month. He has suggested he has the votes of 15 colleagues, but so far, only five have publicly pledged to back him including Michigan’s newly elected Abdul El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel, Merkley, Vermont’s Bernie Sanders, Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan and Michigan’s Elissa Slotkin. Several others have criticized Schumer and called for change but not committed to a vote.

While he is clearly the underdog in the race, Van Hollen insists he has a “path” to win. Whether or not he succeeds in his bid to oust Schumer, the race has significantly raised his national profile as an advocate for Palestinian rights.

Outside the Senate, advocacy groups’ endorsements are largely following divides on Israel. Bend the Arc, a progressive Jewish group, noted that “the midterm elections proved that a majority of Americans are hungry for change and American Jews are no exception”. The Institute for Middle Eastern Understanding’s Policy Project cited Schumer’s record as the only current Democratic senator to vote against the Iran nuclear deal as “paving the way” for the current war in Iran.

“Senator Van Hollen is committed to rights-respecting policy and understands that accountability is necessary to comprehensively challenge impunity,” said Brad Parker, associate director of policy at the Center for Constitutional Rights.

“The recent electoral lesson over the past year is that incumbents who ignore the overwhelming and shifting electorate demands to end US complicity in Israeli crimes operate at their own peril.”

Last week, dozens of protesters with the Sunrise Movement, a youth climate organization, were arrested outside Schumer’s Washington office, where they called on the senator to “step up or step aside”.

But Schumer – a titan of the party and the highest-ranking Jewish elected official in US history – has much of the political establishment behind him. He also has the backing of major pro-Israel groups.

“Jewish Americans have been a critical component of a winning Democratic coalition, including in the 2026 midterms,” said Halie Soifer, the Jewish Democratic Council of America’s CEO, which endorsed him. “We’re confident that he’ll lead Democrats to deliver for the American people in a way that is consistent with the values of the Jewish community in the 120th Congress.”

On election night, before Van Hollen announced his challenge, Aipac also issued a statement congratulating Schumer and incoming House speaker Hakeem Jeffries for their caucuses’ wins.

Despite significant shifts in rhetoric, Democratic officials have moved more slowly than their base. Earlier this year, 103 House Democrats voted to slash military aid to Israel – an unprecedented rebuke, but still less than half the party’s caucus (only one Republican voted in favor). The Senate has been even more cautious.

While he has tried to focus on other issues since announcing his challenge, Van Hollen did reference his differences with Schumer on Israel – most notably when he accused him of having “joined with Aipac and crypto” to try to defeat Michigan’s El-Sayed. Schumer favored El-Sayed’s Aipac-backed opponent, Haley Stevens, during the primary, but he supported El-Sayed in the November general election. In an interview on Fox News on Sunday, Van Hollen spoke about growing settler violence in the West Bank, and the Israeli’s government complicity in it. “I don’t think American taxpayer dollars should be going to that purpose,” he said.

“When I first spoke out about Gaza and what I thought – the bad conduct in Gaza – I was a pretty lonely voice, frankly,” Van Hollen also said in an interview last year.

When he first ran for Senate a decade ago, Van Hollen was backed by some Aipac-aligned donors and regularly voted with most centrist Democrats on matters relating to Israel. But he has also had a longstanding interest in foreign policy, human rights, and the Middle East, and in his decade in the Senate he has frequently invoked the “Leahy law”, which demands accountability for abuses by US-supported foreign militaries – including Israel’s.

His criticism of Israel has grown more forceful over time. Following the 2022 West Bank killing of the Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, by an Israeli sniper, Van Hollen repeatedly met with her family and led the congressional response to the killing, aggressively pressing the Biden administration for accountability. (To this day, there has been none, and despite Van Hollen’s repeated efforts, an official report on Abu Akleh’s killing remains classified). Van Hollen’s office said that Abu Akleh’s killing “underscored for him the impunity with which the Israeli government was increasingly acting with regard to the West Bank”.

In recent years, he has also championed the families of other US citizens killed by settlers and soldiers – including Rachel Corrie, Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, and Sayfollah Musallet. He also met with Mahmoud Khalil, the Columbia University student that has become the face of the Trump administration’s crackdown on pro-Palestinian speech, shortly after Khalil was released from ICE detention. (When he was arrested, by contrast, Schumer issued a statement saying that he “abhor[s]” Khalil’s views, though he added that if the Trump administration could not prove Khalil had committed a crime, his speech was protected by the US constitution.)

The contest is the latest proxy war over the future of the US-Israel relationship. It played an outsized role in mayoral elections in New York and Los Angeles, and defined heated Democratic primaries. It is dividing Republicans, and turning groups like Aipac into a liability for candidates.

Kidus Girma, campaign director for the Sunrise Movement, told the Guardian that while the speaker majority vote was about whether the Senate would respond to voters’ calls for change from tackling climate action to getting money out of politics, support for Palestine had become “a litmus test issue for Democratic voters”.

articles.title: Swift assurances from officials after wave of nationwide outages raises questions, expert says
articles.excerpt: As federal officials and major institutions called a string of critical infrastructure disruptions isolated technical glitches, a longtime security veteran warns that hasty assurances can mask stealth...
articles.body_text:
As federal officials and major institutions called a string of critical infrastructure disruptions isolated technical glitches, a longtime security veteran warns that hasty assurances can mask stealth intrusions, and give adversaries room to linger undetected.

Amid a slew of high-profile disruptions that struck major pillars of American life over the past week, including a nationwide ground stop that halted air travel, banking outages at JPMorgan Chase and other lenders, and a service disruption at Microsoft, officials were quick to reassure the public that nothing nefarious was behind the failures.

During the ground stop, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the homeland and the banking system remained secure, insisting that the disruptions showed no signs of a cyberattack or malicious activity.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton similarly stated that officials saw no evidence of a coordinated or state-sponsored attack, pointing instead to routine patching and system upgrades.

DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE'

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testified Wednesday to reiterate intelligence shows the recent outages are neither related nor a result of a 'state-sponsored' attack. (Brendan Smialowski / AFP)

"Based on what we know today … these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes," Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday. "They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack."

Major companies, including Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase, also attributed the disruptions to internal technical issues or software bugs rather than malicious intrusions.

US INFRASTRUCTURE CRUMBLES AS ADVERSARIES POWER UP – LEAVING AMERICANS DANGEROUSLY EXPOSED: CYBER EXPERT

To Danny Cooper, CEO of critical infrastructure security firm SMET, the speed with which those assurances were issued poses a problem.

"A blanket statement like 'there's no malicious activity associated with any of the outages' is almost impossible from a probability perspective," Cooper told Fox News Digital.

THE OUTAGES AMERICA HAS SUFFERED WEREN'T AN ATTACK, BUT THE NEXT FAILURE COULD BE

A Chase ATM is pictured outside the bank as technology disruptions impact banking services. (Ava Palschakov for Fox News Digital)

Public anxiety tends to spike around a single question in the aftermath of a major disruption: Was it a coincidence or an attack? Public skepticism is understandable given how many critical systems stumbled within a five-to-six-day window, Cooper said.

"How plausible is it that all these pillars or whatever all suffered major independent technical failures within a five- or six-day window?" Cooper asked. "I think highly improbable. And I understand why the American public is calling this into question and deeply empathize with that. The pattern recognition is there."

DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK

Even when officials point to routine maintenance or aging hardware, Cooper argued that ruling out foul play too quickly skips investigative steps that take time to execute properly, which could potentially undermine efforts to fix vulnerabilities and prevent future incidents.

A person looks at a departures board showing delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on Nov. 13, in New York City. The Federal Aviation Administration had ordered a nationwide ground stop on all departing flights, one of several critical infrastructure that experienced outages or issues last week, raising questions about the cause of the stoppages. (Getty Images)

"If a company or the government is making a statement that is as bold as 'we are certain there is no malicious activity here' without having the time to actually do an appropriate investigation, in the case of this sort of cyber domain, some cyber forensics and a full audit of what transpired, that's not quite how it works," she said.

PERPETUAL PARALYSIS: WHY EVERYTHING IS GRINDING TO A HALT

"On the physical side, being able to fully interrogate what has happened in the environment, who was there, and so on about what is happening in the periphery and what led up to that moment in time, those things take time."

An instant "nothing to see here" message can also deepen public suspicion, Cooper said, particularly when multiple institutions and agencies echo that conclusion before audits can be completed.

JOIN THE CHAT: RECENT TECH OUTAGES LOOM OVER MULLIN TESTIMONY ON WORLDWIDE THREATS

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) also sounded the alarm over conflicting statements coming from the Trump administration.

A general view of Charlotte Douglas International Airport in Charlotte, North Carolina, United States, on November 13, 2026, as passengers face delays and strandings after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for all flights. (Peter Zay/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"The administration has repeatedly offered conflicting statements about the causes of the outages," DNC Deputy Communications Director Kendall Witmer said in a statement. "Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that SI – Trump’s preferred name for Artificial Intelligence (AI) – is responsible for the multiple outages that have occurred in recent days, according to a "very smart" tech guy he talked to. Then, yesterday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio contradicted Mullin and would not attribute the outages to AI."

MICROSOFT’S MASSIVE OUTAGE OFFERS A LESSON IN HOW TO BRING THE WORLD BACK ONLINE

Much of the official explanation surrounding the November disruptions centered on software updates and system upgrades. Organizations frequently schedule maintenance and can experience downtime when rolling out changes at scale, especially if teams move too quickly, Cooper noted.

However, those windows are what sophisticated adversaries watch closely, she warned.

"If companies are disproportionately moving to execute these sorts of upgrades en masse, then yes, it's possible that you would have a higher number of downtime or outages," she said.

"But it's also quite possible that, particularly given the sophistication of cyber adversaries, whether it's hackers, whether it's non-state entities, whether it's nation-state entities, it's also possible that they are using those software updates or upgrades or patches and in those moments actually injecting malware and exploits and so on."

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: DEPROGRAMMED: He lived as a woman for six years, hit ‘rock bottom’ and found Jesus. Then he detransitioned.
articles.excerpt: Diego Arellan moved to America from Peru as a teenager, and encountered gender ideology he’d never been exposed to that led him into "rock bottom" of a life living as a woman — until an encounter with...
articles.body_text:
Diego Arellan moved to America from Peru as a teenager, and encountered gender ideology he’d never been exposed to that led him into "rock bottom" of a life living as a woman — until an encounter with Jesus changed everything.

This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 800-273-TALK (8255).

Diego Arellan said he had never encountered transgender ideology until he moved to the United States from Peru as a teenager. He said people later encouraged him to transition because of the way he behaved. Ultimately, he lived as a transgender woman for six years before becoming a Christian and detransitioning.

"I started hanging out with a lot of people that were living that lifestyle and that also recommended me to live that lifestyle because [of] the way I acted," Arellan told Fox News Digital.

"I found that out of like this clinic who offer that pretty much transitioning to become your opposite gender. And so, through that process … in my mind it was like, 'I definitely have to do this because this is the right path. Everything that I'm seeing out there, like in social media, or anywhere I go I see, like this is a way you have to go in order for you to feel fulfilled, at least because I always struggle with my identity,'" he continued.

PRISHA MOSLEY: AS A DETRANSITIONER AND MOM, I KNOW WHAT GENDER IDEOLOGY STOLE FROM ME

Diego Arellan while living as a transgender woman in Miami. (Diego Arellan)

"I transitioned when I was 18 and a lot of things happened during that season just because I was very immature in that season … I went through a lot [of] gender dysphoria," Arellan said.

He went on to describe what he said were side effects of the hormone pills he took, saying his body was reacting to something that was "not natural."

"[I had] a lot of like, pain on my body and just changes, but I still went through it because I really thought that this was gonna be the path that was gonna make me happy … There was a lot of rejection as well from the people I start[ed] dating … I was lying not only to me, but I was lying to the people out there who thought they were dating any other woman, but in reality, [I] was not," he continued.

WOMAN WHO LIVED AS MAN SAYS SHE GRIEVED ‘UNWANTED BODY PARTS’ AFTER TRANSITION

Diego Arellan lived as a transgender woman for six years before finding Jesus at his lowest point, detransitioning to his biological gender after becoming a Christian. (Diego Arellan)

"There was a lot of confusion, a lot of stress, a lot like just also wanting to kill myself at one point because of all these things I was building and thinking that this was the right path again," Arellan added.

Arellan said he had breast augmentation surgery, a Brazilian butt lift and Botox injections in different areas of his face.

"It was turning into an addiction because it was never enough. Everything I see on my face … I started to hate it because I just kept looking at myself and I look[ed] at the mirror and I look[ed like] I'm a man just having long hair," he said.

"I achieved everything I wanted [and] I still felt so empty and that's where a lot of things changed," Arellan said.

WOMAN WHO UNDERWENT DOUBLE MASTECTOMY AT 14 TELLS SURGEON, 'YOU STOLE MY GIRLHOOD'

Diego Arellan now runs an online Christian clothing store called "D-King Merch."  (Diego Arellan)

According to a research paper by Eric Kaufmann, published on the Social Science Research Network (SSRN), the share of surveyed university students identifying as transgender fell from nearly 7% in 2023 to under 4% in later survey data. The paper also reported a decline of approximately 10 percentage points in the share identifying as non-heterosexual.

Arellan discussed his move to Miami, where he dated "a sugar daddy" and experienced "crazy" things that opened his heart to his sister’s testimony of her experience with Jesus Christ.

"I was [at] rock bottom, I hated myself. I had a lot of money. I did a lot [of] things that were really bad. But my sister — she shared with me her testimony of how she encountered Jesus — and that was it," he said.

Arellan, who now runs an online shop called "D-King merch" selling Christian clothing, offered advice to people reconsidering their gender transitions.

"Following Jesus is not easy. It can be narrow, it can be hard, but it's so worth it," he said.

Alba Cuebas-Fantauzzi is an Associate Producer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories
articles.excerpt:
Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes

Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication fo...
articles.body_text:
Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes

Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.

In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.

What happened during the escape from Myanmar – a journey through forests and over hills and rivers while being battered by monsoon rains – was a key part of the ruling made this week in The Hague that Myanmar had carried out a genocide against the Rohingya.

The international court of justice (ICJ) said it was not enough to say they had faced ethnic cleansing when soldiers had also killed those trying to escape – Myanmar was trying to destroy the group as a people.

Stories of that violence in 2017, of organised mass killing, sexual attacks and the complete destruction of their villages, came with the refugees who arrived in neighbouring Bangladesh, eventually numbering more than 700,000 and settling in what has become the world’s largest refugee camp.

For months, they would arrive from places such as Tula Toli, where thousands were rounded up, killed and buried in mass graves. In other villages, men were captured and killed by the security forces.

Many survivors had escaped an attack on their own village, only to watch their relatives being killed in the villages where they had sought safety.

Almost a decade later, the majority of Rohingya who arrived in 2017 remain in the refugee camps, joining those who had already been there since the early 1990s, having escaped previous military operations and ever-increasing persecution.

The ICJ ruling has come at a particularly harsh time for Rohingya refugees, in a year in which hundreds have died at sea trying to escape the refugee camps, and in which countries such as Malaysia and India have spoken about returning the Rohingya to Myanmar.

Rohingya campaigners are hoping that this ruling will put an end to that.

Rohingya refugees still live in fragile shelters made of bamboo and tarpaulin sheets. They are denied the right to leave the camps, to work or to seek education.

Below are some of the stories from Rohingya who arrived in Bangladesh in 2017, having escaped Tula Toli and the surrounding area.

Sitting in the background, almost unnoticed as Momtaz Begum recollected how Myanmar forces had killed her husband and children and then raped her in front of her lone surviving child, was a woman who seemed to know every word of the story.

It was not because she had heard it before. Dildar Begum had experienced exactly the same violence as her sister had, in their village, Tula Toli.

In fact, they had for months believed each other dead until they discovered that they had both made it to Bangladesh and lived in different parts of the camp.

Each had only one surviving daughter, both of whom had similar scars along the back of their heads.

Twice previously Anwara Begum had lived as a refugee in Bangladesh. Once as a child in 1978 and then again in the early 1990s, as a young mother who lost her son to a respiratory disease during a rainy season spent in a flimsy tent.

When she was forced to return to Myanmar, though the persecution she fled there had not stopped, Anwara swore to herself that she would never become a refugee again.

She broke that oath when she saw the river by her village filled with bodies floating from Tula Toli.

Her husband first pulled from the river as many bodies as he could to bury and then they gathered some belongings and headed westwards to the River Naf – the border with Bangladesh.

To cross, she handed over all the gold she owned, equal to US $200 (£150), to a Bangladeshi boatman.

Elderly people were not spared the Myanmar military’s attacks. Like so many others, Nur Alam had to be carried on the shoulders of his children on his journey to Bangladesh.

His 10-year-old grandson, Mamoon, held his hand. Once in the camp, they stuck to each other.

Alam’s arrival in Bangladesh was his fourth time being a refugee there. He was first expelled from Myanmar – known as Burma until 1989 – during military operations in the 1950s when Bangladesh was not yet an independent country.

articles.title: Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer Chad Smith to join Wu-Tang Clan for Lions' Thanksgiving halftime show
articles.excerpt: Danny Parkins makes his picks for Week 11, including the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Denver Broncos, and Chicago Bears. Plus, Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if the NFC North is the best ...
articles.body_text:
Danny Parkins makes his picks for Week 11, including the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Denver Broncos, and Chicago Bears. Plus, Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if the NFC North is the best division ever, and if the Los Angeles Rams are in trouble without Puka Nacua.

This Thanksgiving, NFL fans will once again have the opportunity to enjoy three games spread across the afternoon and evening.

The Detroit Lions will open the day with their traditional early afternoon matchup, hosting the Chicago Bears. The Cowboys will follow with their long-running home game in the late-afternoon window on Fox. The third game of the day will be played at the new Highmark Stadium, where the Buffalo Bills will host the Kansas City Chiefs.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductees Wu-Tang Clan will headline the Lions-Bears halftime show.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The legendary hip-hop group will be joined by Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer Chad Smith.

Chad Smith, drummer of Red Hot Chili Peppers, performs during the first day of Lollapalooza Buenos Aires 2018 at Hipodromo de San Isidro on March 16, 2018, in Buenos Aires, Argentina. (Santiago Bluguermann/Getty Images)

The Lions announced Smith’s special guest appearance Friday.

Detroit rapper Eminem and his manager, Paul Rosenberg, serves as the executive producers of the Lions’ Thanksgiving Day halftime show.

Friday’s announcement marked the second year of their three-year deal to oversee the event. Last year’s performance featured Jack White and a surprise appearance by Eminem.

A general view of Ford Field during a game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions on Dec. 31, 2017, in Detroit, Michigan. (Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

BUFFALO BILLS TAP HOMETOWN HEROES GOO GOO DOLLS FOR THANKSGIVING NIGHT HALFTIME CONCERT

The Lions have been an NFL Thanksgiving Day staple nearly every season since 1934.

Drummer Chad Smith of the Red Hot Chili Peppers performs live on stage at Palau Sant Jordi in Barcelona, Spain, on Dec. 15, 2011. (David Ramos/Getty Images)

Country music artist Miranda Lambert is scheduled to put on a show at the Cowboys-Eagles matchup later that afternoon.

Last month, the Bills announced the Goo Goo Dolls will perform during halftime of their Thanksgiving night game on Nov. 26. The rock band was originally formed in Buffalo.

"The Goo Goo Dolls halftime performance will take place on the Bills Legends Deck, creating a unique concert experience that can be seen throughout the stadium," the Bills said in a statement. "Fans will also receive PixMob light-up bracelets at their seats, transforming the crowd into an interactive part of the show with synchronized lighting effects throughout Highmark Stadium."

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: ‘A new record for entertainment’: Grand Theft Auto VI sales hit $3.8bn on first day of release, developer says
articles.excerpt:
The announcement from Rockstar Games would mean GTA VI has already earned more than the entire box office run of the highest-grossing film of all time

Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail ...
articles.body_text:
The announcement from Rockstar Games would mean GTA VI has already earned more than the entire box office run of the highest-grossing film of all time

Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games has announced, calling it the biggest launch for any entertainment product in history.

The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game launched. Rockstar said also it had sold 32.5m units of the game on prerelease, setting a record across platforms.

“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a statement.

The company said the sales set “a new record for entertainment across any medium … becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.”

The figure is nearly five times the roughly $800m that predecessor Grand Theft Auto V attracted during its first 24 hours in 2013.

It also exceeds the entire box office run of Avengers: Endgame, which became the highest-grossing film of all time last month at about $2.9bn worldwide after a rerelease pushed it past Avatar.

The game went on sale Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, launching first in New Zealand and rolling out market by market as each reached midnight local time.

The release quickly became a global phenomenon, generating more social media posts than this year’s World Cup, according to monitoring platform Visibrain.

Critics praised the game, which has a score of 99 on review aggregator Metacritic.

Rockstar said that made it the highest-rated game ever.

Like its predecessors, “GTA VI” is an open-world action game in which players roam freely through a sprawling city, stealing cars, pulling off heists and carrying out missions for criminal gangs.

Its busy streets, neon-lit nightlife and beaches are rendered in striking detail, and non-player characters go about their lives whether or not the player is involved.

While critics have raved about the game, it has also prompted real-world warnings from authorities.

With the game’s release on Thursday, police departments across the US reminded people that the car thefts, reckless driving, violence and other criminal mayhem depicted in the blockbuster title should not be re-enacted on the country’s streets.

There is insufficient evidence supporting a scientific causal link between violent video games and violent behaviour, according to the American Psycyhological Association. Nonetheless, several police departments took to the internet with warnings – and even jokes – aimed at keeping GTA VI’s lawlessness firmly in the virtual world.

The Atlanta police department delivered one of the clearest messages in a social media post.

“GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is!” the department warned. “Don’t confuse virtual entertainment with real-life decisions.”

articles.title: Three French police officers sentenced over racist assault on Black man
articles.excerpt: A French court has sentenced three police officers to serve time for assaulting a Black music producer in 2020, acknowledging the racist motives of the beating in a rare ruling against police brutalit...
articles.body_text:
A French court has sentenced three police officers to serve time for assaulting a Black music producer in 2020, acknowledging the racist motives of the beating in a rare ruling against police brutality.

In the judgement delivered on Friday, the Paris criminal court found the victim, Michel Zecler, 47, consistent in his account and deemed that racism was an aggravating factor in the assault.

An investigation into the incident showed that the officers pushed into the entrance of Zecler’s office and beat him.

The officers attacked Zecler outside his studio in Paris on November 21, 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, justifying the assault as being for his failure to wear a mandatory mask and allegedly grabbing one of their weapons.

Zecler’s security cameras recorded the attack, which left him with head trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon.

The court noted that Zecler told a Black police officer who was handcuffing him after the beating that he had been subjected to racial slurs. He repeated the allegation at the police station and again on the way to the hospital, and he also told his loved ones.

The court added that the officers’ falsification of the police report damaged their credibility when they denied using racist insults.

The court sentenced Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, to five years in jail, including three suspended.

Philippe Tondeux, 50, was sentenced to five years, including three-and-a-half suspended.

Pierre Plantier, 37, was sentenced to five years, four of which were suspended, and was to serve the one year with an ankle tag instead of behind bars.

A crowd applauded Zecler as he stepped out of the hearing, according to the AFP news agency.

“Justice has been done. It has restored a man’s dignity and allowed him to begin rebuilding himself,” his lawyer, Serge Money, said.

All three officers apologised to Zecler earlier on Friday, with Plantier in tears, AFP reported.

French victims and researchers say police violence is systemic, but guilty verdicts in alleged police brutality cases are rare in the country.

In 2024, a judge handed suspended prison sentences to three officers who caused permanent rectal injuries to a Black man, Theo Luhaka, during a stop-and-search in 2017.

Last year, a report by France’s rights chief found that young men “perceived as Arab, black or from North Africa” are four times more likely to be stopped than the rest of the population.

articles.title: Alabama woman pleads guilty after reportedly using smart glasses to target drug trial witnesses
articles.excerpt:
Woman reportedly used Meta smart glasses, ChatGPT in alleged witness intimidation campaign

An Alabama woman accused of using Meta smart glasses to secretly record witnesses in a federal drug trial ha...
articles.body_text:
Woman reportedly used Meta smart glasses, ChatGPT in alleged witness intimidation campaign

An Alabama woman accused of using Meta smart glasses to secretly record witnesses in a federal drug trial has pleaded guilty.

Tierra Shatalia Douglas, 36, on Thursday admitted to conspiracy to retaliate against a witness in the January prosecution of Glennie "Little Man" McGee and his wife, Echandza Maxie, according to local outlet AL.

The couple, along with Maxie’s sister, Exavieria Maxie, were involved in a multimillion-dollar drug trafficking organization that distributed bulk cocaine and fentanyl and used children as couriers, according to the Justice Department.

DRUG RING BUSTED, ILLEGAL ALIENS CUFFED BY HOMELAND SECURITY TASK FORCE IN SOUTH CAROLINA: DOJ

Tierra Shatalia Douglas pleaded guilty to retaliating against three witnesses, using smart glasses and AI in a months-long intimidation campaign. (Escambia County Sheriff's Office)

In the eight months following the prosecution, Douglas repeatedly harassed the witnesses and attempted to obtain their personal information before her arrest in September.

"Douglas disseminated the videos to publicly identify and intimidate the witnesses," court records said, according to AL.

The harassment included secretly recording witnesses as they left the courthouse after testifying, according to Fox10TV.

On Jan. 16, one of the witnesses said he received a video from a friend showing him exiting the courtroom after testifying, the outlet reported.

'SEE A TRUE HOLOCAUST': RELIGION PROFESSOR INDICTED AFTER ANONYMOUS ANTISEMITIC POSTS EXPOSED

In one of the videos she recorded of a witness, Douglas asked someone whether they recognized him, saying, "This guy telling, do anyone know him, he needs to be hurt," according to AL.

An Alabama woman secretly filmed federal witnesses with Meta smart glasses during the trial against Glennie "Little Man" McGee and his wife, Echandza Maxie. (Fabian Strauch/picture alliance via Getty Images)

She also used ChatGPT to generate and distribute a flyer identifying one of the witnesses as a "snitch," the outlet said.

Reports added that Douglas sent Discord messages identifying one of the witness's minor children and the school the child attended.

In one case, Douglas allegedly sent text messages to a witness she had saved in her phone contacts as "The Rat," taunting him repeatedly for testifying.

An Alabama woman secretly filmed federal witnesses with Meta smart glasses and used ChatGPT to create a "snitch" flyer, according to reports. (Meta)

Douglas reportedly confessed after officials confronted her with evidence that included internal surveillance footage from the courthouse.

Douglas was arrested in September and pleaded guilty Thursday.

Her sentencing is set for February 2027, according to reports.

She faces a maximum sentence of life in prison, though prosecutors reportedly agreed to recommend leniency, reports say.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

articles.title: Trump calls for Nvidia to reinstate ‘brilliant’ Jensen Huang
articles.excerpt:
US President Donald Trump has said he would welcome Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO, more than a week after the company’s founder stepped down over a scandal involving extramarital affairs.

“Yo...
articles.body_text:
US President Donald Trump has said he would welcome Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO, more than a week after the company’s founder stepped down over a scandal involving extramarital affairs.

“You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go?” Trump told reporters on Friday. “I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance.”

Trump also described Jensen Huang as “a good man” who “made some bad decisions”.

“I’d like to see Jensen make a big apology and go back, because he created something with Blackwell,” Trump said, referring to Nvidia’s most advanced chips.

Huang resigned on November 12, following media reports of an intimate relationship with an alleged spy for Beijing who may have helped route restricted chips to China. US intelligence officials are said to have previously known about the possible espionage link.

Two more affairs have since been reported. The New York Times reported on Friday that the suspected spy, Alice Huang, has extensive ties to China’s defence industry through her family and associates.

Trump also appeared to contradict Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who had said earlier on Friday that Jensen Huang did not come up in talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.

“I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, ‘Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He’s a brilliant man,'” said Trump of his meeting with the Chinese president.

In a post on X on Tuesday, Jensen Huang offered to return to the company.

However, Nvidia’s board has ruled out his comeback. Board chairperson Harvey Jones said on an earnings call later that day that the directors unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and do not plan to reinstate him.

The scandal has also drawn in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Republican Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas told The Wall Street Journal that Lutnick had repeatedly ignored warnings about AI chips being smuggled to China before the scandal broke, though he stopped short of calling for the commerce secretary’s resignation.

“I have not lost confidence,” Trump said, calling Lutnick “a different kind of a guy, very good businessman”.

Democrats, who will take control of Congress in January, are investigating whether Lutnick used his office to help Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm run by his sons, avoid losses tied to scrutiny of Nvidia’s links to a Chinese company.

articles.title: Can Africa’s new credit rating agency change how the continent is assessed?
articles.excerpt:
Abuja, Nigeria – On October 7, the African Union officially launched the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), bringing to fruition an initiative first endorsed by African leaders in 2017.

The agency,...
articles.body_text:
Abuja, Nigeria – On October 7, the African Union officially launched the Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), bringing to fruition an initiative first endorsed by African leaders in 2017.

The agency, based in Port Louis, Mauritius, is designed to provide independent assessments of African governments and corporate borrowers, drawing on local data and expertise to complement ratings issued by international agencies. Its first sovereign ratings are expected by the end of March.

Its interim chief executive, Sifiso Falala, says AfCRA is already in discussions with 15 African governments with research planned in countries that include Mauritius, Kenya, Togo, the Seychelles and Burundi.

The case for AfCRA rests partly on the cost of how African economies are perceived by financial markets. A 2023 study by the United Nations Development Programme estimated that subjectivities in sovereign credit ratings cost African countries $74.5bn through excessive interest payments and foregone lending.

African governments have long argued that international rating methodologies do not adequately account for the continent’s economic structures and circumstances.

The major international agencies – Moody’s, S&P Global Ratings and Fitch Ratings – have disputed suggestions that their assessments systematically disadvantage African borrowers. At a Chatham House discussion in June, Moody’s Marie Diron argued that the agency’s analysis of four decades of global sovereign default data showed that African countries with a particular rating had broadly the same probability of default as equally rated borrowers elsewhere.

For example, she said, a sovereign with a B rating had an estimated one-year default probability of about 5 percent regardless of whether it was African or from another region.

That is an important counterargument. AfCRA’s challenge will not simply be to produce different ratings but to demonstrate that its assessments are more comprehensive, transparent and predictive of actual credit risk. Its credibility will ultimately depend on the evidence behind its conclusions, including when those conclusions are unfavourable to African borrowers.

For Falala, the agency’s priority is to ensure that assessments better reflect the economic realities of African countries.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, he said: “A significant number of African countries carry speculative-grade ratings despite having no history of sovereign default.

“This raises legitimate questions about whether prevailing models adequately capture African economic realities. We believe our analytical framework can contribute to a constructive reassessment of these assumptions, encouraging the entire industry to examine whether the indicators used to determine creditworthiness remain relevant, proportionate and sufficiently predictive of actual default risk.”

Falala said the agency was not seeking more favourable ratings for African borrowers but greater accuracy through engagement with established rating agencies.

“Our objective is not to manufacture better ratings for Africa, but to produce more accurate ratings of Africa in collaboration with established rating agencies. Importantly, we believe that a stronger AfCRA will contribute to a stronger credit rating industry overall,” he said.

That distinction will be central to the agency’s credibility. An institution established partly in response to dissatisfaction with existing ratings must demonstrate that its own assessments are independent of political pressure and the interests of the governments and companies it evaluates.

Falala acknowledged the scepticism surrounding the industry, saying AfCRA has an opportunity to rebuild confidence through transparency and analytical independence. He said the agency was not seeking confrontation with established rating providers but saw considerable scope for collaboration and mutual learning.

Beyond sovereign ratings, AfCRA intends to assess companies, municipalities, banks and local-currency debt. This broader coverage could address gaps in information about borrowers that receive limited attention from international agencies while providing domestic investors with additional assessments of credit risk.

The potential benefits extend beyond the ratings themselves. African pension funds, banks and other institutional investors need reliable information to assess domestic borrowers and allocate capital. More comprehensive coverage, supported by stronger local data, could help reduce information gaps and support the development of domestic capital markets.

However, additional ratings will not automatically translate into cheaper borrowing. Their influence will depend on whether investors consider the assessments credible and useful in making investment decisions.

Abdussalam Muazu, an associate chartered economist at the Institute of Chartered Economists of Nigeria, said limited information about African borrowers has contributed to the uncertainty investors factor into lending decisions.

“African governments and companies often pay more to borrow than their ratings suggest, partly because investors know too little about them and price in the uncertainty.

“The big agencies have few analysts on the ground, and much of Africa’s economy runs through informal trade, mobile money and community finance that is hard to measure from outside. An African agency can bring local knowledge into credit ratings and help build the data that is missing today, which gives investors less reason to charge for guesswork,” he told Al Jazeera.

The argument points to a wider problem: The availability and quality of economic data can shape how creditworthiness is assessed. Informal economic activity, for example, is not always adequately captured in conventional indicators, even though it contributes significantly to livelihoods and economic activity across the continent.

Methodology is another part of the debate. Different approaches to assessing sovereign risk can produce different conclusions about the same country’s ability and willingness to meet its financial obligations. AfCRA, therefore, will need to explain clearly how its models account for factors that may be overlooked or insufficiently reflected in existing assessments.

Dayo Obisan, a financial market professional, told Al Jazeera that African countries need rating methodologies that better reflect their economic circumstances and their access to capital.

“The compelling question is how does Africa ensure its peculiarities are factored into the determination of its perception as a sovereign and its access to much-needed capital, which rides on this perception?”

He said an African rating institution could bring greater understanding of these circumstances through its presence across the continent, improved data and methodologies that complement existing approaches.

“The value proposition for the creation of an Africa-focused credit rating agency centres on richer local data, contextual insight, wider coverage and support for domestic markets,” Obisan said.

But local knowledge alone will not be enough. AfCRA will also have to demonstrate that its methodology is rigorous, consistent and transparent and its ratings can withstand scrutiny from investors beyond the continent.

Its ownership and financing arrangements will also be important. The agency describes itself as privately owned and self-funded while its planned sovereign assessments will operate on a solicited basis, meaning governments pay for ratings and provide access to officials and financial information.

This is a model also used by established rating agencies, but it makes safeguards against conflicts of interest particularly important. The African Union says governments may not own shares in AfCRA, but the agency will still need to demonstrate that commercial relationships with the borrowers it assesses cannot influence its analytical decisions.

Ultimately, AfCRA’s credibility will not be determined by how many African countries it rates or how far its assessments differ from those of Moody’s, S&P and Fitch.

It will depend on whether investors trust its analyses, whether its methodology withstands scrutiny and, above all, whether it can remain independent when its findings are politically inconvenient.

Its defining test may come when an African government rejects an unfavourable assessment and the agency refuses to change it.

As Falala put it, “What strengthens AfCRA should ultimately strengthen the credibility of the entire credit rating industry. Africa needs more credible assessments, not competing narratives.”

clusters.topic_label: Kinetic and Civil Tensions Related to Israel-Gaza Conflict
clusters.synthesis: The reported events concern disparate kinetic and civil incidents tied to the ongoing Israel-Gaza conflict. Physical actions include an Israeli airstrike in Gaza targeting family members of Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya, resulting in injuries to relatives but the survival of his son Izzeldeen. Concurrent non-kinetic events include the detention of UN rapporteur Francesca Albanese by Costa Rican immigration authorities at Juan Santamaria International Airport, and violent clashes between Turkish and Israeli football fan bases in Batumi, Georgia, during a UEFA Europa League match, which caused a 30-minute suspension of play. Additionally, media institutional action occurred in the U.S. where NBC removed a paid advertisement criticizing Israeli military funding following public pressure.
consensus: An Israeli airstrike targeted the family of Khalil al-Hayya in Gaza, resulting in injuries to family members but the survival of Izzeldeen al-Hayya.
UN rapporteur Francesca Albanese was detained by Costa Rican authorities at Juan Santamaria International Airport.
Violence occurred between Turkish and Israeli fans in Batumi, Georgia, leading to 16 arrests and a 30-minute suspension of the Besiktas vs. Hapoel Be'er Sheva match.
NBC removed a broadcast advertisement containing imagery of a Palestinian child and claims regarding U.S. funding to Israel.
divergence: Al Jazeera characterizes the Israeli actions as a 'genocidal war' and emphasizes the failure of a ceasefire, while omitting the strategic military context of the strikes.
Fox News frames the NBC ad removal through the lens of public backlash and political controversy, omitting the specific financial claims made in the advertisement text.
Costa Rican official communications label Francesca Albanese a 'risk to national security,' whereas Albanese characterizes the detention as a 'disgrace.'

UEFA and related reporting classify the relocation of the match to Batumi as a safety precaution, while media narratives emphasize the political animosity between the two fan bases as the driver of the violence.

The school administration has initiated an investigation into the physical confrontation.

impact.title: US Federal Aviation Administration Nationwide Ground Stop and Telecommunications Failure
impact.why_it_matters: A critical telecommunications failure within the United States air traffic control system forced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to execute a nationwide ground stop for all departing flights. The interruption, lasting over four hours, impacted all 22 regional air traffic control centers, resulting in approximately 8,500 flight delays and nearly 8,000 cancellations on the primary day of the event, with cascading effects extending into subsequent days at international transit hubs including Sydney and Melbourne. Federal authorities confirmed the cessation of operations was prompted by internal system instability rather than external kinetic or cyber-attack vectors, though the outage represents the largest disruption to US civilian aviation since 2001.
